name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Max Engling claims defamation over driving allegations in new Beau Bayh ad
text:
Max Engling speaks with reporters after winning the Republican secretary of state nomination on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican Max Engling is threatening to sue Democrat Beau Bayh over a new television advertisement in their increasingly bitter Indiana secretary of state election campaign.
Engling alleges that references in the ad that he had been convicted of reckless driving is “defamation on its face.”
The Bayh campaign is defending the commercial, which features a uniformed sheriff’s deputy saying Engling “has been convicted and investigated at least eight times for reckless driving and reckless behavior.”
Engling’s campaign acknowledged in a weekend statement that his driving record “includes eight speeding tickets, the most recent from 16 years ago, all traffic infractions, not misdemeanor charges or convictions.”
“Beau Bayh can spend money repeating this claim, but he cannot produce a reckless driving charge against me because there isn’t one,” Engling said in the statement. “If Beau has evidence, release it. Otherwise, pull the ad and tell Hoosiers the truth.”
A search of online Indiana court records show Engling with eight speeding tickets in Hamilton or Marion counties between 2006 and 2010 — when he was 19 to 23 years old — but no other court cases.
The Bayh campaign provided the Capital Chronicle with a timeline supporting its ad that also included an expunged misdemeanor criminal reckless case from 2007 in which Engling threw eggs at passing vehicles from a U.S. 31 overpass in Carmel, along with a 2023 speeding ticket in Arlington, Virginia.
That timeline includes no “reckless driving” criminal charges against Engling.
Who’s a real Hoosier? Secretary of state candidates spar over time in Indiana.

Bayh, meanwhile, was initially charged in 2018 at age 22 in Brunswick County, Virginia, with misdemeanor reckless driving for driving faster than 85 mph. That charge was reduced to an infraction for defective or unsafe equipment and Bayh was fined, according to Virginia online court records.
Engling’s campaign said Bayh should “withdraw his latest attack ad and correct its false claim about Engling’s driving record, or face a lawsuit.”
Bayh’s campaign responded to the Capital Chronicle that it “is reckless for Max to drive 87 in a 60mph zone. It is reckless of Max to throw things from an overpass at moving cars.”
“His driving is reckless. His behavior is reckless. His threats of frivolous lawsuits are reckless,” Bayh campaign manager Jack Tormoehlen said in an email. “This ad is accurate and Max Engling needs to take a deep breath.”
The dispute over Engling’s driving record follows attack ads from Engling over Bayh’s voter registration history.
Bayh first registered to vote in 2014 while still a high school student in Washington, D.C., using the address of an Indianapolis condominium owned by his father, former U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh. 
An Engling ad says Beau Bayh “voted in Indiana elections 14 times. Had his ballot mailed to his parents’ D.C. mansion. Sounds like voter fraud.”
Bayh, who has never been charged with voter fraud, cast ballots regularly in Indiana through his time as a student at Harvard and during services with the Marine Corps — often by mail but sometimes voting early in person. He moved full time to Indiana in 2024 after graduating from Harvard Law School.
Bayh has defended voting in Indiana, saying he always considered the state home despite mostly growing up in the Washington area after his family moved there when he was three with his father’s election to the U.S. Senate.
The Indiana Supreme Court ruled in 1988 — in a case involving Evan Bayh’s residency — that physical presence in a place is only one circumstance in determining domicile, and that a person’s residency hinges on intent.

name: VTDigger
title: What can we do? An answer from Vermont’s premiere theater.
text:
By Leslie Swackhamer, Executive Director, Susan Smith Blackburn Prize, and Jay Wahl, Executive Director, the Flynn
We began with an impossibly large question: What is the current state of democracy in America?
But underneath it was a smaller and much more personal one: What can we do? What should we do?
What can a couple of Vermonters who run a performing arts organization and a playwriting prize do? Some days, hiding under the bed seems like a reasonable option. The world feels frightening. The 2026 midterm elections are approaching. Our country seems increasingly divided not only about politics, but about reality itself.
We’re not politicians or constitutional scholars. But we believe in the power of theater to bring people together, to ask difficult questions, and to help us see the world through someone else’s eyes. That’s what we have to offer.
So we teamed up, leaning into Susan Smith Blackburn’s belief that both our stories and our civic life are richer with women’s voices at the center. And we invited some of the most influential playwrights of our time to take on this question with us.
We thought maybe six or seven playwrights would say yes to an invitation to write short plays or monologues. Instead, our invitation opened a floodgate. Thirty-four plays by award-winning women+ playwrights make up the project. They are funny and furious, intimate and unruly, historical and speculative. They contradict one another. Some make us uncomfortable. Others make us laugh. All ask us to pay attention.

Together, these plays do not argue for a single point of view or prescribe a single course of action. They offer something more interesting: an invitation to consider perspectives we might not otherwise encounter.
That is why we’re producing all of them throughout a full day at the Flynn on October 24.
A play can’t encompass democracy. A conversation won’t allay all our fears. But something can happen between people who gather to listen to a story that would not have happened otherwise. That is a critical beginning.
And we didn’t want that conversation to happen only in Burlington.
We’ve invited theaters, schools, colleges and universities, libraries, museums, community organizations, and independent artists to bring these plays into their own communities across the United States and beyond. More than 100 groups have answered the call, with free performances planned around the country and the globe in the weeks leading up to the midterms. We are approaching our goal of participation in every state and Washington, D.C.
Some will present a single play around a kitchen table. Others will gather hundreds of people in a theater. Each community will decide which stories matter most to them and what conversations they want to have.
There is something particularly meaningful to us about this national conversation beginning in Vermont, a state whose motto, Freedom and Unity, holds two ideas that can be difficult to reconcile. We believe the arts can help us practice both.
The election will pass. The arguments that seemed all-consuming in 2026 will give way to others. And these plays will still be here. They will be available in an anthology, though that collection is not a time capsule containing the correct thoughts about American democracy in 2026. It is a record of artists being brave enough to look directly at their moment and make something.
Democracy requires more than agreement. It asks us to share a public life with people who see the world differently. To listen, to question, to disagree, and to remain in conversation even when it would be easier to walk away.
We can’t promise that 34 plays will change the course of American democracy.
But we can invite people into a room together.
And right now, that feels like something very worth doing.

To learn more and reserve free tickets for the Saturday, October 24 world-premiere of all 34 Women+ on the Edge of Democracy plays at the Flynn in Burlington, VT, visit: https://www.flynnvt.org/see-and-do/democracy/.
To explore the full Women+ on the Edge of Democracy project, visit: https://www.democracy.flynnvt.org/.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Letter with white powder addressed to Utah Lt. Gov. Henderson intercepted, given to FBI
text:
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks to reporters about the launch of Utah's digital apostille program after a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson is among several election officials across the country that have been sent suspicious white powder and threatening letters ahead of the midterm elections. 
Reports of the letters in Arizona, Ohio, Oklahoma and Louisiana began last week, prompting building evacuations and an FBI investigation with just over two weeks to go until the Nov. 3 elections. 
 


View on Threads

 

In Utah, Henderson said in a social media post that on Sunday “our local postal inspector was able to intercept ours and hand it off to the FBI before it could be delivered to my office.” 
“We are grateful for his diligence and service!” Henderson wrote. “Also, nothing is going to disrupt the midterm election. We won’t let it happen.” 
Last week, when reports of the letters began surfacing and Utah News Dispatch asked about whether Henderson’s office had received any, the lieutenant governor’s office said in a prepared statement that U.S. Postal Service staff were keeping an eye out for any suspicious packages. 
“We have been in contact with postal service employees who are actively monitoring our mail for a similar letter so they can intercept it before it reaches our office,” Henderson’s office said Thursday. 
It’s not the first time threatening packages have been sent to Henderson or other election officials across the country. It happened in September 2024, when the FBI found a letter containing white powder addressed to Henderson’s office. It was signed by the “United States Traitor Elimination Army.” 
FBI intercepts ‘suspicious’ envelope containing white powder addressed to Utah Lt. Gov.

“This incident is the latest tactic in a nationwide trend of threats and intimidation toward election officials. But we will not be intimidated,” Henderson said in a statement in 2024. “I am grateful for the swift action of postal workers and law enforcement and the perseverance of election workers who show up and do their jobs every day despite all the rhetoric and risk. We love them. We owe them. They are heroes.”
In her post on Sunday, Henderson’s message was short, saying “nothing is going to disrupt” the election.
She also took the opportunity to point out that early in-person voting starts this week, and that Utahns can sign up for ballot tracking notifications at trackmyballot.utah.gov. 
Henderson has been in a national spotlight this year, including on CBS’ 60 Minutes over the weekend, as she has pushed back against an order from the Trump administration to turn over sensitive information from Utah’s voter rolls including social security numbers, full birth dates and driver’s license numbers. 
Her resistance has elicited both a lawsuit against the state and a personal investigation against her from the U.S. Department of Justice.

name: Delaware
title: Hayrides, Hope and Helping Hands: Building a Foundation for Recovery in Delaware
text:
Annual Friends of Delaware Hayride at Milburn Orchards invites supporters of its healing mission to enjoy family time while strengthening connections centered on recovery.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
A hayride and a bonfire might seem like simple ingredients for an autumn outing. For Firm Foundation Recovery, they are also opportunities to bring families together around a mission that reaches far beyond a fall evening.
The nonprofit hosts its annual Friends of Delaware Hayride at Milburn Orchards each October, inviting supporters of its healing mission to enjoy family time while strengthening connections centered on recovery.
The gathering is one example of how the organization combines community activities, peer support and service to address substance addiction in Delaware.
Firm Foundation Recovery grew out of what its website describes as an enormous need for a long-term, God-centered recovery resource in the state. Its approach brings people and fellowships together around shared principles for healing, with an emphasis on addressing needs that can leave individuals and families struggling to find support.
“Together we can help to heal our communities one recovery at a time,” the organization states on its website.
That mission includes an ambitious undertaking: building a long-term, God-centered recovery facility with transitional living and a work program. The planned facility reflects the organization’s focus on sustained support and helping people establish a foundation for their lives in recovery.
Its broader vision extends throughout Delaware. Firm Foundation Recovery seeks to develop a recovery culture rooted in principles, service and community involvement, with people in recovery taking active roles in strengthening the communities around them.
Family events are one way it works toward that goal.
The organization reports hosting seven annual statewide family and community events focused on awareness, education, prevention and resources. Community donations help secure venues and allow those gatherings to grow.
In May, its Skating For Change events bring the mission to the rink. The owners of Christiana Skating Center and Dover Skating Center partner with the nonprofit to offer Delaware youth and families opportunities to skate while supporting its work.
October brings a different setting, with hayrides and bonfires at Milburn Orchards. The Friends of Delaware Hayride combines a familiar fall tradition with the organization’s efforts to unite people around healing and recovery.
Together, the activities reflect an approach that makes room for families and community members to participate through shared experiences.
Service is another central part of the organization’s work.
Firm Foundation Recovery reports carrying out three service projects annually in and around Delaware. Its service activities include improving housing, providing food and clothing to people experiencing homelessness, hosting speaker jams and creating supportive recovery environments.
These efforts connect recovery with practical ways to help others. They also give participants opportunities to contribute their experience and energy to needs within the wider community.
The nonprofit’s peer-driven initiatives reach children, families and people new to recovery. According to its website, lived experience helps those involved connect with others and respond to gaps in support.
“This ‘we’ concept of serving with our lived experience is life changing,” the website states.
Community partnerships help sustain the effort. Firm Foundation Recovery offers sponsorship and advertising opportunities for businesses and other supporters interested in contributing to its mission while building relationships within their communities.
For the organization, the larger goal is a Delaware where helping people affected by addiction becomes a shared commitment, and where those building lives in recovery have opportunities to serve others.
A skating rink, a service project or an evening beside a bonfire offers a different doorway into that work. Each creates space for people to gather, participate and support a mission built around healing.
Through those connections, Firm Foundation Recovery is working toward a future in which recovery has a place in everyday community life, one helping hand and one changed life at a time.

name: Mississippi Today
title: DOJ reaches settlement with Lexington Police Department over civil rights violations
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice has announced it reached a settlement forcing reforms in a Mississippi city and its police department, which the DOJ found discriminated against Black people, used excessive force and retaliated against critics.
The settlement announced Friday comes after a scathing 2024 DOJ report said the Lexington Police Department routinely violated citizens’ civil rights in the rural, poor, majority-Black city located about 65 miles north of the state’s capital. Police targeted Black people for arrests, made arrests for low-level offenses to generate money for the police department and locked people up for extended periods of time if they could not afford to pay fines, according to the report.
The out-of-court settlement requires the City of Lexington and its police department to reform practices on a number of issues — from fines and bail to stops, searches and use of force — and bring them into compliance with state and federal law.
The Associated Press called and emailed city and police department officials but did not immediately receive responses.
The agreement bars the Lexington police from continuing to jail people for unpaid fines without first assessing whether they can afford to pay them, a practice that violates the Fourteenth Amendment. The 2024 report found the city court had issued arrest warrants for more than 650 people, roughly half of the city’s population, for unpaid fines.
The city and the Lexington Police Department must also dismiss all existing warrants for unpaid fines and fees that violate the law and move to expunge the records of all unlawful fine-based convictions.
Additionally, the city and the Lexington Police Department are barred from creating and implementing a quota or incentive system for stops, warnings, citations, arrests or related revenue. The DOJ previously found that between 2022 and 2024, the Lexington Police Department made one arrest for every four people in town, more than 10 times the per-capita arrest rate for the state of Mississippi.
The department will also require DOJ-approved trainings on stops, searches, arrests and use of force, in addition to implementing documentation and review systems to ensure such actions are lawful.
“Through these reforms, we seek not only to address the concerns identified in our investigation, but also to strengthen public trust and promote practices that respect the rights and dignity of every person,” U.S. Attorney J.E. Baxter Kruger for the Southern District of Mississippi said in a news release.
The DOJ said it would work with the city and police to “ensure that they remedy the alleged violations.” The agreement lasts for three years, but could be cut short or extended depending on whether the parties mutually determine the city and police department have reached compliance.
The DOJ launched a probe into the Lexington Police Department in 2023, after citizens accused officers of using roadblocks to target Black drivers, engaging in excessive force, committing sexual assault and arresting people without justification, among other claims.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Lawsuit alleges feds gathered sensitive data on Kentucky voters
text:
A polling location is open for early voting at Paristown Hall in Louisville on Saturday in May, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
This story first appeared on Louisville Public Media. It’s republished here as part of the Appalachian News Exchange reporting partnership to strength Kentucky journalism.
A lawsuit filed in a federal district court Thursday alleges the Department of Homeland Security has systematically collected sensitive data on Kentucky voters, despite the state’s refusal to share it.
In the court filing, voting rights and electronic privacy groups cited emails and memos obtained from the DHS through records requests.
The lawsuit points to an email attachment dated July 6, 2026, which said the DHS investigative unit had “enriched” something from Kentucky and five other states, and the information was “pending Palantir entry into ELITE.”
ELITE is a tool developed by AI-company Palantir which they describe as being used for “identifying the location of known foreign nationals who meet criteria for removal.”
The voting rights group paired that memo with a recent federal whistleblower disclosure warning lawmakers that DHS employees are being told to use “voter data of dubious origins, that is being compiled with ‘supplemental magic.’”
This summer, courts dismissed Department of Justice lawsuits against Kentucky and many other states when election officials refused to hand over unredacted voter data with confidential information.
Afterwards, the DOJ said Kentucky Secretary of State Michael Adams was “under investigation” for not complying with federal demands for sensitive voter data.
“We see this as an attempt to work around what courts have found is a violation of the Privacy Act,” Marcia Johnson with the National League of Women Voters said about their lawsuit against DHS.
Johnson added that if voting data is used by immigration enforcement agents, it could have a chilling effect at the polls in November.
“I could be a citizen, I could be eligible, but I could be concerned about being prevented from voting,” she said.
A spokesperson for the Secretary Adams’ office said they are not a party to the suit but offered assurances that Kentucky’s voter rolls have not been improperly accessed or altered. They said they don’t know if the federal government developed its own voter file, but that it wouldn’t impact Kentucky’s elections even if they did.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Follow the Money: Churchill Downs gives big to groups helping Sen. Adams and other GOP candidates
text:
Race-goers gather in Churchill Downs' paddock ahead of the Kentucky Derby. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Churchill Downs contributed $570,000 during the last three months to Republican PACs that have been spending big on independent advertising aimed at electing State Sen. Julie Raque Adams and other Republicans to the General Assembly in November.
The flood of campaign money from Churchill since July 1 is documented in disclosure reports filed last week by GOPAC Inc., the Republican State Leadership Committee, and the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition.
Combined with donations it made earlier this year, Churchill has contributed $712,500 this year to the three Republican committees combined.
These three committees combined have reported spending a combined $668,158 on independent ads to help Adams win reelection.
That’s far more independent spending than any other candidate for the Kentucky House or Senate has benefitted from this year.
Adams, of Louisville, is hoping to win her fourth consecutive term in the state Senate. She is opposed by Democrat Sarah Cole McIntosh, a former member of the Jefferson County Board of Education.
Adams chairs the Senate Licensing and Occupations Committee which handles legislation related to the horse racing and gambling legislation.
Records posted on the Kentucky Registry of Election Finance show that GOPAC, a long-established national Republican committee dedicated to helping elect Republicans at the state and local level, has reported buying $479,158 in advertising to independently support Adams’ election.
The Republican State Leadership Committee, also a national group that supports state and local GOP candidates, has bought $149,000 in ads supporting Adams or opposing McIntosh.
Election registry records show that GOPAC and the RSLC have bought ads in Kentucky this year only for Adams, and no other candidate.
Commonwealth Conservative Coalition is a Louisville-based Republican PAC registered with the Federal Election Commission that has spent money on advertising advocating the election of many Republican candidates for the Kentucky General Assembly including $40,000 in ads that oppose McIntosh.
KY teachers PAC donated to conservative group to try to influence GOP primaries

While the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition is a local PAC with many Kentucky donors, reports it has filed with the Federal Election Commission show it has been mostly funded this year by GOPAC and RSLC.
Those records show that GOPAC has given $450,000 to Commonwealth Conservative Coalition this year, and RSLC has given it $300,000. The combined $750,000 represents 53.4 percent of all the money contributed to Commonwealth Conservative Coalition this year through Sep. 30.
Disclosure reports filed with the Internal Revenue Service and Federal Election Commission show that Churchill Downs contributed:

$270,000 in the recent quarter to GOPAC, bringing its total contributions to GOPAC for the year to $355,000.
$250,000 in the recent quarter to the RSLC, bringing its total contributions to RSLC for the year to $307,500.
$50,000 to Commonwealth Conservative Coalition on Sept. 8.

Churchill’s contributions represent only a small part of the total contributions taken in this year by GOPAC and RSLC, which work in all states and get contributions from across the country. (GOPAC reported getting $13 million in contributions in the recent quarter, RSLC reported getting $27 million in the quarter.)
Churchill is the largest donor from Kentucky, but at least 25 Kentucky-based corporations and associations that lobby the General Assembly have donated to one or both of these national Republican PACs. Reports show Sazerac Company, Louisville, has given $100,500, and Brown-Forman, of Louisville has given, $59,185.
And although lobbyists themselves are forbidden by state law from donating directly to the campaign committee of a candidate for the General Assembly, lobbying firms based in Kentucky are allowed to donate to groups like GOPAC and RSLC. 
And they do. 
So far this year Kentucky lobbying firms have donated a combined $150,000 to GOPAC and RSLC. Here’s the breakdown:  Commonwealth Alliances, $55,000; McCarthy Strategic Solutions, $45,000; Top Shelf Lobby, $25,000; HCM Governmental Relations, $10,000; Government Strategies, $10,000; and Stoll Keenon Ogden, $5,000.
GOPAC and RSLC also get their biggest contributions from some other groups that lobby the Kentucky General Assembly but are based in other states such as: Altria Client Services, of Richmond, Virginia; Reynolds American, of Winston Salem, North Carolina; the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, of Denver; and Charter Communications, of St. Louis.
Beshear’s big Pennsylvania donor gives more
Gov. Andy Beshear’s friend from Carlisle, Pennsylvania, is continuing to pour big money into the Beshear super PAC that is a forerunner to the  campaign for president that Beshear is exploring.
Ashish Patel donated another $150,000 to Beshear super PAC In This Together in August, bringing the total Patel has contributed to that PAC to $1 million, according to reports filed by In This Together with the Internal Revenue Service. All of that money was contributed since Aug. 1, 2025 and the recent contribution solidified Patel’s standing as the top donor to the super PAC since Beshear created it soon after his reelection as governor in 2023.
Beshear’s top political strategist Eric Hyers, who oversees In This Together, has declined to provide more identifying information about Patel. Louisville Public Media recently reported that Patel declined to provide more information about himself or why he supports Beshear in such a big way.
Patel has emerged as a big political donor in just the past 18 months. He has given more than 70 contributions to different political committees during that time according to reports filed with the IRS and FEC. But by far his largest contributions have been to Beshear’s In This Together. Also this year, Patel has donated $82,500 to the Democratic Governors Association, a group chaired this year by Beshear.
In This Together reported only two other large contributions in its recent report with the IRS: $100,000 from Andrew Hauptman, of Beverly Hills, California, founder of an investment firm called Andell Holdings who hosted a fundraiser attended by Beshear and other Democratic governors earlier this year for the DGA; and $50,000 from Nachiketa Bhatt, a regular donor to Beshear political committees. Bhatt, of Prospect, is identified in the report as an administrator of Healthy Living Primary Care.
Beshear formed In This Together to raise contributions that he, in turn, could donate to other political causes and campaigns around the country.
In This Together’s new report shows that it donated $275,000 in the last three months to Democratic political committees in Nevada, the site of a hotly contested  governor’s race this year. The Beshear PAC made much smaller contributions to political committees in South Carolina, Michigan, Maine and Wisconsin.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Jeffries talks AI concerns at roundtable with Macomb County community leaders
text:
Former special victims prosecutor and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines and U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) at a roundtable in Eastpointe on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)During a roundtable in Eastpointe on Saturday, U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries argued that Congress must take a more aggressive approach to regulating AI as multiple panelists raised concerns about how artificial intelligence will affect American workers and the economy.
Jeffries joined former special victims prosecutor Christina Hines in the southern Macomb County community to hear from faith leaders and local elected officials. Hines is the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, where she is running against Republican Michael Bouchard Jr.
Jeffries’ visit comes as Democrats seek to reclaim control of the U.S. House in the Nov. 3 election, a shift that could position him to become House speaker if Democrats win a majority.
During the roundtable, Jocelyn Howard, executive director of Citadel of Perpetual Learning, a training and development organization, questioned how AI would impact the nation’s frontline workers, telling Jeffries she’d like to see Congress reinforce the value of being human.
Pastor Lance Pittman of First Praise Pentecostal Church also asked Jeffries about transparency around AI and what Congress is doing to make sure the U.S. doesn’t fall behind in developing this technology.
Jeffries said House Democrats’ approach to AI has centered on ensuring that the technology benefits the American people.
“That could be in the healthcare space. That could be educational attainment and closing resource gaps. That could be helping to ensure that people have additional tools available for them to bring their entrepreneurial ideas to life,” Jeffries said. 
However, Jeffries said technology can be very disruptive and if the right guardrails are not in place, AI could exacerbate an economy that “already has not been moving in the right direction.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He spoke out against a provision in the House version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which would have barred state and local governments from enforcing regulations on artificial intelligence for 10 years. While this would have put AI regulation solely in the hands of the federal government, Jeffries argued there was no federal legislation to fall back on. 
“Basically, we were saying that these companies should just do whatever the heck they want to do,” Jeffries said, noting that House Democrats hoped to take a more aggressive approach focused on safety. 
He called back to Howard’s early comments on human value while discussing the OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident, in which roughly 1,200 AI agents, which were meant to be isolated, found a way to communicate. Seven hundred of these OpenAI agents would go on to hack Hugging Face, an AI development platform.
“This is a movie-like situation that we’re dealing with, but it’s very real and has a real possible impact,” Jeffries said, arguing that Congress cannot bury its head in the sand and ignore security concerns around AI.
Macomb County Commissioner Michael Howard discusses community concerns during a roundtable on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
“We as House Democrats will decisively act to protect the American people,” Jeffries said.
While discussing the ways AI could exacerbate inequality, Jeffries also argued that the risks of AI extend beyond the technology itself to the infrastructure, such as data centers, needed to support its growth, noting that these facilities also dig into concerns around the costs and burdens placed on communities.
Speaking with reporters after the roundtable, Jeffries was asked whether he would support legislation to establish a federal moratorium on AI data centers until further regulations can be enacted.
“We’ll take a look at all of the bills that have been introduced, including those related to data centers,” Jeffries said. “My personal view has been – and I support the one-year moratorium that has been put into effect by my home state governor, Kathy Hochul – that this should be left to the states and localities at this particular moment in time until Congress can act decisively to protect the health, the safety, and the economic well-being of the American people.”
Hines said she would support a moratorium.
“This is a top concern,” Hines said. “We’re right next to Lake St. Clair. People are very worried about protecting our water.”
She also pointed to the concerns with hyperscale data centers contributing to higher energy rates. 
“People are already struggling with the high cost of gas and groceries and healthcare. We cannot afford for our bills to keep going up,” Hines said, adding that “we need a strong Congress that is actually going to, you know, engage in sensible regulation to protect the American people.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: GOP focuses on fraud, seeking to redirect voters’ ire over healthcare costs
text:
Addressing hundreds of supports at the Bangor International Airport, Vice President JD Vance accused Maine's Democratic leadership of enabling Medicaid fraud on May 14, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)Heading into the midterm elections, high healthcare costs rank among voters’ biggest concerns. But lately, there’s a twist giving the issue new momentum on campaign agendas: a focus on fraud in government health programs.
The administration of President Donald Trump has used claims of widespread wrongdoing to justify investigations, suspensions of billions of dollars in payments to states, and the cancellation of Affordable Care Act health coverage for hundreds of thousands of people.
The effort has opened a broader political fight over the extent of fraud and the administration’s response to it. Republicans say they’re safeguarding taxpayer dollars by going after bad actors. Democrats contend the administration has relied on insufficient evidence to target blue states and cut programs Republicans have long tried to shrink. Meanwhile, Trump’s pardons of executives convicted of healthcare fraud, administration moves to weaken some protections against abuses, and a high-profile error by Trump regulators stand in contrast with the administration’s proclaimed fraud-fighting goals.
After months of GOP criticism, Maine shares details of Medicaid fraud enforcement

The dispute is becoming a talking point for both parties leading up to the November election.
Republican candidates are trying to win voters’ confidence by emphasizing their efforts to halt what they say is the misuse of taxpayer dollars in federal health programs.
“Going after fraud gives Republicans a healthcare message when they would otherwise just be defending cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. The approach, he said, helps “blunt” those attacks.
Democrats, however, traditionally have an advantage on healthcare in general, with polls showing voters are more likely to trust them with such issues. Now Democrats are portraying Republicans’ fraud crackdown as a cover for the GOP’s weakening of safety net programs. But the GOP messaging could resonate at the ballot box.
About 44% of voters — and 54% of Republican voters — say say fraud in government programs is “extremely important” for candidates to talk about, according to a KFF poll conducted in mid-September, suggesting the fraud focus might be connecting with the GOP base. Such fraud is also the top issue rural Republican voters want candidates to talk about, based on a separate survey by KFF and the Associated Press.
It’s an issue that is hardly new, and government watchdogs have repeatedly documented fraud by health providers and brokers, as well as improper enrollment in government health programs. A report by the Government Accountability Office in March warned that the “sheer amount of payments in the Medicare program creates significant fraud risks.” And in a separate probe, GAO investigators were able to get subsidized insurance for fake ACA enrollees.
What has changed is the prominence the issue now occupies in national politics.
Administration’s fraud targets
Trump administration authorities have this year charged hundreds of people, including doctors, in alleged billing schemes. It has announced audits of state Medicaid fraud units and increased scrutiny of enrollment in federal programs, withholding billions of dollars in federal Medicaid payments over claims of lax oversight — with what Democrats say is a laser focus on blue states despite a lack of evidence.
The administration’s more expansive claims about fraud — and the actions it has taken in response — have generated fierce political clashes.
Most recently, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services canceled ACA enrollments covering 760,000 people. While Democrats have questioned the methods that found them to be fraudulent, federal officials said they included nonexistent consumers whose applications were submitted by brokers or agents who can earn commissions from insurers.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said at a press event that the cancellations included people who had coverage through the ACA but hadn’t used it. He also said some had no Social Security numbers, calling that evidence of problems.
“About 35% of current people on the Obamacare system — 35%, more than a third — had never used the program. They haven’t bought a prescription medication. They haven’t seen a doctor. That just is not possible,” Oz said. “So we know there is fraud.”
Democrats and some health policy analysts challenge that conclusion. They say that younger and healthier people are much less likely to use their insurance and that not using their coverage doesn’t mean they were improperly enrolled. Critics also say the absence of Social Security numbers doesn’t necessarily establish fraud; for example, newborns can be added to their parents’ plans before receiving a number.
“This is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to kick hundreds of thousands of vulnerable Americans off their healthcare,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) posted on the social media site X. “Millions are already struggling to access healthcare—and this is their plan?”

DR. OZ AND I VISITED YESTERDAY HERE IN MAINE over coffee to talk about Maine people’s needs. As Administrator of the United States Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Dr. Oz has worked to modernize his agency, to provide better healthcare outcomes for Americans, and to tackle the massive amounts of welfare fraud we see reported across the country. His enforcement efforts from the Medicaid Fraud War Room (MFWR) have stopped more than $203 million in potentially improper welfare Medicaid payments in just its first 90 days. As our next Member of Congress I want to ensure our Seniors get the care they need at the lowest possible cost, taxpayers are protected, the truly needy get the help they need, and fraudsters face the consequences they deserve.
— Paul LePage (@MainePaulLePage) August 4, 2026

There are political risks for the GOP as well. The disenrollment of alleged phantom accounts is likely to ensnare legitimate consumers, say health analysts and ACA advocates, leading to a potential backlash against Republicans if scores of people lose coverage just before the midterm elections.
States that tend to deliver for GOP candidates will be hit especially hard, they say, because ACA enrollees are concentrated in those states. The 4.5 million people in Florida and 4.1 million in Texas who have marketplace coverage account for nearly 40% of the country’s ACA enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.
Conservative health policy advisers say the administration took multiple steps to avoid canceling legitimate coverage, including attempts to contact consumers and requirements that additional criteria be met before coverage was terminated.
“Those criticizing the action either don’t understand it or see some political advantage in mischaracterizing it,” said Brian Blase, president of Paragon Health Institute and a former Trump health policy adviser.
Democrats, meanwhile, highlight inconsistencies in the administration’s broader anti-fraud campaign.
They note that the Department of Health and Human Services last year recertified hundreds of insurance brokers and agents who had been suspended in 2024 by the Biden administration for suspected fraud or abuse. The Trump administration also laid off about 200 employees from a CMS office involved in regional oversight of the ACA marketplace.
On Oct. 3, Trump called on Congress to pass legislation with mandatory prison terms for defrauding Medicare and Medicaid, eliminating probation as an option.
But Trump has also pardoned health industry executives convicted of major fraud schemes, including people who are connected to his political allies or who spent heavily on lobbying on their behalf. The pardons included a nursing home operator sentenced to three years in prison for a nearly $40 million tax scheme and, in Trump’s first term, five executives at a Florida company convicted for Medicaid fraud.
Trump’s pardons in 2021 of executives who profited from massive public healthcare fraud spurred criticism from the National Health Care Anti-Fraud Association. Critics now say the administration is portraying cuts to Medicare and Medicaid as necessary for weeding out waste, fraud, and abuse while exonerating criminals who have engaged in some of the biggest schemes in federal health programs.
Blue State Allegations
HHS has raised concerns about Medicaid fraud and program integrity in several states, and the administration has deferred or threatened to cut federal Medicaid funding while disputes are investigated.
Democrats say the administration is itself engaging in fraud by using unsubstantiated allegations of abuse to politically target blue states.
One of the most striking clashes occurred in New York.
Federal officials launched an investigation of the state’s Medicaid program after claiming that personal care services — including help with bathing, dressing, and meal preparation — had been provided to more than 5 million people, which would have amounted to roughly three-quarters of the state’s Medicaid population — an almost impossibly large proportion.
“It is time for New York to come clean about its Medicaid program,” CMS’ Oz posted in March on X.
CMS later acknowledged its calculations were wrong. The agency said that it had misunderstood the state’s billing codes and that the actual number of beneficiaries who received the services was closer to 450,000. The administration continued its scrutiny of the New York program, however, and later suspended millions of dollars in federal funding for the state’s Medicaid fraud unit, saying the division wasn’t producing enough indictments.
The administration also withheld about $2 billion in Medicaid funding from California, citing concerns about program integrity and oversight of some home medical services. State officials deny the allegations, saying spending on home services has grown because of factors such as higher wages for home health aides and an increase the number of older people receiving care.
The White House announced plans to defer more than $500 million in federal funds from Minnesota, claiming the state had failed to protect its Medicaid program from abuse. State officials have defended their oversight and gone to court to challenge the decision.
Vice President JD Vance, who chairs Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, and other administration officials announced the state deferrals at the White House, giving what traditionally would have been technical disputes between state and federal health officials a much higher political profile. Vance’s office did not respond to KFF Health News questions about the administration’s anti-fraud activities related to healthcare.
“I’ve never seen anything like this,” said Andy Schneider, a Georgetown University research professor and a senior adviser at CMS during the Obama administration. “It’s a deferral, not a finding of fraud. This is being elevated by political decision-makers.”
Republican candidates have pounced on the investigations and allegations. In Minnesota, Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth, who is speaker of the Minnesota House, released a September ad claiming that her Democratic opponent, U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, “has never done anything to stop the fraud here in Minnesota.” Klobuchar has said that as governor she would “launch a top-to-bottom audit of state government to root out fraud.”
Dunlap and LePage continue campaign quarrels in final debate

In New York, Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat whose office runs the Medicaid fraud unit, criticized the decision to withhold funds and said weakening the operation would benefit criminals. Her Republican challenger in the November election, Saritha Komatireddy, has cited the Trump administration’s claims during her campaign, telling Fox News Digital that James is “totally failing to prosecute Medicaid fraud.”
The administration says its actions are necessary because fraud diverts taxpayer money from people who legitimately qualify for government programs.
“The fraud doesn’t just steal money — it steals our trust,” Oz said in August on CBS’ Face the Nation.
Democrats and healthcare advocates say the White House’s anti-fraud crusade is being used by Republicans to distract from criticisms over its sweeping funding cuts to Medicaid, the ACA, and other federal health programs.
Republican-backed legislation enacted last year is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade.
Congressional Republicans also declined to extend enhanced ACA premium subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, increasing premium costs for many people who buy insurance through the marketplaces. Enrollment has since declined by millions.
Overall, the combined effect of GOP-led changes will result in 16 million more uninsured people by 2034, according to an analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Those changes have given Democrats an opening to campaign on protecting healthcare coverage and affordability while Republicans seek to shift some of the debate toward fraud and government spending.
“It’s really a way to distract and reframe the cuts in a different way, to say it’s part of an anti-fraud effort,” said Anthony Wright, executive director of Families USA, an advocacy group focused on expanding health coverage. “Fighting fraud shouldn’t result in people losing coverage.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: General Assembly calls off Oct. 26 special session to elect judges
text:
The Virginia Capitol on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)An Oct. 26 special session to elect judges to the Court of Appeals of Virginia has been called off because of scheduling conflicts, scrapping lawmakers’ return to Richmond. 
The session was expected to last at least three days, which Senate Majority Leader Sen. Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said was difficult for many lawmakers to plan around.  
“Members were planning on all kinds of travel plans and family plans and all kinds of stuff. Scheduling special sessions is difficult outside of the regular session,” Surovell told The Mercury in a phone interview Monday.
A special session brings lawmakers together outside their annual regular session to conduct legislative business. Under the Virginia Constitution, the governor can call one when the interests of the state require it and must do so if two-thirds of elected members of each chamber request it. 
This planned meeting was part of the on-going special session that lawmakers have kept open by recessing rather than adjourning after completing their business. That allows them to return at the request of leaders in both chambers.
Surovell said the reason for the session was intended to address a backlog of judicial appointments that could delay some panel decisions. 
Disagreements over taxing data centers delayed final passage of the state budget until June, months after the regular session ended.  That, in turn, delayed funding for the positions and pushed back the vetting process, he said. 
Aside from selecting the judges, Sen. Glen Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, had planned to bring a data center moratorium up for debate ahead of the regular session in January. 
“We’re trying to lower power bills for Virginians and make data centers pay their own way instead of passing their costs on to families,” Sturtevant said in a statement Monday.
Sturtevant has been an early voice in the growing chorus calling for some form of pause on data center development in the commonwealth while lawmakers pass more guardrails and regulations. Multiple such bills have been introduced, or are expected to be, for the regular General Assembly session that begins Jan. 13. 
“The problem exists today. Virginians are dealing with rising power costs now, and we need to make sure data centers pay their own costs rather than shifting them onto families,” Sturtevant said. “If everyone agrees this needs attention, there’s no reason not to start the work Monday.”
However, even if the session had moved forward, bringing Sturtevant’s bill up for a vote would have violated a procedural resolution limiting the introduction of legislation that the House adopted earlier this year. 
Surovell also said the tight schedule did not accommodate committee hearings, which would be necessary to pass legislation such as a moratorium, because the session was focused on electing judges.

name: WyoFile
title: Yellowstone receives record $105 million gift for infrastructure, conservation, access
text:
Yellowstone National Park and Tallgrass, a Colorado company building an AI power hub near Cheyenne, have launched a $105 million conservation and stewardship fund for the country’s first national park, calling it the largest single private gift in the agency’s history.
The park announced creation of the fund this morning in conjunction with its nonprofit conservation partner, Yellowstone Forever, and Tallgrass, a Blackstone Infrastructure portfolio company. The fund will establish a permanent source of support for long-term stewardship, the groups said.
Among the projects the effort will fund is a $35 million visitor center at Norris Geyser Basin, Steven Davidson, senior vice president at Tallgrass said in an interview with WyoFile.
“There’s no place for you to sit and engage with a ranger directly,” he said of the sprawling basin. The center will offer opportunities for experiences that are “a bit more interactive,” he said.
Bison graze near Roosevelt Arch in the spring. (Jacob W. Frank/Yellowstone National Park)
The fund will advance conservation and research, invest in infrastructure and expand opportunities for Wyoming residents and students to visit the 2.2 million-acre reserve. The groups said the donation will establish the Tallgrass WYld Yellowstone Initiative, named for the company that’s been operating in Wyoming for more than a decade.
“The focus is for Wyoming,” Davidson said. “If you are a Wyoming kid, family, we are going to target these programs for you. Let’s be proud and selfish for Wyoming kids.”
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called the investment “historic,” and said in a statement it brings together “the best of American enterprise and conservation.”
“We’re grateful to Blackstone, Tallgrass and Yellowstone Forever for their partnership and extraordinary commitment,” his statement reads.
For Blackstone, the gift “reflects our belief that infrastructure investment can and should be a force for good, helping us invest in Yellowstone’s future and the growth of the communities that surround it,” Sean Klimczak, the company’s global head of infrastructure said in a statement.
Gardner River floodwaters in 2022 obliterated many stretches of Yellowstone National Park’s North Entrance Road, which runs from Gardiner, Mont., to Mammoth Hot Springs, Wyo. (Kyle Stone/National Park Service)
Lisa Diekmann, president and CEO of Yellowstone Forever, called the gift a transformational investment. “It gives us the ability to meet urgent needs today while building enduring support for the research, education, stewardship and visitor infrastructure that will protect this park for generations to come.”
The gift comes at a time of change and challenge for Yellowstone, the country’s first national park. The Park Service estimates $1.2 billion in deferred maintenance and repairs. Barclay Trimble just assumed duties as Acting Superintendent of Yellowstone National Park. He replaced Cam Sholly, who left his post after eight years.
Tallgrass, a “multi-commodity infrastructure” company based in Colorado, operates more than 10,000 miles of pipelines. Early this year it received approval to build an AI data center south of Cheyenne. Google will be Tallgrass’ partner, according to Measured AI, a recent switch from original partner Cruso.
Tallgrass is building the gas-fired Cheyenne Power Hub for the 1.8 gigawatt project. Tallgrass’ $7 billion project is located on more than 1,000 acres in the Switchgrass industrial park south of Cheyenne. The data center will occupy more than 700 acres, according to plans. The data center has faced pushback from rural neighbors in Laramie County concerned about lost views and potential water contamination.
On Monday, Tallgrass President and CEO Crystal Heter said, in a statement announcing the donation to Yellowstone, that the company is proud to strengthen the park’s connection with the next generation.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana laws to protect domestic abuse survivors only go so far
text:
People grieve in front of the home where a shooting spree occurred on April 20, 2026 in Shreveport's Cedar Grove neighborhood. Eight children were killed and two women were wounded at two homes during a domestic violence incident in the early morning hours on April 19, according to local authorities. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Director Deeyah Khan had been fighting violence against women for 15 years when she made the 2022 documentary “Behind the Rage: America’s Domestic Violence.” 
“There is a greater consequence in the United States for killing a bald eagle than there is for assaulting your wife,” says an interviewee in the film. 
In Louisiana, a first conviction for domestic abuse battery carries a fine of $300 to $1,000 and 30 days to six months of jail time. Under federal law, killing a bald eagle can result in a fine of up to $100,000 and a year in prison for a first offense. 
Charles, one of the men Khan interviewed for her documentary, said he once went to jail for domestic violence twice in one night. Between the two arrests, he found the woman and beat her for calling the police. 
When asked whether the women he abused got restraining orders, he said, “Restraining order ain’t nothing but a piece of paper. That ain’t gonna stop me from doing nothing. It ain’t over till I say it’s over.”
A restraining order and firearms restrictions are legal boundaries available to survivors of domestic abuse, but they are not sufficient when an abuser is determined to punish, control, stalk or kill their victim.
Under Louisiana law, a person subject to certain qualified protective orders is prohibited from possessing firearms or carrying concealed weapons when a court finds they represent a credible threat. Since 2018, courts have been required to order some abusers to surrender guns they already own.
A restraining order relies on a chain of people and institutions — judges, clerks, police, prosecutors, service providers and often the victim —  to work effectively. When that chain fails, or when the abuser takes offense at the court order because it challenges their authority, the paper meant to protect the victim can become evidence of danger rather than a guarantee of safety. 
In Louisiana, Gwen’s Law allows a judge to hold a person charged with domestic abuse battery, stalking or a protective order violation without bail for 48 to 72 hours. The law weighs warning signs such as threats and strangulation, but it also has weaknesses. The bail hearing Gwen’s Law once required has been optional since 2015, and a judge may order a jail hold but isn’t required.
Protection also weakens before the bail hearing. A temporary restraining order issued in Louisiana without notice is generally set for a hearing within 21 days. The state’s firearm-prohibition statute does not include a temporary restraining order, which gives the perpetrator time and leverage to do harm.
Women are killed with and without guns. In 2024, according to the Violence Policy Center, firearms were used in 63.4% of killings of women by men. This means that more than one-third involved another weapon or method. 
The central issue is not merely what weapon an abuser can access but whether he is using what Rutgers University scholar Evan Stark calls coercive control: a pattern of violence, intimidation, isolation and control used to dominate a partner.  
Loyola University New Orleans criminologist Rae Taylor’s research points to the same root: sexual proprietariness, a man’s sense that a woman belongs to him. A woman is not made safe simply because one weapon is removed from her home if the system does not address the person who believes he has the right to control her body, movement, relationships and future.
Although Louisiana has a preferred risk tool that predicts whether an abuser will assault again, there is an additional tool that exists. The Lethality Assessment Program screens women at the scene and connects high-risk victims with an advocate on the spot. 
An Oklahoma study reported promising results from the program. In a state health department report published in February, Louisiana’s Domestic Abuse Fatality Review Panel recommended that officers use both tools.
Louisiana must measure a victim’s safety against the full pattern of abuse, including coercive control and lethal violence committed without a firearm. We continue to try to protect abuse survivors one weapon at a time while the danger remains the same.
Restraining orders are not enough as long as we continue to measure the danger by the gun in the house instead of the man who believes it isn’t over until he says it’s over.

title: WATCH: The ‘License to Kill’ documentary
text: CalMatters and Evident team up to investigate what happens to truck drivers in California after they kill someone on the road.

name: California
title: They killed people with their big rigs, and California let them keep driving
text:
Loren Chow looked in the rearview mirror and had a terrifying realization.
We’re going to get hit.
There’s nothing I can do to get out of this.
Traffic outside Fresno had slowed. A semitruck loaded with fertilizer from Missouri, cruising at 65 miles per hour, hadn’t. By the time the driver, Baljit Singh, hit the brakes, it was too late. A fully loaded big rig traveling at that speed takes the length of nearly two football fields to stop.
Chow, his wife and their 17-year-old son were headed home from a college visit in June 2022. Singh’s red Freightliner smashed into the back of their SUV and flipped it. Jenny Chow died. Law enforcement said Singh caused the crash by driving too fast.
Loren Chow can’t talk about the details of the collision because of an active lawsuit against Singh, the trucking companies and vehicle manufacturers. But court filings, police reports and driving records lead to a simple conclusion:
If the California Department of Motor Vehicles had done its job, Jenny Chow would still be alive.
That’s because in July 2021 — 11 months before he killed Chow — Singh let his semitruck drift over the median on Merle Haggard Drive in Kern County on his way to an Amazon distribution center, killing a 26-year-old man on a motorcycle. 
The collision report from that crash shows police found pages from a log book, meant to keep track of Singh’s hours behind the wheel, “ripped into small pieces” in an overhead compartment. Investigators with the California Highway Patrol alleged that Singh was fatigued at the time of the crash after driving more than the 12-hour limit and recommended he be charged with vehicular manslaughter.
But while the DMV knew about the earlier fatal crash and had the authority to suspend Singh’s driving privileges, it let him continue to drive a big rig until he killed again.
“The death was completely avoidable. That accident never should have happened,” Chow said, barely choking back grief during an interview in his Bay Area living room, which is blanketed in smiling photos of Jenny and their two boys.
Loren Chow holds a photo of his wife, Jenny, at the home they shared in Los Altos. Skeeter, the family dog they adopted shortly after Jenny’s death, snuggles next to him. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters



First: Jenny Chow’s car after the collision with Baljit Singh’s semitruck. Screenshot via KGET Last: An altar dedicated to Jenny Chow who died after the family’s car was hit by a truck.  Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters
“I would have had my partner still. We’d be a family of four. Jenny would have seen Dylan and Tyler graduate from high school,” Chow said. “She would have seen so much if only the DMV had done what any person in his right mind would have done, which is to suspend the license.”
A CalMatters investigation found that the DMV often lets professional drivers with a history of dangerous behavior behind the wheel stay on the road and command massive vehicles —  buses filled with passengers, semis packed with goods, and tankers loaded with hazardous chemicals — even after a fatal crash.
Under California law, a truck driver convicted of manslaughter is disqualified from driving big rigs for 12 months. And any driver convicted of felony vehicular manslaughter is generally supposed to receive a three-year license revocation. But criminal cases can drag out, sometimes for years. Singh wasn’t convicted of manslaughter in Kern and Fresno counties until 2024. It was only then that the DMV took his license. Singh and his attorney did not respond to requests for comment.
State law empowers the agency to investigate drivers involved in fatal and serious-injury collisions and suspend their licenses — with or without a conviction. But the DMV routinely does nothing.


Even when the agency does act, records show it can take years to do so. We examined court filings and DMV records for more than 130 commercial licensees charged with vehicular manslaughter from 2019 to early 2024 following a fatal crash on the job or off-duty in a personal vehicle. Nearly half had a valid Class A or Class B license as of late May. That includes a dozen drivers who got a ticket for unsafe driving in a commercial vehicle after having already killed someone.
What’s more, vehicular manslaughter is supposed to be a three-point violation for a truck driver, but in almost every DMV record we reviewed, it was listed as two, the penalty for a regular driver. The agency in a written statement said it relies on the courts to notify it when a conviction involves a commercial vehicle so it can assess the appropriate number of points.
Despite such examples of bureaucratic indifference, we did find one area of enforcement in which the DMV is aggressive: making sure people pay fines.
In 2023, months before the agency finally suspended Singh’s license, it started sending Loren Chow letters threatening to garnish his wages, seize his property and put a lien on his home.
The DMV said he was late paying his vehicle registration fee on the SUV that was totaled, by the truck driver it allowed to stay on the road.
The DMV notice Loren Chow received warning of delinquent registration fees on the vehicle involved in the fatal crash. Graphic composite by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
‘You’re gonna kill somebody’

The DMV’s inaction against commercial drivers is all the more consequential because of the clear risks they pose. Truck driving is a grueling job involving long hours over vast distances. A fully loaded semi can total 80,000 pounds — 20 times the weight of a car. A speeding semitruck doesn’t do fender-benders; it obliterates.
“One thing goes wrong, you’re gonna kill somebody,” said Joe Rajkovacz, a longtime owner-operator and advocate with the Western States Trucking Association. 
About 4,000 people died in large-truck crashes in California from 2015 through 2024, the most recent decade for which federal data is available. 

California’s licensing decisions have an impact beyond the state’s borders. Supersized trucks, long the backbone of our economy, haul billions of dollars of food from the state’s farms and online orders from teeming ports to destinations across the country.  
Tami Friedrich, president of the Truck Safety Coalition, a national advocacy group, said that’s why regulators need to do more to flag truck drivers who shouldn’t be on the road. She got involved in road safety issues after her sister and brother-in-law and their two children — Kris, Alan, Anthony and Brandie — died in a crash with a big rig just after Christmas in 1989. 
“There’s a certain level of responsibility above and beyond a regular car driver that they should adhere to,” Friedrich said.
The cases we examined suggest California is not holding them to that level.
A truck driver killed a 55-year-old man in Bakersfield in 2023, four years after court records show he allegedly injured a woman with his semi in a Sacramento crash. There’s nothing on his driving record to indicate that the DMV did anything in response. He got in yet another truck collision in 2025. 

One driver was convicted of reckless driving and a hit-and-run, got in a collision in San Joaquin County in 2023, failed to show up to court in Sacramento on a traffic ticket and killed someone while driving in Amador County. Just this year he got a speeding ticket in Sacramento and in another collision in Amador. The DMV didn’t suspend his commercial driver’s license until  September, after we asked about the case. 
Another driver with five prior collisions — including one in 2021 in which he veered onto the shoulder in a semitruck and killed someone in Riverside County — was able to renew his license last year and almost immediately racked up two tickets for speeding in a commercial vehicle. He had a valid trucking license as of September.
While regular drivers can easily drive on a suspended license, a trucking company isn’t likely to turn over a loaded semi to a driver without a valid commercial license, experts said. That means DMV action would be all the more meaningful. But the agency often acts only when it’s legally required to and doesn’t use its immense discretionary power to ensure that unsafe drivers get off the road.
The DMV’s hands-off approach comes at a time of turmoil for the trucking industry. Experts say a proliferation of fly-by-night operators and training schools has undercut safety standards and fueled a race to the bottom for driving conditions. At the same time, the Trump administration has alleged California is improperly giving commercial licenses to people who don’t meet immigration or language standards. The court files and DMV records we reviewed do not include drivers’ immigration status.
We sent the DMV a list of commercial drivers along with questions for this story. The agency declined an interview request and wouldn’t comment on specific cases but, shortly after, took action against a dozen of the drivers, such as suspending licenses or stripping commercial driving privileges.

In an email, DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote that the agency recently updated how it handles fatal crashes and manslaughter convictions.
“During this modernization process, the DMV identified some cases that had not been previously reviewed and have now been processed or are currently being processed,” according to Groveman’s email.
He also wrote that law enforcement and the courts need to report information to the agency in a timely manner in order for the DMV to act.
‘What the hell?’

Jon Israel knew what kind of damage a fully loaded big rig could do. He used to drive one. And as a tow truck operator in California’s vast Inland Empire, he’d spent years towing away mangled wreckage from crashes on one of the state’s busiest trucking corridors.
So Israel would have been cautious one summer morning in 2018, when he pulled his overheating tow truck to the side of Interstate 10 and got out to check the radiator fluid, traffic whipping by. 
But there’s not much you can do when a semi veers your way.
A police report shows that Marco Rodriguez let his tractor-trailer drift onto the shoulder. The massive side mirror struck Israel. He died on the roadway he’d long patrolled. 
Rodriguez’s DMV record shows he kept driving commercial vehicles even after the fatal crash, for which he was ultimately convicted of manslaughter. Police caught him speeding in commercial vehicles three separate times from 2022 through last year, and ticketed him one more time for a lane violation.
Despite that record — a vehicular manslaughter conviction, plus four tickets for unsafe driving in commercial vehicles — the agency renewed Rodriguez’s trucking license in March, declining to use its discretion to keep him off the road.
Jon Israel with one of the tow trucks he used to patrol California’s vast Inland Empire. Photo courtesy of Maxine Israel
“What the hell?” said Maxine Israel, Jon’s widow. “Are they waiting for him to kill somebody else?”
Rodriguez’s criminal defense attorney, Mukund Arun, called the fatal crash “a very unfortunate, tragic incident” and emphasized that his client was only charged with a misdemeanor. Prosecutors can charge vehicular manslaughter as a felony or a misdemeanor, with the more serious charge typically involving extreme behavior like drunk driving or excessive speeding. 
Maxine Israel comes from a trucking family. She missed her high school graduation to go on a run in her dad’s semi. For years, she and Jon lived near a notoriously strict Riverside County checkpoint where the CHP weighed trucks and drivers could buy T-shirts that said, “I survived the Banning Scales.” 
But over time, she and her husband noticed that truck drivers seemed to get younger and younger. They drove fast, and their eyes often drifted from the road ahead. The big thing she and Jon talked about was how, unlike in some other states, truck drivers here often failed to slow down and switch lanes to pass people on the shoulder.
“California used to be really, really strict on the big trucks,” Israel said. But now, it’s “like they don’t care.”
It’s been more than six years since Rodriguez was convicted of killing Jon Israel. In July, after CalMatters asked the DMV about the case, the agency finally disqualified Rodriguez from driving commercially. 
DMV records show it’s a one-year ban; he should be eligible to go back to driving trucks next summer.
Court research by Robert Lewis, Lauren Hepler, Anat Rubin, Sergio Olmos, Cayla Mihalovich, Ese Olumhense, Ko Bragg, Andrew Donohue and Jenna Peterson.
