name: Minnesota Reformer
title: How much PFAS is in Minnesota fish? We often have no idea.
text:
A citizen has found that government agencies are far behind when it comes to analyzing PFAS contamination in the fish in Minnesota waterways. Pictured here: Bigmouth buffalo, right and common carp. (Photo by Frank Bures/Minnesota Reformer)Hundreds of Minnesota lakes, rivers and creeks lie downstream of industrial sites where well sampling shows significant groundwater contamination. 
In most of them, state agencies have yet to sample fish — or at least publish the results of completed tests — for PFAS, the so-called forever chemicals associated with a slew of adverse human health impacts.
That’s according to a suburban Twin Cities resident’s analysis of publicly available data from three state agencies, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and the U.S. Geological Survey. 
The findings show nearly 1,000 lakes and about 4,200 river miles downstream of 93 named facilities where sample wells show concerning levels of PFAS contamination in groundwater. Most are closed landfills that operated during the mid- to late 20th century, when consumer and commercial products containing PFAS and other harmful chemicals were common and their impact less widely known or understood.
Last year, samples taken from at least 19 wells at the closed Gofer Landfill near Fairmont showed PFAS concentrations far in excess of human exposure thresholds set by the Minnesota Department of Health. One well had levels of PFOA — a PFAS chemical used in nonstick cookware and other common consumer products — 2.2 million times higher than the state health department’s benchmark for elevated lifetime cancer risk.
In 2021, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency told the Minnesota Star Tribune that PFAS was leaching into Elm Creek, a Minnesota River tributary near Gofer Landfill. Five years later, public data show that the state has yet to publish fish testing results from Elm Creek or several named lakes in its watershed — nor from waters near Louisville Landfill, a Shakopee facility MPCA also flagged in 2021.
“These are two examples where they went out of their way to name those locations and there was no apparent follow-up,” said Beau Parrish, the Mendota Heights resident who compiled the data onto an interactive website in his spare time. 
On the website and in an interview with the Reformer, Parrish stressed that the project does not accuse state health or environmental authorities of a coverup, draw conclusions about how PFAS spreads in surface and subsurface waters, or suggest that PFAS contamination is rampant in Minnesota’s fish population. 
But the findings do show a yawning gap in testing that would take years to close at the current pace, Parrish said. State agencies and local authorities have monitored and mitigated PFAS in drinking water supplies for two decades across swathes of the east metro contaminated by PFAS from 3M industrial sites, but certain PFAS compounds can reach concentrations hundreds or thousands of times greater in fish tissue than in the water itself, he said.
“It’s the worst way you could consume (PFAS), in my opinion,” he said.
Staff from Minnesota’s Pollution Control Agency, Department of Health and Department of Natural Resources have analyzed fish from about 160 different waterbodies since 2021 through an interagency collaboration called the Fish Contaminant Monitoring Program, pollution control spokesperson Adam Olson told the Reformer in an email. 
In 2024, the agencies ramped up testing thanks to a cash infusion from the state’s constitutionally protected clean water fund. They now have about $250,000 per year to monitor PFAS in fish. That’s enough for about 500 fish from 25 lakes or river segments, with priority going to “waters with known PFAS contamination risks, waters of Tribal significance, and popular fishing sites,” Olson said.
At that pace, it would take about 40 years to test the 997 lakes Parrish found to have no record of fish-tissue sampling for PFAS contamination. State health department data collected by Parrish shows fish in about 200 of those lakes were tested for other toxins, such as mercury, while about 800 have no record of fish-tissue testing for any contaminants.
“That is still a drop in the bucket,” Parrish said, of the added funding. The three agencies could clear the backlog much faster with a relatively modest investment: about $3 million per year for five years, he added.
Olson suggested the agencies may have a shortcut. This month, health and environmental officials from Minnesota, Wisconsin and Colorado published the results of a long-running joint study that found a clear correlation between surface-water and fish-tissue concentrations of PFOS, a common PFAS compound. 
Using surface-water analysis as a “pre-screening tool” for fish-tissue test selection, as the researchers recommend, could be more cost-effective and humane than the status quo, Olson said. 
“Surface water analysis is faster, cheaper and can be done at scale without the ecological impact of killing the equivalent number of fish,” he said.
It’s not clear whether accelerated testing would significantly change public understanding of PFAS risk in Minnesota fish. Closed landfills are only one potential source of PFAS contamination in surface or subsurface water, along with industrial activity, wastewater, stormwater, firefighting foam and more, Olson said. 
“While it is a significant source, it’s impossible to say what percent of Minnesota’s known PFAS pollution has passed through landfills,” he said.
None of the 86 waterbodies for which the health department provides PFAS-related fish consumption guidelines are directly fed by water from closed landfill sites, and fish-tissue testing in lakes near closed landfills — including Mille Lacs Lake, one of the state’s richest fisheries — produced PFAS results too low to prompt waterbody-specific consumption guidelines, Olson added.
But those guidelines are not necessarily set in stone, Angela Preimesberger, fish consumption guidance program lead at the state health department, told the Reformer.
“PFAS science is a very active area of research,” Preimesberger said in an email. “(The) information we have today is based on our current understanding. As we learn more about PFAS in fish, MDH will update fish consumption guidance as needed.”

name: Delaware
title: State Police Investigating Strong-Arm Robbery in Wilmington
text:
POLICE LOG – October 19, 2026
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware State Police are investigating a strong-arm robbery that left two employees injured early Sunday morning in Wilmington.
Troopers responded at approximately 3:20 a.m. on October 18 to a business in the 3300 block of Old Capitol Trail.
Police said two employees were walking to their vehicles after work when they were approached by two male suspects wearing pink masks. The suspects allegedly assaulted both employees, stole personal property and fled in a vehicle.
Both victims were taken to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
The Delaware State Police Criminal Investigations Unit is investigating. Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective M. Kerrigan at 302-365-8487 or Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Northern NH maternal health organizations receive grants from border commission
text:
Fourteen organizations across New York, Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine are receiving a collective $1.67 million from the commission. (Getty Images)The Women of the Mountains Birth Initiative, also known as WOMB, and Families Flourish Northeast Inc. received $119,705 to help tackle the maternal health crisis in northern New Hampshire, the Northern Border Regional Commission announced.
They’re two of 14 organizations across New York, Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine to receive a collective $1.67 million from the commission. The money came through a partnership between the commission and the federal government aimed at addressing various gaps in the region’s healthcare network.
WOMB plans to use the money to develop “a network of community-based birth workers and regional healthcare partners,” including “a doula peer mentorship network and a centralized nonprofit hub to support administration, billing, referrals, and connections to prenatal and postpartum services,” per the grant announcement. Families Flourish Northeast plans to develop “a coordinated, family-centered healthcare network” for pregnant and parenting women struggling with substance use disorders in rural New Hampshire and Vermont.
This comes as New Hampshire and rural New England’s maternal care infrastructure is shrinking. Eleven maternity wards have closed in New Hampshire since 2000, the Bulletin has reported.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Bill Clinton and others pay tribute to women ‘Warriors of the Civil Rights Movement’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SAN FRANCISCO – These eight women and their families fought in a war known as America’s Civil Rights Movement. Over the weekend, they gathered, perhaps for the last time, as former President Bill Clinton and others cheered their courage and their grace.
“Throughout the course of their lives, these women have proved that love and compassion are better than bitterness and hatred,” Clinton said in a videotaped message. “They have led with courage, strength, dignity and grace to help build an America that more closely lives up to our founding ideals of equality and justice for all. And through their actions and their example, they have inspired millions of people, including me.”
He wished four of the women happy birthdays: Minnijean Brown Trickey and Elizabeth Eckford, two of the Little Rock Nine who integrated Central High School in 1957; Reena Evers-Everette, whose father, Mississippi NAACP leader Medgar Evers, was assassinated in Jackson in 1963; and Lisa McNair, whose sister, Denise, was among the four girls whose lives were stolen by the Ku Klux Klan in the 1963 Birmingham church bombing.
Lisa McNair, Minnijean Brown Trickey, Elizabeth Eckford and Reena Evers-Everette celebrated their birthdays Oct. 17, 2026, in San Francisco at a Sojourn Project gathering for the women.  Credit: Jerry Mitchell/Mississippi Today
“To the four of you celebrating your birthdays, I thank you for the life you have lived and continue to live,” Clinton told them. “We’re all better off because of you.”
The other women gathered at the event, sponsored by the Sojourn Project, included: Kim McNair, the other sister of Denise McNair; Bettie Dahmer, whose father, voting rights activist Vernon Dahmer Sr., died defending their family from a Klan attack in Hattiesburg in 1966; the Rev. Gwen Webb, who took part in the 1963 Children’s March; and Angela Lewis, whose father James Chaney was among the three civil rights workers killed by Klansmen in Neshoba County in 1964.
Salute from San Francisco officials
Bettie Dahmer, the daughter of Vernon Dahmer Sr., is honored by the city of San Francisco on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.  Credit: Jerry Mitchell/Mississippi Today
On Friday, the city of San Francisco, county supervisors and the sheriff’s office honored these women.
“Your courage changed history,” Mayor Daniel Lurie told them. “It changed the course of history, and your example continues to inspire generations and generations.  I know we still have a whole lot of work to do, but your example will help guide us forward.”
Sheriff Paul M. Miyamoto praised the women. 
“We know their names, the events and some of the photographs, but we don’t know the people,” he said. “You’ve helped change our history by being part of our history.”
The history of the Civil Rights Movement includes some in law enforcement “who failed to protect people at that time, who failed to protect you in our community, and, in some cases, were responsible for the very injustices that people experienced during this time,” Miyamoto said. “That’s not an easy part of our history to confront, but it’s one that we have to accept and understand and move on from.”
More than 20 Klansmen, including some Mississippi law enforcement officers, killed three civil rights workers, Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, on the first day of summer in 1964 and buried their bodies 15 feet down in an earthen dam.
Three years later, seven Klansmen were convicted of federal conspiracy charges, including a deputy sheriff. In 2005, a Neshoba County jury convicted Edgar Ray Killen of orchestrating the killings of the trio. He was sentenced to 60 years in prison, where he died.
Miyamoto has taken some of his deputies on the Sojourn trip, walking across some of the same ground that the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. once walked.
“He’s always been, from birth, an influence on my life,” Miyamoto said. “It meant something very special to me as a history major and also sharing Martin Luther King’s birthday.”
He said it’s important for young people and for those in law enforcement “to learn together, to remember the past and make sure that it’s our responsibility to make sure nothing comes close to repeating it again.”
District Attorney Brooke Jenkins praised Trickey and Eckford for “stepping up at that time to make that sacrifice. You were so strong and brave.”
San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins speaks to the eight women honored at a City Hall Ceremony on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.  Credit: Jerry Mitchell/Mississipi Today
She told Evers-Everette, who now heads the Medgar & Myrlie Evers Institute, ”Your father died doing the work to give us the chance to be here, to give people like me the chance to serve in these positions. Thank you.” 
In 1994, his killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted of murder. Beckwith was sentenced to life in prison, where he died.
Through photos of the children marching in Birmingham or the Black students entering school in Little Rock amid a screaming mob, “we see strength, and we see beauty,” Jenkins said, “but what nobody wants to talk about are their scars.”
She said she hopes “we can set aside all the many differences that so many of us have and make sure we continue to work together to maintain their legacy — people who lost parents, who lost siblings, who lost so much of themselves to give us the chance to just go to school together.”
‘Women Who Dared, Women Who Cared: Warriors of the Civil Rights Movement’
She noted the upcoming elections in November. “I’m not telling you how to vote,” she said, “but you have to vote because we have multiple people who lost their fathers trying to make sure we had the right to do so.”
Reena Evers-Everette and Elizabeth Eckford listen as the city of San Francisco honors them on Friday, Oct 16, 2026. Angela Lewis is sitting to the left behind them.  Credit: Audra Gray
In 2023, Jenkins took her first of four Sojourn’s trips to civil rights sites in the South, where she met these women and visited landmarks where history was made. Through these trips, “we gain a deeper understanding of the courage it took, and continues to take, to change our country for the better,” she said. “These lessons matter.”
On Saturday, Sojourn celebrated these “Warriors of the Civil Rights Movement” with songs, speeches and birthday cakes with photos of the women.
Jenkins pointed toward the historic photos of the women and their families. She told them that she keeps a photograph of the four Dahmer sons dressed in military uniforms, standing over the rubble of what had been their home.
“Vernon Dahmer Sr. spent his life and lost his life over voting rights, over making sure that we could vote,” she said. A part of Medgar Evers’ work “was making sure that Blacks got the right to vote,” she said. “James Chaney and the others lost their lives to give us the right to vote.”
There is no more critical time than now, she said. “Their spirits are calling upon us to act, or else we will see this time again.”
Jenkins said when she walked inside the 16th Street Baptist Church, where the bomb killed four girls and injured dozens of others, “I had no idea how I would feel.”
But after hearing the McNair family speak, “I was overcome with emotion, not just because of their story, but because I, too, had buried my child,” she said. “When you think about losing your baby because of hate, there’s nothing worse.”
What led her to the path of becoming a prosecutor was the loss of her son, she said. “We have to look at these experiences of loss and of grief and of trauma, and use it as our purpose to act. Find the purpose out of our pain.”
When she thinks of Eckford and Trickey, she thinks of her grandmother, who graduated from a segregated high school in Texas and what it meant for her younger siblings to attend an integrated high school, she said. “It was because of your sacrifice that they had that opportunity.”
She praised Webb, who as a teenager faced the dogs and firehoses of Birmingham police to march for justice, only to later become one of the first Black police officers.
“She said, ‘I won’t be turned away by my experience,’” Jenkins said. “I’m going to come into this institution and make it change.”
Sojourn’s founder, Jeff Steinberg, said his nonprofit organization aims to amplify stories that people should know beyond King and Malcolm X — people such as Dahmer, Medgar Evers and the Rev. Fred Shuttlesworth, who was repeatedly beaten for his activism in Birmingham and whose home was blown up by Klansmen.
“They live up to America’s ideals,” Steinberg said. “They set the standard of what we all should aspire to be.”
Lewis said if people want the world to change, they need to become part of that change. “It has to start with us,” she said. “We all want to see things change in a major way, but the way things change is in small amounts over time.”
When it comes to voting, “a lot of people think that their vote doesn’t count, but it does count,” Lewis said. “It begins with us being responsible by voting, because we have to make sure that we have a say in how this country is being run.”
Eckford said she tells “young people today to use your voice, ’cause if you don’t use your voice, somebody else is speaking for you.”

title: Live debate: Should Mass. adopt all-party primary elections?
text:
EPISODE INFO

GUESTS: Danielle Allen, Convening Chair of the Coalition for Healthy Democracy, and Jordan Berg Powers, Chair of Voting Rights MA








PERHAPS THE MOST controversial of the nine ballot questions that will appear before Massachusetts voters in November is Question 3, which would replace partisan primaries with all-party primaries for most state, federal, county, and district offices, allowing the two candidates receiving the most votes to advance to the general election.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Early voting for Alaska’s general election opens in Juneau, Nome and across the Railbelt
text:
Voters line up on Aug. 17, 2026, at the early voting station set up in Anchorage's Midtown Mall. Voters reported waiting about an hour to cast their primary election ballots. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Most state offices may be closed on Monday for Alaska Day, but officials with the Alaska Division of Elections are planning to be at work for the first day of early in-person voting in the 2026 general election.
In Anchorage, early voting will be open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday at Midtown Mall and Anchorage City Hall. 
Other voting locations will be open in Eagle River, Fairbanks, Juneau, Kenai, Nome, Palmer and Wasilla.
A full list of locations and operating days and times has been posted online by the division. All votes must be cast before or on Election Day, Nov. 3.
Dozens of in-person absentee voting locations will also open starting Monday across the state, but there is a key difference between early voting and absentee voting, which has also been taking place by mail and fax for weeks.
In early voting, the voter’s identity is checked up front, before voting, so the ballot is guaranteed to count. With absentee voting, whether in person, by mail or fax, the voter’s ID isn’t checked until the ballot reaches the Division of Elections.
If the voter’s identity can’t be verified, or if there’s another procedural problem, the ballot may be rejected and not counted. Alaska doesn’t offer a way for absentee voters to fix procedural problems.
In addition, absentee ballots can be affected by delivery delays. In this year’s primary election, dozens of absentee ballots cast in person were rejected because they didn’t reach a hub location in time for review.
The division said it has changed its procedures for the general election in order to prevent that problem.
But mail delays may still keep some absentee ballots from being counted.
Under state law, a mailed ballot must arrive within 10 days after Election Day if mailed from within the United States,or 15 days afterward, if mailed from outside the country. Those ballots will be counted as long as they were postmarked on or before Election Day.
Any ballots that arrive after that deadline will not be counted.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
text:
U.S. consumers aren’t just frustrated with high prices. They’re angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices.
Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product.
Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve.
“There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney.
Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper.
“We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote.
But companies aren’t always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it’s used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said.
Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law.
Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny.
Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices
What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber’s practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing.
Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager.
Digital price labels are coming to more US stores
What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags.
Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology.
The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced.
“Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said.
Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data
What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing” for the same practice.
Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers.
Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut’s legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases.
California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer’s app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside.
Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using so-called geofencing technology to increase prices.
Target said the app functionality at issue was used to “provide guests with accurate pricing, which can vary across stores and channels.” The retailer said it didn’t personalize prices based on a guest’s data or behavior and remains “committed to clear, transparent pricing.”
Different prices do not necessarily mean personal data was used. Last year, an investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that shoppers on Instacart were shown different prices for identical products at the same stores. Instacart subsequently ended what it described as tests that randomly assigned shoppers to groups rather than setting prices based on their personal information.
Algorithmic pricing gets an assist from AI
What it is: Algorithmic pricing uses software to recommend or automatically set prices. Companies have used such systems for decades. AI can help the software identify patterns in sales, competitors’ prices and other information to predict demand and estimate how different prices would affect sales and profits. These tools can support both dynamic and personalized pricing.
Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely retailers use AI to help set prices, but research suggests businesses across industries are adopting it.
Simon-Kucher, a global consulting company, surveyed more than 2,200 business leaders in 28 countries and 39 industries last year, and 41% said they used AI software to gather market intelligence, including competitors’ prices. Another 28% said they used it for “real-time price optimization.” Price optimization means choosing prices that advance business goals, such as increasing profits, attracting shoppers or clearing unsold goods.
The National Retail Federation, which represents big and small stores, said algorithmic pricing is a new method of doing what retailers have always done: monitor and adjust prices depending on supply, demand, seasonality, competitors’ prices and other factors.
Some lawsuits have alleged companies used pricing algorithms to undermine competition.
A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged, among other practices, an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie. The agency alleged Amazon used the tool to identify products whose prices it could raise with competitors likely to follow, generating more than $1 billion in excess profits.
A trial is scheduled for next year. Amazon said the FTC allegations “grossly mischaracterize” the pricing tool.
Project Nessie was intended to stop retail price-matching practices from creating unsustainably low prices, the e-commerce giant said. Amazon said it tested the tool for a few years but it didn’t work as intended and was scrapped before the federal agency’s lawsuit.
A recent consumer lawsuit against McDonald’s alleged that its pricing system use nonpublic sales data from competing locations to coordinate prices. The Chicago-based burger giant said the lawsuit was “filled with inaccuracies” and that the company makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Democrat running for SC secretary of state wants to change the office’s duties
text:
Republican Secretary of State Mark Hammond (left) is running for re-election against Democrat Jason Belton (right). (Photos by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The Democrat seeking to oust South Carolina’s longtime secretary of state wants to change the job description.
Jason Belton’s campaign platform includes “restoring election integrity” to bring “accountable leadership at the ballot,” his website reads. But in South Carolina, the secretary of state has nothing to do with the ballot. The office plays no role in registering voters or conducting elections.
Belton believes that should change.
South Carolina’s secretary of state leads the office where businesses, corporations, and charities file their paperwork. Other duties of the agency include regulating professional fundraisers and approving notaries. The secretary’s very limited role in elections is to certify every four years who South Carolinians chose for president — weeks after vote-counting stops.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


Republican Mark Hammond, first elected in 2002, last did that in December 2024, when he signed the document officially declaring that Donald Trump received South Carolina’s nine votes in the Electoral College.
In 40 other states, the secretary of state is the chief election officer, according to the Council of State Governments. But in South Carolina, that job goes to the state Election Commission, an agency governed by five board members and the director they choose. By law, the director can’t be in elected office or even a candidate for at least a year before the appointment.
But Belton believes the secretary of state should head the Election Commission or at least have a “senior adviser role,” saying the voters should elect who’s in charge of elections.
“We’re talking about somebody that’s over the most important thing in this state, and that’s voting and I think they should be held accountable to the voters, but that’s hard if none of these roles are actually voted in by the people,” Belton said, adding the secretary of state “should have statutory power as it comes to the Election Commission.”
That would require the Legislature changing the law. Belton said he’d advocate for that.
“I would love to talk that over with the General Assembly” on the specific changes, said Belton, who won the June primary over Edwina Winter to be the Democratic nominee.
Hammond, who had no GOP opponent in his bid for a seventh term, said he’d accept the new role if legislators put the secretary of state in charge. But he doesn’t think they will.
Under existing law, all Election Commission board members are appointed by the governor to four-year terms, who can technically hire and fire the director. But the Senate gets the final say over a hire through the confirmation process, a role they’re loath to give up. The chances become even slimmer that the GOP-dominated Legislature will make changes to give an elected Democrat power over elections.
Other plans
As for the secretary of state’s existing duties, Belton said he entered the race because of its role with charities, which must register and file annual reports with the office in order to solicit donations from South Carolinians or risk suspension.
During Hammond’s tenure, that information became more easily accessible. Charities’ financial reports are searchable online and through an app called “Give Smart SC.” People can submit an online complaint about a charity’s solicitation.
Every November, the office recognizes 10 charity “angels” that spend at least 80% of donations on their mission.
Belton said he’ll advocate for a law requiring big, out-of-state nonprofits to work through a local nonprofit. He believes that will result in less spending on administration. He said he wants to create a referral program to help small businesses and nonprofits get loans and grants.
“A lot of times, to thrive as a business is more about relationships. It’s about having access to banks,” Belton said.
And he wants to broaden the office’s reach by putting an employee or artificial intelligence station in every county. He did not have a cost estimate but says it shouldn’t cost a lot because they’d use space in existing government buildings.
But Hammond, former clerk of court in Spartanburg County, called whatever Belton’s plan would cost a “waste of money.”
“If you want to do business with the Secretary of State’s office in South Carolina, all you need is a cellphone, and I don’t know anyone starting a business that doesn’t have a cellphone or a checking account,” he said.
The office has about 30 employees and operates on less than $1.7 million in state taxes. Its total budget this fiscal year is $5.5 million, funded mostly by the filing fees it charges.
Asked about his plans, Hammond said he’d like to take more noncompliant charities to the Administrative Law Court to suspend their legal fundraising operations.
And while online services make in-person filings unnecessary, he says there’s still work to do to make the office more “business friendly.” He’s looking to add an AI assistant to the agency’s website to answer questions and help filers navigate the system.
“I still feel like there’s more to do, and I think that we’re getting a lot accomplished,” Hammond, 62, said about why he’s running again. “You know, I have always wanted to have a Secretary of State’s office that is very transparent, that is user friendly and never closes. Right now, the South Carolina Secretary of State’s office technically never closed.”
Belton, 39, is the former state director for the AFL-CIO union and co-chief of a political and business consulting firm. He’s also vice president of the AFL-CIO’s Greater Columbia Central Labor Council, a liaison between the national union and local unions in 12 counties. In that role, he helps train local union leaders in a state that’s among the least-unionized nationwide.
It’s been 40 years since South Carolinians elected a Democrat as secretary of state.
In 1990, John Campbell lost his bid for a fourth term to Jim Miles, the first Republican to win the job since Reconstruction.
Hammond won the last open contest in 2002, when Miles ran unsuccessfully for governor.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. upgraded from least competitive elections in the country to second-worst
text:
FOR THE FIRST time since Barack Obama was president, Massachusetts did not land in dead last place in one assessment of electoral competitiveness.
It came in second to last.
Thanks to a slight uptick in the share of state legislative races with multiple choices for voters this election season, the Bay State climbed from the basement up one single rung higher in Ballotpedia’s biennial competition index.
The nonprofit online political encyclopedia examined all 46 states that have legislative races this fall. Massachusetts ranked 39th for the share of open seats (8 percent), 35th for the share of incumbents who faced primary challenges (14 percent), and 45th for the share of its 200 races where both a Democrat and Republican are on the general election ballot (23 percent). Averaging those three inputs, Ballotpedia awarded Massachusetts an overall “competitiveness index” of 15 on a 100-point scale, lower than every other state except Rhode Island.
All 160 seats in the Massachusetts House and all 40 seats in the Massachusetts Senate are up for reelection every two years. Three out of five of those races are completely uncontested this year, leaving most voters with no choice in their state lawmakers at the same time they will face a record-tying number of ballot questions.
The lack of options is far from a new development. In every two-year cycle from 2016 to 2024, Massachusetts landed at the bottom of Ballotpedia’s national competitiveness rankings.
Republicans are outnumbered about six to one in the Legislature, and while many Democrats avoid drawing primary opponents, the lack of competition is especially fueled by the low rate of GOP challenges.
Democrats are contesting 94 percent of Massachusetts seats, while Republicans are only vying for 30 percent, according to Ballotpedia. That’s much lower than many other safely blue states like Connecticut (where 80 percent of districts have a Republican candidate) and New York (where 71 percent of districts are being challenged by Republicans).
In California, where Democrats control three-quarters of the state Legislature, Republicans are in fact vying for a slightly higher share (95 percent) of the 100 seats up for grabs this November than Democrats are (93 percent). That fact, plus a high rate of incumbents drawing same-party challengers, prompted Ballotpedia to rank California number one overall in its 2026 competitiveness index.
Other states that see significant competition tend to have split party control or the prospect of one party seizing a majority. In Michigan, where Democrats hold a two-seat margin in the Senate and Republicans hold a six-seat margin in the House, every single legislative district except one has a candidate from each of the major parties.
Little is at stake in the Massachusetts Legislature this November. With so few races, Democrats are guaranteed to retain a veto-proof supermajority in both chambers. Only two other states have a supermajority locked in before votes are cast: fellow Democratic hotbed Rhode Island, and Arkansas, where Republicans dominate.
House Speaker Ron Mariano has not faced an opponent since 2020, and Senate President Karen Spilka has been unopposed in every one of her reelection campaigns since 2010.
Laura Giordano, a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Democratic Party, said the latest Ballotpedia rankings showing the Bay State second-to-last in the country on electoral competition is not itself a worrying sign. The party does not get involved in contested primaries, she noted.
“We did see some really competitive races this cycle, which brought some excitement for some people, but on a whole, it’s not something [about which] we’re incredibly concerned,” Giordano said.
Beacon Hill critics across the partisan spectrum have long lamented the lackluster competition, arguing that entrenched leadership leads to a sluggish pace of work and elected officials out of touch with what their constituents want. Reformists pushing a dramatic change to the state’s electoral landscape made that a central pitch of their ballot question campaign.
If voters approve Question 3 this fall, Massachusetts would cease to operate separate Republican and Democratic primary elections and instead place all candidates onto a single, “all-party primary” ballot. The top two finishers would advance to the general election, even if they are both from the same party.
“Without competition, elected officials don’t have to listen to voters. Everybody feels stuck, and nothing is changing,” Danielle Allen, a Harvard University professor and the campaign’s chief proponent, said in her opening remarks at a CommonWealth Beacon-hosted debate last week. “You don’t get movement on housing and affordability and other issues.”
It’s not a view shared by those dissatisfied with the status quo nor by the people who control the system. Opponents of Question 3 include progressive organizers who think the Legislature’s Democratic supermajority has been too slow to respond to the most pressing issues as well as well as both the state Democratic and Republican parties. While they disagree on how well the system functions today, that constellation of voices agrees that altering how primary elections work will not automatically encourage more candidates to run.
“Under the system proposed with Question 3, there are instances where the top two for November might be Democrats. You wouldn’t have the representation of an independent or a Republican” on the ballot, Giordano said.

name: California
title: Unsure about how to vote in California Supreme Court election? You’re not alone
text:
The California Supreme Court during a court session at the Ronald Reagan State Office Building in Los Angeles on April 3, 2024. Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo




Why do we vote on judges, and how are we supposed to decide? It’s a recurring question we’re hearing in our conversation with voters this fall.
Judges aren’t exactly household names, although one on your ballot shares a name with a certain multiplatinum-selling musician. They generally don’t campaign, either. 
The simple answer to the question, though, is that our state constitution requires it. California justices serve 12-year terms rather than the lifetime appointments that federal judges receive. 
Unlike conventional elections, state Supreme Court and appeals court judges don’t run against opponents. Instead, voters are given a simple yes-or-no question on retaining a judge. If a majority votes a judge out, the governor appoints their replacement. 
That’s why your ballot asks whether two California Supreme Court justices, Kelli Evans and Joshua Groban, should keep their jobs. You’ll also see a number of appeals court justices depending on where you live.

Thomas Wilhite, a retired California Court of Appeals justice: “It does give the court of appeal a measure of independence because you don’t stand for election constantly. But it gives the voters a chance to have a say and confirm the continued service of the justice.”

Californians only used their power to unseat sitting justices once. That was in 1986 when voters swept three state supreme court justices off the bench over their rulings against death sentences.
You can search for any disciplinary actions against justices at the Commission on Judicial Performance. 
It’s common for voters to skip over the judicial elections. In 2022, for example, about 8.3 million Californians voted in elections for state supreme court justices. That’s about 2.5 million fewer than the number of people who voted in our U.S. Senate race.
Retired California Supreme Court Justice Martin Jenkins was up for retention that year. He wants Californians to understand the care and commitment judges put into their work, saying he worked six or seven days a week throughout his career. Voters should research the justices just as they would any other politician or ballot measure, Jenkins said. 



Join CalMatters, AAJA Sac, ABC 10 and The Sacramento Observer for a free VotingMatters event Wednesday in Sacramento. The event enables attendees to learn and discuss the upcoming election and focuses on the ballot propositions and insurance commissioner race. Register here to attend in person.

Abuse and retaliation inside CA women’s prison


Incarcerated women walk through a yard at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED




We’re publishing a special report today by our partners KQED on what led up to the mass pepper-spraying of incarcerated people in California’s largest women’s prison.
That incident took place at Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla, the same site where former guard Gregory Rodriguez last year was convicted on dozens of counts of raping and sexually assaulting incarcerated women. 
As the rate of sexual misconduct complaints against staff increased, a pattern of retaliation against those who reported assault also emerged, as did a failure to investigate those assaults, report KQED’s Madi Bolaños and Sukey Lewis.
On Aug. 2, 2024 officers confined 159 women for more than four hours in a dining hall without food, water or medication, and then unleashed streams of pepper spray and chemical blast grenades on them.
Angela Kent said in her 27 years of law enforcement, she had never seen anything like the use of force that day. She was an administrator for the state’s two women’s prisons when it occurred.

Kent: “I absolutely felt that every officer, supervisor and manager involved should be fired.”

Read more.



GOP’s push to unseat Merced congressmember


U.S. Rep. Adam Gray (left) and Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln. Photos via the U.S. House of Representatives and Lincoln’s campaign website




Rep. Adam Gray won the closest U.S. House race in 2024 by a mere 187 votes. This year, the Merced Democrat faces more favorable odds for reelection due to the state’s recent voter-approved redistricting that favors Democrats.
But former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln, a Republican, aims to unseat Gray to represent California’s 13th District — which stretches from Stockton to Merced — and he’s getting a lot of help and money from national Republicans, writes CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller.
A super PAC aligned with House Republican leadership has spent more than $4.34 million on the race this year so far, and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana went to Chowchilla to rally support for Lincoln. Part of the reason for the GOP’s strong support likely stems from having few other prospects for winnable races elsewhere in California after last year’s gerrymander.
House Democrats, meanwhile, have spent less than $400,000 this year on the race, according to campaign finance records.

And lastly: What do you want public health officials to know?


A certified lab specialist looks through a microscope at Hazel Hawkins Memorial Hospital in Hollister on March 30, 2023. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




Have an opinion on what health issues should be prioritized in California? CalMatters is partnering with Your Local Epidemiologist to make the real concerns and questions from Californians heard by public health officials and journalists.
