name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrat connects with voters by pointing out ‘we were all lied to’ on inflation, immigration
text:
Lauren Reinhold, a Kansas Democratic candidate for a U.S. House seat, appears for a recording of the Kansas Reflector podcast on Oct. 12, 2026, in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Democratic U.S. House candidate Lauren Reinhold says she has found a way to connect with disaffected Republicans and independent voters.
She has traveled more than 35,000 miles as she campaigns in the 1st District, which thanks to GOP gerrymandering now stretches from her home in Lawrence to the western half of the state. She is running against Republican Rep. Tracey Mann, a three-term incumbent who won by 39 percentage points just two years ago.
But, Reinhold said on the Kansas Reflector podcast, a lot has changed in two years. People in the district are hurt economically and “fed up with some of the radical policies” of President Donald Trump’s administration, she said.


“As I like to point out on the trail, we were all lied to,” Reinhold said. “We were told that we would make more money, that inflation would go down, that prices would go down, that the immigration enforcement surge would only be to get out the worst of the worst, the criminals, and we would stay out of wars. And none of that’s true. It’s the opposite, and people are starting to realize it.”
Reinhold’s foray into the political world was spurred by last year’s firing spree by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. She accepted a buyout and left her job at the Social Security Administration. Faced with a “big, unexpected void” in her career, as she put it, but still wanting to serve, she decided to run for office.
She defeated Colin McRoberts, a business law professor at the University of Kansas, to win the Democratic nomination in the August primary.
On the campaign trail, she expected people in the ultra-conservative congressional district to say, “Go away, you Lawrenceite.”
Instead, she made personal connections.
“When I’m out there talking to folks, I’m just a mom — a middle-age mom, a regular person, who’s just hearing the issues and letting them know my experience and what I want to do in Washington,” Reinhold said.
And they are telling her “they are fed up with irrational wars and unstable tariff and trade policies and affordability,” she said. “They’re worried about being able to afford their lives.”
Reinhold said economic security is the defining issue of the campaign. She said Congress needs to reform healthcare, raise the minimum wage, balance the tax system and end “crazy military engagements” around the world.
The first piece of legislation she would introduce or support if elected would be immigration reform.
“The reason why we have so many undocumented people, and the reason why we have this divide, and now this ICE enforcement terrorism, really, in a way that is dividing us a lot, is because we’ve been overdue for comprehensive immigration reform for decades,” she said.
She said Congress needs to create classes of visas for agriculture, both seasonal and year-round, as well as visas for construction and other fields. There also needs to be a path to citizenship, she said.
Congress also needs to provide oversight over U.S. Immigration and Customs and Enforcement, she said. The recent raids in southwest Kansas, which disrupted the agriculture sector, she said, were examples of “militia-type behavior” that needs to be stopped.
“Congress needs to get ICE back operating as it should be under the law,” Reinhold said. “And the lies — we’ve been told that they’re prioritizing taking people with criminal records. They’re not. They’re taking anyone they can.”
Reinhold said the Republicans’ most recent proposal for a farm bill is inadequate because it lacks sufficient funding for the Supplemental Nutrition and Assistance Program, conservation efforts and foreign aid.
“But everything in Congress is compromised,” she said, ” so I might end up voting for a farm bill that’s pretty similar to that one, if that’s the only compromise we can reach.”
She said it was time to consider legalizing marijuana for both medicinal and recreational use. On abortion rights, she said she believes in a woman’s complete and unfettered right to choose.
She said she supports background checks for firearm purchases and that she has applied for a concealed carry permit.
“I decided I needed to understand and learn how guns work and learn to shoot and all that before I could weigh in on such a difficult issue,” she said.
Mann’s office didn’t respond to repeated invitations for a podcast interview.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 2 weeks of early voting in SC is underway
text:
In South Carolina, the Nov. 3 ballot includes a U.S. Senate contest between Republican Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews. (Illustration from iStock/Getty Images Plus)Voting is underway in South Carolina in an election that could change control of Congress and is guaranteed to usher in new administrations in state government.
Two weeks of early voting began Monday morning. Locations are open from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. through Oct. 31, with one exception: There is no voting Oct. 25. State law forbids voting on Sundays.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


The race getting the most attention nationally will decide whether U.S. Sen. Darline Graham wins her first election to keep the seat she was appointed to following the death of her older brother, Lindsey Graham, or whether Democrat Annie Andrews flips it blue.
South Carolina hasn’t had a Democrat in the U.S. Senate since Fritz Hollings retired in January 2005.
Voters will also decide who will be South Carolina’s next governor, attorney general, agriculture commissioner and comptroller general. Other statewide races with incumbents running are superintendent of education, treasurer, and secretary of state.
All 46 counties have at least one early voting location.
Four counties have seven locations open, the maximum allowed by state law: Charleston, Florence, Greenville and Horry.
The counties with six locations open are Aiken, Berkeley, Lexington, Pickens, Richland, Spartanburg and York.
Voters can choose whatever location is most convenient within the county where they’re registered, whether that’s close to home, work or shopping. Early voters aren’t bound by home address.
That changes for Election Day, Nov. 3, when people must vote in their assigned precinct.

name: California
title: ‘Put them down with gas’: Abuse and retaliation inside a California women’s prison
authors: Madi Bolaños and Sukey Lewis of KQED
text:
Hear more of the story on the podcast We Are Jane Doe, from KQED’s Snap Studios.
Aliksandria Prout was at home the evening of Aug. 2, 2024, when her phone rang. It was her former cellmate at the Central California Women’s Facility. Catrina Cameron was nearly incoherent over the prison phone line. 
“She told me she couldn’t see outta one eye,” Prout recalled. Cameron told Prout that correctional officers had sprayed her and dozens of other women with tear gas and pepper spray. “Our other cellmate had gotten beat up by correctional staff.”
Prout could barely grasp the enormity of the incident. As the public would later learn, correctional officers had removed 159 women from a prison housing unit, confined them for more than four hours in a dining hall without food, water or medication, and then unleashed streams of pepper spray and chemical blast grenades on them when tensions escalated. 
Later, as the prisoners sat outside on the hot, dusty yard with their hands zip-tied behind their backs, officers again used tear gas and pepper grenades on them.
Surveillance footage obtained by KQED through a public records request shows officers throwing chemical blast grenades at incarcerated women in the dining hall of the Central California Women’s Facility on Aug. 2, 2024. Screenshot via the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
A retired prison administrator who reviewed footage of the incident told KQED: “It looks like they’re lining ’em up for the firing squad.” 
Women suffered injuries including stroke, blindness and seizures. “I didn’t know what they were doing to us or why, but I needed help, and I need somebody out there to know,” Cameron later recalled. 
On the phone with her friend, Prout felt sick. The 33-year-old nursing student and mother of three had been out of prison for nearly two years, but she hadn’t been able to leave it behind. 
In just a couple of months, Prout was set to testify against the now-infamous former correctional officer, Gregory Rodriguez, who’d been charged with sexually assaulting more than a dozen women at the facility in Chowchilla, about 35 miles from Fresno. 
And now, her close friend and former cellmate had been attacked by officers in the chow hall. She couldn’t help but think her efforts to expose Rodriguez were connected to what had just happened to Cameron and more than 150 women in her old unit.
Aliksandria Prout surrounded by legal paperwork in her home office, on Aug. 19, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
Prout’s concerns were well-founded, according to a two-year KQED investigation into “Operation Breakdown,” as the incident was called in internal documents.
Interviews with more than a dozen women, a KQED analysis of six years’ worth of sexual assault complaints, trial transcripts, court filings, leaked internal affairs interviews and hundreds of disciplinary documents revealed a pattern of retaliation against incarcerated women who reported assault, failure to investigate those assaults and the dysfunctional accountability system that allowed staff sexual exploitation of women to flourish.
A recent U.S. Department of Justice investigation reached a similar conclusion, finding an “unbroken pattern” of sexual abuse and retaliation in California’s women’s prisons dating back more than two decades. Central California Women’s Facility is one of just two women’s penitentiaries in the state and is one of the largest women’s prisons in the world, with a population of more than 2,000 women, nonbinary and trans people held inside.
In the wake of the Justice Department report, and as KQED neared publication of this investigation, the warden at the women’s prison, Anissa De La Cruz, was demoted and transferred, and multiple officers were put under investigation for sexual abuse. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) said the agency cannot comment on personnel decisions or the ongoing investigation. It said the agency is “fully committed to protecting victims of sexual assault.” 
Corrections department Press Secretary Terri Hardy said in an email that the department conducted its own investigation into the events of Aug. 2, investigating 95 employees and disciplining 34 for their conduct, including firing three for excessive force and dishonesty. Initially, the department moved to discipline 41 staff members, but that number dropped as correctional officers filed appeals, some of which are still pending. 
The corrections department said the case was the largest corrective action stemming from a single incident in its history. Yet, key questions about the operation’s connection to a rising tide of sexual assault complaints remain unanswered. 



First: Rape crisis center signs hang in a housing unit at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. Last: Resources hang on the wall at the housing unit. Photos by Beth LaBerge, KQED
A KQED analysis of six years of Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA) data obtained from the corrections department showed that the rate of sexual misconduct complaints against staff at Central California Women’s Facility increased by about 1,800% from 2022 to 2023. The department did not answer questions about this data.
Prout’s experience illuminates a pervasive culture of sexual abuse at Central California Women’s Facility, helps explain why women suddenly started coming forward in 2023, and reveals what the officers charged with keeping people safe in custody did in response.
Ali’s story
In May 2022, Prout had been at the women’s prison for just a few days when correctional officer Gregory Rodriguez stopped her as she walked to a medical appointment. He asked her to pull down her N95 mask so he could verify her identity.
“He said, ‘You have beautiful lips and beautiful eyes,’” Prout told KQED.
Aliksandria Prout at her home on Aug. 19, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
Three days later, an officer gave Prout a paper pass, known as a ducat, allowing her to move through the prison. 
“They told me I had an attorney visit,” she said. An officer escorted her to the Board of Parole Hearings room, where such visits are usually held.
But there was no attorney visit. Instead, she saw Rodriguez. This is the first time she has spoken to the media about what happened in that room. 
Rodriguez came close and tried to kiss her. He lifted her shirt and then turned her around on a chair beneath a window. Prout remembers staring at the officer’s boot, propped against the left side of the green upholstered chair. 
“What really upset me was he didn’t use protection,” she said. 
When it was over, Prout said, Rodriguez warned her that if she told anyone, she could face disciplinary action, which could mean more time in prison. 
A pass issued for a fraudulent attorney visit on May 20, 2022, is among the evidence Aliksandria Prout saved following her sexual assault. Courtesy of Aliksandria Prout
A screenshot of an internal affairs investigation report obtained by KQED through a public records request from an investigation led by Special Agent Dustin Baker. Screenshot via the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
KQED heard similar stories from other women at the prison. Eight women said they feared disciplinary write-ups, repeated cell searches and other retaliation if they reported sexual assault by staff. In a statement, the corrections department said it is committed to protecting victims of sexual assault and that “sexual abuse, harassment and retaliation against incarcerated people is unacceptable.”
At the time, Prout stayed silent, but she made sure to keep track of the multiple times Rodriguez called her back to that room. When she was paroled after just a few months in prison, Prout began contacting attorneys. 
She found out that the corrections department’s Office of Internal Affairs was already investigating Rodriguez. They ultimately identified 22 potential victims, including Prout, and worked with the Madera County District Attorney’s Office to arrest the former officer in May of 2023. The case, in which Prout testified as a Jane Doe, attracted national attention. Rodriguez was convicted on 64 counts of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual battery. He was sentenced to 224 years in prison.
Aliksandria Prout holds documents related to her case at her home. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
In an email to KQED, a prison spokesperson wrote that Rodriguez’s sentence “reaffirms CDCR’s own internal investigation” and that the department “condemns any staff member — especially a peace officer who is entrusted to enforce the law — who violates their oath and public trust.”
The department also said that then-Warden Michael Pallares was transferred to Pleasant Valley State Prison, where he was made associate warden.
However, documents recently obtained by KQED reveal troubling new details about that investigation. The internal affairs report showed there was a six-month window in which investigators and CDCR leadership were notified of Rodriguez’s misconduct and failed to act. During that period, he assaulted at least six women, including Prout, numerous times. 
Before Prout even arrived in the Chowchilla prison, a woman had already told investigators that Rodriguez summoned her to the Board of Parole Hearings room for fake attorney visits and sexually assaulted her on three occasions. 
Still, Rodriguez remained at his job until Aug. 17, 2022, when he was finally reassigned to the mailroom. He retired shortly after that. The corrections department did not answer questions about why it took so long to stop Rodriguez’s abuse.
Rodriguez had been flagged before. All the way back in 2014, someone had reported potential relations between Rodriguez and a young woman identified in the trial transcripts as Nicole Doe. An investigation was done at the time, but the allegations against Rodriguez were dismissed. 
Nicole Doe was sent to solitary confinement for more than six months and then transferred to another prison.
“I was treated like I was the problem,” Nicole Doe said at trial. 
In 2019, a female co-worker reported Rodriguez for sexual harassment. Rodriguez tried to kiss her and get her to go into the staff restroom at work, this woman told investigators. 
“I’ll be quick, I’ll be quick,” she recalled Rodriguez saying, according to internal documents.
Rodriguez was reprimanded and told not to do it again, according to trial testimony. 
A sign hangs above a doorway to a housing unit at the Central California Women’s Facility on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
The internal affairs report appeared to show that no other officers were disciplined in connection with Rodriguez’s years of criminal abuse.
Prout said other officers must have known. They were often responsible for issuing ducats like the ones she received. The police of the prison, Investigative Services Unit officers, had an office right across the hall from the room where Rodriguez repeatedly called women in order to assault them. Prout, concerned she might be pregnant, had also gone to the prison clinic after that first assault.
“They told me that if I wanted a pregnancy or STD test,” Prout testified at trial, “I had to admit to engaging in risky behavior, and that if I did that, it would add more time onto my sentence.”
Ripple effects
Rodriguez’s 2023 arrest also drew the attention of state lawmakers, who convened a special hearing on sexual abuse inside California’s women’s prisons. 
While allegations of sexual abuse by officers have persisted for years, the Rodriguez case, along with the wide-ranging scandal of abuse at the federal prison in Dublin brought renewed urgency to the issue.
“It was a real pivotal moment,” said Amika Mota, executive director of the prison advocacy nonprofit Sister Warriors Freedom Coalition, who spoke at that hearing. “I feel like it’s kind of when Pandora’s Box opened.”
The Legislature allocated funds to create a sexual-abuse response and prevention working group. As part of that, Central California Women’s Facility began allowing incarcerated people to gather inside the prison gym for town halls organized by Sister Warriors and other advocacy groups.
A fitness facility at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
Advocates stood watch at the doors of the gym to ensure correctional officers did not enter.
“ In the 30 years that I had been there, never had the prison allowed such a large group of us to gather with guests and without staff present,” said Elizabeth Lozano, one of the incarcerated women who was there. 
For the first time, Lozano spoke about the terror and violation she felt when being groped by a correctional officer. “There’s things that happen where it’s out of your control,” she told KQED.
In October of 2023, the state agreed to pay Prout $1.2 million to settle a civil suit she’d filed. Hundreds of lawsuits have been filed against the corrections department since Rodriguez’s arrest, alleging sexual abuse by him and dozens of officers. The cases became so numerous they were consolidated into a single coordinated proceeding that is still moving through the Sacramento Superior Court.
As civil claims and Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA) complaints began to rise, five women, including Antoinette Yancey, who served on the prison’s inmate advisory council, said in interviews with KQED or in legal filings that they were warned that the complaints needed to stop. 



First: Rape crisis center and Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA) informational signs hang in a housing unit at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla. Last: Incarcerated women walk through a yard on June 30, 2026. Photos by Beth LaBerge, KQED
During a smaller search about a month before Operation Breakdown, Yancey said that Sgt. Isidro Arroyo confronted her, saying, “The PREA, the staff assaults, the complaints and all the 602s [prison grievances] all of that stuff needs to stop.
“If the complaints do not stop, then I’m going to lock you guys down, take all your privileges, and this is gonna continue until the complaints stop,” Yancey recalled Arroyo saying.
Yancey said she told him this was neither legal nor fair and refused to discourage women from filing sexual-abuse complaints. She also said she brought up this incident with Arroyo during a regular inmate advisory council meeting with leadership of the prison.
The corrections department declined to make Arroyo available for an interview and did not respond to questions about this incident. 
‘These bitches needed to know’
In the days leading up to Operation Breakdown, then-Warden Anissa De La Cruz was not at the prison, so Chief Deputy Warden Cynthia Rojas was in charge.
On Aug. 1, 2024, acting Capt. Carlos Mendoza and Associate Warden Stephanie Torres came to Rojas about problems with prisoners smoking and being “disruptive” in a housing area called D Yard, according to internal affairs interviews that were leaked on YouTube and later taken down. 
“We need to gain control of that f—— unit,” Rojas said, according to one of those leaked tapes.
Rojas and her staff planned a massive search-and-seizure operation to look for contraband and enforce prison property limits for the entire unit. Under state prison regulations, each incarcerated person’s state-issued and approved personal belongings must fit within 6 cubic feet of space — about the size of a mini-fridge.
Torres’ name was redacted in the investigation report, but KQED was able to identify her by comparing her statements to leaked internal affairs interviews and details about her role in the prison. She said the chief deputy warden gave her and Mendoza about a four-and-a-half-hour window to plan a search that would normally take days. 
Incarcerated women walk through a Receiving and Release yard at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. The R&R yard is used to process incarcerated people entering and leaving the facility. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
Torres and Mendoza later told internal affairs investigators that they “questioned the reasoning and urgency” for the search, according to the report. The two senior staff members said that Rojas told them, “these bitches need to know who’s in control,” and that De La Cruz had directed her to “do what I know how to do.” 
Mendoza sent an email to De La Cruz, Rojas, Torres and other prison leaders late that Thursday afternoon, laying out the basics, including breaking the prisoners down to 6 cubic feet, using K-9 and searching the building.
Operation Breakdown was set for the next day.
‘Fun, fun, fun baby’
On Aug. 2, Torres described a “skeleton crew of managerial staff” on site. Prison officials had to bring in officers who were still in training, according to the report. Two trainees said it was their first day working inside a prison. And despite initiating and planning Operation Breakdown, Rojas was also not at work that day. But when the acting captain of D Yard called her around midday, she answered. 
“Boss, we just went code three,” Mendoza said, according to Rojas’ leaked interview with internal affairs.
“What the f—? What do you mean we went code three?” Rojas replied.
The 159 incarcerated women on D Yard had been taken out of their cells and crowded into the dining hall first thing that morning. As the morning wore on, the scope of the search became apparent, according to a dozen women who were there that day. 
A cafeteria at the Central California Women’s Facility on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
They watched through the windows of the chow hall as their pillows, shoes, clothing, TVs and even some mattresses were taken or thrown away.
“People been here for 20 years,” said Wisdom Muhammad, who is out of prison now. “You throwing away they sentimental things that they have. You feel me? Like stuff that’s unreplaceable, and all that stuff is just hot trash.”
Around 12:20 p.m., one of the people being held in the dining hall had a seizure. An alarm sounded, and officers filed into the dining hall in a skirmish line carrying MK-46 pepper sprayers and chemical grenades, surveillance footage and internal records showed. Things quickly escalated.
After more than four hours in the sweltering Central Valley heat without food, water or medication, the people being held in the dining hall were frustrated, according to at least a dozen women who were there. They shouted at the officers. They banged on the tables and windows.
Yancey said she pointed to Arroyo and then to herself, trying to signal that she wanted to speak with him. He did not acknowledge her.
Mendoza handed Arroyo a chemical blast grenade and instructed him to “put ’em down with the gas,” according to internal disciplinary documents obtained by KQED.
Mendoza was recorded on body camera directing officers to “go gas” and placing chemical grenades in the hands of subordinates, according to disciplinary documents. He later told them he “took the initiative to be the response supervisor” at the dining hall.
The scrimmage line unleashed chemical blast grenades and pepper spray on the crowd of incarcerated people, sending them scrambling toward the back of the room, surveillance video reviewed by KQED showed.
According to a leaked internal affairs interview, correctional officer Jordan R. Chavira told another officer that he had entered the dining hall and “started dumping it, dude,” referring to chemical agents. 
One by one, the women’s hands were zip-tied behind their backs and eventually were walked outside to the yard, surveillance footage showed.
Yancey assumed the officers were going to start letting them go back into their housing unit. 
Instead, as the incarcerated people sat under the baking sun in 90-degree weather, the officers formed a half circle around them, according to surveillance footage.
One woman, hands zip-tied behind her back, got up and took four steps to sit by another woman. Just then, the officers started throwing grenades filled with tear gas or pepper spray at the entire group. At least 15 blast grenades were deployed, according to KQED’s analysis of the disciplinary documents. 
As the assault died down, multiple women were carried off the field on stretchers. According to leaked internal affairs tapes, Chavira was captured on his body-worn camera approaching another officer and saying, “Fun, fun, fun, baby.”
Chavira told investigators he made those remarks in “the heat of the moment” and that he was being sarcastic.
Surveillance footage obtained by KQED through a public records request shows an incarcerated woman secured to a stretcher outside the dining hall at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on Aug. 2, 2024. Screenshot via the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
Mendoza and Chavira were charged with inexcusable neglect of duty, dishonesty, willful disobedience and excessive force; both were fired. Arroyo received a 10% salary reduction for seven pay periods and has returned to work at the prison.
KQED was unable to reach Mendoza. Multiple attempts to reach Chavira were unsuccessful.
“To me, if you can openly spray people as if they’re rats or roaches, like they’re not human, you completely disregard their humanity,” said Lozano, who was there on Aug. 2. “You’re sadistic. You’re an abuser.” 
Two investigations, different questions
Thirteen women, including Catrina Cameron and Antionette Yancey, filed a suit against the state for their injuries during the Aug. 2 incident, alleging the incident was tied to reports of sexual assault. The corrections department admitted no fault, but paid the group $1.9 million to settle the case. A separate class action lawsuit is still pending.
The corrections department’s internal investigation focused on the conduct of individual employees during the operation: who gave orders, who followed them and whether the force they used complied with department policy.
But newly disclosed documents obtained by KQED reveal that the operation was plagued by staffing shortages, lack of planning and oversight failures. Vital questions about why this operation was rushed out were never answered. 
“I still don’t understand that,” Torres told internal affairs. “I wish to understand it, and in some ways, I don’t wish to understand it. It doesn’t make sense.”
Officers escort an incarcerated woman wearing a spit hood through a yard at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
Corrections department Administrator Angela Kent is retired now, but at the time she served as the associate director of Female Offender Programs and Services. In her 27 years in law enforcement, she had never seen anything like the use of force on Aug. 2, she told KQED. 
“I absolutely felt that every officer, supervisor and manager involved should be fired,” Kent said. At the time, she urged the department to release the body-worn camera footage along with a statement, “immediately, in line with the industry standard.” As of publication, the corrections department still has not released the body-worn camera footage.
Chief Deputy Warden Rojas, who’d approved the operation but wasn’t there to oversee it, was not disciplined, according to documents obtained by KQED. In a leaked interview, she was questioned about the statement that Torres and Mendoza told investigators about. 
“Did you make the statement, ‘These bitches need to be reminded who’s in charge,’ or words to that effect?” the investigator asked.
“Not that I recall,” she said.
Rojas was later promoted and is now acting warden at the second-largest men’s prison in the state, the Correctional Training Facility in Soledad, which currently holds about 4,000 people in custody, according to corrections department’s website. The department declined to make Rojas available for an interview.
In the documents obtained by KQED and the leaked internal affairs tapes, the department did not determine why the operation was launched or whether it was connected to the growing number of sexual-abuse complaints.
“There is no doubt in my mind that if you start to empower women that are incarcerated and you start to give credibility to their voice that there’s gonna be tremendous resistance,” Kent said. 
A month after the Aug. 2 incident, the U.S. Department of Justice launched a broad civil rights investigation into sexual abuse and retaliation at California’s women’s prisons. 
Federal investigators examined the incident within the context of rising reports of sexual misconduct, allegations that staff punished women for speaking up and what the department described as longstanding failures to protect them. The department released its findings last month.
“Women were not being protected,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexandra Young told KQED. “It was the cycle that’s continuing to happen.”
In response, the corrections department said it takes every allegation seriously and remains committed to accountability and safety. The agency pointed to federal Prison Rape Elimination Act audits that found both women’s prisons met all 45 standards evaluated.
Those audits measure whether a facility has policies and practices designed to comply with the law; they do not determine whether abuse occurred in every reported case.
A mural covers the side of a fitness facility at the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla on June 30, 2026. Photo by Beth LaBerge, KQED
KQED’s analysis of Prison Rape Elimination Act complaint data obtained from the corrections department showed that in 2025, the year following the Aug. 2 incident, the rate of complaints being filed against staff at Central California Women’s Facility fell by about 75%. The department did not answer questions about this data. There are likely many reasons for this sudden decline, but multiple people at the prison said they no longer felt safe to file complaints.
One incarcerated woman, who was a victim of Rodriguez’s and spoke to KQED on the condition of anonymity because she is afraid for her safety, said if she had to do it over again, she would not report Rodriguez. 
KQED’s analysis of Prison Rape Elimination Act complaints found another trend: As complaints rose in 2023 and 2024, the department appeared unable to keep up. As of the most recent data, more than 2,000 complaints across California’s state prisons had not been adjudicated. The corrections department did not answer questions about this data. 
For many of the women who remain incarcerated at Central California Women’s Facility, Operation Breakdown has left lasting scars. Cameron said she has not set foot in the dining hall since Aug. 2 and that she still has not regained sight in one of her eyes. 
Yancey said she still sees officers who were involved in the operation regularly. “They work in this building. They’re still antagonistic towards us.”
When asked whether the operation had succeeded in frightening women into silence, Cameron said it may have deterred many, but not everyone.
“Hopefully, the more of us who start to speak, the more will follow,” she said. “What happens in the dark always comes to light.”
Anna Sussman contributed reporting to this story. 
Jeremy Sanchez Rue, Associate Professor of Practice for UC Berkeley Journalism School, was the data editor for this series. A.I. tools were used to assist with the data analysis for this story.

name: Nevada Current
title: An unaffordable economy’s ‘culminating venue’: Eviction court
text:
Jonathan Norman, policy director for the Nevada Coalition of Legal Service Providers, and housing organizers call for reforms to the summary eviction process.  (Photo: Michael Lyle/Nevada Current)No place illustrates the affordability crisis quite like an eviction court, say advocates seeking reform of Nevada’s notoriously fast and landlord-friendly eviction laws.
“The eviction courts are the culminating venue of our state’s housing crisis and affordability crisis,” said Ben Iness, the coalition coordinator with the Nevada Housing Justice Alliance, said at a press conference last week attended by attorneys, elected officials, and other tenant advocacy organizations.
The Nevada Housing Justice Alliance has conducted eviction court-watching sessions over the past several years to monitor the process. The press conference Wednesday followed observation of eviction cases that morning.
Tens of thousands of evictions each year in Nevada reflect the increasingly unaffordable cost of living combined with a state that “lacks protections against rent hikes and rent gouging,” Iness said.
Last week’s press conference was a rare appearance for the eviction issue on the campaign trail this year. Advocates say it shouldn’t be.
“I would like to see what the agenda is for the working class and the poor,” said Jonathan Norman, the advocacy, outreach and policy director for the Nevada Coalition of Legal Service Providers.
Reforming the state’s lightning-fast eviction system is the baseline. 
There have been several failed efforts over the last few years to change Nevada’s quick summary eviction process, which in addition to being hasty, requires tenants rather than landlords to initiate a court proceeding — or be evicted summarily. 
“The idea that a tenant files the first pleading with a court is just contrary to every other civil process in the United States, not just evictions,” Norman said. 
Legislation to convert the process was initially sought in 2021, when Democrats controlled the governor’s office as well as both houses of the Legislature. But Democrats thwarted the opportunity for reform by turning the legislation into a mere study bill. 
State lawmakers were able to pass legislation that would have reformed the eviction system in the 2023 and 2025 Legislative sessions. 
Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo vetoed both bills along with a slew of other eviction reforms and tenant protections. 
Lombardo’s veto message on the summary eviction bill in 2023 said the legislation would “impose additional and unnecessary delays” and costs “make our summary eviction process more time-consuming” on property owners.
His office wouldn’t answer questions on whether he would re-evaluate his stance on summary evictions or tenant protections. 
But the governor’s office via email did point to legislation Lombardo signed in 2025 allocating $21 million in eviction diversion rental assistance to county governments as well as a bill he signed enabling modest transparency around rental prices in leases.
Lombardo had vetoed a nearly identical rental transparency bill in 2023.
In an email to Nevada Current Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is currently running against Lombardo, said he “would support efforts to bring Nevada’s summary eviction process in line with the rest of the nation and put the burden of eviction on the landlord instead of the renter.”
Norman said he expects Democratic Assemblymember Elaine Marzola, who is presumed to be the Speaker of the Assembly, to carry another summary eviction reform bill in the 2027 Legislative Session.
‘Money never sleeps’
There were 78,000 total eviction filings in Nevada in fiscal year 2025, according to a report from the Nevada Supreme Court. Roughly 54,000 of them were filed at the Las Vegas Justice Court.
The number of eviction filings skyrocketed in fiscal 2024 when the state had nearly 85,000 eviction filings. The growth in filings followed the expiration of eviction era protections and rental assistance funding. 
State lawmakers had passed a bill in 2021 that paused eviction proceedings while rental assistance applications were being processed. That legislation expired in 2023.
Legislation seeking to implement a scaled back version of that protection was vetoed by Lombardo the same year.
While the number of evictions in 2025 dropped from the 2024 spike, they are still wreaking havoc on people’s lives, organizers warned on Wednesday. 
“How many thousands of people have to be evicted for this to be considered a crisis,” Norman asked. “If there are 40,000 facing eviction this year, that’s enough people to fit in the A’s Stadium. That’s more people that fit in T-Mobile.” 
Democratic Assemblymember Erica Mosca and Democratic U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford joined Wednesday morning.
Iness suggested every Nevada elected official making decisions regarding housing policy and laws should witness eviction hearings. 
Seconding the sentiment, Norman said observing evictions is the only way to truly understand “the carnage and the speed.”
That was the case of a mother of three children – aged 9, 13, and 14 – who was behind $3,287 in rent from August. Her proceeding, which was conducted by hearing master Daniel Westmeyer, lasted roughly two minutes. 
A representative for the landlord, who appeared remotely, told Westmeyer that the failed rent payments resulted in financial distress for the landlord.
“Is there any reason why the court shouldn’t grant your landlord’s request for an eviction order,” Westmeyer asked the tenant.
She said she was starting to rebuild her life after experiencing homelessness. Then her daughter got sick, she missed work, and fell behind on rent. 
“I’m just starting to save money to be able to pay back,” she pleaded with Westmeyer. “I just need a little bit more time.”
The summary eviction was granted, but the judge stayed the eviction for 10 days, giving the tenant a little more time. 
Norman said many people who haven’t observed an eviction would assume if a tenant fails to pay rent it’s a moral failing, rather than acknowledging “they live in a society that has priced them out and pays wages that don’t allow them to live.”
“It’s easy just to say if you’re facing an eviction you did something wrong,” Norman said. “When you see it, you start to think in a more nuanced way.”
Lawyers at the Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada filed a lawsuit last month arguing it is unconstitutional for a hearing master – not an elected judge – to make a ruling in summary eviction cases. 
“At the end of the day, justice shouldn’t depend on what ZIP code you’re in,” Norman said. “Every other justice court in the state of Nevada uses an elected justice of the peace to hear eviction cases,” he said, adding that it’s only at Las Vegas Justice Court where evictions are overseen by “unelected hearing officers.”
While he believes the courts are the best place to challenge the role of hearing masters in granting evictions, Norman is still advocating for tenant protections at the legislative level.
Ford’s campaign said he would support legislation that makes price-fixing on essential goods such as rent illegal and limiting rent increases for seniors.
Ford put forward a price-fixing bill in 2025 but it was vetoed. 
Lawmakers also passed legislation in 2023 and 2025 seeking to cap rent increases for seniors – first a 10% cap followed by a 5% limit. Both were vetoed by Lombardo.  
State lawmakers announced a plan to reintroduce a 10% rent cap for seniors in 2027 Legislation.  
Norman said there are also plans to bring back other failed bills seeking to reform the state’s habitability laws and enable automatic record sealing for evictions after a certain time.
“Right now, it can be on your record for up to seven years,” Norman said. “How do you live in our society with that?”
Both bills passed during the 2025 Legislative Session but were killed by Lombardo.
“We can’t expect to win in one or two sessions,” Norman said of enacting tenant protections. “Money never sleeps. The money interests are going to engage in every session all the time. We have to bring that same level of energy.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan spends billions chasing jobs. There’s a better way
text:
Michigan Economic Development Corporation in Lansing. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceRegardless of who wins the Michigan governor’s race next month, the state’s approach to economic development is likely to undergo sweeping change. 
Republican candidate John James says he will completely overhaul the troubled Michigan Economic Development Corp., the state’s quasi-public development agency, and initially focus it on retaining existing businesses. 
Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson says she’ll fire MEDC President and CEO Quentin Messer Jr.  and replace him with a “seasoned administrator,” possibly from the business community. 
Benson says she might also create a separate agency focusing on the needs of small and micro businesses. 
The MEDC has been mired in controversy over the alleged theft and misuse of a $20 million grant by former board member Fay Beydon that led to state Attorney General Dana Nessel charging her with 16 felonies. 
Declining tax revenues from Native American casinos recently led the MEDC to lay off about 15% of its staff. 
And there have long been complaints that MEDC’s business attraction spending isn’t delivering promised jobs.  
Tim Bartik, senior economist at the W.E. Upjohn Center for Employment Research in Kalamazoo and an expert on business attraction incentives, agrees with the gubernatorial candidates that Michigan must radically change its economic development course if it is to become a more prosperous state.

How States Can Design Better Economic Development Incentives 
His exhaustive,186-page new study on business attraction incentives found that the $95 billion a year states spend on these giveaways doesn’t move the needle much on boosting per capita income, a basic measure of a state’s economic wellbeing. Those incentives include cash payments, tax credits and other forms of cash-based incentives. 
Michigan, for example, has fallen into the bottom-tier of states in per capita income over the past 30 years despite spending tens of billions of dollars trying to get new businesses to invest here and create jobs. 
Bartik’s report, which received financial support from the Rockefeller Foundation, recommends the state slash expenditures on cash-based incentives and redirect the money to three areas: customized services for businesses, targeted incentives to distressed areas and housing construction. 
His economic modeling, which included examination of cash-incentive programs in Michigan, California, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, found that every $1 spent on business attraction incentives delivered $1.75 in overall economic benefit and 17 cents in new tax revenues. 
Adopting Bartik’s recommendations could balloon a long-term economic benefit of between $10 and $28 for every dollar spent and between $1 and $3 in new tax revenues, his study found. 
“We must do a lot more than subsidize a few mega projects” that often don’t pay off, Bartik told me. 
Businesses value customized services, job training and infrastructure assistance, Bartik said, but less than 18 cents of every incentive dollar go to providing those services. 
“That ratio is backwards,” he said in the report. “A small, but specific, incentive, tailored to a business’s unique needs, can provide an outsized benefit.” 
Targeting incentives to those communities most in need, places like Flint, Benton Harbor and northern Michigan can put more jobless people living in those areas to work, making the whole state more attractive to business investment. 
Giving incentives to businesses to locate in wealthier communities where unemployment is low means many of the new jobs will go to people living outside those markets.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That means the employment status of those living inside the labor market doesn’t change much, “and neither does the state’s fiscal return,” Bartik said. 
And if the state wants more jobs, it needs more housing. States should pair business incentives with zoning and permitting reform and focus on funding housing projects in areas already committed to housing policy reform, Bartik’s study says. 
A well-designed economic development strategy incorporating Bartik’s recommendations can raise residents’ per capita income by 5% and boost state and local tax revenues by 4% over 20 years, the study claims. 
Traditional economic development policies boost per capita incomes by less than half a percent and cut state and local tax revenues by 3 percent, the study found. 
Bartik said he’s under no illusion that policymakers will completely shift away from offering businesses cash, tax abatements and other goodies to invest in their states. 
Governors score political points by announcing they’ve landed big projects promising thousands of new jobs. 
And getting businesses to invest in distressed areas with a low quality of life and unskilled labor will likely be difficult. 
But Bartik believes there could be a big payoff for Michigan if it would allocate more of its economic development dollars and business assistance to places that need them. 
“Let’s take it one step at a time and see how things work out,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How a housing co-op in CT became the victim of fraud
text:
Success Village, a housing cooperative located on the border of Bridgeport and Stratford, has been in the news repeatedly in recent years. 
The hundreds of co-op members living in the community lost their heat in the middle of winter in 2024, and shortly after, officials in Bridgeport and Stratford filed a case in court, asking a judge to appoint an attorney to take over the housing complex’s finances. 
Now, more than two years later, federal prosecutors have found that the co-op and its members were victims of fraud and conspiracy. 
In the past month, three people have pleaded guilty to taking part in a kickback scheme that resulted in millions of dollars being stolen from the co-op and its members. And federal court records suggest that more criminal charges could soon be filed. 
Here’s what to know about what’s happened so far in the investigation and how much money was involved. 
Who was charged and why? 
Federal prosecutors have charged three people thus far with participating in the alleged conspiracy to siphon off money from the co-op’s bank accounts. That includes the complex’s former general manager, Charles Pitcher, and Richard Messina and Carmine Gentile, two contractors whose companies were paid to perform work at the co-op property. 
All three men have entered plea deals in federal court acknowledging their involvement in a yearslong scheme, which prosecutors say drained the co-op’s bank accounts and left the organization unable to pay for needed repairs.
Prosecutors allege that between June 2022 and September 2024, Messina and Gentile submitted fraudulent or inflated invoices for work at Success Village and later diverted roughly 20% of those payments back to Pitcher and “person-2,” another unnamed co-conspirator who is identified in court records as the co-op’s president. 
How did the alleged scheme work?
Success Village Apartments Inc. is a residential cooperative with 96 buildings and 924 units. Residents pay monthly common charges intended to cover expenses, including heat and hot water.
Pitcher was appointed general manager in May 2022 and was paid $250,000 per year in that position, according to court documents. At the same time, Pitcher also owned and controlled two companies, Real Estate Company of New England LLC and Pitcher Enterprises LLC.
According to prosecutors, Messina and Gentile used the other businesses owned by Pitcher to redirect part of the money they received through contracts with Success Village. 
To conceal the payments, Messina and Gentile allegedly submitted invoices for work that was never performed or charged artificially inflated prices. The documents also describe unreasonable markups and charges for goods and services that were not provided.
The contractors then allegedly made payments to Pitcher and “person- 2” through cash, electronic transfers and checks. Some of the checks that were written to Pitcher’s company included descriptions such as consulting, construction management and project management. 
How much money was involved?
Altogether, prosecutors alleged that the two contractors netted more than $2.7 million from the co-op and allegedly kicked back more than half a million dollars of that money to Pitcher and “person-2,” the co-op’s former president. While the criminal complaints don’t identify “person- 2,” the description in the court records only fits one person: Tyreke Bird, the former president of Success Village. 
Prosecutors also alleged that Pitcher received at least $232,479 in purported “consulting fees” from Success Village for services he did not perform.
As part of their plea agreements, Pitcher agreed to pay at least $2.5 million in restitution, while Gentile and Messina each agreed to pay at least $1.5 million. The agreements also include forfeiture of payments to the government.
These amounts are part of the plea agreements and should not be treated as a final accounting of all losses to Success Village.
The investigation is being conducted by the FBI, the Internal Revenue Service’s Criminal Investigation division and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.
Will anyone else be charged?  
There have been some clues that suggest Bird could become a target of the federal criminal investigation. 
In May, federal agents executed a search warrant at Bird’s residence. The FBI declined to comment on the investigation at the time, and the public reporting did not establish what evidence agents were seeking.
Bird has not been formally charged or accused of committing any crimes at this point. But federal prosecutors made it clear in press releases that the criminal investigation tied to Success Village is not over.

name: California
title: CARE Court can profoundly change lives, and California’s justice system, if given the chance
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Charles F. Adams
Charles F. Adams, an associate justice of the California Court of Appeal, Sixth Appellate District, served for eight years on the Santa Clara County Superior Court.


When most people think of courtrooms, they picture places where disputes are settled, laws are enforced and justice is delivered. When I was a superior court judge, I presided over many types of cases — criminal, civil, family, and more. 
But after serving in the court’s probate division and managing the CARE Court calendar, I have come to believe a courtroom can be much more than a venue for adversarial proceedings. It can be a catalyst for profound change in a person’s life.
For too long, Californians with serious mental illness have faced barriers to achieving long-term stability. Family members who for years have sought to assist their loved ones often became disappointed by a lack of options. 
CARE Court is changing that — and changing the role of California’s judges in ways I never expected. The CARE Act calls for a new kind of judicial leadership, grounded in trust, empathy and relationship-building. 
Unlike most court proceedings, everyone in a CARE Court courtroom — judges, participants, family members, providers and county agencies — works toward the same objective: helping someone find a path to stability and hope, where perhaps that path previously was lost or difficult to find.
My experience as a CARE Court judge showed me how powerful a courtroom can be when it has the right tools and the right people. I have seen real change in people. 
CARE Court offers participants — who are usually unmedicated and impaired by an illness they did not choose or understand — an opportunity to become engaged in their own recovery and to make remarkable progress toward self-sufficiency and independence. 
This often means resolving criminal cases, transitioning from incarceration to treatment and finding housing. Perhaps most importantly, it means finding hope out of what were hopeless circumstances. 
In the process, participants rediscover themselves and make sustainable connections with service providers and family members.
Witnessing transformations like this is deeply moving. It reminded me that when someone is met with persistent, coordinated support, the courtroom can be a place of healing and possibility. 
CARE Court is a new tool in California’s behavioral health continuum, helping thousands access treatment, medication, housing and supportive services. It strengthens coordination across systems that too often have operated independently. 
Many CARE participants have cycled through hospitals, behavioral health programs, emergency departments, jails and other public systems without achieving lasting stability. Now these fragmented systems are brought together through a structured, person-centered process.
Participants who once associated courtrooms with judgment and consequences begin to see them as places of resolution and care — proof the justice system can work for them, not against them. 
My role was to ensure CARE plans meet participants’ unique needs and that agencies remain active, responsive and accountable.
Long-term recovery cannot be forced. Counties invest in relentless outreach and relationship-building to earn trust and engage participants. Family members, providers and partners now have meaningful avenues to advocate for individuals in need of structured support.
CARE Court is a work in progress, and it is not the right fit for everyone. Different pathways exist for different people, and the courtroom can be a place where those pathways begin. 
Challenges remain, as they do with any new approach to a complex issue, but that is not a reason to abandon a worthy cause.  
As California implements the CARE Act, members of the judiciary should advance its promise. By approaching these cases with compassion, accountability and collaboration, judges can ensure more Californians have meaningful pathways to care and long-term recovery.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut General Election 2026 Voter Guide
text:
Connecticut General Election 2026 Voter Guide
How to register, vote and know who’s running.

IN THIS GUIDE:    KEY DATES    FAQ CANDIDATES    GENERAL ASSEMBLY    COVERAGE
Connecticut voters go to the polls on Nov. 3 to cast ballots for governor and the other statewide constitutional offices, the General Assembly and U.S. House. Many will have questions about where to vote, how to vote and for whom to vote when Election Day rolls around. The Connecticut Mirror, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization, is here to help with this voter guide — a look at the key dates to know ahead of Nov. 3, a one-stop-shop for election-related information.

November 3: Election Day! Polls open 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Same-Day Registration is available to all residents eligible to vote.  
KEY DATES FOR THE 2026 GENERAL ELECTION


Oct. 2
First day absentee ballots are issued.


Oct. 16
Last day to register online, by mail, at DMV or Registrar of Voters.


Oct. 19
First day of early voting.


Nov. 1
Last day of early voting.


Nov. 2
Last day to request absentee ballots. Last day to return them in person.



FAQ
Any questions we haven’t answered here? Send us an email and we’ll try to answer them for you.
Am I eligible to vote?
Connecticut residents are eligible to vote if they are a U.S. citizen and turn 18 on or before Nov. 3, 2026. If a person has been convicted of a felony, they must also have completed confinement.
Voters do not need to be affiliated with a party. 

How do I register to vote?
Those eligible to vote can visit the state’s online voter registration portal to check their registration or sign up. The deadline to register online, by mail, in person at your town’s Registrar of Voters or at the DMV was Oct. 16.
Or, voters can use Same-Day registration.  

What if I miss the deadline? What is Same-Day Registration?
Same-Day Registration is available to everyone eligible to vote who is not already registered by Oct. 16. or has moved to a different town since last registering.
Voters can register during early voting by visiting their town’s early voting location to cast their ballot. On Election Day itself, voters can also register and cast their ballot at their town’s Same-Day Registration location. To find out where to go, contact your town’s Registrar of Voters. 

Tell me about early voting. Who can vote? When does it begin? Where do I go?
Anyone eligible to vote can vote during the early voting period. Early voting begins on Oct. 19 and runs through Nov. 1. Early voting locations will be posted on a rolling basis on the state’s Early Voting Locations page.

What time are the polls open on primary election day?
Polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. If you are in line at 8 p.m., you will still be able to vote.

Do I need to bring an ID to vote? 
No, but you can. Before you receive a ballot at the polls, you will be asked to provide a government-issued ID, a different ID with your name and photo, or a document such as a utility bill or checkbook that has your name and address. You may use your current driver’s license at the polls even if it is marked “not for federal identification.”
If you can not provide any of these, you will be asked to sign an affidavit instead.

Can I vote by using an absentee or mail-in ballot? 
Anyone eligible to vote can request an absentee ballot. Voters can submit requests through the Online Absentee Ballot Request Portal, or mail or hand-deliver a printed ballot to their town clerk. Voters do not need to specify a reason for requesting an absentee ballot. The deadline to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.
Absentee ballots will be issued and mailed to voters starting Oct. 2. The ballot must be returned to the voter’s town clerk by using the United States Postal Service, in person at the town clerk’s office or in a drop box in their town. The deadline to return an absentee ballot in person is Nov. 2. Voters must return their absentee ballot in the same envelope that housed the ballot and ensure that they print and sign their name on the envelope. 
All ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3 to be counted. Voters can check if their ballot has been received on the state’s Voter Registration Lookup and should contact their town clerk if their ballot has not been received.
For additional questions about absentee voting, contact the state Legislation and Election Administration at LEAD@ct.gov or (860) 509-6100.

I’m a college student. How do I vote? 
Students eligible to vote can do so in one of two ways: vote by absentee ballot in your home town or register to vote in your college town.

GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATES
Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat seeking a third term that could make him Connecticut’s longest-serving governor since statehood, is challenged by Republican state Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich. Both appear on two ballot lines, with Lamont cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party and Fazio by the Independent Party.
Lamont, 72, of Greenwich, is running as a fiscal centrist who has presided over eight years of budget surpluses and a social progressive who has signed legislation creating a paid family and medical leave program and produced one of the nation’s highest minimum wages.
Lamont is waging his fifth statewide campaign and his fourth for governor. He challenged U.S. Sen. Joseph I. Lieberman over the war in Iraq in 2006, winning a Democratic primary but losing the general when Lieberman continued as an independent. Lamont lost a gubernatorial primary to Dannel P. Malloy in 2010 then won an open race in 2018 and a second term in 2022.
Fazio, 36, is the youngest major-party gubernatorial nominee since John G. Rowland won the GOP nomination as a 33-year-old in 1990. Fazio was elected in a special election to the 36th Senate District of Greenwich, New Canaan and Stamford in 2021, getting national notice as the first Republican to flip a Democratic seat after Joe Biden won the White House. Fazio was reelected in 2022 and 2024, difficult cycles for Republicans in Connecticut. To win in the presidential year, Fazio had to outperform Donald Trump by 17 percentage points.
He is the ranking Republican senator on the legislature’s Finance, Revenue, & Bonding Committee and the Energy & Technology Committee, perches Fazio has used to advocate for lower taxes and electric rates. In 2025, he contributed to a bipartisan energy bill that lowered rates by authorizing state borrowing to cover the costs of some public benefit programs that had been borne by rate payers.

OTHER STATEWIDE CONSTITUTIONAL CANDIDATES
All six of Connecticut’s statewide constitutional officers are seeking reelection, but they occupy only five lines on the ballot. Voters cast a single vote for governor and lieutenant governor and vote separately for secretary of the state, treasurer, comptroller and attorney general.
Lieutenant Governor
Susan Bysiewicz, a Democrat from Middletown, is a former state representative and secretary of the state whose career to seemed to end in a misstep: running in 2010 for attorney general, only to be deemed ineligible by the state Supreme Court over a lack of a courtroom experience. She lost a U.S. Senate primary to Chris Murphy in 2012. Bysiewicz rebounded in 2018, ending a gubernatorial campaign to become Ned Lamont’s running mate.
Her opponent, Republican Matthew Corey of Manchester, is a Navy veteran and businessman and six-time electoral loser. With the exception of 2022, Corey has been on the ballot every two years since 2012, losing races for the U.S. House against Congressman John B. Larson in 2012, 2014 and 2016, two for U.S. Senate against Murphy in 2018 and 2024 and one for the state Senate in 2020. 
Secretary of the State
Stephanie Thomas, a Democrat from Norwalk and former non-profit adviser and small business owner, was elected in 2022 after a single term as a state representative from the 143rd House District. She won the convention endorsement in a five-way race and then a two-way primary. Thomas is the first Black person to hold the office, which oversees elections and business filings. The Democrat is on three ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party and Independent Party.
Her opponent, Republican Peter Lumaj of Fairfield, is a real estate investor and former immigration legal adviser born in Albania who has run unsuccessfully for statewide office four times, twice for U.S. Senate, once for governor and secretary of the state. His only time on November ballot came as the GOP nominee for secretary of the state in 2014.
Treasurer
Erick Russell, a Democrat from New Haven, made history in 2022 as the first Black openly gay person elected to any statewide office in the United States. He is a lawyer who specialized in issues related to municipal financing and pension issues prior to his election. Connecticut is the only state where the treasurer is the sole fiduciary with control over pension investments. In fiscal year 2026, the state reported returns of 15.1% on its investments, better than three quarters of other states. He is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party.
His opponent, Republican Fred Wilms of Norwalk, is a senior banking executive and former two-term state representative who lost his seat in 2018 and failed to win it back in 2020. He previously served as a city councilman and chair of Norwalk’s Board of Estimate and Taxation. Wilms is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Independent Party.
Comptroller
Sean Scanlon, a Democrat from Guilford, was elected comptroller in 2022 after four terms as a state representative from the 98th House District. He won the Democratic nomination for comptroller without opposition. By working on healthcare reform and other issues, Scanlon has raised the profile of an office responsible for monitoring state finances, payroll and retirement benefits. Scanlon is on the three ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party and Independent Party.
His Republican opponent is Jennifer Tooker of Westport, a retired reinsurance executive who was that community’s first selectwoman from 2021 to 2025 and previously served on its Board of Education and Board of Finance. Tooker is a former global marketing and communications manager at Gen Re.
Attorney General
William Tong, a Democrat from Stamford, is a litigator who was elected attorney general in 2018 after six terms as a state representative. He has filed or joined more than 40 lawsuits challenging federal policies since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including the president’s efforts to end birthright citizenship. Tong is the son of immigrants, the first Asian American elected to state office and the first Chinese American elected as an attorney general in the U.S. Tong is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party.
His opponent, Republican John Bolton, is a lawyer with a solo practice in his hometown of Westport, where he formerly served on the Planning and Zoning Commission. His campaign bio highlights his representation of 40 teachers who objected to required vaccinations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

CT CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT CANDIDATES


Connecticut’s congressional map is little changed since revisions after the 2000 Census, which resulted in the state losing one of its six U.S. House seats. The oddly shaped 5th District was drawn in a bipartisan deal to accommodate two incumbents, a Danbury Democrat and New Britain Republican, running for the same seat after the downsizing. Republicans won three of the five seats in 2002 and 2004 but lost two of them in the 2006 midterm and the last one in 2008. Democrats since have won every congressional race.
The respected Cook Political Report rates all five seats as safely Democratic this year. Based on voting in the past two presidential elections, 4th Congressional District of Fairfield County is deemed the most Democratic, closely followed by the 1st of Greater Hartford.




1st Congressional District
The district is centered on Hartford but reaches awkwardly around a hammer-shaped portion of the 5th towards Torrington in the north and Bristol in the south. It is the only open seat, a consequence of Luke Bronin defeating Congressman John B. Larson in a Democratic primary, the first primary challenge to an incumbent congressman in Connecticut.
Bronin is the former mayor of Hartford, elected in 2015 to the first of two four-year terms. He served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve and was deployed to Afghanistan in 2010. Before becoming mayor, he worked in the Obama administration and was general counsel to Gov. Dannel P. Malloy. 
Amy Chai, the Republican nominee, is a physician who lives in North Haven, outside the 1st District. In a questionnaire, she described government or political experience as a liability: “Representatives are supposed to represent people, not the government. When people do nothing but rise through the ranks from dog catcher to organizer to mayor, they are entering a bubble that actually excludes them from the reality of the people that they serve.” She registered as a Libertarian candidate for the seat in 2021 and as a Republican in 2025. She was unopposed for the GOP nomination.
Mary L. Sanders of the Green Party also is on the ballot.
2nd Congressional District
The 2nd District encompasses Eastern Connecticut and has been represented by Democratic U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney of Vernon since he unseated Republican Rob Simmons in 2006.  Courtney serves on the House Armed Services Committee and is the ranking Democrat on the Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces, an important assignment for a congressman who represents a district with a submarine base and the Electric Boat shipyard.
His challenger, Republican George Austin of Suffield, is a first-time candidate. Austin is a contractor and the son of Mexican immigrants. He says his campaign is about “standing up for families, protecting the unborn, defending the Second Amendment, and pushing back against oppressive taxes that make life unaffordable.” He was unopposed for the GOP nomination. Austin is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Independent Party.
3rd Congressional District
Democrat Rosa L. DeLauro of New Haven, who began her career as adviser to a New Haven mayor and then to a U.S. senator, is the senior member of the congressional delegation, representing a district centered on the city, winning an open seat in 1990. She is the ranking Democrat on Appropriations Committee and stands to return as chair if Democrats retake control of the House, as expected.
Her Republican challenger, Christopher J. Lancia of Milford, is a former Coast Guardsman and police officer at the Naval Submarine Base New London who now is  a manager at TNI, a provider of fiber networks. He says he is running “to give the people of Connecticut a voice — and to help President Donald Trump finish what he started: putting America First.” He won the nomination on a roll call vote at the convention.
Thomas Egan of Ansonia also is on the ballot as a nominee of the Independent Party. He is a lawyer who has run unsuccessfully for mayor and state representative.
4th Congressional District
The compact 4th District of lower Fairfield County includes the state’s two largest cities, Bridgeport and Stamford, and some of the nation’s richest suburbs, including Greenwich and Darien. Once a Republican stronghold represented by a succession of maverick GOP moderates, it has become the state’s strongest Democratic district, as judged by the Cook Political Report.
Democrat Jim Himes unseated Republican Chris Shays in 2008, ending the GOP’s 40-year-old hold on the seat and leaving Connecticut without a Republican in Congress. Himes is the ranking Democrat on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and on the House Financial Services Committee. As a key member of the Intelligence Committee, Himes is part of the “Gang of Eight,” members of Congress who are briefed on classified intelligence matters.
His Republican challenger, Michael Goldstein of Greenwich is running for Congress for the third time. He is a physician and a lawyer. He says on his campaign site, “In surgery, you can’t fake it. You diagnose the problem. You fix it. You take responsibility for the outcome.” He lost a primary in 2022 but won the GOP nomination in 2024 and this year.
Benjamin Wesley of Norwalk also is seeking office as the nominee the Independent Party for the second time in two years. He is a mechanical engineer.
5th Congressional District
Democrat Jahana Hayes of Wolcott, a national teacher of the year in 2016 in the Waterbury public schools, won the open congressional seat in 2018, running with the encouragement of U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy. She is the first Black woman elected to Congress from Connecticut and the first of two from New England. She had a close call in 2022, winning with only 50.39% of the vote. The district sprawls from Danbury on the New York border to Litchfield County on the Massachusetts line. Hayes is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party.
Her Republican challenger, Chris Shea of Cheshire, is a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy Seal. In his acceptance speech at the GOP convention, Shea talked about his military service, his Christian faith and an experiment with “imaginative prayer” that helped inspire him to run. He said, “I actually had an experience with Jesus Christ himself sitting next to me in a chair.” He won the nomination in a primary.
