name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s GOP Legislature left out key info on property taxes state question: the financial impact
text:
The downtown Oklahoma City skyline is pictured. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)If any emoji best represents the property tax state question Oklahoma lawmakers have placed before voters, it would be the grimace.
For those who need a translation, we use that face to express tension. In this case, it’s because our Republican-controlled Legislature, in all its wisdom, tacked on this disclaimer to their proposed constitutional amendment: “If passed, this measure would have a fiscal impact on the state, but the exact impact is unknown.”
(Insert eye-roll emoji.)
Lawmakers, in their zest to convince us they are cutting taxes as inflation rages on, decided that taking the time to suss out how eliminating a chunk of revenue via State Question 847 will affect senior citizens, public schools, CareerTechs, counties and some municipalities wasn’t as important as having a talking point on the campaign trail.
Because that’s where our property taxes go. Reminder: property taxes typically fund the functions of municipal and county governments. State government doesn’t get a dime from these taxes.  
Maybe that’s why they weren’t sure about the fiscal impact?
I don’t know whether this oversight was sheer laziness, a blatant disregard for voter intelligence or if legislators’ effort was a rush job that overlooked the finer details – including how complicated it probably is to calculate the impact.
But in any case, this is an unfair scenario for Oklahoma voters who have to make a decision on Nov. 3 about whether to change the structure of our property tax system. Voters deserve to have all the facts ahead of time, and lawmakers should not be permitted to omit them.
Since they did, though, I’ll fill in the gaps.
An Oklahoma Tax Commission analysis estimates local jurisdictions would lose about $45.78 million in revenue in the first year if voters approve this question. Over the next 10 years, that lost revenue could top $450 million.
That’s a whopping sum of money for a ballot measure that lists its fiscal impact as being “unknown.”
State Question 847 is one of the most convoluted and complicated state questions on the ballot this year, and that’s saying a lot given some of the other issues that lawmakers have placed before voters. (Who can forget that manufacturing tax credit that voters soundly rejected in August?)
Right now, the fair cash value of a home can’t increase by more than 3% a year for homesteads — better known as the homes we own and live in — and for most agricultural land. Commercial property values are capped at no more than a 5% annual increase.
Lawmakers have decided it’s time to lower that cap to a seemingly random 1.75% a year for homesteads and agricultural properties and to 4% for commercial properties. 
They also have decided to muck around with the income cap that senior citizens must meet to qualify for a valuation freeze. The amount of the increase would be calculated on a tiered system ranging from 0% to 1.75% based on a formula that is way too complicated.
Supporters argue that the measure would create the “lowest cap on growth” for homesteads in the U.S. and save cash-strapped Oklahomans money.
Critics, though, point out that besides the previously mentioned budget cuts for public schools, CareerTechs, county governments and some municipalities, it would also make it harder for those entities to borrow money for future needs.
They say this is not really property tax relief. The value of properties will continue to go up, and so will Oklahoman’s taxes. This merely just slows the rate of growth a bit.
But they also warn that because it will reduce revenue, many Oklahomans should expect to see their tax rates go up to pay the existing bills.
That’s because bond debt – that borrowed money I just mentioned – will not miraculously vanish. All bonds are set based on the revenue expected to be generated from existing property taxes. When someone screws around with the formula, it messes up those expected revenue streams.
The only feasible way right now to make up that lost revenue is to adjust the millage rates — better known as the tax rate assessed on real estate. That means everyone will see an increase in their taxes, but I suspect senior citizens living on fixed incomes could feel the pinch more.
Lower-income senior citizens’ home valuations have long been frozen to provide them an idea of what their tax bills will look like each year. Most probably have not budgeted to abruptly pay higher taxes.
How much millage rates will increase depends on how reliant an entity is on the revenue source and whether local jurisdictions have enough resources to adjust. 
Rural residents in particular will likely be harder hit because those entities have less resources to draw on. 
So instead of cutting expenses at the state government level that they control, lawmakers plan to force those cuts on local governments. How is that fair?
Oklahomans’ wallets definitely need relief from soaring property insurance and utility rates as well as high gas, diesel and grocery prices, but this plan doesn’t do anything to address that.
Maybe rather than monkeying around with our property tax formulas, lawmakers should first look at why their policies have resulted in us having the highest homeowners insurance rates in the country — more than double the national average. Reducing those rates would certainly provide welcome relief without harming our local revenue streams.
But it seems like state leaders prefer to live in a fairy tale where instead of apples or peaches, money grows on trees for the benefit of our cities and towns. And instead of doing the hard work of confronting insurance lobbyists and fixing broken state spending, it’s easier to ask voters to pass a plan with an unknown budgetary impact.
Here’s the reality: No business wants to come to a community that doesn’t have good schools, good roads and bridges and solid public services. Those services are primarily paid for by property taxes. 
To put this plan back in emoji speak: big red question mark.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV native teaching next generation about products made in state, bringing supply chain back home
text:
Ed Ryan, founder of Reshore WV, speaks to lawmakers at the West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Sept. 14, 2026, about his college course on import substitution and manufacturing. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)A West Virginia native with expertise in trade operations is taking his passion to state college campuses, hoping to connect the upcoming workforce with skills to bring supply chains back home.
There’s a goal, too, of keeping more students in state to curb the population decline, particularly among young adults. 
The initiative has earned the support of many in the Statehouse, including House Speaker Roger Hanshaw. 
There’s nothing but an upside to it, he said.
House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“We need to do everything that we possibly can to help students, young people, aspiring entrepreneurs and potential founders of companies here in West Virginia see what the scope of the possible is,” said Hanshaw, R-Clay. 
Ed Ryan, who grew up in Nitro, is the brainchild behind the economic and education initiative, Reshore WV, and his company, Reshore Technologies.
He has a background in U.S. customs and international logistics and worked outside of the state before returning home.   
Ryan said that initially, he wasn’t “a great student.” Professors at Marshall University introduced him to international relations, Chinese world history and economics.
“I learned to love learning, and fell in love with international trade and economics and world affairs and how trade is this unifying force that can end wars. It has such a power on people,” Ryan said. “I thought, ‘I’m not gonna let any of that go to waste’ and try and do as much as I can here to help companies and communities.”
Products made in West Virginia are on display at the West Virginia Manufacturers Association headquarters in Charleston, West Virginia, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)
West Virginia has a wealth of products made in the state, including well-known exports like coal, engines and car parts made at the Buffalo Toyota plant, glass, HVAC filters, aircraft parts, wood products and more. 
Aluminum plates from the Artemis II spacecraft were made by Constellium in Jackson County, and recently earned the honor of “Coolest Thing Made in West Virginia” by the West Virginia Manufacturers Association.
West Virginia companies don’t always know of the resources made in their backyard, opting to import needed products from overseas. Ryan’s work focuses on identifying products West Virginia companies currently purchase overseas and connecting those buyers with manufacturers making those products in state or that have the capability to.
Next, he took that passion to the classroom, first teaching a class at the University of Charleston in spring of last year to MBA students. The course focused on import substitution and manufacturing.
“I think with this curriculum, we’re going to build just so many knowledgeable students who think about maybe not a career in manufacturing, but understanding how manufacturing can then connect to what they do,” Ryan said. “Whether they’re a finance major, a supply chain major, an education major, a marketing major, it just opens up manufacturing … We have thousands of students here in West Virginia that I think this education could benefit.”
Students prepared an import substitution proposal connecting a West Virginia manufacturer product to a real import demand of an in-state company. Students compared costs of importing the product versus purchasing it in-state.
Kelton Boblits
Kelton Boblits, a Fayetteville, West Virginia native and MBA student at U.C., wants a future career in West Virginia after interning at the state Department of Economic Development. Ryan’s course opened Boblit’s eyes to in-state manufacturing possibilities. 
“I had studied supply chains and international commerce in different classes, but this was a seven-week deep dive, and so to get that understanding was valuable,” he said. “Not only that, to find out that the manufacturing base that we have here in West Virginia, I think that that’s something that’s very meaningful … I think if people were to take a look at what is here, they would be very impressed, and I think it would break a lot of stereotypes.”
Ryan has now taken the course to West Virginia University and will soon expand it statewide through a partnership with the West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission.
Ryan also shared his idea with state lawmakers at the Capitol, explaining how this education is valuable to students statewide.
“Our customer base does not have to be limited to just the 1.8 million West Virginians,” Hanshaw said. “We have to think at least regionally, if not nationally and globally. What Ed and his team are doing in helping to expose young people to those kinds of opportunities is really awesome.”
Del. Lori Dittman, R-Braxton. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Lori Dittman, R-Braxton, is chair of the House of Delegates’ Higher Education Subcommittee. Dittman, who works at a middle school, praised Ryan for returning to West Virginia and investing in the state. 
“I just think anytime you have students that can get their experience outside of just the text, or just outside of this theoretical learning, and they are actually doing it, that is an incredible experience for them,” she said. “It will help them build a life and a career and be able to stay in West Virginia, and then it’s going to help our West Virginia manufacturers either expand or they’re going to see new ones created because of the demand for the products that are needed.”
Boblits said hundreds of students across West Virginia participating in the course and drafting usable proposals is likely to produce a real impact on the state’s economy.
“They will hit a home run and change their communities for the better, and that’s the impact that I see that’s having on the state long term … It’s going to create opportunity,” he said. 
Reshoring tax credit bill expected in 2027 
Tariff policies from the Trump administration and escalation in supply chain vulnerability played a role in Ryan creating his company in West Virginia, along with his desire to raise his family in the Mountain State. 
Businesses operating in West Virginia imported approximately $4.8 billion in foreign manufactured goods during the calendar year 2024.
Ryan estimated that 15% of West Virginia imports could be substituted for in-state products. 
In the 2027 legislative session, Ryan will be advocating for the “West Virginia Reshore Manufacturing Act,” which creates a tax credit to incentivize the replacement of imported goods with goods manufactured in West Virginia.
“We want to create an economic incentive for a West Virginia company to make that change when it makes sense,” Ryan explained.



Quotation







I think if people were to take a look at what is here, they would be very impressed, and I think it would break a lot of stereotypes.


– Kelton Boblits


The bill was introduced by two Republican senators in the last legislative session, but didn’t make it to the governor’s desk. 
Lawmakers have been working on it since then, according to Hanshaw. Economic development will again be a focus in the House of Delegates next year. 
“If we have the capacity to make it here, and you bring that demand back here, we’ll provide you with a credit of some sort against one or more of the taxes that you pay just for the just for the the benefit of having brought that manufacturing demand back here to West Virginia,” Hanshaw said. 
The speaker said he’s an “enthusiastic supporter” of Ryan’s work with Reshore WV.
“Hats off to Ed and his team for launching it, and I’m really proud of the companies that are taking advantage of it too,” Hanshaw said. “I love everything about this. It’s the kind of thing we got to really be leaning into.”
Kentucky recently launched its own reshoring initiative, drawing on the experiences of Ryan and Reshore WV. Manufacturing leaders in Kentucky credited Ryan for his expertise and work in West Virginia as they launched their initiative on Oct. 14.

name: WyoFile
title: A problem with our ‘them’ and ‘us’ mentality
text:
All good people agree, And all good people say, All nice people, like Us, are We And everyone else is They.” — Rudyard Kipling

Opinion

To date, more than 230 people have been killed by our armed forces in the Caribbean. They were presumed to be drug smugglers, but there has been no process whatsoever to assess their guilt. How do we account for this outrage? Even the criminals slaughtered for entertainment in Rome’s Colosseum had been adjudicated. 
Human use of mood-altering substances and psychotropic drugs goes back thousands of years. After the Civil War, unregulated opiates flooded the country to treat the war wounded, and addiction became epidemic. Our government attempted to rein in this problem by passing the Harrison Narcotic Act in 1914. This federal law sharply reduced the legal supply of narcotics. This had the effect of making most attempts to obtain narcotics illegal, and created the problem of “those” people and “those” drugs. 
The furor over “those” people and “those” drugs reached a peak in 2023 when over 70,000 people in the U.S. died from fentanyl overdose. This led to the chapter of the “narcoterrorist” in our War on Drugs. However, this number is dwarfed by 178,000 deaths from beverage alcohol and 480,000 deaths from tobacco in the United States that year. 
In Wyoming that year, 50 people died from fentanyl overdose; 178 people died as a direct consequence of drinking alcohol; and indirect deaths from alcohol totaled 48 from alcohol-related motor vehicle accidents and 57 from suicide. One-third of people who died by suicide test positive for alcohol. The day after heavy drinking there is a seven-fold increase in suicidal behavior. 
A fundamental truth is that legality does not protect from lethality. The separation of mood-altering substances into legal and illegal has created a “them and us” construct. There are many problems with this construct, and the War on Drugs is a big one. So far this war has cost us $1 trillion with 60% going to incarceration, 20% to interdiction and 20% to treatment. 
A commonality between legal and illegal drugs is that human beings have feelings — physical and emotional. Some people use chemicals to alter these feelings. Not infrequently, they have problems with the chemicals they use. 
What you see in life often depends on where you sit. I possessed the unique perspective of a board-certified dermatologist who was also trained and certified in addiction medicine. I saw that there was little difference between people who had been using the wrong substance to treat an itch and made their problems worse, and those who treated their physical or emotional issues with mood-altering substances and made their problems much much worse. 
The solutions for the former were much easier. I became a voluntary combatant in this drug war in 1989, and was involved with community, tribal and professional treatment programs. I witnessed over and over the astounding similarities in the nature of the problems of addiction. Whether the drug is illegal or legal, upper, downer, all-arounder, whether the person is rich or poor, educated or not, white, black, Native American, it’s all the same. What differs most is the availability of support and treatment. The 80% of drug war dollars currently being spent on interdiction and incarceration are largely wasted. 
Interdiction addresses the supply side of this war. We hear that X tons of drugs and XX dollars are seized. Although this gives the impression that our government is doing something, there is always an adequate supply. Even C.J. Box thinks they can make fentanyl in the Bighorn Mountains. 
Incarceration manifests the thinking that the problem is “those” people and “those” drugs. Some 43% of federal inmates and 20% of state inmates are there on drug charges, with minority populations disproportionately represented in prison populations — “those people.” 
Addiction to illegal or legal drugs is a giant health problem. Right now, the greatest health and social problems in the state of Wyoming are legal drugs: alcohol and tobacco. The slaughter in the Caribbean won’t fix these, but just turn our heads elsewhere. Politicians and the media feed on each other, focusing us on “those” people and “those” drugs. 
Humanity has an endemic addiction problem; we need humane solutions. A strong step in the right direction is to protect and expand Medicaid and protect and expand funding for mental health and substance abuse treatment. We need to keep an honest assessment of the drug and alcohol culture in Wyoming. The “Them and Us” delusion is not functional. Honesty is essential. Addiction is an endemic affliction of humanity. We should look for humane solutions.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers advance draft bill to close legal loopholes for giving alcohol to minors
text:
LANDER—As things currently stand in the state of Wyoming, adults can at times provide alcohol to minors without consequence. A minor may end up in legal trouble for underage drinking — but the adult who supplied the minor with alcohol, if the two are related or the alcohol was consumed for religious or medical purposes, often walks away without a charge. 
Meanwhile, the youth faces a misdemeanor citation.
Fremont County Youth Services representatives have previously reported that some of the kids in the county report drinking at a very young age. It’s not just a countywide problem, Wyoming Highway Patrol Colonel KC Ramsey told the Legislature’s Select Committee on Tribal Relations that there’s a cultural drinking problem in Wyoming.
After hearing about the issue earlier this year, the committee directed the Legislative Service Office to draft legislation to tighten up, if not close, some of those legal loopholes. The bill draft LSO brought back doesn’t remove the exceptions, but it does place a limit on them.

Sen. Cale Case, R-Lander, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“I think untangling the list of exceptions … that would be very divisive,” said Sen. Cale Case, R-Lander, committee co-chairman. “I do think this is an intelligent and clever way to approach this, and I appreciate it.”
The limit suggested by the bill is a minor’s blood-alcohol content of 0.02%. Below that, the exemptions for parents, legal guardians, religious uses, and medical uses would still apply. Above that, the adult or adults providing alcohol to the minor could face a misdemeanor citation of their own.
“The way the law reads … is a prohibition against any person selling, furnishing or causing to be sold alcohol, and then there are some exceptions to that rule. So in this case, if a minor is above a 0.02%, then it is the person who furnished that alcohol who no longer gets the exception,” LSO’s Ian Shaw explained.
According to Alcohol.org’s blood alcohol calculator, for a 130-pound boy approximately half a glass of wine, or about 2.5 ounces, would likely result in a blood-alcohol content of 0.02%; for a full glass of wine or one 12-ounce beer, the blood alcohol content is estimated to likely fall to 0.02% within about an hour. Most NyQuil is about 10% alcohol by volume, a little less than a standard glass of wine; the standard dose of NyQuil is just over one ounce.
Half a glass of wine is significantly more than is typically used in religious ceremonies. 
Since the bill draft proposes that its new lack of exceptions kick in only if a minor’s blood-alcohol content is over 0.02%, it is unlikely that consumption of a small amount of wine or other alcohol for religious or medical purposes would place a minor over that legal limit.
And, Ramsey assured, the Highway Patrol would not stake out churches or places of worship to try to catch people. As it does now, he said, Highway Patrol would look for signs of intoxication, which would prompt testing as part of a traffic stop. That is to say, the way the bill is currently written it would not alter investigation procedures, only what the consequences of that investigation might be.
“It’s another way for us to ensure that the highways are safe,” he said.
Ramsey originally phrased the Highway Patrol’s position on the bill draft as neutral. After some probing from committee members, including Case and Rep. Pepper Ottman, R-Riverton, he said that the agency regards it as a positive step – but implied that unless it shifts the cultural needle, it may not be the silver bullet that solves underage drinking in Wyoming.
The committee had invited a number of law enforcement agencies to attend and comment on the bill draft, including the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office, the Riverton Police Department, and the Lander Police Department as well as the Highway Patrol. Ramsey was the only law enforcement officer who provided comment on the bill.
Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, expressed some reservations around the bill draft, noting that he feels it’s important to ensure that exceptions are carved out for things like religious use. Nonetheless, he voted in favor of the committee sponsoring the bill.

Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Case said the bill strikes the right balance between allowing some exceptions and holding adults responsible when they provide minors with opportunities for excessive consumption. 
“It’s the best of all worlds in this,” he observed. “I mean you’re really not exactly going after the kids, you’re going after the person that did it in an irresponsible manner. If you have a house party … people really get intoxicated, then you’re no longer covered by the exception.”
Case moved for the committee to move the bill forward; Ottman seconded him. Despite his reservations, Salazar voted in favor of advancing the bill, as did committee Co-chairman Rep. Ivan Posey, D-Fort Washakie.
“I’m going to vote yes today, but I’m eager to hear the conversations come January,” Salazar said. “I do need the exceptions in this bill. I need them.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The race for Idaho’s top election official, the secretary of state, is a rematch
text:
"I Voted" stickers are available for voters to pick up after casting their ballot in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Lowell Elementary School in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In the race for Idaho’s top election official, two familiar names are headed to the ballot.
Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane, who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. 
Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation.
McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. 
The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election.
The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands.
The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690.
In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic secretary of state decades earlier. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Who is Shawn Keenan, the Democratic candidate for secretary of state?

Idaho Democratic candidate for secretary of state, Shawn Keenan. (Photo courtesy of Shawn Keenan)
Keenan, 49, has not worked in election administration but said he has been involved in politics from a young age and has worked on several Democratic campaigns in North Idaho. His parents moved to Idaho with him when he was 1 years old, he said. 
Keenan runs a nonprofit, called the North Idaho Kindness Project, that focuses on fostering acts of kindness — like love letters around Valentine’s Day and kindness tokens, which his group encourages people to hand out to people they see doing random acts of kindness. 
He said his initial bid for secretary of state four years ago came out of fear of growing distrust in election results — including among some of the then-Republican candidates for secretary of state. Years later, Keenan is still campaigning on that.
“When people start crafting these stories about elections not being secure or safe in Idaho, I wanted to be a voice for the truth: that they are indeed safe and secure and have been and always will be,” he said. 
Keenan praised McGrane, the incumbent, for his “due diligence.” And he said he and McGrane are on the same page on at least one policy priority: Establishing a state-issued voter guide, like other Western states have, that mails information on candidates and more directly to voters. 
As a Democrat in a reliably red state, he said he acknowledged that his odds of getting elected are tough — unless he puts in years of doorknocking. He said his campaign has largely focused on digital outreach to voters, compared to travel across the state.
With less than three weeks until the election, Keenan’s campaign has not raised any money, according to the state’s campaign finance database.
 Who is Phil McGrane, the Republican incumbent seeking a second term as secretary of state?

Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane (center) enters the House of Representative chambers to listen to Gov. Brad Little give his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
McGrane, 45, first started in election administration in Ada County in 2005 — years after a contentious recount of the George W. Bush v. Al Gore presidential election in Florida that brought concerns over partially hole punched “hanging chads.”
In the two decades since, he went to law school and worked in several areas of election administration — like operating voting equipment, training poll workers and entering voter registration cards into the state’s system. 
In 2018, McGrane was elected Ada County clerk. In 2022, he was elected as secretary of state, widely defeating Keenan with more than 72% of the vote.
McGrane said he’s proud of his work to improve access to election information — pointing to his office revamping a website that hosts resources for voters and candidates. The office also has updated the state’s campaign finance data dashboard and the state’s lobbying transparency website. 
“I’ve been working in elections my entire career. I think … the work I’ve done at Ada County, both in the elections team, but also as the elected clerk, and then here as Secretary of State, I think I’ve had a long history of making sure that voting is easy, that voting is secure, and that Idahoans can have confidence in their elections,” he said.
If re-elected, McGrane said his priorities would be to overhaul the state’s business registration system, update the state’s dated campaign finance laws, re-establish the presidential primary election and ask the Legislature for approval to create a voter guide with information on candidates
McGrane’s campaign has raised more than $440,000, and has about $171,000 in cash on hand, according to the state campaign finance database, which his office manages.
 How would the candidates approach running elections?

Keenan said the key difference between him and his opponent is the type of pressure they’d face from their political parties. 
“He does a good job of trying to hold the line when it comes to just the important work of delivering fair and safe elections,” Keenan said. “I don’t think I would have any — the same kind of party pressure to deal with that Phil (McGrane) has to.”
But Keenan reiterated an assurance he offered ahead of the 2022 general election: That the state would be OK if his opponent won.
“At the end of the day, I don’t feel like the office of secretary of state is being threatened by a candidate that is not capable of performing well for the citizens of Idaho,” Keenan said. “So I have full confidence, win or lose, that myself or Phil (McGrane) will be able to fulfill the necessary duties for the citizens of Idaho.”
But McGrane said he doesn’t see it as him working against partisan pressure. 
Even when he disagreed with the Idaho Republican Party — over regulations around closed primary elections — or the Trump administration when it comes to sensitive voter roll data, he said he’s maintained good relationships with them.
The same week that the U.S. Justice Department sued McGrane over refusing to turn over sensitive information in voter records to the Trump administration, McGrane said he was in the White House celebrating St. Patrick’s Day with President Donald Trump. 
And he said he talks frequently to Dorothy Moon, the chairwoman of the Idaho Republican Party, who McGrane narrowly defeated in the 2022 GOP primary election for secretary of state.
“It shows that it is not so simple as what people read in the news and the way things are framed in the news,” McGrane said. “That the best form of government — whether that’s state and federal government or it’s just here within the state, state officers, us with the Legislature — is government that works together and coordinates together. And that’s part of my leadership and something, if I have the good fortune of being reelected here and serving Idaho some more, I’m going to continue to work to pull people together — pull people together in the state of Idaho, and pull people together across the country.”

title: Friends of Minidoka symposium connects Japanese-American incarceration to immigration debate
text:
The Minidoka National Historic Site in southern Idaho offers 1.6 miles of gravel walking trails. Visitors may explore the site and the exteriors of historic structures at their own pace. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service)
The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization.
The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said.
In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration)
The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II.
The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section.
On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law.
Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience.
The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues.
“History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.”
All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. For event details and registration information, go to minidoka.org/2026-civil-liberties.
 


2026 Civil Liberties Symposium events

“Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman” — Film and legal discussion

The event begins at 5:30 p.m. Thursday at the University of Idaho College of Law’s Boise campus, Room 221, at 501 W. Front St. in Boise. This event is free, but registration is required.

“Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do” — Distinguished lecture featuring Kari Hong, director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law

The reception for this event begins at 5:30 p.m., and the lecture begins at 6:30 p.m. at LED at Dixon, 3300 W. Chinden Blvd. in Garden City. This event is free, but registration is required.

“Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do — Online lecture featuring Kari Hong, followed by a moderated question-and-answer session.

The lecture will begin at 6:30 p.m. Dec. 8 online via Zoom. This event is free, but registration is required.



Friends of Minidoka worked with the University of Idaho College of Law, the ACLU of Idaho, Idaho State Bar Diversity Section, Boise State University, Boise State Public Radio, Boise Valley Japanese American Citizens League, and LED, to organize the symposium.

title: In Alabama congressional races, incumbents hold fundraising advantages
text:
The U.S. Capitol on May 7, 2025. Alabama congressional incumbents outraised their opponents over the summertime, according to Federal Election Commission reports filed last week. (Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom) 
 How to register to vote
Oct. 19 is the last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 election. If you haven’t registered to vote, you can do so here. And if you’re not sure of your registration status, you can double-check it here.


Incumbents in Alabama’s congressional races outraised challengers over the summer, according to federal campaign finance reports filed last week. 
Officeholders in six of Alabama’s seven U.S. House districts, whether Democratic or Republican, took in more money than challengers. In the state’s two open congressional races, Republicans outraised their Democratic opponents. 
Republicans mostly led the field, but U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, seeking re-election in the redrawn 2nd Congressional District in southeast Alabama, raised $1 million in campaign donations, the most of any candidate running for Congress, through the end of September. The 2nd Congressional District is considered the most competitive in the state; state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the Republican nominee, is considered the frontrunner. 
The reports cover fundraising from July 1 to Sept. 30. 
U.S. Senate
Republican U.S. Senate nominee Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, significantly outraised his Democratic opponent Everett Wess. Moore raised $685,600 to Wess’ $36,300.
Messages seeking comment were left with Moore and Wess Friday.
Moore also spent $466,800 to Wess’ $43,400. Wess did not receive money from political action commitees (PACs) while Moore received $151,000 from PACs. Moore leads in cash on hand with $218,900 to Wess’ $11,300.
Alabama 1st Congressional District
In the state’s only open seat, former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl, R-Mobile, the Republican nominee, significantly outpaced Democratic nominee Clyde Jones in fundraising. Carl raised $277,500 while Jones raised $97,500.
Jones said in a statement Saturday morning he wasn’t surprised by the fundraising gap.
“Money is important in a campaign, but our team consists of over 100 volunteers who are knocking doors and registering voters,” Jones said. “We’ve attended hundreds of community events and not seen Jerry Carl at one of them since he won the primary. I may not have out-raised him, but I’m confident we can out-work him.”
A message seeking comment was left with Carl on Friday.
Both candidates took donations from PACs. Carl received $216,500 and Clyde received $7,000. The gap in spending was slightly smaller, with Carl spending $299,000 to Jones’ $105,200. Carl also maintains the edge in cash on hand with $345,200 while Jones has $20,400.
Alabama 2nd Congressional District
In Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, Congressman Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, was the only candidate to raise $1 million, according to campaign finance reports. Figures’ opponent, Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, raised $316,800. 
Messages seeking comment were left with Figures and Marques Friday.
Figures also outspent Marques through the end of September, spending $338,100 to Marques’ $176,900. 
Both candidates received PAC donations. Figures received $268,500 from PACs while Marques received $106,000 from PACs. 
Figures has $1.4 million on hand, while Marques has $327,600.
Alabama 3rd Congressional District
Republican nominee and incumbent U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks, raised $318,300 and spent $245,000 over the summer. According to campaign finance reports, he received $97,000.00 from PACs. He has $2.7 million left on hand.
A message seeking comment was left with Rogers Friday.
Campaign finance reports for the third quarter for Lee McInnis, the Democratic nominee for the 3rd Congressional District, were not present on the FEC website as of Saturday morning. 
Alabama 4th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, raised $207,600 between July 1 and September 30. Amanda Pusczek, Democratic candidate for Alabama’s 4th Congressional District, did not submit campaign finance reports.
A message seeking comment was left with Aderholt Friday.
Aderholt received $35,700 from PACs and spent $179,200. He has $778,000 left on hand.
Third-quarter campaign finance reports for Amanda Pusczek, the Democratic nominee for the district, were not present on the FEC website as of Saturday morning. 
Alabama 5th Congressional District
Fundraising between the candidates in Alabama’s 5th Congressional District was closer than other races. Republican nominee and incumbent U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, raised $236,500. Democratic nominee Andrew Sneed raised $214,400. Strong retains the edge for cash on hand with $1.2 million to Sneed’s $220,900.
“As I’ve said from the very start, the people are tired of the politics of division and career politicians whose priorities are out of touch with the people of north Alabama,” Sneed said in a statement Friday. “They want a representative that will actually fight to get these costs down, will hear every voice, and has a plan to fix what’s deeply broken in Washington; and I do.”
A message seeking comment was left with Strong Friday.
Sneed outraised Strong in the July quarterly report with $162,000 to Strong’s $125,600. 
Strong spent  $449,072.53 to Sneed’s $163,100. Both candidates received PAC money with Strong getting $90,100 from PACs while Sneed received $4,500.
Alabama 6th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, raised $84,600 in the third quarter. Palmer received $53,000 from PACs and spent $241,300. He has $104,000 on hand.
A message seeking comment was left with Palmer Friday.
Third-quarter campaign finance reports for Maurice Mercer, the Democratic nominee for the seat, were not present on the FEC website as of Saturday morning. 
Alabama 7th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, raised $245,200 to Republican nominee Ammie Akin’s $112,200. Sewell also spent $504,000 to Akin’s $176,000.
Messages seeking comment were left with Akin and Sewell Friday.
Both candidates received PAC donations. Sewell received $206,000 from PACs and Akin received $5,000. Sewell maintains the lead with cash on hand with $3.5 million to Akin’s $52,000.
The election is on Nov. 3.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A tale of two farmers: Ager, Balkcom compete for NC-11 seat
text:
Jamie Ager hosts a concert rally at Asheville Yards on Oct. 13, 2026. Ager is the Democrat running for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District against state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)ASHEVILLE — About 3,000 people gathered at Asheville Yards last week for a concert rally with Jamie Ager, who’s running against GOP state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to represent North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. The contest could play a pivotal role in the control of the U.S. House. 
Wearing trucker hats, shirts, or buttons in the campaign’s signature kelly green saying “Ager for U.S. Congress,” attendees encouraged each other to knock on doors and work the polls. Others waved signs claiming, “I’m a mountain Democrat and proud of it.”
The Cook Political Report rates the seat as “toss up,” and Democrats see Ager as their best chance to win in the district, which has been reliably red for most of the past 35 years.
“Jamie’s a great guy,” Patricia Derrough said. “He is honest, hardworking, and has good values. Just what Western North Carolina needs by working for all the people, not just the wealthy.”
Derrough says she’s known the Ager family her entire life. Her ancestors moved to Western North Carolina in the 1700s; Ager’s came later. His great-grandparents moved to Fairview in 1916, where the family has been ever since.
“They used to have square dances regularly. Everybody in town went,” Derrough said.
Ager’s grandfather, Jamie Clarke, represented NC-11 in Congress. His older brother Eric serves in the North Carolina House, in the same seat their father John once held.
Jamie Ager at Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
As a fourth-generation farmer, Ager and his wife sell grassfed beef, pastured pork, and fresh eggs to grocery stores, restaurants, and individual customers. They also host events at Hickory Nut Gap Farm — along with barn dances, there’s stargazing, meditation, and hayrides.
“My boys drive the tractors,” Ager said with a smile, referring to his sons Cyrus, Nolin, and Levi. “It’s a good job for them, to give a little hayride and give those people a little perspective on growing up here on the farm.”
But Ager’s rival also has deep roots in Western North Carolinian, where her family has lived for eight generations. Balkcom grew up on her family’s apple farm in Henderson County and is well known in her community, where she’s a mortgage loan officer. 
The campaign trail
NC-11 is geographically vast, spanning 16 counties and about 6,200 square miles. The mountain terrain means many routes contain switchbacks or tunnels, requiring slower speeds. 
President Donald Trump has handily won the district three times. It has elected only one Democrat, Heath Shuler, to Congress since 1991. Many thought this year would be no different. 
In August, incumbent GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his bid for reelection, after reports of inappropriate conduct. The U.S. House voted to censure him in September. 
The North Carolina Republican Party selected Balkcom as his replacement, leaving her with roughly three months to campaign. 
Ager, on the other hand, launched his campaign about 18 months ago. Since then, he’s traveled extensively across Western North Carolina, speaking with voters about their priorities. He’s held events from Cherokee to Burnsville to Hendersonville. 
“I’ve met so many wonderful people that are too busy to worry about politics because they’re too worried about how to make payroll on Friday afternoon,” Ager said. “One thing I hear over and over again is that people in this country are sick and tired of partisan politics, and we need leaders in this country who are going to work hard for the people in our community.”
Goals for Washington
Ager said his top priority in Congress would be securing funding for Hurricane Helene relief. 
At Hickory Nut Gap, the storm knocked out the power and toppled trees. The farm typically earns more than half of its revenue during harvest season, and with local restaurants closed, it temporarily lost some of its biggest customers. 
“We were devastated, and all we knew to do was get chainsaws out, start sawing our way out, checking on neighbors, doing everything everybody did here in Western North Carolina at that time,” Ager said. “We came together to put ourselves back together and do everything we can, and I think we need some of that kind of spirit up in Washington, D.C.”
Like Ager, Balkcom has been active in Helene relief and recovery efforts. She helped secure funds at the state level and wants to do the same in Congress. 
A member of the state legislature since 2023, her primary accomplishment so far has been sponsoring a bill banning transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports.
“I want to work hard for the people that live here, and that’s what we were voted in to do. I want to do that in Washington, just like I have in Raleigh,” Balkcom told Spectrum News. “I’ve been serving in the General Assembly, helping farmers for the last four years.”
She’s gotten funding from national Republican House leaders like Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, and Majority Whip Tom Emmer, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. Balkcom also received donations from most of the GOP members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation and some of her state House colleagues. 
But she’s still building name recognition across the sprawling district. Her campaign website reveals almost nothing about her policy priorities. 
And when Spectrum News asked Balkcom if she thought Edwards should resign from Congress, she took a lengthy pause before saying she wasn’t sure. She gave similar answers to other questions.
Balkcom declined to be interviewed for this story.
“It’s certainly not ideal,” political scientist David McLennan said. “She’s had some interviews that have shown a bit of inexperience. When you have a real short window of opportunity, it makes it difficult to campaign.”
Republican Reps. Jennifer Balkcom, front, and Erin Paré speak against allowing transgender athletes to compete against female students in sporting events at the NC General Assembly in April 2023. Balkcom is now running for NC’s 11th Congressional District. (Screenshot from livestream of committee hearing)
Homegrown candidates
Before Edwards, Republicans Madison Cawthorn and Mark Meadows held the seat. Each left office under a cloud. It’s left Western North Carolinians hungry for change, Democrats say. 
Ager tells voters he wants to lower the cost of living and remove corruption from politics by overturning Citizens United and banning members of Congress from trading stocks. 
“The whole place looks like a big old coin-operated machine. If you don’t have any money to put into that machine, you don’t get any favors out of that machine,” he said. “We need somebody who’s going to fight for the people here in Western North Carolina.”
Last month, both candidates debuted ads aiming to appeal to the same mountain community. 
Ager’s ad, titled “Barn Dance,” featured live music as he rallied his supporters at one of his events. 
“Nobody cares what politics you are when you’re in the middle of a square dance,” Ager told NC Newsline. 
Image from Balkcom’s “Mom” ad, one of two unique spots currently running in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. (Photo: YouTube)
Balkcom aired an ad, titled “Mom,” where she talks about her mother teaching her to be strong.
“When someone broke into her house, she shot them,” Balkcom said in the video.
The national political scene
Republicans are facing a tricky political climate amid rising costs across the board and declining approval ratings for President Donald Trump. 
Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has consistently polled ahead of former Republican National Committee and NCGOP chair Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat. National fundraising groups have temporarily paused spending on campaign ads for the race, focusing on other states instead. 
NC Republicans Tillis, Moore prepare for GOP losses in upcoming election

Republicans currently hold a 218-212 majority in the U.S. House, with four vacancies and one independent caucusing with the GOP. 
The GOP has deployed Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other Republicans to North Carolina to stump for candidates like Whatley and Balkcom. Vance is scheduled to hold a rally in Hendersonville Monday. 
Even so, despite the district’s newly competitive nature, not all residents have been following politics closely. Some don’t get to know the candidates until they head to the polls.  
“It’s really dependent in part on the Democratic wave, and whether it’ll be a ripple or a tsunami, it’s impossible to tell right now,” McLennan said. “The next few weeks and overall turnout are going to be very important.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado activists call for transparency measures as they attempt to track ICE flights out of Denver
text:
Dana Miller, Kristen Aldretti and Amy Farrar watch a plane scheduled to transport people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement out of the Signature Aviation terminal at the Denver International Airport on Sept. 13, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)On a Sunday morning in September, three Colorado women met at the cell phone lot near Denver International Airport and waited for a flight from Texas to arrive.
They watched a flight tracker as the plane flew closer to Denver, and prepared to meet it as it landed. But they did not go to the typical arrivals terminal, and they were not awaiting visiting family and friends. This was a plane scheduled to pick up people detained in Colorado by U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement and transport them to Mesa, Arizona.
Dana Miller, Kristen Aldretti and Amy Farrar drove to the Signature Aviation terminal immediately southeast of the main airport and waited behind a fence near the perimeter of the runway. An Air Wisconsin plane pulled into view, and the typical choreography of an ICE flight began: An unmarked bus pulled up, people began loading white bags of personal belongings onto the airplane and officers laid out silver shackles on the tarmac.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Typically, the women would watch people exit the bus, get shackled and then directed onto the airplane. They carried a handheld tally counter to track the number of detainees, and planned to count the pairs of feet they could see under the bus, since it blocked their line of sight to the plane stairs that day.
But then a security guard pulled up and asked the trio to leave, and they left the terminal, which is private property, without protest. It wasn’t the first time they were kicked out during their dozen or so outings to the airport. Once they got back into their car and pulled out onto the road, a private security vehicle trailed them for about a mile and then turned around.
“Regardless, we learned things,” Aldretti said, categorizing the outing as a success even though they did not witness people getting on the flight. “We learned that they are still parking the buses in front so we can’t see (the stairs). We learned that sometimes the pilots come out. Those are all things that need to be documented, and it goes into our learning for next time.”
Two days later, they were back, and saw 32 people led onto an ICE flight. On Sept. 29, it was 33.
“The general public, at this point, has a common view of what happens when people get picked up from ICE,” Miller said. But there’s still a gap in understanding what happens between someone’s initial detainment and their release or eventual deportation, she said.
“We want people to see what it really looks like,” she said of ICE flights. “It’s when the shackles are all laid out on the pavement, and the sun is shining on them, and then you see them getting put on people, and then people struggling to walk. People should know.”
Calls for cameras
Domestic ICE flights happen on a semi-regular basis out of the Denver airport. There were 118 flights between January and August this year, according to research from Human Rights First. They are part of the Trump administration’s program of mass deportations. Aldretti and Miller began heading to the airport to observe the flights in mid-July, and Aldretti posts about them on a dedicated Instagram account that has grown to almost 1,000 followers. Farrar joined more recently and lives the closest to the airport among the three.
“We have privilege, and if we’re not going to be the ones doing this important work and standing up for others who are vulnerable, who will be?” Aldretti said.
People in shackles are led off a plane flight-tracking databases show is operated by Arapahoe County, Colorado-based Key Lime Air at Alexandria International Airport, Louisiana, on Oct. 11, 2025. (Photo by Madelyn Murphy/Colorado Newsline)
Their goal is to physically witness and count the people being boarded onto these flights and feed it into a national network of volunteer ICE flight observers called Habeas Flight Watch. That website hosts a live dashboard of confirmed ICE flights and volunteers rely on it to track when a flight lands in their city. Other “birders” in the network are able to take clear photos of passengers in an effort to connect people with lawyers and family. The setup at Signature Aviation, with a nearly opaque fence and no clear sight line to the plane, makes that hard.
“If we could even get pictures of these passengers to share with their family members, to share with their lawyers … to make sure that their family knows where the hell they are (would be ideal),” Farrar said.
The group, as well as other immigrant advocacy organizations, have called on city and airport leadership to increase transparency and local surveillance around ICE flights. They see an example in King County, Washington, near Seattle, where county officials in 2023 ordered the airport to log every flight and maintain a livestream to show ICE flight operations. The county recently hired a flight monitoring and outreach coordinator to count passengers and flag safety violations. Activists pressured county officials for years over the issue.
“I hope (we get) the live camera feed, where the public and folks who are monitoring this from a legal perspective can identify (people) and just document this,” Denver City Council member Stacie Gilmore told Colorado Newsline. She said she has heard commitments from airport leadership that they are working on evaluating the feasibility of such a measure.
Signature Aviation did not reply to a request for comment.
The transparency concerns in Denver came to a head recently as council members debated whether to approve a lease for regional passenger service through a subsidiary of Key Lime Air at the airport. Key Lime Air is a Colorado-based company that has operated hundreds of ICE flights since last year, when Colorado Newsline first reported that it was flying for the agency.
An airport spokesperson wrote in an email that leadership has been in discussion with a “number of stakeholder groups to hear their concerns and ideas” over the issue.
“Obviously, it’s not nearly enough, but I think monitoring of these flights is a good first step to actually be able to see what’s happening, and bring a wider lens to the broader public,” said Brandon Gehrke Quintanilla, an organizer with Aurora Unidos CSO who met with airport leadership. He said the Key Lime lease coming before City Council was enough leverage to put pressure on the airport and city leaders about the ICE flights.
City Council delayed the lease approval vote, but then passed it 11-1 on Oct. 13 under the promise from airport officials to continue conversations about transparency measures with advocates like Miller. Gilmore was the lone “no” vote. No council member directly mentioned cameras or livestreams.
“The things I expect moving forward is that the collaboration continues with the community organizations — collaboration and partnership, not lip service,” council member Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said during that meeting. “I also would like that we implement and maintain transparency measures, such as tracking ICE activity. I know other airports have done this. I want us to be creative and think about how we are doing this.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Explained: How to vote early in the 2026 midterm election
text:
Signs direct voters inside the Lee County Courthouse in eastern Arkansas in February 2024. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Early voting begins Monday in Arkansas and continues for two weeks leading up to the general election on Nov. 3. 
Arkansas voters can head to their local polling location to cast their ballots in the races for U.S. Senate, Arkansas governor and the state Legislature, among others. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
More than 1.85 million voters are registered to vote in Arkansas, according to the secretary of state’s office. Over 1.6 million are registered as “Party Optional,” meaning they have no party affiliation. 
Roughly 155,000 Arkansans are registered Republicans and 85,000 are registered Democrats. The state also has more than 755 Libertarians and 125 Green Party members. 
Here’s what to know about early voting in Arkansas:
How do I know if I’m eligible to vote?
To participate in the Nov. 3 election, you must have registered to vote in Arkansas by Oct. 5. 
Your local county clerk will send you a personalized voter registration card once your application is processed, and it could take several weeks. 
Arkansans should not assume they’re registered until they’ve received their voter registration card, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
You can check your voter registration status by calling your local county clerk or visiting www.voterview.ar-nova.org.  
What if I need to update my voter registration?
You can update your information at an early voting site if your name or address has changed, according to the secretary of state’s office.
When is early voting?
Early voting runs Oct. 19 through Nov. 2. Election Day is Nov. 3.
During early voting, polls are open from 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Saturday. Early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Monday prior to the election. 
Where can I vote?
In most counties, early voting is conducted at the county clerk’s office, according to the secretary of state’s office. Local newspapers will publish designated sites in counties with polling locations other than the county clerk’s office. 
A 2025 law requires an early voting location in cities with more than 15,000 residents. The legislation was proposed in response to a 2024 legal battle over early voting in Crittenden County. 
You can find polling sites by calling your local county clerk or visiting www.voterview.ar-nova.org.
Do I need an ID to vote?
Yes. Arkansas voters are required to verify their voter registration with photo identification, such as a driver’s license or passport. 
If you don’t bring an ID with you to the polls, you can cast a provisional ballot. 
In order for the provisional ballot to count, a voter must present a document or photo ID to verify their registration to the county board of election commissioners or the county clerk by noon on the Monday following the election.
How do I know what races I can vote in?
To view sample ballots, call your local county clerk or visit www.voterview.ar-nova.org.
Information about candidates running for federal and statewide office, as well as the Arkansas House and Senate, is available on the Advocate’s 2026 Voter Guide.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New group seeks to help US small towns lead the clean energy transition
text:
Mayor Mondale Robinson, of Enfield, North Carolina, at the town’s aging substation (Photo: Elizabeth Ouzts/Canary Media)
As the mayor of tiny Enfield, North Carolina, Mondale Robinson has huge clean energy ambitions. Among them: building a solar farm to power the entire town of about 2,000, replacing the town’s decrepit substation to distribute those renewable electrons, and building a thermal energy network to provide heating and cooling and reduce exorbitant electric bills.


But Enfield is one of the poorest towns in the state, where the average household income hovers around the poverty line. As mayor, Robinson earns $500 a month. There are no sustainability officers, no grant writers, no policy teams to help him push this plan forward.


One way Robinson is trying to overcome these hurdles is by working with allies from the closest major metro area. Lawyers from Chapel Hill’s Southern Environmental Law Center, for instance, are negotiating the town utility’s next electricity contract so that it can produce its own solar energy. Researchers at Durham’s Duke University are helping design the geothermal project.


Yet too many doors remain closed to Robinson. The U.S. Conference of Mayors, which has galvanized city leadership on climate solutions, doesn’t extend full membership to leaders of towns as small as Enfield. And most foundations tend to overlook such communities.




Mayor Mondale Robinson and Canary Media contributing reporter Elizabeth Ouzts at a Climate Week NYC summit on rural America and the clean energy transition (Photo: Daniel Krieger/Canary Media)



So Robinson, a longtime political organizer, decided to do what he’s always done: Join together with his cohorts to fight for change. At a Canary Media summit on clean energy in rural America in September, he announced that he’s launching a new small-town coalition. If towns like his work together, he believes, they can help get new federal policies enacted, attract new donors, and have greater access to experts who can help them confront a host of challenges, from the climate crisis to housing and food insecurity.


“One small town can be ignored,” he said. “Thousands of organized small towns become a national constituency.”


Robinson’s National Conference of Small Cities and Rural Mayors is designed for officials of locales with fewer than 30,000 people. The figure is not arbitrary: the U.S. Conference of Mayors serves mayors of cities with populations above that benchmark.


“The national organization that speaks for mayors doesn’t even allow us to be full members,” he said. Yet census data shows that towns like Enfield make up 93% of all incorporated municipalities and house some 60 million people, he said. “America is a nation of small towns.”


At the same time, Robinson points out that 90% of philanthropy goes to urban areas. “If you consider rural people as a collective, we will be bigger than the largest populated state in this country,” he said, referring to California. “And yet, we are not being invested in in a way that makes sense.”


Robinson’s new coalition is still in the early stages. “Right now, we’re trying to recruit the first 100 founding mayors,” as well as anchor foundations, he said.
As economic damage from climate change grows, NC experts urge ‘pre-recovery’ planning 



Longer term, his goals for the group include training, peer-to-peer networks, regional collaboration, and a shared voice in federal advocacy. He also believes that small towns, with minimal footprints and more ability than big cities to be nimble, are the best places to test and refine new clean energy models, just as Enfield is aiming to do.


Already, the town has helped form a new nonprofit, Enfield Energy Futures, which has won a small seed grant to pursue the thermal energy network. Its utility could become the first to run such a project in the Southeast.


“What we’re doing here in Enfield,” Robinson said, “with no resources, or very little resources, is how we change the lives not just of the people in Enfield but everybody who is living in a small town across this country.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Opportunity Zones can help bring investment, development to Idaho areas that need it most
text:
An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026.  (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings.
This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1.
An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity.
In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise. These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included.
In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls.
The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries.
The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here.
Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward.
Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value.
Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership.
For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services.
Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Attorney General touts success of Trump task force in Memphis
text:
Joined by U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and U.S. Marshals Director Gady Serralta, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche visited Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 17, 2026, to discussed the Memphis Safe Task. (Photo: U.S. Department of Justice)U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche joined federal and state leaders in Tennessee on Friday to tout the record of the Memphis Safe Task Force a little more than one year after President Donald Trump first established the multi-agency crime-fighting force. 
Overall crime in Memphis is now at a 25-year low, Blanche said, giving the task force credit for the reduction in violent crimes, robberies and vehicle thefts. Crime, local officials have noted, began trending downward in the city in the year before the task force was convened. 
Family demands answers after Memphis Task Force agent kills man at Burger King

Blanche gave no timetable for a potential end to  the enhanced law enforcement presence, saying the task force will remain in the city “as long as it takes.” 
“We haven’t won yet. It’s not over,” he said. Blanche did not define terms for a successful completion of the task force’s mission in Memphis.  
He also reiterated the Trump administration’s goal to replicate the model across the country, singling out Chicago as a goal. Like Memphis, the city is minority white, and majority Democrat.
“If you think about a place like Chicago, if Chicago called me and said, ‘we want to replicate Memphis in Chicago,’ we could transform an entire city, one of the most pivotal cities in this country, in the same way that we’ve transformed Memphis,” he said
Since September 2025, the task force has brought hundreds of federal law enforcement officers to the city and surrounding Shelby County to serve warrants, make arrests, detain immigrants, conduct traffic stops and recover missing children, often working in tandem with the Tennessee Highway Patrol and other state and local law enforcement officers.  Gov. Bill Lee deployed hundreds of soldiers with the Tennessee National Guard to support the effort. 
ACLU claims Memphis Safe Task Force harassing plaintiff

The task force has been welcomed by Republican leaders, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee for governor, who praised the task force at Friday’s roundtable discussion in a Memphis warehouse alongside state Sen. Brent Taylor and Memphis Police Chief CJ Davis.
But it has faced pushback by many in the Democratic-leaning city as a form of over-policing of predominantly Black and brown communities — pushback that grew earlier this year after the fatal shootings of four Black men by task force members in four separate encounters earlier this year. 
Critics and community groups have also highlighted dangerous high speed chases and the heightened presence of officers conducting immigration enforcement in areas of Memphis with large immigrant populations. 
Several lawsuits filed by journalists, local leaders and community groups have alleged intimidation against bystanders attempting to monitor enforcement activity and the refusal by state agencies participating in the task force to provide public records.

title: Michigan Data Centers: The Weekly Download
text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Tyrone Township officials have begun developing regulations to prohibit data centers that require more than 60 megawatts of electricity, The Livingston Post reported. Officials in the Livingston County township say their moratorium blocks data center applications until about the end of February or beginning of March.

Updates
