name: Maine Morning Star
title: All three candidates for governor promise tax relief. How feasible are their plans?
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles unveiled his plan to cut property taxes at an Oct. 6 press conference outside a supporter's house in Lisbon. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)All three candidates for Maine governor are promising property tax relief through an expanded homestead exemption, but questions remain about how their proposals would be funded and how much relief they would deliver to homeowners.
Mainers’ property taxes increased by 22.7% from 2019 to 2024, whereas the average home value went up by 74%, the highest rate in the country, according to a national analysis. 
Republican nominee Bobby Charles was the latest candidate to unveil his plan, which proposes the most sweeping change. He said if elected he would increase the homestead exemption, which the state subtracts from property values before calculating taxes, from $25,000 to $100,000 over the next few years.
“Property tax relief is essential,” Charles said at a press conference earlier this month at a supporter’s house in Lisbon. “It’s actually central to the ability of anybody to afford anything, and that ultimately is how we get affordability back.”
While he’s the only candidate promising such a high exemption to all homeowners, the idea is not unique to the Leeds resident. Democrat Hannah Pingree has promised to double the homestead exemption, while independent Rick Bennett said he would increase the homestead exemption for homeowners 65 and older to half the median home value in the state.
“I think there is a fair amount of overlap here with three different candidates trying to tackle this in slightly different ways but all trying to get at the same thing,” said James Myall, a policy analyst at the Maine Center for Economic Policy.
“Increasing the homestead exemption has the advantage of making it so that people with wealthier homes end up paying a larger share of that in taxes than people with less wealthy homes.”
Despite vow of bipartisanship, gubernatorial candidates spar in first televised debate

Charles has focused much of his campaign on lowering taxes. During the event in Lisbon, he explained that he would raise the homestead exemption in two steps: increasing the exemption to $50,000 during his first budget and eventually raising it to $100,000.
Property taxes in Maine account for more than 50% of local revenue, the fourth highest rate in the nation, according to a report by the Maine Legislature’s property tax relief task force this January. That’s why it’s important for all gubernatorial candidates hoping to lower taxes to ensure towns are reimbursed by the state for what they lose in property tax cuts.
Currently, municipalities are reimbursed 76% of  tax revenue lost to this exemption; in fiscal year 2025, the state reimbursed municipalities just over $85 million. Charles plans to increase that to a 100% reimbursement, which his campaign estimated would cost the state $285 million annually with a $100,000 exemption.
“Potentially the level of increase that he’s suggesting could help a fair number of folks,” Myall said about Charles’ plan. “I think the part where maybe it’s a little trickier is how he’s proposing to pay for it.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Charles has blamed unchecked government spending, fraud and “unfunded mandates” for recent spending increases and the projected $1.3 billion budget gap.
“We have so much waste, so much largesse … so much duplication, and so much fraud in this government budget that we have got to start over again,” he said last week.
He said he would offset lower property taxes by eliminating 100 mostly vacant state government jobs, promising there would be no layoffs. On the campaign trail, he has also vowed to audit two of the largest state agencies: the health and education departments.
Myall explained that the money from empty state government positions is currently reallocated to other services in the budget, so “it just feels like there’s still some questions to answer, I think on where this money is coming from.” 
Charles’ campaign said that until departments are audited it is not possible to predict how much money can be reallocated to property tax relief.
“Everyone likes the idea of the government being more efficient but generally what tends to happen is like when people come in, they find there’s not actually that much to cut,” Myall said.
“Even with Elon Musk’s effort in the federal government, they cut plenty of programs, but I don’t think they actually uncovered large, widespread amounts of actual abuse in those programs.”
Other tax relief plans
In addition to focusing on the homestead exemption, Bennett and Pingree have proposed increasing the property tax fairness credit, which helps low- and moderate-income homeowners and renters. 
Bennett’s plan would apply the credit directly to property tax bills, rather than requiring families to wait until they file their returns.
Pingree has proposed taxing second homes owned by non-Maine residents at a higher rate, which she said during a debate last Thursday would “both deliver tax relief but also ensure that we can invest in the infrastructure that desperately needs it.”
The proposal will likely require a constitutional amendment, which Myall said, “might not be an impossible ask since there is bipartisan agreement on some of this.”
However, Pingree’s Republican and independent opponents dismissed the idea.
“It really doesn’t deal with the underlying issue, we need to get spending in check, and we need to have meaningful property tax relief soon to Maine people,” Bennett said during the second debate. “The proposal she has pushes the can down the road some more, and I don’t think it’s viable.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: What if Tom Tiffany casts doubt on the November election results?
text:
Voting rights activists and others gathering at the Midtown Center in Milwaukee on the first day of early voting in July, 2022. (Photo | Isiah Holmes)If Tom Tiffany loses in November, it’s not irrational to think he might try to overturn the election results. On Nov. 4, the day after the election, Tiffany might repeat the same, old, tired argument he made when he tried to overturn the 2020 election results in Arizona and Pennsylvania and said that, if he’d had the chance, he would have voted against certifying the results in Wisconsin. Tiffany might again accuse Dane County election officials as being “unscrupulous.” He might say that Milwaukee County allowed “hundreds of thousands of illegal votes to be cast and counted.” 
Tiffany only recently admitted that Joe Biden won the 2020 election, and has said he supports an FBI probe into the 2020 election results in our state. 
Mayor Cavalier Johnson has offered Tiffany an open-ended invitation to observe Milwaukee’s elections procedures himself. “I invite you to see our election operation, to talk to officials who conduct our elections and scrutinize, first hand the extensive security and accuracy in place.”  Unsurprisingly, Tiffany has not accepted this offer. 
When Tiffany welcomed FBI agents this spring to investigate Milwaukee election officials, it wasn’t just to sow doubts in the 2020 election or to ensure election integrity. The real goal was to set the stage in case he loses in November. Then, he might  ask Donald Trump to help overturn Wisconsin’s election.
When facing this very real impending emergency to November’s election, what are Wisconsinites to do? Noted decent human being Mr. Fred Rogers has this advice.
“When I was a boy and I would see scary things in the news, my mother would say to me, ‘Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping.”
So who are our helpers? Let’s start with the people you already know. Once you begin to ask around, you will discover that you know several helpers who volunteer at the polls in every election.  Personally, I attend weekly church services at First Unitarian Society of Milwaukee. A high percentage of our congregants volunteer at the polls. If you ask more than one of them, you hear a consistent story. 
Election volunteers care deeply about ensuring  free and fair elections and they do it year after year. They receive extensive training to carefully follow transparent procedures. They are given advice such as, “It is better to go slow, ask questions and get it right.” Additionally, there are so many people involved at the polls and so much transparency that, once you are a part of it, you have full faith in the integrity of Milwaukee elections. So ask around. Share these helpers’ stories before our city’s integrity is questioned this November. Want to join their ranks? They will gladly put you to work.
But what are we to do on Nov. 4? Luckily, you will always find people who are helping.  This winter, our city faced a real threat from federal ICE immigration agents. Before the victories of everyday helpers in Minneapolis, it was reasonable to believe that level of federal overreach would spread to our city. We know this because of the treatment of our neighbor Yessenia Ruano and the detainment of Elvira Benitez-Suarez and Salah Sarsour. Masked ICE agents detained at least 39 of our neighbors in July.  The ICE Out MKE coalition stood up on those dark days and those Milwaukee helpers are still here. I trust the League of Women Voters of Milwaukee County, Souls to the Polls, Milwaukee Turners, and Voces de la Frontera. Wisconsin has plenty of non-partician, non-for-profit helpers and these are just a few.
Your relationship with the nonpartisan not-for-profits that are working to defend our democracy will need to be deeper than digital. Go to a meeting and find out now which local helpers will be your trusted voice. Empowered with this connection, on the day after the election, your plan should be to listen to follow the guidance from these groups and join the organized, active citizens who are standing up.  
Most importantly, don’t relax into believing that Tiffany and Trump are interested in anything but autocracy. The dance of democracy is not choreographed by a single caller. It is not a solo act. It depends on all of us moving together.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio again spent more than a billion dollars on private school vouchers during latest fiscal year
text:
A school bus. (File photo by Getty Images)For the second year in a row, Ohio spent more than a billion dollars on private school vouchers, this time for the 2026 fiscal year. 
The total amount for Ohio’s five private school voucher programs was $1.173 billion, according to data from the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. Nearly half of the money ($532.8 million) was from the Education Choice Expansion vouchers. This is the third full year with near-universal school vouchers. 
“It’s frustrating to see this amount of money going to vouchers when our public schools still are not fully and fairly funded,” said Melissa Cropper, president of the Ohio Federation of Teachers. 
“Right now, they’re funneling a lot of money to private schools and not fully funding our public schools.”
Ohio Education Association President Jeff Wensing also said the state needs to fully fund public schools. 
“I think our policymakers … diverting more than $1.1 billion a year, maybe $1.2 to private schools probably isn’t the best decision because of the fact …  that these are public tax dollars going to largely unaccountable private schools, and that’s a concern when that happens.”
Ohio appeals court rules state’s private school voucher system unconstitutional

An Ohio appellate court ruled on Thursday that the EdChoice voucher program is unconstitutional. The program will still be able to exist, as the judges expected the state to appeal. 
Interim Ohio Republican Attorney General Andy Wilson said in a statement last Thursday that he would appeal the decision to the the 6-1 Republican-controlled Ohio Supreme Court. Ohio Republican state lawmakers made Ohio Supreme Court races overtly partisan by adding party labels in 2021.
Wensing said that it’s incredibly obvious that it’s an illegal use of taxpayer money.
“The students using the EdChoice vouchers and EdChoice expansion are students already enrolled in private school,” Wensing said. “These families have been paying for their students to go to private schools, mostly wealthy families, and it’s a handout to the wealthy, a handout to the rich.”
The $1.173 billion figure is just under the estimated $1.18 billion the nonpartisan Ohio Legislative Service Commission predicted for the voucher programs for fiscal year 2026.  
The five private school scholarship programs are the Autism Scholarship Program, the Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship Program, the Cleveland Scholarship, the Education Choice Scholarship and the Educational Choice Expansion Scholarship Program. 
Lawmakers expanded the Education Choice Expansion eligibility to 450% of the poverty line three years ago through the state budget — creating near-universal school vouchers.
K-8 students can receive a $6,166 scholarship and high schoolers can receive a $8,408 scholarship in state funding under the EdChoice vouchers. 
There were more than 105,000 EdChoice Expansion scholarships awarded, averaging $5,114 per participant, according to the ODEW data.

There were more than 42,000 traditional EdChoice scholarships awarded for a total of $284.6 million — with an average of $6,807 per participant. 
For the Cleveland scholarship, there were more than 8,000 scholarships awarded for a total of $55.09 million — with an average of $6,875 per participant. 
There were more than 6,000 autism scholarships awarded for a total of $186.7 million — with an average of $30,318 per participant. 
For the Jon Peterson Scholarship, there were more than 9,000 scholarships awarded for a total of $114.2 million — with an average of $13,511 per participant. 
There were 1,629,346 students enrolled in Ohio’s public schools during the 2025-26 school year, according to ODEW, but the number of students enrolled in the state’s public schools has been on the decline.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Growth of data centers becomes a defining issue of the midterms, entangling some Georgia candidates
text:
Candidates for Georgia Attorney General (left to right) Tanya Miller and Brian Strickland had a fiery exchange at the Atlanta Press Club general election debates on Oct. 12, 2026, when Miller pressed Strickland on a data center project proposed on his family farm land that he now says is “dead.” Pool photo via J Glenn PhotographyGeorgia candidates up and down the ballot are campaigning on an issue that has struck a nerve across the political spectrum: data centers. 
A wave of data center projects across Georgia has been met with outrage in many communities in the last year or so, causing state lawmakers from both parties to push a flurry of legislative solutions during the 2026 legislative session. But in the end, none of the bills passed. 
Since then, Georgia has become the leading state for data centers. Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited and leaving office after this year, has welcomed the facilities, saying at a data center-related event in Washington this summer that “we cannot let China win this race, and that’s what some people want,” referencing the race between the U.S. and China to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models.
The November election will decide to what extent Georgia embraces the energy-hungry facilities in the future, with voters choosing a new governor, the lawmakers who shape the state’s policies on data centers and other state leaders who play a role in carrying out those policies. 
At the top of the ballot, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, has criticized Republican nominee Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, for his investment in a data center in Texas through a company Jackson was the head of until recently. Though his campaign has tried to distance itself from that development, in his campaign financial disclosure, Jackson is listed as the CEO and president of Datahub Developers, the company that is advancing the data center in Texas that the local community is fighting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bottoms and Jackson had a fiery exchange at a recent debate where they swapped accusations of being involved in advancing data centers. 
“There is a community asking him to not build a data center, a massive data center in their community, and he is moving forward. So, if he is an investor in data centers, if he builds data centers, he cannot be trusted on this,” Bottoms said in the debate organized by Atlanta News First and Gray Media.
Jackson fired back, accusing Bottoms of approving three data centers during her time as mayor of Atlanta, but Bottoms said that she was “not sure what data centers he’s referencing,” saying there was only one at Georgia Tech that wasn’t one of the hyperscale data centers that cause concerns today.
Attorney general candidate says family has ‘moved on’ from data center project once planned for their farmland 
At least one other candidate, Georgia state Sen. Brian Strickland, a McDonough Republican running for state attorney general, held a personal financial stake in a proposed data center as recently as the summer of 2025. But the proposal has since been shelved, according to public records and interviews.
The Georgia Recorder examined financial disclosure documents for all candidates running for statewide office in November. The Recorder also reviewed other public records and reached out to all of the candidates and their campaigns to ask whether the candidate has a direct financial stake in a data center. 
In phone calls, text messages and emails with candidates and their campaign staff, all except those described in the story reported having no financial interest in data center projects.
Public records show that Strickland, a lawyer who represents a suburban district southeast of Atlanta, was involved in advancing a $1.2 billion data center on his family’s farmland in Henry County. On May 15, 2024, he authorized a real estate development firm focused on technology to pursue rezoning for the project. 
Strickland’s personal financial disclosure statement shows that the state senator holds a greater-than-5% stake in Strickland Road Farms, which was a co-applicant in the rezoning application for the proposed 1.25 million-square-feet data center.
The project came close to being finalized mid-2025 – about the same time Strickland launched his bid for higher office – but Strickland told reporters last week that his family backed out over concerns about the noise that would come from the data center and now says the project is “dead.” 
A public hearing before the Henry County Board of Commissioners was scheduled to consider rezoning part of the farmland on June 17, 2025, but Carlotta Harrell, the commission’s chair, said at the top of the meeting that the agenda item, along with other rezoning public hearings, “have all been removed at the request of the applicant and we will hear these items at a later time.”
County and local development officials confirmed the project is now inactive.
The Democratic nominee for attorney general, state Rep. Tanya Miller, pressed Strickland on the project at last week’s Atlanta Press Club debate. 
“It wasn’t until days – and mind you, we’re talking days – after he announced his run for attorney general, did he remove the agenda item from the public hearing. He didn’t remove the data center application. He’s playing with words. He’s shape shifting,” Miller said to reporters after the debate. 
Opponents of the data center project, like Connie Snow, a member of Conserve Henry County, a local advocacy group focused on zoning issues, say they’re worried the project will be revived after the November election. 
“They’ve all told us that he’s withdrawn and all this other stuff, but I don’t think that it’s going to go away,” Snow said in an interview. “You have to also remember that all this happened coincidentally enough as it was getting close to election time.” Snow also participated in a press call organized by the Democratic Party of Georgia. 
But Strickland said the decision to halt the project was not related to his decision to run for office and says the family now plans to add to an existing residence on the property and that his “parents decided to keep the entire farm intact.”
“The family has moved on and my dad is back working the land,” Strickland said in a text message.
Strickland says that the family listened to the community’s concerns about the project but that the family also ultimately did not want a data center next to them either.
“We said ‘no data center for us’ because the closest neighbor to the data center was actually my parents. They had their own concerns, and they said no to this,” he said at the debate.
The project also raised environmental concerns during a regional review process, with officials in the nearby city of Hampton saying potential hazardous material handled at the site could threaten the Towaliga River and Indian Creek watersheds and risk contaminating drinking water. The Atlanta Regional Commission concluded in their review that the data center project did not align with the commission’s planning policy for Atlanta’s developing suburbs and proposed ways the project could move forward by mitigating environmental impacts, such as using undeveloped areas around streams as a buffer, a plan to manage the proposed preservation areas and providing a fund “to support conservation land acquisition elsewhere in the County.”
In an earlier interview on Sept. 30, Strickland said that the proposal started when developers approached his father about using part of the family’s farmland for “some sort of commercial development.” Strickland said he became directly involved with the project to help with discussions and evaluate the contract since he is the only attorney in the family.
Strickland said that his father, once he learned more about the project, had concerns that noise from the data center could compromise their quality of life. Strickland’s father declined a request for an interview made through Strickland. 
Strickland also said that the developers had purchased another parcel nearby that is not owned by his family, and he’s unsure about the status of that particular development. The land is owned by a Delaware-registered corporation called 0 Rocky Creek Road, LLC, and owned by Aaron Wolofsky, who also authorized the same real estate development firm to pursue rezoning for the land. Wolofsky is also the head of Red Wolf DCD Properties, the company that proposed developing on Strickland’s family farmland. 
While Wolofsky did not return an email and phone messages seeking an update on the projects, Strickland provided a letter signed by Wolofsky that “Red Wolf has no relationship, by way of contract or otherwise, with Strickland Road Farms, LLC and there are no proposals to construct anything on any property owned by Strickland Road Farms, LLC.” There was no date on the letter, but its metadata shows that the document was created on Oct. 12 shortly before Strickland faced his Democratic opponent on the debate stage. 



More on how we reported this story: 
We checked all of the statewide candidates’ financial disclosure documents. As of Oct. 16, four candidates’ required financial disclosures have not been posted on the State Ethics Commission’s website: Democratic insurance commissioner candidate Keisha Sean Waites, Republican Public Service Commission candidate Fitz Johnson, Democratic Public Service Commission candidate Shelia Edwards and Democratic agriculture commissioner Katherine Juhan-Arnold. The deadline was April 1. 
Juhan-Arnold’s LinkedIn lists her current occupation as BIM & Document Control Site Lead for the Rohadfox Corporation with Google Data Center Services as a client.
“I do not own, invest in, develop, or hold any direct or indirect financial stake in a data center, nor do I receive compensation based on the approval or expansion of data-center projects,” Juhan-Arnold said in an email.
“For transparency, my professional background includes paid work in data-center infrastructure and operations,” she added. “That experience has shown me both the importance of digital infrastructure and the significant demands these facilities can place on land, water, energy, and surrounding communities.”



Georgia Recorder Deputy Editor Ross Williams and Reporter Maya Homan contributed to this report.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Emails reveal local police were more involved in Montour County ICE raid than initially admitted
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen as ICE conducts a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Avenue on Aug. 30, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)While questions remain over how a Sept. 2 Immigration and Customs Enforcement raid in Montour County unfolded, emails between ICE and a participating police department shed more light on what happened.
Along with further interviews with law enforcement, the emails obtained through public records requests also show police chiefs — particularly Mahoning Township’s Frederick Dyroff III — downplayed the scope of the raid and their role in it.
The records also confirm some of the accounts of witnesses who claim the total number of arrests made in connection with the operation was far higher than federal and local authorities have stated. It’s still unclear how many people were ultimately detained.
The ICE operation last month – assisted by police – led to the arrests of a number of immigrant workers leaving a construction site on the Geisinger Medical Center campus in Danville. 

What happened at Geisinger? Arrests near Danville hospital show difficulty tracking ICE activity.


When news of the operation first broke, statements from ICE, police chiefs and witnesses painted conflicting pictures about the scope of the raid.
Citing witnesses, immigration advocates claimed as many as 40 people were detained as part of the workplace raid. A statement from ICE claimed federal officers ultimately arrested “10 illegal aliens in Danville … after they were encountered by local law enforcement during vehicle stops.”
Police chiefs made contradictory statements about their involvement and whether they had even targeted individuals suspected of immigration-related crimes.
But the newly released records reveal at least 11 federal agents were assigned to the operation and received assistance from police officers from five departments in nearby communities. They used drones to track their targets as they left work at the construction site, and the operation resulted in several foot chases.
The police departments involved were Mahoning Township, Danville Borough, Riverside Borough, Hemlock Township and Montour Township. All are part of what’s known as the 287(g) program, which allows local law enforcement to partner with federal immigration agents, often receiving funding and training as well.
The Daily Item reported that the Mahoning police department received $160,000 through the program and the Danville police department received $167,000.

Federal funds for local police enforcement accelerated Trump immigration crackdown


While five officers from Mahoning were involved, each other department appeared to provide one or two officers.
Neither Montour Township nor Hemlock police chiefs responded to requests for comment from the Capital-Star.
‘Redacting my statement’
When the Capital-Star first reached Dyroff roughly a week after the raid, he confirmed that his department and police officers from neighboring Danville Borough assisted federal agents, but provided conflicting statements on the scope of their involvement.
“ICE was in the area at the time we were conducting traffic stops,” he said. “Vehicles were stopped for traffic violations, and if those persons were wanted by ICE, they were turned over to ICE.”
Asked whether his officers intentionally targeted anyone because of questions about their immigration status, Dyroff said “No … It was run-of-the-mill policing.”
Asked in a later interview how his officers knew where to stage to provide the most assistance, Dyroff said it was “no secret we know where there’s a concentration of people who are here illegally … It does not take a rocket scientist to find out where they’re working at.”
But emails between ICE and Dyroff obtained through a public records request show an organized and targeted operation. 
An ICE employee emailed Dyroff the day before the operation with specific information on where and how the raid would play out, what police officers’ roles would be, and who was being targeted.

ICE enforcement around healthcare facilities in Pa. leads to fears about immigrants who need care


An attachment to the email called “targets.docx” was given to the Capital-Star, but was heavily redacted. It appeared to contain information on 13 individuals.
The email, from someone with a redacted email address, also included detailed instructions about what role federal agents would be playing and how they were planning to track people as they left the construction site.
Eleven officers, the sender wrote, were to ride along with police, who would conduct traffic stops.
They would be guided by a “drone operator” who would track and call out the movement of construction workers’ vehicles as they left a parking lot near the site. 
Four officers were assigned to “transport,” two in a “white express van,” and two others each in “separate caged vehicle[s],” to take custody after traffic stops.
“The idea is that this will take place as quick as we can safely do it,” read the email. “We are going to make sure the van is loaded with restraints and extra handcuffs. When you take custody of one, you will provide the arresting officer with a pair of handcuffs (one for one exchange). Restraints will be applied when safe to do so.”
Two officers were assigned as “floaters in separate vehicles to assist with Spanish and any other issues that may arise.”



Quotation







“Why was my letter not true to what we’re talking about now? That’s a good question. There was some truth — I guess I can’t answer that. I don’t know how to answer that.”


– Mahoning Township Police Chief Frederick Dyroff III


Two others, including a supervisor, were assigned to conduct record checks off-site.
Because of redactions, it’s unclear if there was overlap between the roles.
Asked how the information squared with his previous claims that his officers were not targeting individuals at ICE’s bequest, Dyroff hedged.
“I’m redacting [sic] my [previous] statement,” he told the Capital-Star last week. “I’m telling you now it was an operation, and they were looking for certain targets, and we assisted in stopping those targets if they were violating the law.”
Danville Borough Chief Greg Watson and Riverside Police Chief Kerry Parkes also told the Capital-Star that they were asked to assist in the operation by Dyroff himself, and not ICE.
“Mahoning, they orchestrated that event,” said Parkes, though he noted it is common for officers from Riverside, Mahoning and surrounding municipalities to assist one another.
Watson also said he was not provided the kind of detailed information about the raid ahead of time that Dyroff was.
“I wasn’t involved in any of that planning, but my understanding is that my officers were only doing vehicle stops,” he said. 
Copies of incident reports received through records requests from the Danville Borough Police Department show multiple people fled from officers, leading to at least one foot chase that resulted in a use of force report.
“Three males took off,” the officer wrote about the aftermath of a traffic stop in his use of force report. “I chased after a male and escorted him to the ground. The male got away and I could not locate him. A reasonable amount of force was used in attempt to get him into custody.”
The report is hand-written and the word “escorted” appears to be written in different color ink than the rest of the form.

An excerpt of a Danville Police Department use of force report filled out by an officer after the Sept. 2 operation with ICE. The document was obtained by the Capital-Star through a public records request.
The officer checked boxes noting the suspect was not injured before or during the interaction.
After news of the operation emerged, it wasn’t just media inquiries Dyroff was addressing. In the weeks after the raid, Mahoning Township supervisors faced pushback over police involvement in an ICE operation so close to a major hospital. As conflicting stories emerged from police, witnesses, and immigrants’ rights advocates, some community members sought answers.
On Sept. 14, Dyroff addressed a township supervisors meeting attended by roughly 35 people who were primarily there to oppose the operation and to hear from the chief exactly what happened.
Mahoning Township Supervisor John Whelan estimated the audience was 10 times larger than the “typical three to five.”

“We recognize that the September 2 operation has generated questions and concerns within our community, and we appreciate the opportunity to provide clarification regarding the role and actions of the Mahoning Township Police Department,” Dyroff wrote in a letter that was read at the meeting.
But little clarity was provided
“It is important to make clear that MTPD is not a federal immigration agency, nor are our officers attempting to assume that role,” Dyroff’s letter read. “…Our department’s role was to support effective law-enforcement coordination while continuing to serve the residents and visitors of our community.”
Asked why the letter he read seemed to characterize his department in more of a supervisory role when it appears to have participated more actively, Dyroff said he couldn’t say.
“Why was my letter not true to what we’re talking about now? That’s a good question,” Dyroff said. “There was some truth — I guess I can’t answer that. I don’t know how to answer that.”

ICE looks to sell two Pennsylvania warehouses and others initially planned for detention center


Emails confirm witness reports of surveillance drones
In the weeks after the raid, witnesses told advocates and the Capital-Star they believed drones were used to surveil workers as they were leaving the hospital. 
A construction worker who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation from ICE and his employer told the Capital-Star that he and his co-workers spotted a drone circling above them as they prepared to get in their vehicles to leave work on Sept. 2.
“We noticed that there were some electrician guys working, and we thought it was them maybe, but it just looked very suspicious that it immediately came and hovered over us,” he said.
At the time, ICE refused to answer questions about the claim when asked by the Capital-Star.
“We would never divulge investigative practices or procedures,” an ICE spokesperson told the Capital-Star.
Dyroff similarly said he would not answer questions about how information was gathered.
After the Capital-Star received emails showing ICE deployed a drone operator to monitor construction workers as they left work, Dyroff stressed that ICE was the agency choosing and monitoring targets, and not his officers.
“It was an operation that was with ICE,” Dyroff said. “They were looking for certain targets, and we assisted in apprehending those targets. I’ll just leave it at that.”
ICE also reiterated that they would not discuss tactics when asked whether the use of drones was typical.
“For operational security and the safety of our officers, DHS will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations, strategy, or tactics,” a spokesperson for the agency said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Elon Musk donates $7 million to help incumbent Ohio Republican US Sen. Jon Husted
text:
CEO of Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk speaks last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Maryland.(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)As part of unprecedented spending on U.S. elections, the world’s richest man Elon Musk is funneling more than $7 million to try to reelect incumbent Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, according to an analysis of federal election data by a group demanding regulation of AI companies.
The contributions by Elon Musk are not directly to Husted’s campaign, but instead to independent groups seeking to help Husted’s chances in the Nov. 3 midterms. 
Musk’s expenditures on Husted’s behalf are second only to those on behalf of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican who is in a closely fought U.S. Senate election there. Musk is contributing a whopping $18.8 million to that effort, the analysis by Guardrails Action said.
As with Paxton, Husted is in a tight race. 
Husted’s is against former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat. Husted was appointed in early 2025 to fill the seat, which was vacated when JD Vance became vice president.
President Donald Trump is highly unpopular — in part over his coziness with Big Tech figures like Musk. And Republicans are in danger of losing one or both houses of Congress. 
That raises the prospect of investigations into Trump and an industry that Americans view with increasing suspicion. 
The New York Times on Monday reported that Musk has contributed $276 million to his super PAC and to Republican groups since July in a desperate effort to keep that from happening.
Musk is worth an estimated $966 billion. In 2024, he spent a quarter-billion dollars backing Trump and Republican candidates.
Guardrails Action bills itself as “a nonpartisan advocacy organization fighting for common-sense AI accountability — protecting workers, families, and democracy from unchecked AI power.”
Evidence has mounted that AI is already causing social harm, and luminaries such as Bill Gates worry that much worse is already possible.
In addition, it’s causing localized job displacement, and people around the world fear that it will cause big job losses in the future. Experts also worry that AI-driven misinformation and deepfakes pose a serious threat to democracy.
Some people working within the industry share those fears so much that dissident OpenAI employees gave $215,000 to support Guardrails Action, Wired reported in July.
The group’s mission statement was posted before the most recent report on Musk’s political spending.
“A small group of Silicon Valley billionaires is spending over $125 million to elect politicians who will block AI safety laws — and hand control of the most powerful technology ever built to a handful of unaccountable companies,” it said. “Guardrails Action organizes workers, parents, and citizens to fight back. We believe AI can be transformative and good — but only if it’s built with accountability, transparency, and democratic oversight.”
Husted’s office didn’t respond to questions for this story.
Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Action parent organization Guardrails Alliance, said the massive spending by Big Tech is aimed at keeping Congress from regulating AI. It also shows that the industry knows how unpopular it is, he said.
“The AI industry realizes they have a political problem on their hands, and they never met a problem they didn’t think they could solve just by throwing money at it,” Blaettler said in an interview.
After getting hundreds of millions from Big Tech leaders, Trump last month agreed to allow the companies to regulate themselves. Blaettler said tech oligarchs need to be regulated.
“This agreement demonstrates the extent of the rot and corruption in this administration, where many of the AI executives who are party to this agreement have funded Trump’s super PACs, his inauguration, his pet projects,” he said. 
“You have Silicon Valley billionaires who are spending millions of dollars to do anything Donald Trump wants. In exchange they’re getting to set the regulations for their own industry. No industry should be allowed to set the regulations for itself — let alone the technology that is the most transformative that humans have ever known.”

title: New Ohio bill proposes task force to address childcare, early childhood education
text:
(File photo by Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).New legislation coming at the tail end of the current Ohio General Assembly seeks to study early childhood education regulation in the state.
Ohio House Bill 1023, sponsored by Republican state Rep. Josh Williams of Sylvania, would establish an “early childhood education governance and outcomes task force,” according to the language of the bill.
“The Task Force’s work should seek to answer the fundamental policy question of whether Ohio’s existing early childhood investments, governance structure, and programs are effectively preparing children to enter kindergarten ready to learn and providing the foundation necessary for long-term academic success,” the bill states.
The task force would “evaluate whether Ohio’s regulatory structures governing early childhood education optimally support” everything from kindergarten and school readiness to the use of state and federal funding.
The state has received federal funding for Head Start, funded a Publicly Funded Child Care program for low-income households, created vouchers to assist with child care costs, as well as overseeing a star-rating system for childcare and early education facilities.
“Some children are set up to struggle long before they ever walk into a kindergarten classroom,” Williams said in a statement. “We need to understand what is working, where the gaps are, and how to give every child a stronger start.”
Under H.B. 1023, the task force would be made up of three members each of the Ohio House and Senate, all appointed by the leaders of the chambers. At least one appointee from each chamber has to be from the minority party.
Other task force appointees would include a member of the Ohio departments of Children and Youth, Education and Workforce, Medicaid, Health, and Developmental Disabilities. Outside of state departments, the task force would have a representative from the Children and Youth Advisory Council “with expertise in early childhood education and care,” an expert in early childhood education and kindergarten readiness, an educator licensed in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade, an early childhood education provider, experts in child development and education data, and a parent or guardian of a child in or recently out of early childhood education.
The group would be tasked with making recommendations about the administration of early childhood education programs within state government, and “whether the existing governance structure in Ohio provides sufficient coordination, accountability, and educational focus across early childhood programs,” according to the bill.
One thing that won’t be under the purview of the task force is a review of childcare licensing, health and safety regulations, or the daily operations of childcare providers “except to the extent that such matters directly affect educational quality, kindergarten readiness, program participation, or educational continuity.”
A final report will be due by Dec. 1, 2027, including an inventory of programs and funding sources, enrollment and eligibility information, and identification of “gaps or unnecessary duplication,” along with recommendations on improving the system as a whole.
Many child advocacy groups are still reviewing the legislation before it goes to committee hearings, where testimony will be heard from those for and against the measure. Tami Lunan, organizing director for the CEO Project, a program within the Ohio Organizing Collaborative focused on the childcare system, said she appreciates lawmakers working to improve the early childhood education system and coordinate among agencies, but no study or coordination will bring childcare out of its funding shortage.
“Underinvestment has reduced childcare capacity, leaving parents unable to work and businesses without the workforce they need,” Lunan told the Capital Journal. “If Ohio wants better outcomes for children and working families, meaningful investment must be part of the solution.”
The national group First Five Years Fund found Ohio had a 13% gap in the supply of childcare services for the more than 800,000 children in Ohio aged five and under, and the 67% of households with children whose parents or guardians are all in the workforce.
Child care is a top issue in the upcoming November election, with the affordability concerns being raised as candidates for governor and the legislature face the voters.
This is not Williams’ first foray into legislation related to early childhood education and childcare. His previous measure had to do with enforcement of fraud regulations related to childcare facilities, with Ohio House Bill 649 looking to use the power of the Ohio Auditor of State’s Office and the Ohio Attorney General’s Office, if needed, to prosecute any potential claims that funding from the Publicly Funded Child Care program were being used inappropriately.
While he said he does not allege there is “widespread fraud in Ohio,” in arguing in support of that bill, he said the Ohio Department of Children & Youth “is not doing a good job of investigating it.”
The Ohio legislature has pushed different legislation in an attempt to address concerns about the lack of access and cost challenges related to childcare. Childcare vouchers were included in the last budget, and the Publicly Funded Child Care program was also funded, though lawmakers didn’t increase the funding, as childcare experts had urged them to do.
Lawmakers also approved a pilot program that would allow employers who apply to be a part of the program to share the cost of childcare. Participating employers would split the cost between them, the state, and the eligible employee.
The newest legislation will have to have a quick turnaround to be implemented, since the current General Assembly’s current term ends Dec. 31. If it isn’t approved before then, the bill will need to be reintroduced at the start of the new General Assembly in 2027.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: 9 years ago, gun violence took my father. Today, Ohio political silence is costing more lives
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal)Oct. 12 marked nine years since my father was murdered.
Nine years. Nearly a decade of birthdays, holidays, milestones, and ordinary moments marked by the absence of someone who should still be here.
People often talk about grief as something that fades with time. What I’ve learned is that grief never ends. It evolves, but it never leaves.
It shows up in empty chairs at family dinners. It lingers in the silence during holidays. It appears during life’s happiest moments, reminding you of the person who should have been there to celebrate with you.
Since my father’s life was taken, our country has endured an unprecedented era of gun violence. Families across Ohio and throughout the nation have joined a club that no one ever wants to become a member of.
Children have buried parents. Parents have buried children. Communities have been rattled by bullets and forever changed by violence. Local economies have felt the tremendous cost that gun violence imposes.
Hospitals, victim service providers, mental health professionals, schools, law enforcement agencies, and community organizations have stretched resources to meet growing needs.
Behind every statistic is a family.
Behind every number is a name.
And behind every act of violence is grief that never truly ends.
Some families are experiencing that grief for the first time today.
At this very moment, someone in Ohio may be receiving a phone call that will divide their life into a “before” and an “after.” They are planning a funeral they never imagined having to arrange.
They are answering impossible questions from children. They are helping parents navigate a loss no parent should ever experience. They are trying to understand what life looks like without someone they love.
Many of these tragedies are preventable.
While America has recently seen encouraging declines in homicides, early data suggests some of the largest decreases on record. Yet another crisis continues to grow in the shadows. Suicide rates remain at all time highs and continue to claim lives, often erasing much of the progress made elsewhere.
Since the beginning of 2017, the year my father was murdered, an estimated 409,640 Americans have died from firearm-related causes and another 321,721 have been injured.
The United States has experienced 4,973 mass shootings and more than 17,000 unintentional shootings. Most troubling of all, at least 47,725 children and teens have been shot or killed. Behind every one of those numbers is a family, a community, and a future forever changed.
Those aren’t just statistics. One of those numbers is my dad. They are our neighbors, classmates, teammates, friends, sons, daughters, mothers, and fathers. They are empty chairs at dinner tables, missed birthdays, unfinished dreams, and families forced to navigate a lifetime of grief.
That reality forces us to ask an important question:
What can we do when someone is experiencing the darkest moment of their life?
How do we intervene before a tragedy occurs?
How do we protect a person from themselves while also protecting those around them?
One answer is the adoption of common-sense policies such as Extreme Risk Protection Orders.
This is not about taking away constitutional rights. It is about creating a legal, temporary intervention during a crisis. It is about giving families and communities another tool to save a life.
The same is true for secure firearm storage laws. We have witnessed far too many tragedies involving children who gained access to loaded, unsecured firearms. In a matter of seconds, lives are forever altered.
Responsible gun ownership includes responsible gun storage.
That should not be controversial.
In fact, it should be a conversation we have more often.
And yet, as we enter another election season, I cannot help but notice the silence.
Candidates are asking for votes. Campaign signs are appearing in our neighborhoods. Speeches are being given. Promises are being made.
But where are the conversations about firearm deaths?
Where are the discussions about protecting children from their leading cause of death?
Where are the proposed solutions for reducing suicides, preventing accidental shootings, supporting families impacted, and saving lives?
Too many candidates seem afraid to engage in these conversations because they are difficult. Some fear being labeled “anti-gun.” Others avoid the topic altogether because it is politically uncomfortable.
But difficult conversations should not make us silent.
They should challenge us to think creatively.
They should encourage us to ask hard questions.
They should inspire current and future leaders to seek solutions.
Most importantly, they should help us save lives.
Gun violence has been the leading cause of death for children and teens in America for years. It surpasses car crashes and many diseases that once dominated those discussions. This is a uniquely American crisis, and it demands uniquely American leadership.
The conversation should not be about choosing between the Second Amendment and public safety.
We can support both.
The Second Amendment is a constitutional right. But with every right comes responsibility.
Responsible gun ownership means storing firearms securely and away from children. It means recognizing that guns are not toys. It means understanding the consequences when firearms fall into the wrong hands.
It means having honest conversations about risk, accountability, and prevention. And it means coming to terms with that guns are dangerous and should be viewed that way by both gun owners and non-gun owners alike.
These discussions are not attacks on responsible gun owners.
They are opportunities to define what responsible ownership looks like.
For nine years, I have carried the pain of losing my father. Other families have carried that burden for decades. Some are carrying it for the very first time today.
That is why I am asking every candidate running for local office, state office, governor, or any position of public trust a simple question:
What will you do to save lives?
What policies will you support to protect children?
How will you encourage responsible gun ownership?
How will you address suicide prevention?
How will you handle the mental health crisis in our state and country?
How will you support survivors and victims’ families?
What difficult conversations are you willing to have?
The answers matter.
Because leadership is not measured by the conversations we avoid. Leadership is measured by the challenges we are willing to confront.
Ohio stands at a crossroads. We can choose action. We can choose prevention. We can choose policies that save lives and support families.
Or we can choose silence. And silence is not a political strategy.
Silence is not leadership, it’s complacency.
Silence is surrendering our responsibility to protect our children and accepting preventable tragedies as inevitable.
Silence is accepting that another family will receive the phone call that changes everything and failing those who can no longer speak for themselves.
Silence is avoiding the difficult conversations because they are politically uncomfortable and refusing to confront a problem that continues to devastate families across Ohio and our nation.
Silence is the absence of courage when courage is needed most.
And silence will not save a single life.
Nine years after losing my father, I know silence has never healed a wound, prevented a tragedy, or saved a life and one thing that I know for certain: every life saved means another family won’t have to experience the grief that mine lives with every day.
That alone makes these conversations worth having.
When the next family receives the phone call that changes everything, will we be able to say we did everything we could to prevent it?
Because the question before us is no longer whether we can afford to have these conversations. The question is whether we can afford another life lost because we refused to.
After nine years without my father, and after more than 738,184 Americans shot, killed, or injured by firearms since his murder, I already know the answer.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Skill games saga ends with outlawed gambling machines removed … for now
text:
State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, where business owners and volunteer organizations urged lawmakers to pass legislation to legalize and tax skill games. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital Star) Pennsylvania’s skill game industry grew for more than a decade in a legal gray area where courts said the commonwealth’s gambling laws couldn’t touch them. 
That changed earlier this year, when the state Supreme Court said the estimated 70,000 skill game machines in small businesses and private clubs across the state were, in fact, unlicensed slot machines and therefore illegal.
Now, those machines sit unplugged and dark, awaiting transfer to storage and an uncertain fate, after state lawmakers were unable to reach a compromise to tax and regulate the industry before the high court’s ruling took effect Oct. 14.
The General Assembly’s inaction, with only five days left in the current session, means a multi-billion dollar revenue stream for thousands of businesses and organizations, such as volunteer fire companies, will disappear, at least temporarily.
While some lawmakers and members of the public held negative sentiments about skill games, citing the expansion of gambling and the associated societal ills, most people favored legalization, according to the Franklin and Marshall College Poll in June. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than seven out of 10 people who responded said they were in favor of regulating and taxing skill games, up from 60 percent in February 2024.
“There was generally public support for this idea of fixing this problem,” Berwood A. Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at F&M, said. 
He added that even if the notion of legalizing skill games had been unpopular, lawmakers had cover from the Supreme Court. In its opinion, the justices noted the General Assembly “has spoken clearly,” by amending the state Gaming Act in 2017 to make clear that skill games are legally indistinguishable from slot machines.
“If interested parties find the application of the General Assembly’s laws to be undesirable, the proper remedy lies with the same legislative body that wrote those laws,” Justice David Wecht wrote for the court.
Those interested parties showed up at the Capitol by thousands, loudly stating what was at stake for skill game operators and their communities. 
At an Oct. 6 rally on the Capitol steps, Delaware County tavern owner Joe McGee said the skill games in his bars have helped him improve his business and support the local volunteer fire companies and youth baseball programs while keeping the price of a Miller Lite at $3 or $4.
Supreme Court denies request to extend deadline for skill games

“All we want is sensible regulation, and we need it now. We can’t wait. We can’t wait till next year,” McGee said, flanked by hundreds of fellow business owners and lawmakers.
So why hasn’t the legislature been able to pass legislation on skill games?
“I don’t think anyone can explain why certain things get done and others don’t in the legislature,” Yost said, adding that the seemingly straightforward task masked layers of ideological complexity even within the same caucus.
He noted Republicans, who control the Senate, are generally loath to increase the size of government by creating new revenue streams, but at the same time are pro-small business and might balk at anything that would harm them.
“Our divided government has kind of led to policy moderation and that means some things that have a lot of support don’t happen because it runs up against something that one of the parties is opposed to,” Yost said. He noted broadly popular initiatives such as privatizing liquor sales and school choice have failed because of partisan ideology. 
State Sen. Camera Bartolotta (R-Washington) said that while she sees the value of skill games to businesses and community organizations, she opposed Gov. Josh Shapiro’s plan to direct much of the revenue from a proposed tax to mass transit, which more heavily benefits large urban areas than her rural district. 
“I’m not going to look my constituents in the eye when they don’t have public transportation and say, ‘We’re going to ship it all to this place where it doesn’t help you,’” said Bartolotta, who was one of the Republican incumbents targeted by skill game interests in this year’s primary.
Spokespeople for Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) and House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) did not return messages from the Capital-Star requesting interviews. 
Yost added that the skill game issue is unique because of the way the industry grew upon shaky legal footings.
“I can’t remember anything analogous to this,” he said. 
Skill games in a Virginia corner store. (Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)
The history of skill games in Pennsylvania
 The company that would become the predominant force behind skill gaming sought to legitimize gambling in spaces where illicit video poker operations had lurked for decades.  
In 2013, Georgia-based Pace-O-Matic (POM) arranged for Pennsylvania State Police to seize one of the earliest skill game machines at the American Italian Club in Aliquippa, Beaver County, according to the company’s website.
After examining the machine, Beaver County Common Pleas Judge Harry Knafelc ruled in 2014 that winning a series of puzzles and memory games was based predominantly on skill. For that reason, the judge ruled, the machine was distinct from a slot machine and “a gambling device per se.”
Neither county prosecutors nor the state attorney general’s office, then led by Attorney General Kathleen Kane, challenged the ruling, and a legal path for skill games was blazed.
Since the 2014 ruling, POM has won five rulings in favor of the machines’ legality, including the 2023 Commonwealth Court ruling that the Supreme Court overturned this year.
Pennsylvania’s casinos launched following the 2004 passage of the Horse Racing Development and Gaming Act. State lawmakers spent years debating how to regulate and tax it to support horse racing and tax relief.



Quotation







“This is one of those situations that I view as the pursuit of the perfect at the expense of the good. A good spot for most Pennsylvanians is a compromise on regulation and taxation that lets businesses keep some of the revenue. That shouldn’t be an unattainable goal.


– Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick


While one owner surrendered his license after being charged with lying to regulators about his ties to a Scranton organized crime family, the casino business grew over two decades into a $7 billion industry with nearly every flavor of gambling in 17 casinos, truck stops and online.
Skill gaming grew too, and while there are no official numbers on its size, Gov. Josh Shapiro’s proposal to tax the industry put the potential new revenue at $2 billion with a 52% levy on gross revenue, allowing an inference that the industry generates in excess of $4 billion annually.
As skill games became increasingly popular with players and business owners, who shared in the revenue, others in the legal gaming business took notice and pushed back. In addition to casinos, which lobbied heavily against plans to legalize skill games, the Pennsylvania Lottery claimed in 2019 that skill games cost it $138 million in sales. 
Lawmakers were divided over the situation. Former state Sen. Tommy Tomlinson introduced a bill that year that would make “a criminal offense for anyone to knowingly make, assemble, maintain, lease or sell Games of Skill.” It was the first of several bills to simply outlaw the devices.
Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) introduced his first legislation to regulate and tax skill games in 2023, with a proposal to require annual licensing fees of $1 million for distributors, $25,000 for operators and $250 for individual establishments. It was estimated to bring in about $300 million in tax revenue.
Yaw’s district includes Miele Manufacturing, which makes the physical machines. He did not respond to a request for comment.
Yaw and other lawmakers have since floated legislation to tax skill games at different rates. 
Senate leaders endorsed a plan to tax skill games at 35%. Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming), whose district includes skill game maker Miele Manufacturing, sponsored competing legislation to tax the machines at 16%. Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) also introduced a bill to impose a monthly fee of $500 per machine.
Miele Group, based in Muncy Township, Lycoming County, manufactures Pennsylvania Skill Games, which have been the subject of legislative efforts to regulate and tax the slot machine-like devices. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Casino slot machines and video gaming terminals are taxed between 34% and 54% depending on the category of casino. While lawmakers broadly agreed that they needed to act before the Oct 14 deadline, no action was taken. 
Four lawmakers, Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) and Reps. Danilo Burgos (D-Philadelphia) and Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne) filed an emergency petition asking the court to extend the deadline to give the legislature more time to work
The petition was later withdrawn and subsequently refiled without Burgos’ name. That was a result of pressure from Bradford, who said support for Burgos’ legislative proposal by rank and file lawmakers undermined the leadership, SpotlightPA reported.
Ultimately, the court rejected the request without comment and the deadline passed without action.
Jonathan Caulkins, professor of operations research and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University, said he wouldn’t view the inaction as a failure on the part of the legislature.
He noted in a commentary for The Conversation that was published by the Capital-Star earlier this month that the focus on taxing skill games overlooks the bigger picture of whether gambling should be freely and widely available.
“One could argue that the error was in the earlier legislation that left it ambiguous as to whether skill games were actually gambling devices, or that the courts took so long to clarify that they are,” Caulkins said in an email.  
Even if the legislature’s inaction resulting in skill games being removed from their places around the commonwealth represents a policy decision, Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick said, simply letting the deadline pass is neither orderly nor decisive.
“I guess if you don’t want these things in the state, I guess you won, but they can come back,” he said. “There’s a lot of opportunity cost for the state and there’s a lot of things that could have been resolved in a more efficient way and that to me suggests that a different policy could have been more productive.”
While the situation appears complex, Borick said the question before the legislature is simple. 
“This is one of those situations that I view as the pursuit of the perfect at the expense of the good,” he said. “A good spot for most Pennsylvanians is a compromise on regulation and taxation that lets businesses keep some of the revenue. That shouldn’t be an unattainable goal.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Catching Our Eye News Roundup, Oct. 19, 2026
text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• The overtly partisan Ohio Supreme Court. The Columbus Dispatch’s Laura A. Bischoff reports, “Democrat Jennifer Brunner loses federal lawsuit over partisan election labels.”
With less than three weeks left before Election Day, a federal court upheld a state law requiring partisan labels for candidates running for appellate and supreme court seats in Ohio.
Ohio Supreme Court Justice Jennifer Brunner, the only Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, filed a lawsuit over the law, saying it violated her First and Fifth Amendment rights. She argued that forcing candidates to carry a party label conflicts with judicial ethics rules.
In July 2021, Gov. Mike DeWine signed into law a measure requiring party labels in general elections for some judges. Since then, Democrats have lost every race for Ohio Supreme Court.
• Jim Jordan’s plans. CNN reports, “House Republicans face a potential clash over who will be GOP leader if they lose the midterms.”
When House Speaker Mike Johnson decided in September to send lawmakers home early to their districts ahead of the midterm elections, House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan quietly made clear that he would have handled the situation differently, according to a source close to Jordan.
In a private conversation with one Republican lawmaker, Jordan said he would have kept lawmakers in Washington longer to hold more votes that would be politically challenging for Democrats. He also expressed interest in holding more votes on President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill that has been blocked in the Republican-led Senate, arguing that would help House Republicans on the campaign trail even if the bill won’t be signed into law.
• Bernie Moreno’s plans. Bloomberg reports, “Senator Expects ‘Last Supper’ Budget Bill if GOP Loses Power.”
Sen. Bernie Moreno wants senators to stay in session from the election through the end of the year without a break to pass a party-line budget bill with all their priorities if Republicans lose in the midterms next month.
• Ohio Womens’ Monument. The Toledo Blade’s Danny Eldredge reports, “State leaders unveil Ohio Women’s Monument.”
A new landmark honoring generations of women who fought for suffrage and equality is now established on the grounds of the Ohio Statehouse.
The Ohio Women’s Monument was unveiled Wednesday after more than six years of work by the Ohio Women’s Suffrage Centennial Commission, Capitol Square Foundation, Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board, and Ohio Arts Council.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: The story Florida’s new driver licenses tell ain’t necessarily so
text:
The new design for Florida driver licenses via DHSMV.Listen up: Florida is back.
WAY back.
Not that we were ever not the free-est, greatest, top-est state in the USA, it’s that we just got even more awesome.
Our governor is presenting us with a brand-new driver’s license design, and it is HAWT.
The old one was, like, so mid, as the kids say, so vanilla.
On the front, there’s a piece of the state seal kind of tangled up in big letters reading “FL,” and on the back, there’s another “FL” and a little Florida outline (in case you forget where you live) with American flag stripes kind of flopping around.
Totally “Ohio,” as the kids also say, or did last month, at least: It can be hard to keep up, even for us hip folk.
But, thanks to the artistes at the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicle the new driver’s license is FIRE.
On the front, it says, “Florida,” like you’d expect, but the “O” is an orange!”
So cute.
Then you got your state seal, some palm trees, and a sweet little gator wrapped around that gold star that shows you’re not an illegal or a terrorist or, as our vice-president likes to point out, some non-European weirdo trying to destroy American culture.
That’s not all, either.

 Something less foreign

“Matanzas” means massacre.

Our governor, who knows Jesus spoke English, chose to call the hurricane Isaiah, which is obviously a fine American Bible name.

The new design for Florida driver licenses via DHSMV.
 Circle of Life

The new license honors the Ghosts of Citrus Past.

Debbie Downers complain the Feds won’t put manatees on the Endangered Species List, and say stuff like, “Jeez, Florida only has around 8,000 manatees total and as of October this year we’ve lost 500, some dying of natural causes, many dying because dudes like to run over them with their jet skis and power boats.”
It’s the Circle of Life!

Moseley was a job-creator, owner of a fully staffed plantation in Jefferson County where at least 80 Africans learned valuable skills such as cotton-picking.

 Freedom!

The libs in Washington didn’t let us alone, so we were forced to fire on Fort Sumter.

Great patriots still cherish the snake and his warning: They waved the flag when the America-hating Barack Obama became president, then they waved it again on Jan. 6, 2021, when True Americans rallied on a Day of Love at the Capitol, trying to stop the communists, the feminists, the gays, the immigrants, and the ungrateful minorities from stealing the election from our rightful liege lord, Donald J.
