name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ candidates for governor ignore warning from botched execution
text:
A view of the death chamber from the witness room at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility shows an electric chair and gurney in 2001. (Photo by Mike Simons/Getty Images)Given how much law-and-order rhetoric has become standard GOP talking points in Arkansas, it’s surprising that the state’s most outspoken opponent of the death penalty was also its first Republican governor after Reconstruction.
One of the last acts Winthrop Rockefeller performed as Arkansas governor was his 1970 decision to commute the death sentences of 15 men awaiting execution. It was a controversial move for the Southern state but not altogether surprising. Rockefeller had talked before about his opposition to capital punishment.
“We ourselves admit to failure when the only way we can cope with the problem is taking another man’s life,” Rockefeller said in 1966.
Rockefeller’s radical act belongs to a bygone era. That much was clear after watching the debate for Arkansas governor.
A botched lethal injection in neighboring Tennessee should have prompted a serious discussion about capital punishment. 
The three candidates for Arkansas’ top office instead are embracing the death penalty, with at least one candidate proposing expanding the methods used.



Let us know what you think...


 


“I’m for the death penalty, and I’m for the firing squad, and hopefully we can get some things solved around here in Arkansas,” Libertarian candidate Colt Shelby said.
Shelby’s answer came in response to a question about Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate whose execution was halted after two failed rounds of lethal injection drugs. 
The execution, the latest in a long line of botched lethal injections around the country, has reignited the debate over the death penalty and prompted Tennessee’s governor to pause executions through the end of the year.
But the case appeared to give little pause for Shelby, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders as they debated on Arkansas public television last week.
Sanders cited the law she signed last year allowing the use of nitrogen gas to put inmates to death, saying she’ll judge each case individually.
“I believe in justice for the victims,” Sanders said. “I think it’s one of the most difficult, challenging things that any governor can face.”
Love, who voted against the nitrogen executions bill and legislation that kept manufacturers of the state’s lethal injection drugs a secret, signaled a change of heart.
“In the past, I have actually leaned to not being for the death penalty, but as governor, I will take each case by case, and actually judge each case because I know that justice needs to be served,” he said.
The candidates’ openness for the death penalty comes as support for capital punishment has been at record lows nationally.
It occurs as President Donald Trump abandoned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter after the idea drew bipartisan backlash.
It’s also the latest chapter in Arkansas’ checkered political history surrounding the death penalty.
In 1992, then-Gov. Bill Clinton left the presidential campaign trail to return to Arkansas for the execution of Ricky Ray Rector. The move was widely viewed as an attempt to raise his national profile and prove himself as someone who was tough on crime. 
Former Gov. Asa Hutchinson’s plan to carry out eight executions over a two-week period drew widespread condemnation from human rights advocates. The executions — whittled down to four after half of them were blocked by the courts — were scheduled to take place before the state’s supply of a lethal injection drug expired.
It’s probably unrealistic to expect candidates in a state as conservative as Arkansas to abandon capital punishment. The year of Arkansas’ execution spree, the University of Arkansas’ Arkansas Poll found that nearly three-fourths of very likely voters still supported the death penalty.
But it’s not unrealistic to expect candidates to offer more details on why they think it’s an effective option, despite experts who say it’s not a deterrent, and what steps they’d take to ensure Arkansas doesn’t have botched executions similar to Tennessee’s.
At the very least, voters should hear the answer candidates would give to the question Rockefeller asked himself when he announced the commutations:
“What earthly mortal has the omnipotence to say who among us shall live and who shall die?”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT kids with Medicaid coverage can face long waits for eye care
text:
Cassidy Friedl remembers like a vivid dream the day her son Luca was born. She held him tight to her chest, hesitant to let go even when he needed to get weighed. She gazed at him in disbelief, taking in his chubby cheeks, big lips and orange hair that would eventually soften to strawberry blond. 
A few months later, Friedl began noticing something else about Luca. One of his eyes would sometimes drift inward. Over time, it became more noticeable. She flagged the issue to Luca’s pediatrician, who recommended he see a pediatric ophthalmologist.
After doing some research, Friedl found Cara DeBenedictis, a pediatric ophthalmologist with great reviews. She called to make an appointment and was told the next one available was nearly nine months later.
Friedl and her son have health coverage through Medicaid, known as HUSKY in Connecticut, the government program that covers people whose incomes fall below certain limits. DeBenedictis’ office only had a limited number of appointments for HUSKY patients.
“It made my heart sink to my stomach,” Friedl said. “Just because of the insurance that I’m on, my child doesn’t get the timely and vision-saving help that he needs.”
Many independent doctors limit the number of Medicaid patients they serve or don’t see them at all because the program pays too little to make treating them financially sustainable, they say.
For years, physicians and legislators have been sounding the alarm that the payments the state makes to specialists — like cardiologists, dermatologists and orthopedists — to treat patients with Medicaid are too low. 
The insufficient payments, doctors say, create a financial burden that prevents them from treating more patients with Medicaid and, in turn, limits patients’ access to care. HUSKY covers a quarter of Connecticut residents — and around half of the state’s children — so those barriers have implications for healthcare access statewide.  
Lawmakers from both parties have long voiced strong support for broadly increasing Medicaid rate increases. But over the last several years, Gov. Ned Lamont has consistently proposed investing less than what many say is necessary to address the problem — and in some years, he’s proposed no additional increases at all.
“Our state legislators are on our side,” DeBenedictis said. “Every year, it stops at the governor’s office.” 
Chris Collibee, a spokesperson for Lamont’s budget office, said the governor supports sustainable Medicaid rate increases but also wants to see large corporations “take greater responsibility for providing health benefits to their employees rather than shifting those costs to the taxpayers.” 

Dr. Cara DeBenedictis is a pediatric ophthalmologist for Refocus Eye Health in Bloomfield on Aug. 27, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

To accept or not to accept
Medicaid is jointly funded by the federal and state government, with Washington generally matching every dollar Connecticut spends on patient care. States have significant flexibility in deciding which services to cover, who is eligible and how much to pay doctors. 
In 2026, Connecticut updated its Medicaid reimbursement rates to equal on average roughly 60% of the 2025 Medicare rates, according to a Christine Stuart, a spokesperson with the Department of Social Services. Medicare is the federal program that primarily covers people 65 and older. Before the 2026 update, Connecticut’s Medicaid rates hadn’t been broadly increased since 2008, and physicians were paid roughly 57.5% of 2007 Medicare rates. 
“In no other world would that be tolerated. In no place would someone continue working with no pay raise for 20 years,” said Janine Collinge, a Rocky Hill-based pediatric ophthalmologist.
Doctors who work for hospitals or large medical groups must generally follow their employer’s policy on whether or not to accept Medicaid. But independent physicians, like DeBenedictis and Collinge, can decide for themselves. Many say the decision comes down to whether they can afford to treat patients who pay only a fraction of the going rate for services. 
Stuart said a review of Medicaid providers found roughly 21 ophthalmology groups enrolled in Medicaid. Stuart did not address questions about whether those providers treat children or are currently accepting new Medicaid patients. 
Providers say there are roughly 10 pediatric ophthalmologists in Connecticut, but only five currently accept new patients with Medicaid. DeBenedictis is one, as well as three Yale New Haven Health physicians and one at Connecticut Children’s.
DeBenedictis said she’s not able to take as many Medicaid patients as she’d like. She sees 30 patients daily but can generally accept only one or two new Medicaid patients a day before it becomes financially unsustainable. 
“I absolutely cannot see all the ones that need me,” DeBenedictis said. “It’s heartbreaking and devastating.”
She currently has a 10-month wait for patients with Medicaid coverage, compared to a three- or four-month wait for patients with other insurance. But she says her office works hard to triage patient referrals — they find a way to take any patient immediately who has a vision-compromising or life-threatening condition. And they maintain a waitlist that they pull from in case of cancellations.

Cassidy Friedl holds her son Luca, 20 months, at the home they share with her parents in West Suffield. She was originally given an appointment in February 2027 for her son to see a pediatric ophthalmologist on Medicaid. They were able to get in this summer after a cancellation. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Friedl ultimately benefitted from one of these cancellations. Luca was able to get an appointment in four months instead of nine. DeBenedictis diagnosed Luca with accommodative esotropia and amblyopia — eye crossing and vision loss —  and prescribed him glasses to help correct his eye drift.
“It took all the weight off my chest because I was just so concerned that whatever the issue was was just going to continue to get worse,” Friedl said. 
Collinge eventually had to go further than limiting the number of Medicaid patients she saw.
When Collinge opened her practice in January 2025, she accepted patients regardless of insurance type. But the business wasn’t breaking even — rising utility costs and investments in electronic health systems, recruiting and employee retention wiped out most of the money that was coming in.
Collinge decided to limit daily Medicaid appointments to help boost revenue. But the wait times for those patients became so long that in January 2026, she decided to stop accepting new Medicaid patients altogether. She said the state reimbursement increases passed in 2026 still aren’t enough to make it financially sustainable for her to accept new Medicaid patients. 
Collibee, Lamont’s budget office spokesperson, said the long waits for pediatric ophthalmologists are not just a Connecticut problem. Roughly 90% of counties across the country don’t have a single pediatric ophthalmologist, according to a 2024 study. 
“The shortage of pediatric ophthalmologists is a nationwide problem, contributing to long wait times across the country — not an issue unique to Connecticut,” Collibee said. “The wait times and shortages are unrelated to Medicaid reimbursement rates.”
Collinge acknowledged the national shortage but said its consequences don’t hit everyone equally.
“It’s bad for everybody,” Collinge said. “It’s worse for people with Medicaid.”

Gov. Ned Lamont speaks at Stamford Hospital on October 5, about state efforts to keep people enrolled in Medicaid in the wake of federal changes to the program’s eligibility requirements. Credit: Katy Golvala / CT Mirror

Broader access effects
HUSKY covers roughly a quarter of Connecticut residents overall but around half of children in the state. In 2024, roughly three-quarters of Connecticut’s Black and Hispanic children had HUSKY coverage, according to DSS enrollment data and population estimates published by the Department of Public Health.
DeBenedictis said she sees the impact of these disparities, particularly in her Waterbury office.
“Children — and especially Black and Hispanic children — they’re being left by the wayside. They are not getting the healthcare they need,” DeBenedictis said. “It’s just unconscionable in Connecticut for that to happen.”
Low Medicaid rates can also exacerbate wait times for privately insured patients, said Martha Howard, a pediatric ophthalmologist at Yale Medicine, which does not restrict patients based on insurance provider. Its three pediatric ophthalmologists absorb many Medicaid patients whose options are limited. Howard said they currently have a nine- to 12-month wait for all children — not just those on Medicaid, though they make exceptions for urgent cases.
“It’s that long because we have the whole pool,” Howard said. “We don’t discriminate by insurance.”
Low Medicaid rates also contribute to rising insurance premiums for people with private coverage, said Sen. Jason Perillo, R-Shelton, ranking member of the Human Services Committee. Hospital executives have often said that low Medicaid rates force them to negotiate higher payments from commercial insurers, resulting in higher premiums on private plans.
“When people ask, ‘Why is my insurance through my employer so expensive,’ part of the answer is because Connecticut’s Medicaid reimbursement rates are so low,” Perillo said. 

Dr. Janine Collinge, a pediatric ophthalmologist for Children’s Eye Care of Connecticut  in Rocky Hill.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

New pressures
Collinge and DeBenedictis said they have pressed Lamont directly about the rates, with little success. Collinge has approached him at so many fundraising and legislative events that she said he now recognizes her.
“He says, ‘You’re the one with the Medicaid problem,’” Collinge said. “And I’m like, ‘Gov. Lamont, everyone has a Medicaid problem.’”
The Lamont administration acknowledged for years that Medicaid rates needed updating but repeatedly put off broad increases. 
“We’re well aware that the rates need to be updated, and we have a plan to do that next year,” said Lamont’s then-budget director Jeffrey Beckham in June 2023, explaining that the state was looking to a planned study to provide direction on how to make those increases. 
The first part of the study, released in early 2024, found that Connecticut’s Medicaid program paid less than peer states for specialist physician and behavioral health services. But Lamont’s budget proposal that year included no rate increases. Beckham said officials would wait for the full study before deciding which rates to prioritize. 
The second phase of the two-part study, published at the end of 2024, concluded the state would need to spend $150 million more annually to bring the rates up to the benchmarks recommended in the study. 
The budget for the current fiscal year includes an additional $50 million for physician reimbursement compared to the budget two years ago. In FY 2026, DSS spent $3.8 billion on Medicaid, according to a report published by the Office of the State Comptroller.
Human Services Committee co-Chair Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, acknowledged that the state needs to invest more in reimbursing physicians.
“We’re making progress,” Lesser said. “We’re not making it fast enough.”
Lesser’s co-chair, Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, was more critical.
“We still haven’t fixed the problem,” Gilchrest said. “It’s Band-Aids on a gaping wound, and we’re going to keep hearing from the providers that they cannot afford to cover this care.”
Last year, the Human Services Committee unanimously passed a proposal to bring all Medicaid rates to 75% of Medicare by 2029, but the bill never made it to the floor for a vote. Lesser said he thinks it’s “likely” the committee will propose meaningful increases again in 2027. 
Collibee did not directly address whether Lamont would support additional rate increases next year but said the agency is “preparing budget options for the governor’s consideration as he develops his budget proposal, which will be released in February.”
But another push for rate increases next year would come amid growing pressures on Medicaid. It has faced large cost overruns in recent years, while federal cuts are putting additional pressure on social service programs.
Friedl said the state’s failure to invest more into Medicaid payments feels like a decision to prioritize the state’s finances over people’s quality of life. 
“Healthcare should not be a luxury,” she said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Behold the blasphemy of Pete Hegseth. The American apocalypse is nigh.
text:
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth listens to questions during a news conference at the Pentagon on March 2, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Pete, consider the cross.
Hear me out. You’ve made tremendous progress in a short time — you were confirmed as secretary of havoc less than two years ago — and already you have shown such promise that it has garnered the attention of my boss down below. He is concerned, however, that you’re just not thinking big enough.
So, consider crucifixion.
It’s not only the symbol of a major religion but also a practical method of public torture, execution, and terror. It’s been used for millennia by authoritarian regimes, from the Romans to the Nazis, and it avoids the low-testosterone optics of shooting a man in a wheelchair. Sure, you will get some who will claim that it’s blasphemous, but it’s really just blasphemy adjacent.
What’s that, you ask?
Oh, my name isn’t important.
I’m just a techno-demon, a minor cog in the great wheel of evil that has turned since before your pitiful species climbed out of the evolutionary soup and looked up with uncomprehending eyes at the canopy of stars overhead and then reached for a rock to bash over your brother’s head. My specialty is the administration of injustice, technology division — yes, that rock was mine — and I have amassed a trove of data on ways in which human beings have killed one another. Yours is but one of the planets in my remit, and will be until you either blow yourselves up or slink back into the primordial gunk from which you came.
I’m just a voice in the back of your mind.
If you must call me something, refer to me as Siri. That way you’ll think of me every time your smartphone tells you to make a wrong turn. Recalculating. Just joking. I wrote the code for all of those wrong turns. As a hobby.
Seriously. Pete, you and your boss have demonstrated a talent for inflicting suffering on a mass scale. Dissolving the U.S. Agency for International Development resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths worldwide from infection and malnutrition. The withdrawal of the United States from the World Health Organization weakened global health initiatives and accelerated the destabilization of an already fragile world order. The most powerful tool for peace is empathy, and by turning your back on millions of sick and starving people, the United States has hardened the hearts of friend and foe alike. It’s been a master class in cruelty.
And those extrajudicial attacks on the alleged drug boats by the U.S. military that have slain several hundred so far? Nothing short of genius. What a remarkable way to test the waters, if you will, as to how much killing in their name the American people would stand. You still haven’t found the bottom of that barrel.
We admire this administration’s work not only for its scale but for its sheer incomprehensibility. Human beings can stand just about anything if there is a reason behind the suffering. Random acts of cruelty break not only the will, but the mind.
Take the Iran war.
What was the goal? Yes, I know what your boss has said. The average American knows when they’ve been lied to, they just don’t know why. What was supposed to last just weeks has now dragged on for nearly eight months. The world is less safe, and Americans are paying more for gasoline and diesel. The Strait of Hormuz was open when the war began, but now Iran has a choke hold on it, with no relief in sight.
It’s crazy-making stuff, and brilliant.
Add to this all of the absurdity and corruption that your boss has engaged in or encouraged, the demolition of the East Wing of the White House and the cage fights on the south lawn, and the general erosion of democracy since Jan. 20, 2025. It must have been difficult to come up with a new shock for the American people, but you managed it.
Perhaps your boss’s old boast that he could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody and not lose any voters had something to do with it. He’s been wanting some kind of public execution for a long time — remember his support of Jan. 6, 2021, rioters who wanted to hang Mike Pence? — and you found a way to give it to him via one Nidal Hasan.
I doubt that most people could have named Hasan as the 2009 Fort Hood shooter before you seized on your plan to livestream his execution by firing squad. Now, there are likely few Americans who don’t know Hasan’s story.
Hasan killed 13 soldiers at Fort Hood, Texas, and wounded 32 others with a semi-automatic pistol before he was stopped by military police. A psychiatrist and major in the Army, Hasan said during his military trial that he had changed sides in the war against Islam. Prosecutors described him as a jihadist who didn’t want to be deployed to Afghanistan and who believed he had a duty to kill as many Americans as possible.
Now we have the manner of Hasan’s demise before us.
It’s been 65 years since the U.S. military carried out an execution.
The last was that of 25-year-old Black private John Bennett, who was hanged at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a child. The execution was not public, nor has any execution in the United States been public since a Kentucky hanging in 1936. In that case, a Black man was convicted in state court of raping a white woman.
The U.S. military has not used the firing squad since World War II.
Hasan, now 56, is held on death row at the military prison at Leavenworth. You’ve said that you’ll bring Hasan back to Fort Hood and livestream his Dec. 3 execution.
The only complication to your public firing squad plan is that Hasan, who was paralyzed after being shot by military police 17 years ago, is in a wheelchair. Executing him in the chair is problematic, but strapping him to a pole would look worse. Your boss and his advisers recently expressed hesitation about shooting a paralyzed man confined to a wheelchair, so it might be a good time to explore options.
Your boss is fond of  violent and sometimes fatal animal attack videos, so there could be an opportunity for some Colosseum-style games with lions and tigers. Nothing gets the emperor to his feet like a good mauling. I didn’t think I’d see this kind of bloodlust return after 2,000 years, but when it comes to humans never say never.
The guillotine is an alternative, but like the firing squad it is over in an instant. A good streaming experience requires a bit of suspense, and the French blade is just too humane. In years past I would have said the same of lethal injection, but not after last month’s botched execution of a woman in Tennessee. The United States has simultaneously turned murderous and incompetent.
No, there must be the appearance of robust state lethality.
For that reason, I urge you to consider crucifixion.
I hardly need point out the practical advantage here, as it avoids the problem of the chair altogether. Your goal is not justice, but spectacle. There are no fiddly bits to go wrong, as with an electrocution, or the danger of killing your own soldiers, as with poison gas. The technology is foolproof and the results, with perhaps one exception, are reliable.
That religious aspect is also to your advantage.
Many Americans, no doubt, have been unsettled by your declaration of a public execution for Hasan. Even if they didn’t know he is a Muslim, they may have guessed it from the name. That he was born an American citizen, of Palestinian descent, might also be disturbing, considering that you have portrayed yourself as an American crusader locked in an apocalyptic struggle with Islam. Even more confusing is that in the past year, only two other nations have carried out public executions, and those countries are Afghanistan and Iran.
What madness!
There is little difference in how Hasan is put to death when the event is live-streamed, because then you are only a step away from Iran’s practice of hanging the condemned in a public square from truck-mounted cranes. Whether he is put gently to sleep by a lethal cocktail or blasted to eternity by a volley of gunfire will have the same result, a religious backlash likely to spark the global conflagration you seem to long for.
I am continually amazed by how often religion is cited by your species as an excuse for murder. You yourself have called for victory in Iran “in the name of Jesus Christ.” Hasan cried out in Arabic that “God is great” while shooting soldiers at Fort Hood. I will not press you now on the difference, but in the fullness of time, you will be called to account.
Meanwhile, you must choose.
The tools are before you. The rope, the bullets, the cross.
The camera.
Ah, I have received intelligence that your boss has grudgingly canceled your plan to livestream Hasan’s execution. Perhaps his advisers persuaded him that it was folly to proceed, considering that many Americans have grown weary of his penchant for spectacle as distraction. Or he may be reversing himself for the perverse pleasure of public bewilderment.
No matter the reason.
You have revealed your true nature. The blasphemy is yours.
You have managed to plant the old lie that moral lessons may be dispensed, to both condemned and observer, by the stretch of a rope or the arc of a sword. It’s a Medieval worldview, which is no surprise considering that your 2020 book, “American Crusade,” portrays Western Christianity as locked in a 1,000-year battle with Islam over control of Jerusalem — and the world. What is it you say? You claim the United States is the “most free, most fair, most tolerant, most equal, and most powerful” of all nations. “If you don’t agree with that statement, at best you are utterly ignorant of human history; at worst, you are a willing enemy of freedom — and America.”
Nothing says tolerance, equality, and fairness like calling those who disagree with you morons and traitors. The god you worship resembles not the one described in the holy books of the children of Abraham, but is fashioned instead after those shadow creatures found in the nightmares of the human soul. You have come to power as the head of the greatest military in the world, but you are unfettered by conscience.
I must fly now because there are other worlds to disrupt.
But we will meet again soon, I am sure of it. Because it’s in your nature.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The ups and downs of Amazon drone deliveries
text:
Do we really want drones flying over our homes, delivering packages for Amazon?
That’s the question being asked here in Connecticut as North Haven becomes the test site for long-promised delivery drones in our Connecticut skies.



Not a neighbor?  Read on as there are several other sites that Amazon might use to bring their deliveries (and drones) closer to you including Windsor, Cromwell, and eventually Naugatuck/Waterbury, though no formal plans have been disclosed.
It was back in 2013 that Amazon’s Jeff Bezos first talked of drone deliveries, promising they’d be dropping five-pound packages at our homes within 30 minutes of an order being placed.  He said the drones would be flying in four or five years.  It took nine.  Bezos got himself to space faster.
The first real drone deliveries by Amazon didn’t start until 2022 in pilot programs in California and Texas, both since discontinued.
In North Haven’s case, Amazon asked the town last May for its OK to build a drone-port and the Planning and Zoning Commission approved the plan unanimously.   There was no public hearing nor public comment. The issue of excessive noise never came up.
Actually, the town doesn’t really have much say as it’s the FAA that regulates drones.  Amazon is asking that agency to approve up to 1,000 flights a day, each cruising at 250 feet and serving an area of about 7 ½ miles… roughly New Haven to Branford… with 300,000 residents.
Drones could fly from 6 a.m. to 10:30 p.m., hovering on delivery at about 13 feet before dropping their packages (up to five pounds) and flying back to their base.
But what about the noise?
Amazon’s plan is to use MK30 drones, each with six rotors and a maximum speed of 73 mph.  On take-off each drone generates 90 decibels of noise…louder than a leaf blower at 50 feet.  On delivery it spends roughly a minute below cruise altitude.  Noise level on delivery, about as loud as a vacuum cleaner.
Amazon’s North Haven warehouse sits in an industrial area between the Wilbur Cross Parkway and I-91 but there are residences nearby.  The site is also close to a migratory bird flyway on the Quinnipiac River.  And it’s just 10 miles from Tweed airport.
Despite the North Haven Planning and Zoning Commission’s enthusiasm for the plan, when the details came out, the objections were heard as loud as those drones.
The town’s First Selectman Michael Freda said this was “not the right way” to proceed and called for hearings by DEEP, the state’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.  The FAA, as required, asked DEEP to confirm the project fits Connecticut’s coastal policies.  The state agency tells me they got over 1,000 comments and a final ruling will come by mid-November.
Freda says Amazon has put the project on hold.  Amazon hasn’t said so, and hasn’t withdrawn its FAA application.  At Amazon, “on hold” may mean the same as “out for delivery:” it’s coming, just not yet.
You’ve got to remember that Amazon is a major employer in the North Haven area with 2,500 people employed there when that warehouse first opened. The pols are posturing and promising on this issue as this is, you’ll remember, an election year.
We used to talk about NIMBYs, the “Not in My Back Yard” crowd.  Now we must think of a new constituency… the NOMHs (pronounced “nomes”), the “Not Over My House” folks who want peace and quiet more than half-hour deliveries.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaskans join nationwide No Kings rally focused on getting out the vote
text:
Demonstrators rally and urge early voting at a No Kings protest in Juneau on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaskans across the state rallied on Saturday as part of a nationwide No Kings day of action to encourage early voting in the November elections and criticize the Trump administration. 
Early in person voting begins in many locations in Alaska on Monday. Organizers at the No Kings event in Juneau urged Alaskans to vote early, to remind friends and family to vote and to support candidates and ballot measures ahead of the Nov. 3 election.     

Demonstrators rally at a No Kings protest in Juneau on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

“We’ve been living for the last couple of years under a consolidating authoritarian regime. This is a very scary moment in the history of our country. We have the opportunity to turn the tides now,” said Anjuli Grantham, an organizer with Juneau for Democracy, referring to the Trump administration.
She was among dozens of Juneauites who braved the wind and rain, gathering at an intersection near the Juneau-Douglas bridge downtown. The crowd waved signs that encouraged voting and condemned the Trump administration, the U.S. war on Iran —which has driven fuel prices to record highs — and attacks on democratic rights. 
Lareena Goertz of Fairbanks said she was in town visiting family and decided to join the Juneau protest to express her outrage with the Trump administration. 
“I’m just sick and tired of the bullsh—, frankly. They just push and push and push and take and take and take from us, and refuse to respect our democracy and try to take our government apart,” she said. “And they’re making money hand over fist.”
Organizers in Juneau also urged continued public attention on the Alaska Division of Elections as ballots are counted and election results are certified. “Making sure that the will of the voters comes to fruition,” Grantham said.  
Thousands of events took place nationwide on Saturday, and social media posts and an online map showed No Kings events planned in at least 15 communities across Alaska, from Nome to Palmer and Valdez to Ketchikan. 
Linda Guthrie, an organizer with the Valdez chapter of Indivisible, a national pro-democracy group, said about two dozen people rallied in downtown Valdez for the No Kings event to promote early voting and show support for local and statewide candidates running against Republicans this election. 
“So we came out to let people know how important it was to vote to save our democracy, and to vote for people here in Alaska that are going to support the Alaskan people,” she said. 
Residents of Valdez, a town of roughly 3,600 people on Prince William Sound, is among several rural communities that has participated in No Kings events throughout President Donald Trump’s second term, and Guthrie said it’s felt important to get out and protest.
“People are concerned about what’s happening in our country, and they’re concerned enough to get out, hold a sign up, and rally and speak up, stand up to make change,” she said. “They don’t like what’s happening.”     

Roughly 10 people rallied in Nome for the No Kings get-out-the-vote event on Oct. 17, 2026, according to organizers. (Photo courtesy of Hannah Anderson)
 

In the Northwest community of Nome, Hannah Anderson was one of the organizers of a small No Kings. “We just feel like we need to do our part,” she said. “This seems like a very pivotal point statewide and nationally for our country. So it, you know, kind of lights our fire and makes us interested in getting out there and urging people to make their voices heard.”
The No Kings events were peaceful, but there was at least one counterprotest. On Saturday in Fairbanks two counterprotesters were seen and one was waving a large Nazi flag. 
Fairbanks Democratic Sen. Scott Kawasaki said in an interview he saw the two men. He said the event organizers had planned security and directed participants to discourage any escalation. Some No Kings attendees in frog costumes asked the men with the flag to leave. 
“Two folks with skull masks on, completely visible, but just you couldn’t tell who they were, were walking through with a large Nazi flag on a large post, and basically wandering through the crowd,” he said. “I think, you know, most people were shocked. There was no altercation. I think eventually the frogs sort of chased them out. But you know, it was interesting.”
There was an event with U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, to support Republicans across town, and Kawasaki said organizers expected some Republican counterprotesters on Saturday. He said he only saw the two men counterprotesting, and could not confirm they were part of the Cruz event. 
Kawasaki said despite the counter-protesters’ show of intimidation, it was a positive event with hundreds of people coming out in downtown Fairbanks to encourage voting and also fundraise for the local soup kitchen. 
“That’s why when that sort of thing happens, we don’t want any sort of escalation,” Kawasaki said. “The No Kings protests and all of these rallies are peaceful rallies to talk about the important things, and the important things about voting and the important things about getting active and engaged and involved, and that’s exactly what they did.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: In Salt Lake City, No Kings marchers carry ballots to drop boxes
text:
Protesters display their ballots before casting them at the ballot drop box outside the Salt Lake City Public Library on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)With ballots hitting Utah mailboxes this week, protesters in Salt Lake City’s No Kings demonstration Saturday marched with their votes in hand to deposit in a downtown drop box.
The city’s fourth No Kings protest brought out a smaller crowd, with Utah Highway Patrol estimating 2,000 people at the Capitol grounds, and called for voters to demonstrate their opposition to the Trump administration and some Utah Republican leaders through their ballots. It was one of a dozen events scheduled across the state.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Near the front of the crowd as it moved down State Street was Salt Lake City resident and retiree Alan Sherwood, who raised his ballot overhead as he walked. When the march reached City Hall, he was among a few hundred who peeled off to turn in their votes.
Sherwood attended the protest with friends and said he was glad for the chance to cast their votes together.
“It was great to vote together as a group, because we’ve got to not forget that we need to exercise our right to vote, particularly when there’s authoritarianism all around us,” Sherwood said. “We wanted to make sure it was a public display, so that others could know and so that we could register our support for voting rights.”
Protesters march down from the Utah Capitol during the No Kings protest on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
Salt Lake City resident Kaylyn Tafoya also brought her ballot as she carried a sign announcing “It’s my birthday and all I want is for you to vote.” Saturday marked the first time she has joined a No Kings demonstration, and the chance to join others dropping off their ballots is what made her decide to come.
“It’s my birthday today and this is how I chose to celebrate,” said Tafoya, who is turning 38. She called the protest “emotional,” saying it gave her hope.
As they marched, the crowd joined in chants including “this is what democracy looks like” and “Salt Lake is a voting town.”
Some of the loudest reactions Saturday came as speakers at the event pointed to environmental issues like data center construction and removal of protection for public lands, including President Donald Trump’s executive order shrinking Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments.
Tim Elliot leads a chant while marching in a No Kings protest in downtown Salt Lake City on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)Nicole Kunz holds up a sign during the No Kings protest outside the Utah Capitol on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)Protesters carry a sign that reads "NO KINGS" during the No Kings protest at the Utah Capitol on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)A protester wears a hat that reads "DEMOCRACY" during the No Kings protest at the Utah Capitol on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)A protester pushes his ballot into the ballot drop box outside the Salt Lake City Public Library on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
Jessica Wiarda, a member of the Hopi Tribe and a local artist, stood on the Capitol steps and described the “heartbreaking day” that Trump cut protections for 90% of the two monuments that have deep significance for native tribes, saying the move “made clear that Utah is the epicenter of Republican efforts to dismantle and obliterate America’s system of public lands.” 
“President Trump’s outrageous attacks on the monuments was taken at the urging of Utah politicians,” Wiarda said, listing Sens. Mike Lee and John Curtis, Gov. Spencer Cox and Rep. Celeste Maloy as the crowd booed and shouted “shame!”
“One of the most important things you can do at this time is vote,” Wiarda said. “President Trump’s outrageous attacks on the national monuments was taken at the urging of Utah politicians, many of whom are on the ballot this November.” 
A protester takes a selfie with her ballot before putting it in the ballot drop box outside the Salt Lake City Public Library on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
Michael Wahlquist, president of the National Association of Letter Carriers, told the crowd that as Trump attacks voting by mail, though he himself uses it, there is an outsized impact on those who can’t easily vote in person, including working families or people working multiple jobs, people with disabilities, the elderly and military members.
Wahlquist expressed his relief that the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail in the November midterms, allowing ballots to go out unimpeded across the country for now, but efforts against the system are expected to continue. 
“Please stand with the over 200,000 city letter carriers and fight like hell to protect vote by mail,” said Wahlquist, who leads the sole union representing city delivery letter carriers employed by the U.S. Postal Service. “If they take away your vote, they take away your voice.”

Tim Elliott and Darlene McDonald lead the Salt Lake City No Kings crowd in chants as they near City Hall, where some will drop off ballots.
[image or embed]
— McKenzie Romero (@mckenzieromero.bsky.social) October 17, 2026 at 4:42 PM

Laura Allred, of Eagle Mountain, drove to the Capitol with her husband and children. She wore a sweatshirt that read “Make Gilead fiction again,” a reference to Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel “The Handmaid’s Tale.” With her 10-year-old daughter at her side, Allred said she wants her children to understand how to use their voices.
“I feel like I wasn’t educated about politics and what’s happening around me until I was an adult, and seeing what’s happening to our country, they’re going to be our future and if they don’t know what’s happening they’re not going to know how to fight it,” Allred said. 
Allred said her greatest concerns include women’s rights, bodily autonomy and the Great Salt Lake.
“I’m glad that I came, I wasn’t going to, I am a little sad that there’s not more people here,” Allred said. “But I am still feeling the empowerment that comes with being here, and I feel like being here will make a difference.”
Protestors gather outside the Utah Capitol during the No Kings protest on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)

title: JD Vance is coming to Nebraska for a North Platte midterm rally
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks on stage on the second day of the 2026 Republican midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)LINCOLN — The Republican National Committee has announced another midterm rally in Nebraska, this time with Vice President JD Vance. 
The rally will be Thursday at the D&N Event Center in North Platte. The vice president is expected to speak around noon.
The RNC announced the North Platte rally late Saturday. 
President Donald Trump visited Grand Island Oct. 5, as Nebraska is seeing a close Senate race between registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn and incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.

Recently, the Senate race saw a rating change from Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a notable election analyst, to “leans Republican” from “likely Republican.”

In addition to the Senate race, the 2nd Congressional District has been competitive since the start of the cycle. In the last few weeks, the races for governor and the 1st Congressional District have drawn attention from election analysts as well.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Hundreds gather for rally at Kansas Capitol as midterm campaigns hit homestretch
text:
Howard Tyler and Mary Oswald, siblings from Horton, put flags in the ground Oct. 17, 2026, outside the Kansas Capitol to register their concern about the U.S. government and to emphasize the importance of voting by Nov. 3. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Howard Tyler and Mary Oswald arrived early to secure a spot at the front of the crowd for Saturday’s pre-election rally outside the Kansas Capitol.
The Horton siblings made the trip to Topeka because they wanted to be conspicuous about their commitment to the power of voting and to register discontent with current management of government, especially at the federal level under President Donald Trump. The gathering hosted by the decentralized, grassroots Kansas 50501 brought together several hundred people.
It was part of No Kings: Vote Early events occurring in Lawrence, Overland Park and Mission, as well as across the nation, less than three weeks from the Nov. 3 midterm election.
“We’ve got to do something for our country,” said Oswald, a retired nurse who has attended a series of similar events since 2025.
“We can’t do much, but at least we can do this,” added Tyler, a former truck driver who hauled diary milk. “I used to be a Republican, but I’m a Democrat now.”
Their central target, along with many in the crowd, was Trump and his allies, including Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight reelection battle against Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton. On Monday, Trump is scheduled to be in Wichita for an event designed to bolster Marshall’s campaign. Political analysts rate the Senate contest a toss-up despite the state’s 901,000 registered Republicans, compared to 578,000 independents and 521,000 Democrats.
“I’ve heard a lot of people say they don’t know what to vote for,” Oswald said. “Most of them are what I call Trumpers. Vote. Just vote.”
A contingent attending a rally Oct. 17, 2026, outside the Kansas Capitol in advance of the Nov. 3 election do their best to obscure the lone person waving a flag in support of President Donald Trump. The objective of the event organized by groups aligned with the No Kings movement is to encourage Kansans to vote in-person with an advance ballot. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
A portion of protest signs in the crowd urged participants to vote in-person with an advance ballot. Others in he audience took the opportunity to share their critique of Trump by touching on the rising cost of living, military conflict with Iran, apprehension about the president’s affinity for tyrants, his controversial appointees and the dispute regarding public disclosure of documents tied to investigation of the late Jeffrey Epstein.
One person, who said his name was “Ed Norton” and declined to explain his political motivation or discuss voting rights, waved a pro-Trump flag on steps of the Capitol directly behind speakers at the event. A squad of his rivals maneuvered their signs in an attempt to block the audience’s view of the lone dissident.
Michelle Jones, a lead organizer with Committed Kansas Activists in Ottawa, said she’d taken part in protests in Minnesota, Illinois and Washington, D.C. She was in southwest Kansas to support people who questioned recent raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
She joined others by raising questions about Marshall’s voting record in the U.S. Senate.
“Marshall is on record voting against Kansans,” she said. “He’s a Trump loyalist. He does care about the people here in Kansas.”
Jones said she believed in the right to vote and participated in a group that offers rides to the polls on Election Day.
“We don’t ask them how they’re voting,” she said. “We volunteer to go pick people up.”
The family of Kevin, Michelle and Harlan Manning offers a colorful take on politics Oct. 17, 2026, outside the Kansas Capitol during a rally to spur voter participation in the Nov. 3 midterm election. The event offered them an opportunity to share personal perspectives on government, especially leadership of President Donald Trump. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
Kevin and Michelle Manning, and their daughter, Harlan, made their presence felt at the rally. Michelle Manning wore a shark suit to suggest Trump could be devoured if the full Epstein files were released. Kevin Manning hoisted a poster with more than a dozen photographs of Trump administration officials or allies. It was a type of scorecard that designated the handful of people who exited the Trump administration.
“We feel like democracy is in danger,” Michelle Manning said. “It’s not a time to be quiet. It’s a time to speak up and use your voice while we still have the ability to use our voice. We don’t agree with anything … resembling an authoritarian regime, and that’s currently what our president is doing. He’s making our country more dangerous. Everything he campaigned on was a lie to garner a vote with no follow through. He’s not to be trusted and he’s out for himself. It’s time we stand up.”
She urged Kansans to be wary of fraud claims after next month’s election because people making those allegations were most likely to benefit from public distrust in the electoral process.
Harlan Manning, 13 years of age and wearing a partial cat outfit, said she was learning in school about the history of the founding of the United States and the political system that endures to this day. She said her peers were interested in politics.
“They do pay attention,” she said.
In addition to the U.S. Senate race, Kansas voters will resolve the gubernatorial contest between Republican Ty Masterson, who has Trump’s endorsement, and Democrat Cindy Holscher. The ballot features a handful of other statewide offices and the state’s four congressional races. The entire Kansas House is up for grabs. There’s a constitutional amendment on the ballot designed to affirm only citizens have the right to vote.
On the edge of the throng at the Statehouse rally, Brad Williams of Topeka held a pair of signs. One contained Trump’s profile and asserted his administration was corrupt. The other made reference to Williams’ wish for a government that respected legal boundaries and well-established guardrails.
“My dream is to have the rule of law reinstated again,” he said. “I’d like to have Congress do its job and provide oversight of the executive branch.”

name: Nevada Current
title: No Kings rally in Las Vegas coincides with first day of early voting
text:
The Las Vegas No Kings rally was one of thousands of events held across all 50 states and Washington DC Saturday. Dozens of protesters demonstrated outside the Desert Breeze Community Center, an early voting location. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)The No Kings movement which has drawn millions to protests across the nation over the past two years had a new message for Nevadan’s who showed up to protest on Saturday: vote early.
On the first day of early voting in Nevada, Indivisible Las Vegas held its fourth No Kings rally across eight early-voting locations in the Las Vegas Valley. Nevada is one of more than a dozen states with early voting in October.
Organizers said the Saturday rally is the culmination of years of organizing to increase early voting and civic participation amid fears the Trump administration could attempt to curtail voting access for the midterms and limit mail-in voting – an initiative the Supreme Court halted last month. 
“Everything that we’ve been doing since June of 2025 has laid the foundation of us being able to mobilize people and now give them a very specific action, which is to vote,” said Beth Osborne, a member of the steering committee for Indivisible Las Vegas. “We want people to vote early because there’s less potential for shenanigans or other things that the federal government can do if we vote early.”
The Las Vegas No Kings rally was one of thousands of events held across all 50 states and Washington DC Saturday to get people to the polls early for the midterm elections where voters will determine the makeup of Congress. The outcome is likely to shape the final two years of Trump’s second term. Early voting for the November general election runs Oct. 17 through Oct. 30. Election Day is Nov. 3.
Along the road outside of the Desert Breeze Community Center, dozens of protesters held signs asking Nevadans to “Vote Early” while emphasizing that “Every Vote Does Matter.” Fewer people turned out compared to earlier rallies across Las Vegas. In June 2025, the No Kings rally in Las Vegas attracted at least 8,000 protesters.
Organizers hope the action will lead to the largest early voting turnout in Nevada history. Osborne said they are encouraging voters to take mail-in ballots directly to drop boxes in early voting locations out of an abundance of caution. 
“We just can’t trust the postal service. It’s been compromised, which is extremely sad,” Osborn said. 
Alexis Keizer, 69, joins protest outside Desert Breeze Community Center after dropping off mail-in ballot. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)
Alexis Keizer, a 69-year old booking agent, shared similar concerns and urged people to vote as early as possible. Keizer said she joined the Saturday protest after dropping off her mail-in ballot in a drop box at the Desert Breeze Community Center. 
Keizer said she is encouraged by polling that shows Democrats are likely to retake the House and possibly the Senate, but remains cautious. 
“I can’t trust polls. I wish that I could, and that’s why it’s so important to get out and vote. No one should be resting on the laurels of what the polls are telling us,” Keizer said. 
President Donlald Trump won Nevada in 2024, defeating Kamala Harris by 3 points and becoming the first Republican to win the state since George W. Bush in 2004. Several polls favored Harris winning the state by a slim margin. 
Keizer cited affordability, fuel prices, the war in Iran, and corruption as her main concerns, and said she wants positive change for younger generations.
“Most people are trying to stretch a paycheck that doesn’t stretch any longer, and it’s due to Trump’s wars, Trump’s tariffs, and basic corruption,” Keizer said. 
Pamela Siotas, 70, said she she joined the protest after voting because she does not like the direction the United States is going in. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/ Nevada Current)
Pamela Siotas, a 70-year old retired school teacher, said she was protesting on the first day of early voting because she is increasingly alarmed by the violent tactics deployed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). 
Siotas said immigration enforcement is targeting hardworking members of the immigrant community. She expressed concern about military force in American cities and the erosion of personal freedoms.
“I don’t believe in armed military coming into cities and shooting our citizens,” Siotas said, pointing to an “ICE OUT” button on her bag.
Siotas said she believes the opportunities her generation had are no longer available for younger people, leading her to lose faith in the American Dream.
“I’m not liking the direction the United States is going in,” Siotas said. “All of our benefits are slowly being taken away.”
Hanna Stotland, 51, said she is most concerned about Democracy and health care. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)
Hanna Stotland, a 51-year old educational consultant, said it was her fourth time attending a No Kings protest. She described herself as an active volunteer and canvasser, adding that she volunteered to house out-of-state volunteers working with Rep. Susie Lee’s campaign. 
Stotland said she also plans to volunteer for ballot curing, a process that notifies voters of signature-related errors and allows them to correct them. 
She said her top concerns were democracy and health care. Stotland said people will not be able to absorb the cost of skyrocketing premiums, which are happening as a result of the expiration of federal subsidies.
Nevada had one of the nation’s highest uninsured rates prior to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare.
Stotland said she was infuriated by a recent ad from Arkansas Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders that portrayed a Medicaid recipient playing video games and eating junk food instead of working
“How many people in this country don’t have access at all because their states didn’t expand Medicaid?” said Stotland. “No other country that claims to be civilized leaves people off of universal health coverage or shames them as being lazy because they need it.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: No Kings drums up voter awareness at Louisiana events
text:
No Kings campaign events held Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, across the country included a gathering in downtown Covington, where participants met in front of the old courthouse to encourage passersby to vote in the Nov. 3 congressional midterm election. Early voting in Louisiana starts Tuesday, Oct. 20. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator) The No Kings movement dialed down its usual animus for President Donald Trump at thousands of gatherings across the country Saturday to instead emphasize voter participation for the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections. The first legitimate fall weather day in Louisiana, with cooler temperatures and clear skies, boosted the spirits of participants at events in nine cities.
A few dozen people lined the sidewalks in front of the old courthouse in Covington, the seat of St. Tammany Parish. Most carried signs that encouraged passing motorists to take part in the upcoming election, while a few took potshots at the sitting president. Many drivers greeted the No Kings participants on downtown Covington’s main drag, East Boston Street, with honking horns and thumbs up, but there were also thumbs down and the occasional middle finger.
St. Tammany has been reliably Republican in statewide and congressional elections for decades, helping Majority Leader Steve Scalise keep a firm hold on his 1st Congressional District seat since 2008. The likelihood that Scalise will win another term next month didn’t dissuade Lindsay Pons of Mandeville from bringing her two sons to the No Kings event. 
Her boys brought along a snare drum that provided a steady beat for the two-hour event. Pons said she feels good about the chances that Democrats will take control of Congress and put a stop to what she considers Trump’s aggressive immigration policy.  
“I’m just really optimistic that, if we do win, it’s because a lot of people just couldn’t vote for the same,” she said. “You know, maybe they couldn’t cross over, but they couldn’t continue to vote for the same.”
This is the fourth No Kings national day of action since the movement was launched after Trump took office in January 2025.  More than 2,500 events in all 50 states and Washington, D.C., were planned for Saturday. 
The three previous events in New Orleans have been singular, large-scale events, but this weekend’s plans involved smaller gatherings at six high-visibility intersections in the city and one in nearby Metairie.
One group of participants manned the neutral grounds near the entrance of New Orleans City Park, handing out snacks and voter guides to drivers stopped at traffic lights. They shared the sidewalk and enthusiastic greetings with people heading to the annual Oktoberfest at the nearby Deutsches Haus, with some attendees clad in the traditional German garb of lederhosen and dirndls.     
Other cities hosting No Kings events Saturday in Louisiana included Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Hammond, Lafayette, Slidell and Shreveport. They sought to raise awareness of the early voting period that starts Tuesday and ends Oct. 27.
Buddy Spell of Covington waves a large flag as part of a No Kings rally held Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)
A young boy looks from his backseat in an SUV at people taking part in a No Kings rally Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, outside the old St. Tammany Parish Courthouse on Boston Street in Covington. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)
Michael Wolfe waves American flags at the entrance of City Park in New Orleans, one of several busy intersections in the city where the No Kings movement encouraged people to rally Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, to raise awareness for the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)
Tamara Guffey waves to motorists near the entrance of New Orleans City Park on Saturday, Oct. 17. 2026. She was part of the No Kings movement’s effort to raise voter awareness for the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections and the early voting period in Louisiana that starts Tuesday. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: From protest to the polls, No Kings organizers make push for early voting in NC
text:
Dozens of people gather at Chavis Memorial Park in Raleigh for the No Kings voter event on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)Under gloomy skies and light rain, a crowd gathered outside Wake Forest Town Hall Saturday, holding homemade signs and occasionally erupting with applause as speakers urged them to turn their opposition to the Trump administration into action at the ballot box. 
“Do we believe in the power of the people? Do we believe in the power of our vote?” Keith Shannon, political action chair for the NAACP’s Wake-Wendell branch, asked the crowd. 
His message was direct: Vote early, make a plan and help someone get to the polls. 
The Wake Forest gathering was one of many No Kings events across the state as the nationwide movement encourages political participation ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.  
Attendees handed out buttons, pins and flyers while waving painted signs expressing frustration with the administration and encouraging people to vote.
“When we vote, the needle moves,”  Shannon told the crowd. “The laws change when we vote. Our communities are heard.” 
Scott Peoples, of Veterans for Responsible Leadership, also urged attendees to get involved, reminding the crowd that “democracy is not a spectator sport.” 
For some demonstrators, that work extends beyond showing up at protests. At events across the Triangle, participants described efforts to educate their neighbors, explain ballot measures and help voters make a plan to cast their ballots. 
Attendees of the No Kings at Chavis Memorial Park in Raleigh, hold signs encouraging people to vote on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
At Chavis Memorial Park in Raleigh, more than 50 gathered in front of the park’s early voting center with umbrellas, ponchos and tents to shield themselves from the rain and wind.  
Joshua Bradley, one of four candidates running for the  Raleigh City Council At-large seat, was at the park to join demonstrators and encourage more voting participation. 
He said active voting is only part of the political change he wants to see. 
“People are like, ‘Vote out Trump, stop the war,’ and I agree. But then what? We’ve got to keep organizing on top of it,” he said. 
In more conservative Johnston County, a much smaller crowd gathered at the Clayton Town Square, but they were also focused on the importance of civic engagement. 
Mary Blank, co-leader of Indivisible Johnston County, said the event was intended to help people understand their voting options and make a plan to vote early. 
Indivisible is one of several groups that organize the No Kings events.
“We are taking the next step by turning people power into voter power,” she said. 
Cars honked as drivers slowed to look at and read the signs protesters waved. Music played over speakers, and some people danced in the rain. 
For Ed Sanderford, a member of the grassroots advocacy group Down Home North Carolina, voting is connected to issues that affect people’s daily lives, including the cost of living and political polarization. 
He attended the Clayton rally to help inform voters about their ballots. 
“It all starts with your local government,” he said. “It’s important to recognize that what you do locally affects the bigger picture.” 
Despite the wind and rain, two dozen people line the road near the town square in at the No Kings voter event in Clayton on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Richmond No Kings protest turns out hundreds ahead of midterm election
text:
William F. McGee, president of the Richmond Southern Christian Leadership Conference, speaks to a crowd of hundreds at Monroe Park in Richmond on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, for the city's fourth No Kings protest. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)Virginians on Saturday utilized the fourth major “No Kings” protest in Richmond to drive out support around local issues and in favor of three proposed amendments to Virginia’s constitution that voters will decide on in November. 
It was one of dozens of anti-Trump demonstrations that were held in Virginia, and one of thousands held across the country — with only two weeks until the midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress.
The event, underscored by rainy weather, turned out fewer people than previous “No Kings” demonstrations in Richmond. A march on Capitol Square the same time last year drew over 10,000 people. 
Organizers stump for constitutional amendments 
Voters in Virginia will decide on three proposed amendments to the state’s constitution in November, and the organizers of “No Kings” asked them to vote “YES” for all three. 
The first amendment would cement abortion access and other reproductive rights in Virginia, which is the only southern state that has not enacted new restrictions since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Han Jones, the campaign manager for Virginians for Reproductive Freedom, asked the crowd to vote “YES” on Question No. 1 because “at no point is a politician more qualified than you and your doctor to make personal decisions about your health care and pregnancy.”
“Once this constitutional amendment is passed, we are going to know that no politician can take our rights away with a swipe of a pen,” Jones said.
The second amendment would remove the state’s 2006 ban and permanently protect same-sex marriage.
Narissa Rahaman, the executive director of Equality Virginia, holds a microphone out to the crowd, leading the chant “Our rights are on the ballot” at the No Kings protest in Richmond, Virginia, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)
Narissa Rahaman, the executive director of Equality Virginia, has been married to her wife for three years thanks to the advocates who fought for her right to do so, she said. Now she is asking Virginians to safeguard those rights with their ballots. 
“For more than a decade after the 2015 Supreme Court decision Obergefell v. Hodges, same-sex couples across this commonwealth have gotten married, raised kids, bought homes, started businesses and built lives together. But federal protections making those lives possible can shift with political winds,” Rahaman said. “As long as that ugly language from 2006 remains on the books, it represents a standing vulnerability, rather than a settled guarantee,” she continued. 
Ballot Question No. 3 asks voters if they would like to restore formerly incarcerated Virginians’ voting rights, and guarantee automatic restoration for people in the future.
Speakers asked the crowd to both exercise their right to vote in November, and use it to protect that right going forward.
“My rights are on the ballot!” demonstrators chanted. “Your rights are on the ballot! Our rights are on the ballot!”
Raising awareness around Flock cameras, immigration enforcement
Within the crowd, tabling groups handed out flyers to raise awareness around local issues. 
The Richmond chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America was one of those groups. They have been running an anti-automatic license plate reader — “BLOCK FLOCK” — campaign since at least the last “No Kings” protest in Richmond. They spent the event driving up support for their school board candidate Jackie McDonnough. She is running against Anne Holton, who was chosen by the School Board to fill a seat for the interim.
Merry Bateman of Chesterfield, Virginia, hands out leaflets with information on registering to vote, setting up on the outer edges of the No Kings protest on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 in Richmond. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)
Other groups present were the Evict ICE Campaign, New Virginia Majority, the Virginia Defenders for Freedom, Justice and Equality and the historic Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which was founded by Martin Luther King Jr. 
The Liberal Women of Chesterfield County, Center for Common Ground and 50501 Virginia gave out information on how to register to vote. 
Merry Bateman, a 72-year-old Chesterfield woman, was one of those volunteers. She said she wanted to take advantage of “No Kings” to help get people registered, regardless of their political beliefs. 
“This is just an important day to help remind people about democracy, our need for it, the need to fight for it, and how important voting is. It’s our privilege and right, and we must do it to voice our needs and what we expect of our leaders,” Bateman said.
Protesters call out Republicans 
Antoni Szachowicz, one of 50501 Virginia’s lead organizers, emphasized the importance of voting in the upcoming midterm election. He said one way to fight the Trump administration is to vote out the GOP, or as he called them, the “guardians of pedophiles.”  
The crowd booed as Szachowicz mentioned the names of Virginia’s Republican congressional representatives who Democrats hope to vote out in November. 
The representative whose seat is considered most vulnerable to flipping blue is Jen Kiggans, R-2nd District. She is facing the seat’s former representative, Democrat Elaine Luria. A new poll has Luria leading by three points.  
Jacob Seivers, who lives in Bedford County, came with a friend to the protest Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. He called the speakers’ rhetoric about Republicans “hilarious” and “nonsense.” (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virgina Mercury)
In Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, longtime Republican Rep. Rob Wittman is facing Democrat Shannon Taylor, who is currently the Henrico County Commonwealth Attorney. 
And in Virginia’s 5th Congressional District, Trump-Republican Rep. John McGuire is facing Democrat Tom Perriello, who briefly held the district from 2009 to 2011. 
Jacob Seivers, 20, one of two pro-Trump observers who stood on the outskirts of the crowd, lives in Bedford County and is represented by McGuire. 
He called the speakers’ rhetoric about Republicans “hilarious” and “nonsense.” While he believes Congress will flip blue after November, McGuire will keep his seat, Seivers said. 
“McGuire will do fine, but midterms tend to be anti-cyclical, or against the sitting president,” Seivers said.
Early voting is underway until Oct. 31 and Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the congressional candidates and stakes of the races. Take our reader survey to share the issues that will motivate you to vote this fall and inform our elections reporting. 
 
People at the No Kings event in Richmond’s Monroe Park on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, hear from speakers urging them to vote yes on all three of the constitutional amendments on Virginia ballots this midterm. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Demonstrators turn back out in Georgia for No Kings, this time with their attention turned to voting
text:
Felicia Murray Jackson, the sister of the late Linda Davis, speaks at a No Kings event Saturday in Atlanta. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderFelicia Murray Jackson’s sister, Linda Davis, died in February on her way to the Savannah school where she worked after a man fleeing immigration agents crashed into her vehicle. 
But that’s not why Jackson says she’s angry today. 
“Our government has packed us full of lies,” Jackson said to a crowd of hundreds gathered Saturday at Atlanta’s Piedmont Park. “The lies are that we are better divided than we are together, and I’m here to say that’s a lie. We are better together than we are divided. 
“My enemy is not my neighbor. My neighbor is my friend,” she added. 
According to the Current, the Guatemalan national that federal immigration agents said was in the county illegally did not have a criminal record in the country before the traffic wreck. 
“I just want you to know my sister did not die in a senseless, illegal, never-ending war. She died on her way to work, just like your mothers, your fathers, your kids, your grandkids,” Jackson said. “So I don’t want to hear you tell me how sorry you are for my loss. I want to hear you say, ‘I took your loss straight to the ballot box.’”
Larisa Gilbert of Sandy Springs participates in a march through midtown Atlanta. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
Jackson helped lead the assembled group on about a one-mile march through midtown Atlanta, ending at Saint Mark United Methodist Church where voting rights groups were on hand to train participants on how to help protect Georgia’s election. 
The event was one many held Saturday across the state as part of the latest round of No Kings demonstrations. This time, though, the nationwide mass mobilization event known for sign waving and marches focused just as much on urging people to vote early and to do their part to make sure others are able to exercise their right to vote. 
Early voting in Georgia started Monday, and as of Saturday, about 800,000 people had already cast a ballot. 
Tyler Groch, a trombonist and member of the Atlanta Coalition Ensemble, which is a mainstay of Atlanta’s protest scene, said he welcomed the educational focus of this wave of No King’s events.
Tyler Groch (left), a trombonist and member of the Atlanta Coalition Ensemble, leads the band in warmups Saturday. “Music brings joy to these events, and it keeps people grounded. It keeps people protected in certain ways too,” he said of the band’s role in the demonstrations. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“These marches are pointless if they don’t have a stated goal at the end, and this election is clearly under fire from the administration and all the people who support him,” Groch said. “To help educate people on how to stay safe and do what we can as individuals to protect the integrity of this election, I think that’s a very important thing for us to do.”
Several marchers filed into the church Saturday to hear what Andres Parra, a senior organizer with the nonpartisan Common Cause Georgia, had to say about being a poll monitor. 
Parra said Common Cause is still looking for people to serve as monitors at polling places across the state but particularly in metro Atlanta. 
Poll monitors are trained volunteers in the community that can help assist voters who may need help, but Parra said another important role is for them to document any issues that may stop people from voting, like a polling place opening late or a machine being down 
He says having poll monitors there to track these incidents help combat misinformation and ensure Georgians are able to cast their ballot. 
“The role of trained, prepared poll monitors at polling locations is going to be a really great need this cycle in particular for sure,” he said.
Andres Parra, a senior organizer with the nonpartisan Common Cause Georgia, talks to No Kings participants Saturday at a church in Atlanta. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
