title: Two Mitscher Road Homes Struck by Gunfire 10-17-26
text:
POLICE LOG – October 16, 2026
Two Dover Homes Struck By Gunfire Friday Evening
DOVER, Del. — Dover Police are investigating a shooting that damaged two homes on Mitscher Road Friday evening.
Officers responded to the 100 block of Mitscher Road at approximately 6:39 p.m. on October 16, 2026, after receiving a report of shots fired.
Police said two residences were struck by gunfire. One of the homes was occupied by two adults, but no injuries were reported. The second residence was unoccupied at the time.
Officers also located multiple spent shell casings in a nearby alley.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the Dover Police Department at 302-736-7111. Tips may also be submitted through Delaware Crime Stoppers or the Dover Police Department’s online contact form. Tipsters may remain anonymous.

name: National
title: No Kings shifts strategy from streets to the ballot box with early voting day of action
text:
Emmett Doyle, a folk musician and and one of 15 defendants facing federal felony conspiracy charges stemming from protests against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s crackdown in Minnesota, performs at the Twin Cities No Kings rally, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Organizers launched more than 2,500 No Kings events across all 50 states and the District of Columbia Saturday, this time focusing their efforts on the midterm elections.
From roadside rallies to letter-writing campaigns and protest songs, this round of demonstrations aimed to get people to the polls early.  
In the bustling and diverse neighborhood of Jackson Heights, Queens, where Bangladeshi street vendors whip up fuska – crispy, potato-filled shells – and Mexican taquerías serve up al pastor and carne asada, volunteers gathered at a popular local restaurant called The Queensboro. The organizers are part of the Jackson Heights chapter of Indivisible, one of the many grassroots organizations that have made No Kings demonstrations happen. 
Arianne Mayer, 49, cofounded the chapter about two years ago after President Donald Trump was elected to his second term. On this “No Kings: Vote Early Day of Action”, she hands out pens and paper to volunteers to write letters to voters in battleground states, encouraging them to get out and cast their ballots as early as possible. 
“The practice of mobilization of bodies is really helpful, especially in New York City, where you’re trying to mobilize many thousands of people,” Mayer said. “When you see those thousands of marches, you understand people everywhere are not OK with this, but it’s nice to have a different approach for this event. ” 
Mayer, like many people here, said she was deeply frustrated and “disgusted” by the presence of federal immigration agents targeting her neighbors. Many people also said the federal government is implementing increasingly authoritarian policies. 
Since summer 2025, the No Kings movement has held multiple massive demonstrations across thousands of sites around the country, attracting millions of people to protest against what they consider to be an overreach of government under the Trump Administration.
Shona Chakravartty, 60, wrote postcards encouraging early voting at a No Kings event in Jackson Heights, Queens, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
This time around organizers shifted their focus, understanding that the midterm elections  will determine which political party controls Congress. If it’s the Democrats, they could put up roadblocks to Trump’s agenda. Organizers are hoping the day of early voting could not only increase the pool of voters, but also ease the burden on poll workers on Nov. 3, Election Day. 
Voting is in full swing across dozens of states, with over 5 million ballots cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. Trump faces a historic low in approval ratings. 
In Minnesota folk musician Emmett Doyle took to a stage in downtown Minneapolis to perform Lluís Llach’s “L’Estaca,” written in the 1960s in protest of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in Spain. 
Doyle is one of 15 defendants facing federal felony conspiracy charges stemming from protests against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s crackdown in Minnesota.
“When I was getting pulled out of my truck by federal agents a couple months ago, one of the first things I asked them was, ‘Hey, is this about the songs?’ And they told me, ‘No, it’s about resisting ICE,’” Doyle said to the crowd of about 1,000. “I told them, ‘Well, you’re going to have to arrest all of Minneapolis if you want to hit me for that.’”
Diane Komsky, 67,drove an hour to the No Kings protest in Sioux Falls, South Dakota,because of the “madness in the White House,” she said. 
“I want to give peace a real chance for families in the United States,” she said.
Mark Lyons of Centennial, Colorado, said he hadn’t been involved in much political activism or organizing before last year. Saturday’s protest was his fourth No Kings event.
With the midterms approaching, Lyons is hopeful that Democrats will take control of Congress and “put all kinds of checks and balances” on the Trump administration.
“They’ve been stealing the country blind for the last two years,” he said. “There has to be accountability, and it can’t be business as usual.”
At an event in the nation’s capital, 25-year-old Octavia Clapp said using her right to vote especially matters as Trump attempts to wield authority over voting. The Trump administration has spent more than a year in court battles with dozens of states and voting rights groups seeking to force states to provide sensitive voter data and curb voting by mail.
“I think cracking down on mail-in voting and restricting people’s ability to vote easily is anti-democratic,” said Clapp, of Maryland. “Democracy is really important to me, and freedom is really important to me.”
Participants in a No Kings day event march toward the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. The Umbrella Walk 4 Change was one of thousands of No Kings events across the nation encouraging early voting. (Photo by Baya Burgess/States Newsroom)
But the No Kings events were also met with pushback, including directly from Trump’s team. 
“The fact that the ‘No Kings’ organizers are talking about voting in the upcoming election proves they should change their name,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson. “This November, Americans have a clear choice between President Trump and Republican’s commonsense policies or the extreme Democrats radical socialist, open-border policies.”
In battleground state Virginia, two pro-Trump observers on the outskirts of the crowd in Richmond watched on.
 “I’ve learned that a lot of a lot of folks here tend to be older, toward the baby boomer side,” Jacob Seivers, 20, said of the protesters, whom he called “more courteous than you might expect” and “willing to talk.” 
Seivers, who lives in Bedford County, called the speakers’ rhetoric about Republicans “hilarious” and “nonsense.” He also said he believes Congress will flip blue after November.
Trump supporter John Hess of Centralia, Washington, was outnumbered in Olympia but took that in stride. Hess said he comes to the Capitol every week and didn’t know of the day’s events until Friday. 
“Normally I don’t get this much excitement,” he said 
Back in New York, another local Indivisible organizer, Katherine Scannell, 35, said it’s important to encourage people to exercise their right to vote.  
Scannell and volunteers set up shop at a neighborhood “open streets” event in Astoria, Queens, where residents could walk within the street blocked off from cars, listen to live music, and pick up fresh and locally grown vegetables. 
“Normally it’s a protest, but the No Kings coalition had nationwide calls talking about how we wanted to turn those protests and eyeballs into action,”Scannell said. “Voting early is a great way to protect everyone’s vote, because when you vote early it’s hard to sabotage those numbers.” 
Alyssa Chen and Maya Betti of Minnesota Reformer, Makenzie Huber of South Dakota Searchlight, Chase Woodruff of Colorado Newsline, Andrew Kerley for Virginia Mercury and Baya Burgess for States Newsroom’s D.C. bureau, contributed.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: No Kings in Des Moines: Smaller crowd but focused on mobilizing voters
text:
Volunteers from Food and Water Action discuss their door-knocking strategy during the No Kings Day of Action in Colby Park in Des Moines, Iowa, on Oct. 17, 2026.  The event encouraged people to vote early. (Photo by Joanna Schroder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)It was quiet in Windsor Heights’ Colby Park Saturday afternoon as volunteers from many organizations were out canvassing neighborhoods encouraging people to vote early as part of the No Kings Day of Action.
It was a contrast with previous years’ No Kings events in Des Moines, where thousands of people rallied on the State Capitol Grounds, waving signs and shouting slogans. Instead, volunteers worked on various projects aimed at motivating and mobilizing voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Marie Herring, an organizer with the organization Indivisible 515, said the Saturday event looks different from previous No Kings rallies held in Des Moines because it was not meant as a day of protest, but a day for organizers to get out the vote in Iowa.
“It’s a much different goal that we are working to meet,” she told a crowd of roughly 40 people gathered at Colby Park in Windsor Heights.
Earlier in the day, participants met at the park before heading out out to door knock and canvass in the region, encouraging Iowans to sign up to vote and early vote. Herring said this was a nonpartisan effort.
“We had over 200 sign-ups for that,” Herring said. “And I think people are still out knocking doors now because its nice out. That’s the real work we’re trying to accomplish today – actual engagement, having one-on-one conversations.”
Overpass activism
One of the day’s events was overpass activism, where volunteers post signage on pedestrian bridges along I-235. Brenda Double, a Des Moines resident, was on the bridge near Roosevelt High School waving her American flag along with several others.
Brenda Double from Des Moines, Iowa, stands on the bridge near Roosevelt High School in Des Moines with protest signs and an American flag encouraging people to vote. She often participates in Fascist Friday events, posting signs calling for people to save democracy. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“I’m out here today to try and get the message out to make sure people get out and vote,” Double asid. “This isn’t a party issue. This is an American issue. This is a global issue.”
She said that the country is losing democracy and needs to, “get these disgusting sycophants out.”
“We have now aligned with Russia and all our allies are now really upset with us and they’re all starting to work against us, you know, work without us,” Double said. “They are making plans and working ways to get together without the help of the United States because they’ve lost faith with us.”
People are often seen on Friday on the same bridge as part of FED UP!!! Fridays. Double said the Friday afternoon protesting is also known as Fascist Fridays, and she can often be found on the same bridge waving as drivers head home from work.
Saturday’s group was “all different neighbors from different areas in Des Moines and in Polk County. So we just get together randomly periodically for this. Sometimes I join with the Invisible Brigade. Some of the girls here do the Fascist Fridays. So we are all over. We’re not one particular organization. We are just neighbors coming together to help fight for our democracy.”
The Des Moines area events were part of a national No Kings event that included rallies and get-out-the-vote activism across the country. Read live updates about events around the country here.

name: Washington State Standard
title: At Washington state Capitol, No Kings rally is all about voting early
text:
No Kings demonstrators carried signs on Oct. 17, 2026, bearing messages about the importance of both voting and voting early to prevent doubt later when results are tallied. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
A smiling Judy Caron sat on a metal bench on the grounds of the Washington state Capitol, her face partially shielded from Saturday’s bright morning sun by a homemade sign, “No Cons, No Clowns, No Kings.”
Caron left her home in Lacey and arrived early for the No Kings rally, an event that eventually drew several hundred people to the lawn surrounding the Tivoli Fountain and the sidewalks on both sides of Capitol Way.
“This is my fourth. Each one does feel differently,” she said. “I’m 83. I feel our best days are behind us, and I am concerned about our future generations. Here, people are excited about voting and democracy, and I will leave feeling a lot better than when I came.”
Saturday’s two-hour event at the Capitol was decentralized. No stage and no speakers though there was music, drumming and singing. Most folks congregated near and along the road where passing cars honked in solidarity.
It was one of more than two dozen events in the state, with the largest expected in Seattle.
Evergreen Resistance and Olympia Indivisible had booths where volunteers trafficked information solely on how best to make sure one’s ballot is received and counted. 
Voting is “an honor and it’s a responsibility. Our election is foundational in America,” said Amy Rehwaldt of Olympia, an organizer with Evergreen Resistance and Olympia Indivisible. “We really want people to know to avoid any last-minute drama, vote early.”
Voting early, the overriding theme of the rally, is the message local and state election officials have been delivering with increasing volume since the August primary when 20,000 ballots arrived late and did not get counted. 
Several counties mailed out ballots more than a week ago to give people more time. Those officials are strongly encouraging use of ballot drop boxes rather than the U.S. Postal Service.
Joyce Schmidt of Olympia, Washington, incited lots of smiles as she moved the crowd at the No Kings rally at the state Capitol on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
As a result of recent changes, there are fewer pick-ups from mailboxes, especially in rural areas. Thus the postal service does not guarantee a ballot will get postmarked on the day it’s put in the mailbox. After Oct. 26, officials are counseling voters to go to the post office and get their ballot return envelope postmarked in person.
Members of the Backbone Campaign, a progressive organization launched by a Vashon Island resident, spent the duration of the event on the lawn holding their lighted sign, “Imagine a better world, vote.” 
“I’m in line with the theme for today,” said Jeff Snyder. “I have different themes in my mind, too. My mantra is vote blue then demand something new. I am not entirely happy with the way things are going.”
Some in the crowd came with props or in costumes.
Joyce Schmidt of Olympia donned a chicken suit and carried a sign — “Gas is too expensive so I had to ride my chicken.” She said she’d been to every No Kings rally at the Capitol.
“I’m a veteran. I am tired of this,” she said, referring to the Trump administration’s reign. “We vowed our oath to the Constitution and not to a man.”
John Hess of Centralia sat in a folding chair clutching a large red banner emblazoned with Trump’s name. Hess seemed to be the lone supporter of the president, though it wasn’t intentional.
Each weekend he comes to the Capitol for a couple hours to pray. He usually has signs opposing abortion or socialism, or concerning another subject. He wasn’t aware of the rally until Friday.
Judging from the steely stares and periodic abusive comments hurled his way, his presence wasn’t welcome. He was surrounded by folks wielding anti-Trump materials. “Normally, I don’t get this much excitement,” Hess said.
John Hess of Centralia, a supporter of President Donald Trump, endured scornful looks and some abusive language as he sat amongst the crowd at the No Kings rally at the state Capitol in Olympia, Washington, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)

name: Colorado Newsline
title: No Kings event in Grand Junction emphasizes early voting, nonpartisan participation
text:
Sally Henry, left, and Mary Hammond Atkinson, both Presbyterian ministers in Grand Junction, said they have personal reasons for attending a No Kings event in Grand Junction that occurred Saturday. Atkinson said her daughter is an immigration attorney in Aurora whose clients are subjected to "horrible conditions” in detention centers where they don’t belong. (Photo by Sharon Sullivan/Colorado Newsline)About 300 people came out for a No Kings rally Saturday in Grand Junction. Organized by Indivisible Grand Junction, the event attracted fewer than the thousands who’ve attended previous No Kings rallies in the city. But it was billed as a “nonpartisan voter participation, education and community connection event,” designed to bring out community members to cast their vote early. 
Attendees gathered for the “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at the Historic Lowell School, just east of downtown Grand Junction at noon where tables were set up with information, both pro and con, about the various state ballot measures. There was also singing, drumming and speeches by various people, including Mesa County Clerk and Recorder Bobbie Gross. Gross urged people to vote early whenever possible.
“Elections are run by your friends, family, coworkers, neighbors,” Gross said. “They take an oath to run fair and accurate elections. The worst thing we can do is lose confidence in our election process.”
Kelley Turner and her brother Brian Dawson, of Grand Junction, attended a No Kings event on Saturday in Grand Junction. “I’ve been volunteering with Indivisible Grand Junction for two years. We want our voices to be heard. What’s happening in the U.S. right now is awful. I’m a Latter-Day-Saint and a lot of us are not heard in our church because we choose not to support Trump.” (Photo by Sharon Sullivan/Colorado Newsline)
By 2:45 p.m., members of the crowd began marching to the Mesa County elections office on the west side of downtown, to deposit their ballots for the November election into the drop box outside the office.
No Kings protests in Colorado meant to help protect the November election

“We wanted to do something a little different this time,” said Molly Heckman, of Indivisible Grand Junction. “One of the most important things is participating in democracy. One of the simplest ways people can do that is by voting” — thus the event was nonpartisan, she said.
Despite the nonpartisan billing, many attendees carried signs expressing their opinions about the Trump administration.
Grand Junction resident Rachel Cowan carried a sign saying her brother died 21 years ago while serving in the U.S. Army and that people should exercise their right to vote. She’s unhappy with the Trump administration. 
“I lost my job because of Trump,” she said. She worked in environmental remediation and restoration. “I’ve been coming to these protests for a while. This one is amazing because it’s focusing on voting.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In Montgomery, ‘No Kings’ demonstration encourages voter registration, turnout
text:
Protestors holding signs at the fourth "No Kings" protest in Montgomery, Alabama, on Oct. 17, 2026. The demonstration focused on voter registration and participation in preparation for the midterm elections in 17 days. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 
 How to register to vote
Oct. 19 is the last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 election. If you haven’t registered to vote, you can do so here. And if you’re not sure of your registration status, you can double-check it here.


More than 250 people gathered in downtown Montgomery Saturday to encourage voter turnout ahead of the midterm elections and Monday’s deadline to register to vote. 
The demonstration was the fourth “No Kings” protest, a national movement protesting President Donald Trump and his administration’s policies. More than 2,500 events were planned across the country for the fourth installment, which focused on early voting. Montgomery’s event was one of 17 in Alabama, with events scheduled in Birmingham, Huntsville, Mobile and other cities around the state.
Alabama does not have early in-person voting or no excuse absentee voting. State Democratic lawmakers have tried for years to pass an early in person voting law passed, but Republicans have objected, claiming high costs. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Do you want early voting here?” said Beth Bowden, one of the event’s organizers, triggering cheers from the crowd.
Alabama’s voter turnout is among the lowest in the country. In 2024, 58.7% of eligible voters cast a ballot, the lowest turnout for the state in a presidential election since 1988, according to data from the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. About 38.6% of eligible voters cast a ballot in the state’s last midterm election in 2022, the lowest turnout recorded since 1986 for a midterm election. 
In lieu of early voting, organizers turned to encouraging voter turnout and democratic participation. The deadline to register to vote in Alabama’s midterm elections is Monday. The election is in 17 days. 
Tabitha Isner, former vice chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, co-founded a nonprofit organization called Atlas for Democracy. Recently, she has been identifying what she calls Super Voters in Montgomery County through state voting records – those that have voted at least 25 times in the last 15 years, or in every election in that time period. 
Isner said that 5% of the county’s registered voters fall in that category. She visits those voters, gives them a Super Voter yard sign and visits with them. 
“The goal is honor and praise, pure and simple,” she said. “I just want people to know that somebody noticed that they’re doing the thing, but also we know it needs to be done.”
Montgomery is a Democratic-leaning city, but Isner visits voters regardless of ideology. She said a Republican asked her why she was at his house, when they both knew each other’s politics. 
“I love democracy more than I love being a Democrat,” she said. 
She said in the last 15 years, 13% of Montgomery County voters have voted at least 20 times, 23% have voted at least 15 times and 53% have voted less than five times. 
Isner was also giving Super Voters signs at the protest and had a red carpet for them to walk down for photos. One was Joanne Compton, who said in an interview that she votes because her ancestors fought for her right to do so. 
“I’m standing on the shoulders of my ancestors, and I’m hoping that I’m making them proud because of the sacrifices that they made just for me to be able to vote. Not only can you not vote, but I can also vote for the future generation that’s coming up,” she said.
Evan Milligan, a plaintiff in Alabama’s redistricting case Allen v. Milligan, which led to the creation of a near-majority Black congressional district in Alabama that was redrawn by the Legislature in May, said Saturday that what he called the king-like power demonstrated by the Trump administration has been used against Black voting rights before. 
“This is a place where I believe we can imagine a different type of outcome, but what will that outcome require of us? We have to stop doing one thing, and that’s lying to ourselves about where and how leadership works in our social movements,” Milligan said. “We say ‘No Kings,’ but we have to – if we’re at a crossroads – question ourselves and even our own slogans.”
The map created in the Milligan case was redrawn following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais and the subsequent special session of the Alabama Legislature that canceled congressional primary elections in four districts and two state senate districts. 
Sheyann Webb-Christburg, who was eight years old when Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. attempted to lead hundreds in a march from Selma to Montgomery in March 1965, said Saturday she has never stopped fighting for voting rights. 
“Regardless of the struggles and the challenges which we are plagued with today, we can’t feel tired because we’ve come too far from where we started from,” she said. 
As of June 16, 3.8 million Alabamians were registered to vote, according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. Montgomery County Probate Judge J.C. Love III, the county’s chief election official, emphasized the importance of voter participation in all elections. 
A recent special Montgomery City Council election was decided by 13 votes, he said, with a turnout of 6.9%. 
“The next time somebody tells you that one vote doesn’t matter, remember those 13 votes, because elections are not decided by the people who intended the vote,” he said at the protest. “They are not decided by the people who talked about voting, and they are not decided by the people who complained about the outcome afterward, they are decided by the ballots actually cast and lawfully counted.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Madison No Kings march focuses on early voting in midterm elections
text:
No Kings marchers round the Capitol on Saturday, Oct. 17 in Madison, Wisconsin (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)MADISON – About 1,000 people gathered at 2 p.m. on a sunny Saturday afternoon for a No Kings protest in James Madison park near Lake Monona in downtown Madison. The crowd swelled to about 1,500 as protesters marched to the Capitol in a long line with police stopping traffic at intersections along the way. The Forward Marching Band played “Solidarity Forever” on tubas, horns and drums as marchers carrying signs protesting the Trump administration rounded the square and converged in front of City Hall to listen to speakers who urged everyone to vote early in the 2026 midterm elections.
Gina Idsinga and Dee Reid (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)
Gina Idsinga came to the rally from her home in McFarland with a homemade sign that displayed the names of her five grandchildren and the statement: “I need to be able to tell my  grandchildren I did not stay silent.” 
“I feel very strongly about what is going on and we just need to band together and keep community in mind,” she said. “No country is a good country without taking care of its people and this administration is definitely not taking care of its people.”
Beside her, Idsinga’s friend Dee Reid carried a sign that said “No crowns for clowns.” She said she came out to support “all the things that this country has worked hard to keep,” including abortion rights, Social Security and Obamacare. She has been thinking about retiring soon, she said, but the cost of living is making her worry about whether she will be able to stop working. Her kids are also struggling with high costs, she said. “Both have really good careers and can’t buy a house. Interest rates are high, housing is not affordable and things are going in the wrong direction, so we need to focus on what’s good for us and not on starting wars in places we really don’t need to right now.”

Dineen Seymour-Nahn, a retired public school teacher in Madison said, “We have to vote in Crowley and Josh Kaul, and just vote in Democrats up and down the ticket, because really, if we don’t win this, who knows what will happen in 2028? With Tom Tiffany in there, he’ll undo everything we’ve done even in the last two years with some really good Supreme Court races. All that will come back – gerrymandering, anti-abortion laws, so that’s why we’re here.”
Sue Jennik, the president of the  League of Women Voters of Dane County stood behind a table in front of City Hall with information on the candidates running in Wisconsin in 2026, the proposed constitutional amendments voters will see on on their ballots and instructions on how to register, vote early and use a ballot drop box: “Everything people need to know to protect their right to vote,” she said.
Lisa Johnson of Madison No Kings marchers head toward the Capitol (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)'Uncle Sam' at the No Kings march in Madison (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Bill Lueders and his dog at the No Kings march (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Ajak Johnson (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Dineen Seymour-Nahn holds up her sign (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Gina Idsinga and Dee Reid (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Raging Grannies singing group members Marie Martini (center) said "I did all this marching back in the 1960s and we're doing it again, only now it's worse. We're all marching for our grandchildren." Melissa Markquart (right) said people who are not yet registered to vote should watch out for misleading emails telling them they are already registered. (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)
“Don’t trust an email that tells you you’re registered to vote if you just moved to Wisconsin,” said Melissa Markquart, a singer in the protest group the Raging Grannies. “We have grannies out registering people to vote, and they’ve had people tell them they got emails that said they were already registered – but there’s no automatic registration in Wisconsin,” she added.
Ajak Johnson, one of the march organizers, ran back and forth along the line directing marchers throughout. “These national events keep happening and we keep organizing things here on the ground,” she said. “I think it’s important for people to come together.” 
Early voting starts in Wisconsin on Oct 20, she added, “and I would just hope that people would leave here with a plan to early vote.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Hundreds gather in downtown Minneapolis for ‘No Kings’ early voting day of action
text:
St. Paul artist Michael Bahl holds up a sculpture he made of an anguished figure painted in the colors of the American flag as hundreds gather in downtown Minneapolis, Minnesota for the national No Kings rally to encourage midterm voting Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Under a sunny sky, people trickled into Commons Park in downtown Minneapolis on Saturday, forming a crowd of hundreds for a “No Kings” event focused on turning out voters for the midterm elections.
Emmett Doyle, a folk musician and one of 15 defendants facing federal felony conspiracy charges stemming from protests against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s crackdown in Minnesota, performed at the event.
“When I was getting pulled out of my truck by federal agents a couple months ago, one of the first things I asked them was, ‘Hey, is this about the songs?’ And they told me, ‘No, it’s about resisting ICE,’” Doyle said. “I told them, ‘Well, you’re going to have to arrest all of Minneapolis if you want to hit me for that.’”
Doyle was also joined by Brian Apland, another defendant in the case of the group of anti-ICE activists who have become known as the Minnesota 15.
Doyle’s first song was “L’Estaca” by Lluís Llach, a song written in the 1960s in protest of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in Spain.
The Minneapolis event was organized by Indivisible Twin Cities, MN50501, Women’s March Minnesota and the Minnesota AFL-CIO. It drew a smaller crowd compared to the Twin Cities rallies on previous anti-Trump No Kings days.
The last No Kings day in March closely followed Operation Metro Surge and drew tens of thousands of people to the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul for the movement’s flagship protest. Organizers estimated 200,000 people gathered. The first two No Kings days were held on June 14, 2025, hours after the assassination of Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark; and on Oct. 18, 2025.
Organizers said they intended the event to be distinct from previous No Kings rallies, which focused on protesting the Trump administration, saying Saturday’s event would be “a day of nonpartisan voter participation.”
Distinct it was — alongside political speeches and signs urging people to vote, food trucks lined the park and activities were set up for kids. It was also not particularly nonpartisan, with Democratic Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison as the second speaker and DFL politicians in attendance.
Emmett Doyle, a folk musician and defendant in the “Minnesota 15” case, performs an anti-fascist Catalan song by Lluís Llach at the Twin Cities No Kings rally, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Mick Foley, 77, a retired U.S. Navy veteran who served during the Vietnam War, said he attended because he was concerned about the current direction of the country.
“I did fight for this country, and I hate to see it go down in corruption and in flames,” Foley said. “So, I’m here because it’s at least something I can do to fight back.”
Foley also criticized the war in Iran, saying it had kept his “fellow sailors” aboard an aircraft carrier for months unnecessarily.
“We can’t go to war without Congress, without a cause, without a solution,” Foley said.
The war in Iran, which started in February, has driven up fuel, gas and grocery prices, becoming a central issue ahead of November’s elections.
Jeff Dichter, 68, and a physician and professor at the University of Minnesota from Eagan, said he showed up to make people more aware of changes in healthcare, especially insurance losses from new Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“I’m really worried about my patients,” Dichter said. “I’m worrying about our healthcare system in general. Because everybody’s cost is going to go up because all of a sudden we have 15% of our population less insured.”
Dichter, who was there as a volunteer with Indivisible, said he voted Democrat on a mail-in ballot last week.
Aiden Ferris, 18, and Caden Laird, 20, both college students in Minneapolis, said that the “importance of voting” brought them to the event.
“Some races were decided by like 10, 50 votes, and it’s really important to get out and vote this year, especially with every House seat on the line. And there’s a lot of close races here, with Peggy Flanagan and Michele Tafoya and then the governor’s race,” Ferris said. “So it’s really important to make your voice heard and shape Minnesota’s future.”
Laird, who works for Democratic state Rep. Kristin Bahner’s reelection campaign, held a sign reading “Vote for people you trust around your kids.”
The event comes as Minnesota faces heightened federal scrutiny regarding its elections. In August, the U.S. The Department of Justice sent election monitors to polling sites to two Minnesota countries. Trump has also made claims, without evidence, of election fraud in the state, and federal prosecutors recently charged 10 people with illegally voting or registering to vote in Minnesota elections.
Zack Filipovich, a DFL candidate for Minnesota state auditor, said the federal scrutiny has increased concerns about voting rights and election security.
“I think people are fed up with federal government overreach, and I think people want to make sure that their voting rights and their voting power is being utilized and not being taken away,” Filipovich said.
But Filipovich said he remains confident in Minnesota’s election system.
“We know that having paper ballots works, and that accountability, that safety, that voting security is important to have here in Minnesota,” he said.
The general election is on Nov. 3. Early voting began Friday. More than 200,000 ballots had been cast statewide as of Friday morning, according to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: No Kings rallies in North Dakota emphasize early voting
text:
Gail Gilliam donned an early bird costume during a No Kings rally in Fargo on Oct. 17, 2026, to encourage people to vote early this election season. Similar events were held in Grand Forks, Devils Lake, Valley City, Jamestown, Bismarck and Dickinson. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Hundreds rallied across North Dakota on Saturday to encourage early voting in the Nov. 3 election, joining similar No Kings events across the country.
Fargo and Bismarck rallies, each with a few hundred attendees, featured tables with information about how and when people can vote. 
Fargo event organizer Lyn Dockter-Pinnick said the group Red Red United Indivisible is working to promote the largest early vote turnout in history. 
“Vote early, that’s what we’re about today,” she said.
Zeely Rush of Hazen smiles while holding a sign in front of the Capitol in Bismarck during a No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Teresa Schneider, left, and Martha Wheeler ring bells to acknowledge someone who had already voted early in Minnesota during a No Kings rally in Fargo, North Dakota, that also included neighboring Moorhead. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)A No Kings: Vote Early rally in front of Fargo City Hall on Oct. 17, 2026., featured information about voting options, encouraging people to vote early. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Hundreds of people take part in a No Kings: Vote Early rally in front of Fargo City Hall on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Darcy Olson of Bismarck, center-right, holds a sign in front of the Capitol in Bismarck during a No Kings protest on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Participants hold signs in front of the Capitol in Bismarck during a No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Ron Jyring of Bismarck holds an American flag and waves at a vehicle during a No Kings rally at the Capitol in Bismarck on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Attendees hold signs in front of the Capitol in Bismarck during a No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Zeely Rush of Hazen, who attended the Bismarck event, already cast her absentee ballot by dropping it off at her county auditor’s office.
“Better to be safe than sorry,” Rush said. She added she didn’t want to worry about any potential problems at the post office to make sure her ballot is counted.
Several people in the crowd at Fargo City Hall raised their hands when an organizer asked who had already voted. More than 21,900 North Dakotans have voted through absentee or mail-in ballots so far. Seven counties also have early, in-person voting.
For Steve Heiland of Fargo and Susan Stockert of Bismarck, two ballot measures in North Dakota are the biggest election issues this year. 
One statewide ballot measure would require 60% voter approval to change the North Dakota Constitution and the other would require schools to provide free school meals to K-12 students.
Stockert, a middle school teacher attending the event in Bismarck, added a local school bond ballot measure as a motivator for voting. 
Ron Jyring of Bismarck, left, holds an American flag next to Susan Hochhalter of Bismarck, right, during a No Kings rally at the Capitol in Bismarck on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
John Trelstad of Fargo said he has changed his thinking on Measure 1. He said he originally agreed with supporters who argue the 60% helps protect North Dakota’s constitution from being overly influenced by out-of-state interests. 
But he said he has decided that he can’t let fewer than 50% of voters prevail. 
“It’s the reverse of a majority vote,” Trelstad said. “I can’t abide by that on any issue.” 
Darcy Olson of Bismarck brought a sign to the protest at the Capitol that read, “Vote early, vote blue and bring two friends.” Olson said he plans to vote early in-person voting at the Bismarck Event Center, which begins Thursday.
“I gotta vote to be able to hold this administration accountable for all the things it’s doing that is outside of the law, outside of the Constitution and outside of decency,” Olson said. 
At a No Kings: Vote Early rally outside Fargo City Hall, volunteer Liz Carlson, left, answers Arlan Steinolfson’s questions about where to vote in November. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Arlan Steinolfson of Fargo said he may vote early after learning he may be able to get a ride to the polls through a volunteer group. 
Steinolfson said he has always been a voter and at times has voted for Republican candidates, but he said that won’t happen this year. 
One of the reasons people are going to vote during this election is gas prices, said Kris Mount of Bismarck, who attended the protest holding a sign listing the area diesel price of $6.19 per gallon.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
“We were promised lower prices. We were promised lower gas. We were promised no wars and we have none of that,” Mount said.
Grand Forks, Devils Lake, Valley City, Dickinson and Jamestown also held events.
The No Kings rally in Jamestown featured about 80 people with pro-voting signs, said Bob Boyar of Jamestown.
After a short march, participants received information from organizers about ways to vote in Stutsman County, he said.
“It’s important that we’re able to disagree with each other and do it in a way that is life-building instead of destructive,” Boyar said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: No Kings rallies in Lincoln, Omaha draw demonstrators opposed to Trump’s policies
text:
A couple hundred protesters in front of the Nebraska Capitol in Lincoln on Oct, 17. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Angela Unruh, a 39-year-old Lincoln resident, said she came to the Nebraska State Capitol on Saturday to remind protesters that everyone is human.
“We’re all humans, and we all matter … we’re not really trying to screw each other over, we just have totally different sources of information,” Unruh told the Examiner. 
Saturday presented another iteration of the nationwide No Kings protests that have been planned throughout President Donald Trump’s second term. As before, signs opposing Trump were everywhere, with a couple hundred protesters in front of the Capitol. There were other protests across Nebraska.
The national organizer of these protests said this month’s rallies are meant to boost early voting. Despite national organizers’ attempt to give the event a “nonpartisan” feel, people who spoke to the Examiner said they hope to put a check on President Donald Trump in the upcoming midterm.
A couple hundred protesters in front of the Nebraska Capitol in Lincoln on Oct, 17. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Unruh said she plans to cast her early ballot soon, and her top issues are women’s rights, healthcare and immigration enforcement.
Jim Cummings, a 70-year-old Lincoln resident, said his top issues are Ukraine and the Iran war. 
“I really think democracy is threatened. … Congress is supposed to stand up to the abuses of the president; this one doesn’t,” Cummings said. 
Republicans are facing headwinds this November; the party in the White House typically doesn’t do well in midterm elections. Democrats are bullish on their chances of taking both the U.S. House and Senate. In Nebraska, several races are viewed as competitive, including the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races. In the last few weeks, the race for governor and the 1st Congressional District race have drawn attention from election analysts as the political environment worsens for Republicans. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
People gather as C.O.R.E Co-founder and Spokes Council member Ro Baker speaks at the Omaha No Kings protest on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Chase Zagurski for Nebraska Examiner)
In Omaha, demonstrators lined N 52nd Street and the NW Radial Highway. Like the rally in Lincoln, they waved hand-crafted signs opposing Trump and Nebraska Republican elected officials – with volunteers handing out Blue Dot and Blue Wave signs.
Local community activists gave speeches to the crowd gathered in Gallagher Park. A vendor village in Gallagher Park hosted organizations like the Omaha Metro Area Humanist Association, Coalition of Citizens Concerned for Democracy and the Democratic Socialists of America. 
Alyssa Price, A 24-year-old student at Creighton University School of Medicine, said she will vote in person. 
Price said having people in office who care about “healthcare and proper education around people’s rights” is top of mind ahead of the midterms. 
Alyssa Price, left, 24, and Cady Nielsen, 25, both medical students at Creighton University, participate in a No Kings protest at Turner Park in Omaha, Nebraska, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Case Zagurski for Nebraska Examiner)
Cady Nielsen, A 25-year-old Bellevue resident, said she is “really frustrated with how this current administration is handling things.” Nielsen said she wants to “stand up for people that might be getting discriminated [against] or anything like that.” 
John Stochl, a 70-year-old Benson resident, already voted by early ballot. Stochl, who is a veteran of the Vietnam War, said his top issue ahead of the midterms is “a general paintbrush of civil rights.” 
“I came here because I have a grandson and I want him to grow up in a non-fascist society,” Stochl said. “I want my daughter to have her rights. I want people of all makes, models, colors, religions, belief systems to be on equal terms.” 
Stochl added that people should know they are not alone in being “oppressed” or “discriminated against.”
“Everyone here is here for a reason. It may not all be that same reason; that’s the nice thing,” he told the Examiner. 
Back in Lincoln, Nancy Brt, a 70-year-old Lincoln resident, said she is “shocked” that Trump has gotten so far. Brt said she is part of a group that protests around Lincoln weekly.
“It feels good to be around people that agree with you,” Brt said. 
Her top issue is the Senate race, Brt said, adding that she wants Dan Osborn to beat incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts. Osborn and Ricketts are in a heated race that has seen Trump rally for Ricketts in Grand Island, and Republicans are putting Osborn in the political crosshairs, trying to cast doubt on his independence, since he will need some Republican support to pull off his prairie upset. 
When asked how she thinks the election will go this November, Unruh said people have to “handle what we’re given.”
“So I don’t know that I feel very optimistic, but I also don’t feel terrified,” Unruh said. “I think that the worst-case scenario rarely happens, and we live somewhere in the middle…so we just have to do whatever’s handed to us to the best of our ability.” 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.
Chase Zagurski contributed to this report.

outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: In the nation’s capital, rallygoers hoist umbrellas at No Kings get-out-the-vote event
text:
WASHINGTON — A couple hundred people carrying decorated umbrellas walked from the former Black Lives Matter Plaza near the White House to the U.S. Capitol lawn Saturday for a No Kings get-out-the-vote event in the nation's capital.No Kings, a coalition that has drawn millions of Americans to protests three times since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, spread out its fourth effort across several Saturday events in Washington, D.C., in addition to thousands across the nation, to encourage early voting. The Umbrella Walk was one of them. No Kings worked with the advocacy group Umbrella Walk 4 Change to hold the street protest. 

 







Octavia Clapp, of Maryland, at the Umbrella Walk on No Kings day in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/States Newsroom)

Octavia Clapp, a 25-year-old protester from Maryland, said using her right to vote especially matters as Trump attempts to wield authority over voting. The Trump administration has spent more than a year in court battles with dozens of states and voting rights groups seeking to force states to provide sensitive voter data and curb voting by mail.“I think cracking down on mail-in voting and restricting people's ability to vote easily is anti-democratic,” she said. “Democracy is really important to me, and freedom is really important to me.”Linda Levine, a Washington, D.C., resident, said restrictions on abortion rights drew her to the march. The U.S. Supreme Court in 2022 overturned the 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling that established abortion as a constitutional right. 

 







Linda Levine, left, of Washington, D.C., and her daughter, Ari Hershey, walk toward the U.S. Capitol during the Umbrella Walk on No Kings day on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/ States Newsroom)

“I am 83 and I can’t believe that my daughter has less rights now than I had,” she said. “We fought for them and this Supreme Court took them away.”Her daughter, Ari Hershey, attended with her two young sons to show them how to protest.It was a record number of participants for the Umbrella Walk 4 Change, according to the walk’s organizer, Peter Stinson.

 







Umbrella Walk organizer Peter Stinson speaks to protesters as the walk ends at the U.S. Capitol West Lawn in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/States Newsroom)

Stinson said he hopes Saturday’s events will lead to larger, more powerful demonstrations in front of the Capitol and eventually impeachment of the president.“We need 30,000 people right here, right here, every day for about four to six weeks,” he said. 

 







Aida Thoj of Lorton, Virginia, leads chants in protest of the Trump administration at the No Kings day event in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/States Newsroom)

Ashley Thoj from Lorton, Virginia, attended with her spouse Aida Thoj. For Ashley, early voting was the walk’s most important message.“Especially now that we're in early voting periods, just getting people to get out to the polls,” she said.Already, more than 8.5 million Americans have voted in the 2026 midterm election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.Unlike past No Kings events, only some of Saturday’s actions involved protests. The events across the United States included help with voter registration, walks to ballot drop-off locations and car pool sign-ups.At the Umbrella Walk, Stinson ended the march with a reminder to participants to vote and help others vote.“Work within your circle of influence,” he said. “Work within your skill set.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota No Kings events emphasize advance voting
text:
The No Kings demonstration in Sioux Falls on Oct. 17, 2026, was at Drake Springs Park near downtown. Demonstrators lined 10th Street along the park's borders. Speakers and a band took the stage to criticize the Trump administration and encourage advance voting. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/101726-No-Kings-web.mp3
  Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: see below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
Nearly 32,000 South Dakotans have already voted in advance of the Nov. 3 general election, and supporters of the No Kings movement want to push that number higher.
The fourth round of nationwide day-long No Kings demonstrations was Saturday. Eight were held in South Dakota, including the state’s largest city of Sioux Falls, where hundreds showed up to support the advance voting message. In Pierre, the state’s capital city, a few dozen participated. Events were also held in Rapid City, Aberdeen, Watertown, Brookings, Yankton and Vermillion.
Ann Holzhauer said “concern for our country” brought her to the demonstration in Pierre, “specifically in regard to elections.”
“We didn’t have concerns about election security and election integrity until Donald Trump came along,” she said. “And as of yet, no evidence has been presented to prove his allegations regarding elections, and I think it’s really important for people to know that.”
Constance Hoffman, left, and Michael Elsasser traveled from Winner, South Dakota, to support the early voting message at the No Kings rally in Pierre on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)Michael Strickland holds a sign that reads "Trump is America's enemy" at a No Kings rally on Oct. 19, 2026, in Pierre, South Dakota. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)Laurie Kelly, left, said her attendance at a No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Pierre, South Dakota, was "necessary" to spread the message about advance voting. She sits next to Char Russell. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)Diane Komsky, 67, lives in Lake Benton, Minnesota, but drove about an hour to the Sioux Falls No Kings protest on Oct. 17, 2026. She was motivated to attend by the “madness in the White House," she said. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The No Kings demonstration in Sioux Falls on Oct. 17, 2026, was at Drake Springs Park near downtown. Demonstrators lined 10th Street along the park's borders. Speakers and a band took the stage to criticize the Trump administration and encourage advance voting. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)While attending a No Kings demonstration on Oct. 17, 2026, in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Frances Walker, 73, from Madison, said she had attended several previous No Kings events and has been “protesting since the Vietnam War." (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Seventy-seven-year-old Sioux Falls resident Chuck Larson said he’s attended every No Kings demonstration in the city because President Donald Trump “has messed up everything he’s touched.”
Larson said he voted early for the general election at the Minnehaha County Auditor’s Office. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
With the control of Congress at stake, President Donald Trump and his aides have refused to rule out interfering in the elections. In an interview with Time magazine published recently, when Trump was asked about sending Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to conduct enforcement actions at the polls, he said only that he hadn’t thought of it. He also addressed whether he’d declare a national emergency to impose regulations on the election.
“I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see,” Trump said.
Actions like those are “un-American,” according to Michael Strickland, who attended the rally in Pierre.
“They’re trying to steal the election and make it harder for people who they think are going to be against them to vote,” he said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Diane Komsky lives in Lake Benton, Minnesota, but drove about an hour to the Sioux Falls event because of her opposition to the “madness in the White House.”
“I want to give peace a real chance for families in the United States,” Komsky said.
Komsky plans to vote early.
“Voting is our voice,” Komsky said.
Millions were expected to participate in No Kings events nationwide Saturday. The events have grown from 5 million attendees across 2,100 individual events on June 14, 2025, to more than 7 million at 2,700 events on Oct. 18, 2025, and 8 million across 3,330 events on March 28, 2026, according to organizers.
Advance voting is underway in South Dakota, and the voter registration deadline for the Nov. 3 general election is Monday. Ballots in South Dakota include four proposed state constitutional amendments and races for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, governor and the Legislature, along with various local races and issues.
South Dakota Searchlight’s Makenzie Huber contributed to this report.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ‘No Kings’ protests across CT focus on voting, democracy
text:
Hundreds gathered at dozens of “No Kings” protests across Connecticut on Saturday, with signs bearing some familiar slogans but with a sharper focus this time, organizers said, on voting.
The demonstrations were part of a nationwide day of protests against what participants described as threats to democracy, civil rights and government accountability, just weeks before midterm elections that will decide which party holds power in Washington, D.C. 
In Bridgeport, elected officials, longtime activists, educators and residents voiced concerns about immigration enforcement, school funding, voting rights, discrimination and the influence of federal leadership on their daily lives. Protesters also emphasized the importance of voting and holding elected officials accountable beyond Election Day.

Demonstrators march through Bridgeport toward the federal building downtown during a “No Kings” protest on Saturday, Oct. 17.  Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror

About 70 people gathered at Ash Creek Bridge in Bridgeport before marching to the federal building downtown.
In New Haven, about 200 people gathered on the Green for an event organizers described as a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting. Four attendees carried umbrellas painted with the word “VOTE” in red, white and blue, while a service dog wore a sign on its harness that read, “Don’t let bad humans keep you from voting.”
Partisan messages were also visible throughout the gathering. Some signs criticized President Donald Trump’s economic and immigration policies, while others praised Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris. One sign called Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, a “malignant polyp.”

Members of the Umbrella Brigade stand outside the New Haven Free Public Library during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Maggie Marcarelli, a member of the steering committee for Greater New Haven Indivisible, said the group organized the event with Greater Westville Indivisible and Indivisible Amity. Marcarelli said 275 people had registered through the No Kings website and estimated that about 200 attended. 
She said organizers declined requests from politicians to speak to maintain the event’s stated nonpartisan purpose. 
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro attended but did not speak. In an interview, DeLauro criticized Trump, attributing rising living costs to his policies, and praised attendees for “speaking about what they think, what they feel.”

U.S. Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, D-3rd District, sings along with a protest song during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Marcarelli said many attendees appeared to view the gathering as a rally rather than an event focused on voting. “Almost everyone here thinks it’s a rally and a march,” she said at the start of the event. “I said, ‘Did you read the description on the No Kings site?’”
Voting outreach was a central part of the gathering. At one table, members of Greater Westville Indivisible asked attendees to fill out postcards encouraging Connecticut residents who vote less frequently to head to the polls. Nan Becker, the group’s 67-year-old founder, said some studies have found that postcards can increase voter turnout.
“If you give people information that they find useful, they stick it on their refrigerators and hopefully remember to vote,” Becker said.
Attendees filled out about 40 postcards and took home another 250, estimated Andrea Ryan, who staffed the table with Becker. Nearby, large sheets of paper invited attendees to respond to prompts such as “I’m voting early because” and “U.S. 2026 federal budget: where would you spend your tax dollars?”

No Kings protesters demonstrate outside the Connecticut state Capitol in Hartford on Oct. 17, 2026.  Credit: Mark Mirko / Connecticut Public

At the state Capitol in Hartford, a rally on the south lawn featured “teach-ins” that covered a variety of topics, including how to document federal immigration agent activity and ranked-choice voting, according to CT 50501, the event host.
The gathering in Bridgeport also drew attendees from across generations, although younger people appeared to be in the minority. Brenda Pastor, a 24-year-old art teacher from Waterbury who learned about the event through social media, said she was “shocked to see a lot of it being older people.” 
Gabe Johnson, a 41-year-old Hamden resident who brought his young children to encourage their civic engagement, also remarked on the age of the crowd. “There’s not even anybody freaking my age or younger than me,” he said.

Attendees listen to a speaker during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Some attendees voiced concerns beyond voting and the economy. David Boscarino, a 63-year-old Bethany resident who attended with his wife, Carol, and three friends, carried a two-sided poster. One side emphasized voting, while the other contained a series of insults directed at Trump. 
Boscarino said he was frustrated by high gas prices, aggressive immigration enforcement and what he described as damaged international relationships.

Attendees cross the street to attend a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

John Miksad, a 67-year-old Bethany resident and coordinator for the Connecticut chapter of the peace activist group World BEYOND War, carried Palestinian and peace flags on a pole. He called for an end to what he described as “forever” wars and argued that military spending should instead address issues such as education, housing and sustainability.
“Unless we change the trajectory of this country, my grandchildren and their generation are not going to flourish,” Miksad said.
Callie Heilmann, founder and co-director of Bridgeport Generation Now and an organizer of the Bridgeport protest, said Bridgeport has a particular connection to the issues raised by the movement. She described the city as “the epicenter of … problems with American democracy and what can happen to a place when people disrespect it or think they’re above the law.” 

Callie Heilmann, founder and co-director of Bridgeport Generation Now and an organizer of the Bridgeport “No Kings” protest, leads demonstrators in chants during the rally on Saturday, Oct. 17. Heilmann said she hopes to channel the energy surrounding the protests into greater civic participation ahead of Bridgeport’s 2027 municipal elections. Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror

Drawing on years of conversations with residents, Heilmann said she hears both frustration and a desire for action. “What you don’t hear in Bridgeport is ignorance about the issue, and you don’t hear people saying they’re fine with it,” she said.
For some Bridgeport protesters, those concerns were rooted in the effects of federal policies on local families. State Rep. Christopher Rosario, a Democrat representing Bridgeport’s 128th House District, said he attended because of what he called the “rampant abuse by ICE in our communities.” Rosario described incidents involving parents taken from bus stops and a young man who he said was detained while walking his dog. 
He also said immigration enforcement was affecting school attendance, with consequences for students beyond immigrant families. “School attendance is down, which impacts all the students, even those that have citizenship, because our funding is based on bodies and student population,” he said.

Katy Mulvaney, of New Haven, and other attendees participate in the “Protest Pokey” during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

State Sen. Sujata Gadkar-Wilcox, a Democrat whose 22nd Senate District includes Bridgeport, Trumbull and Monroe, said she attended to stand with residents and defend democratic institutions. 
“To me, our constitution is definitely under threat,” she said. She urged residents to hold elected officials accountable throughout the year, not only when they cast ballots. “We need to hold those of us in office accountable. So make sure you do that too, 365 days, not just on Election Day.”
That message was echoed by Trish Swain, a former Bridgeport City Council member, who said residents must continue speaking out even in a city and state where Democrats hold significant political power. 
“We need to be vocal. We cannot be silent at a time like this,” Swain said. She also encouraged people to vote in November, raising concerns about participation in Bridgeport elections. “I hope that everybody votes. That is a problem in Bridgeport. We have a very low voter percentage,” she said.

Betty Hancock, 89, and her daughter Paige Ryan listen to a speaker during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.  Hancock’s sign reads “89 and voting in person…What’s your excuse? Vote Now.” Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The upcoming election was also on the minds of protesters from outside Bridgeport. Maire Velade, a Fairfield resident, said she wanted people to recognize the importance of the midterms. “I just want to make sure people get out and vote because I think a lot of people don’t realize how important these midterms are,” she said. 
Fairfield resident Brendan Johnston said he wanted to see changes in government, an end to corruption and discrimination, and “a better society for everyone.” He said he and other white residents have friends and neighbors who are experiencing discrimination and are afraid to go about their daily lives.

A person in a Donald Trump costume crosses Capitol Avenue in Hartford as NoKings protesters demonstrate outside the Connecticut state Capitol in Hartford on Oct. 17, 2026.  Credit: Mark Mirko / Connecticut Public

Amy Guerrero, a Filipino American activist and teacher in Norwalk who previously taught in Bridgeport, emphasized the importance of solidarity across racial and cultural groups. She said she wears a “Black voters matter” shirt to show support for Black Americans and argued that broader cooperation is needed to bring about change. 
“I think it’s … we really need a cross-cultural solidarity movement to … make good change for all of us,” she said. Guerrero also raised concerns about federal funding cuts affecting schools, including Title I schools serving students from low-income families. “As a former teacher in Bridgeport, current teacher in Norwalk, Title I schools are hurting … we are hurting because of the federal funding that’s been cut,” she said.

Attendees listen to a speaker during a “No Kings: Vote Early” rally at New Haven Green on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The demonstrations come as Connecticut voters prepare for the Nov. 3 general election. Early voting runs from Oct. 19 through Nov. 1, giving eligible voters an opportunity to cast ballots before Election Day. 
The midterms will help determine control of Congress and shape federal policy for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term.

Demonstrators hold signs during a “No Kings” protest in Bridgeport on Saturday, Oct. 17. Protesters called attention to civil rights, discrimination and the importance of protecting democratic institutions. Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror

For Heilmann, however, the protest is also part of a longer effort to get Bridgeport residents involved in local government. She said Bridgeport Generation Now plans to use the energy surrounding the demonstrations to encourage civic participation ahead of the city’s 2027 municipal elections. 
“Part of our work is actually taking this energy and talking to people about next year, when it is a local election year and when voting actually will and does shape power and shapes the outcome of their lives,” she said. Her message to residents was simple: “Hang in there because 2027 will be here before you know it.”
Reporting from Connecticut Public is included in this story.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas US Rep. French Hill seeks classified briefing on Trump waiving Russia sanctions
text:
U.S. Congressional District 2 incumbent Rep. French Hill (R) answers questions during the debate against opponent Chris Jones (D) on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)U.S. Rep. French Hill said Saturday he’s seeking a classified briefing to explain President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions against Russia days before they were to take effect.
The Republican congressman from central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District announced the request the day after Trump signed an executive order putting on hold the sanctions package that was in legislation the president signed last month named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. 

[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.] 
“We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up,” Hill wrote in an X post. “We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine.”
Hill, who chairs the House Financial Services Committee, was a lead sponsor of the Rebuilding Prosperity and Opportunity for Ukrainians Act, also known as the REPO Act, a 2024 law ordering the seizure of Russian sovereign assets held in the United States.
Lawmakers from both parties have criticized Trump’s decision to waive the sanctions. Hill has also opposed Trump’s plan to purchase diesel from Russia, which the president announced as an effort to address high fuel prices.
Central Arkansas congressional candidates debate independence from Trump, cost of living

Hill announced his request as he faces a reelection challenge from Democrat Chris Jones. Hill was first elected to the 2nd District in 2014.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has added the district to its “Red to Blue” program targeting Republican-held seats the party believes can be flipped. The Cook Political Report and Larry Sabato have recently moved the race in Democrats’ favor, from safely to likely Republican.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Charleston No Kings organizers ask crowd to vote early in West Virginia
text:
A No Kings rally participant holds a sign that says “Fund Healthcare not ICE” at the West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Organizers of the fourth “No Kings” rally encouraged people to vote early during the general election. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch) Organizers of the No Kings rally in Charleston, West Virginia, had a simple message Saturday for the crowd who showed up to the state Capitol: vote early. 
The general election is Nov. 3 in West Virginia. Early voting starts Oct. 21 and continues through Oct. 31 at courthouses and other community locations around the state. 
“We are here to encourage everyone to vote and everyone to vote early,” said Sarah Lindstrom, president of United West Virginia, which organized the local rally. “Get those votes in early. It saves us time getting counted.”
Saturday was the fourth No Kings rally at the West Virginia state Capitol. The events were held around the country in protest of the Trump administration. Attendees held protest signs and waved flags. 
Lindstrom said organizers were expecting a bigger turnout than the crowd that showed up. Kanawha Boulevard was closed in front of the Capitol by a line of police vehicles with flashing lights at two points on the roadway. 
Lindstrom said organizers had not requested that Capitol Police close the roadway.
“I personally feel like they’re trying to stifle our voice so that (reporters) don’t see as many people here as would be here if they could drive by and park,” she said. 
A line of West Virginia State Police vehicles block Kanawha Boulevard in front of the state Capitol during the “No Kings” rally on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
A handful of Capitol Police officers standing across the roadway from the Capitol building referred a reporter to the state Department of Homeland Security to answer a question about the road closure. A spokesman for Gov. Patrick Morrisey said he would “make some calls” about why the roadway was closed, but did not have an answer by publication.
At their biggest No Kings rally, 1,000 people attended, Lindstrom said. 
“It’s not ruined, but it’s something to observe,” she said. “I find it something to observe for our communities. We want our First Amendment (rights) to be welcomed, not only respected but welcomed. Because if they had something to say, I want them to be able to come out here and say it.”
Marc Adams, of Charleston, carried an “8647” flag at the rally. Adams has a laundry list of complaints about the Trump administration, from immigration officials “seizing” people off the street, to the war in Iran and tearing down the East Wing of the White House complex. 
And while the president is not on the ballot for the midterm election, Adams said his dislike of Trump’s policies is still motivating his vote. 
“He’s not on the ballot, but everyone who has been supporting him, at least half of them are,” Adams said. “So you know, (I’m) definitely voting against all of that. If you have an R after your name, you’re not getting my vote.”
Adams and his partner Carrie Stollings plan to vote early during this election, though they usually like the “vibe” of voting on Election Day. They want their votes to be in and counted early, he said. 
In West Virginia, absentee and early ballots are counted after polls close on Election Day.
A crowd of people attend the fourth No Kings rally at the West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
Adams said he’s concerned that the Trump administration may not count their votes. 
“We have to make sure that everybody votes, whether it’s on that day or early, and that the votes are counted,” he said. “It may take a fight, there may be some struggles in there.
Rally speakers — including Gina Milam of Huntington — led the crowd in protest chants. 
“I want to hear everybody!” Milam yelled. “We the people! We the people! We the people!”
“Go vote. Take somebody else with you,” Milam said. “And make sure that anybody that needs a ride to the polls can get there.” 
Milam helped restart the Huntington chapter of the National Organization of Women. She said she’s inspired to speak against the Trump administration and Republicans because of the younger women in her life.
“I’m a grandmother, and I have six granddaughters,” she said. “For the first time in my life, I’ve had more rights than my granddaughters have. That’s why it was important to me to start a chapter of NOW in Huntington, and just to build that as much as I possibly can. We’ve got to speak out. We cannot sit idly by and let our democracy be destroyed.”
Renee and John Corrie, of South Charleston, West Virginia, hold signs at the No Kings day rally in Charleston, West Virginia, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
Renee Corrie, of South Charleston, held a “vote early” sign at the rally. Her husband John said they’re fighting back because they’re “fed up” with the country and what it’s become.
“We’ve got to change,” John Corrie said. “We can’t change (Trump) but we can change the House and Senate.”
The Corries say they’ll vote early just in case something happens that prevents them from voting on Election Day. They don’t trust the United States Postal Service with a mail-in ballot, he said. 
“I don’t trust anything to do with the federal government right now,” he said.
