name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Osborn’s independence continues to be scrutinized in Nebraska Senate race
text:
Registered nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn leaves a podium in Lincoln on June 11, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Registered nonpartisan Nebraska U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn has vowed repeatedly he wouldn’t caucus with either party if he pulled off the upset in the bitter race against incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts. 
He did so again at a virtual press conference on Monday with Brian Bengs and Seth Bodnar, who are running for Senate as independents in South Dakota and Montana. The trio said remaining independent could complicate their efforts to secure committee assignments, but argued their votes could carry significant weight in a closely divided Senate, allowing them to negotiate for committee assignments. 
Geoff Lorenz, a University of Nebraska-Lincoln political science professor who focuses on Congress, said committee assignments go through the major parties, so Osborn’s strategy, if he’s elected, would require him to prove to his congressional colleagues that he truly is a swing vote. 
“We’re not going to caucus with either party. In fact, we’ll caucus with everybody, you could say,” Osborn said during the press conference. “Independent means independent, and to do anything else would be a slap in the face to the people of Nebraska and our states.” 
The National Republican Senatorial Committee, in a statement, responded that “the Fake Independent circus is fooling nobody.” The Ricketts campaign and national Republicans dismissed Osborn’s answer, contending that he would caucus with Democrats and wouldn’t get committee assignments if he didn’t caucus with either party.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Congressional committees, much like those in the Nebraska Legislature, are an early step in the legislative process. Any legislation Osborn proposed would have to be referred to a committee, Lorenz said, and to advance legislation, it’s best to serve on a committee that deals with the subject. 
Lorenz said Osborn’s hypothetical strategy isn’t impossible, as Senate rules and procedures can change, but there isn’t “necessarily a good template for doing it.” 
“What Dan Osborn would have to do instead, if he wasn’t on committees … he would be to build a reputation for genuine independence,” Lorenz said. “I don’t want to claim that it’s impossible. It’s just atypical,” 
Independent U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn speaks during his rally in La Vista on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Two independents currently serve in the Senate, Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine, both of whom caucus with Democrats. An earlier independent senator was Wayne Morse of Oregon in the 1950s. According to Wake Up To Politics, a Substack from journalist Gabe Fleisher, Morse eventually decided to caucus with Democrats for better committee assignments. 
Osborn has pointed to Senate rules that require each senator to serve on at least two committees. The rule doesn’t guarantee which committees a senator serves on, and Lorenz emphasized that parties control how they divide them up.
Ricketts serves on four Senate committees: Environment and Public Works; Foreign Relations; Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs; and Budget.
The Ricketts campaign and Republicans have cited a story from the online outlet Plains Sentinel that said Osborn had said during a 2025 town hall in La Vista that he would caucus with Democrats. The Cornhusker Majority, a super PAC tied to the Senate Leadership Fund, used the story in an ad showing Osborn on a cereal box. 
The Examiner asked Osborn about the story during Monday’s virtual press conference. When the outlet was mentioned in the question, Osborn said, “Fake news,” while mimicking President Donald Trump. 
“They could have taken any one of my talks and said I won’t caucus with Republicans, or they could say I won’t caucus with Democrats in the same regard. They take snippets of what I say, turn it around to try to work against me,” Osborn told the Examiner. “So you know, all I can say is what we’ve said again definitively here today. I got no interest in caucusing with either party.” 
The Plains Sentinel released a roughly three-minute audio clip of the 2025 town hall exchange after the Examiner reported Osborn’s answer. 
Lorenz said that if Osborn goes to Washington, he should hire at least one staffer with D.C. experience to help navigate the legislative process and “find a balance between people who have a connection to the state and people who know how the Hill works and know how to get things done there.” 
The Nebraska Senate race has drawn national attention for its nontraditional political dynamics, serving as a trendsetter for other red states with independent candidates. Bengs’ race in South Dakota is a true head-to-head against Republican incumbent Sen. Mike Rounds after the Democrats stepped aside. Idaho also saw the Democratic Senate candidate, David Roth, drop out. 
Bodnar, in Montana, wasn’t so fortunate, as the Democrat in the race refused to drop out. The Nebraska Senate race isn’t a true head-to-head, as three other candidates are running for the seat. Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin has suspended his campaign and endorsed Osborn. 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already begun.

name: WyoFile
title: Who showed up for Wyoming’s US House debate and key takeaways
text:
For those familiar with Wyoming political history, it might seem like a foregone conclusion that voters are poised to elect Republican nominee Chuck Gray to be the state’s next at-large representative in the U.S. House. 
Tight general elections have been infrequent, and it’s been 20 years since a Democrat came close to winning — that was Gary Trauner losing to Republican Rep. Barbara Cubin by just 0.5% of the vote. 
The last time Wyoming actually elected a Democrat to the House? That traces back a full half century ago to 1976, when Teno Roncalio was reelected over Republican Larry Hart. 
So even though Gray, the current secretary of state, only won 25% of the vote in the nine-candidate Republican primary, assumptions that he’s on a glidepath to take office in Washington, D.C. are understandable. 
Yet, the frontrunner didn’t show up on Thursday evening for a livestreamed debate between candidates vying to represent Wyoming in the U.S. House. Democrat Lisa Kinney, Constitution Party candidate Jeffrey Haggit and Libertarian Shawn Johnson did partake and pitched Wyoming voters on their candidacies.
Here are three takeaways about the U.S. House race and the hour-long forum, which was hosted by Wyoming PBS, Wyoming Public Media and Cowboy State Daily.
No Chuck Gray
Kinney didn’t waste any time before seizing on Gray’s absence. After thank yous, it was the first thing the attorney and former state senator from Laramie said during her introductory remarks.
“Where is the GOP nominee?” Kinney said. “I still haven’t seen him.” 
Other candidates were more understanding.
“Chuck Gray is his own man,” Haggit said. “I don’t know if he’s being told to not show up here, or if it’s just a personal decision.”
Gray explained his absence in a statement to WyoFile. He pointed out that past Republican nominees in similar positions have skipped general election debates, including current U.S. House Rep. Harriet Hageman in 2022, 2024, and 2026 (she’s now running for U.S. Senate). And he also touted his outreach to voters.
“So far, I’ve hosted over 50 townhalls, done at least 6 debates, dozens of forums, and also attended other events across Wyoming,” Gray said in a text message.
Major party status on the line?
The Democratic Party qualifies as a “major political party” in Wyoming, and the U.S. House race could determine whether it keeps that status. It’s an important classification, because minor and provisional political parties must nominate candidates through a convention instead of primary elections. 
Wyoming law defines a major political party as an “organization whose candidate for any one of the offices of the United States house of representatives, governor or secretary of state, received not less than 10% of the total votes cast for that office in the most recent general election.”
Will Kinney hit the threshold in a four-way race? If the 2024 general election results are any indication, she’s got a shot. Even in the most pro-Trump state in the nation, Democrat Kamala Harris’ box was checked for president on nearly 26% of Wyoming ballots. 
Rapid fire
During the Riverton forum, the three candidates were given just a moment to provide an immediate reaction to a number of topics. Here are some of their answers: 
Haggit on Harriet Hageman: 
“She’s done a pretty good job.” 
Johnson on Harriet Hageman: 
“I’m not running against Harriet Hageman. Good luck to her and her campaign.”
Kinney on Harriet Hageman: 
“I taught Harriet Hageman when she was going through law school. I’ve known her for years, but she is dead wrong about taking away our public lands.” 
Haggit on ICE and immigration: 
“A lot of people look at them as the brown shirts of Nazi Germany. But a lot of the stuff that they run into problems with is because the local sanctuary outfits don’t do it, so they got to come in with force. Immigration is broken and needs reformed.”
Johnson on ICE and immigration: 
“I think ICE is overly overfunded. I think they’re being used improperly. We do need to ensure that our borders are secure, because I believe that borders define a nation. There’s a right way of doing it and a wrong way of doing it, and ICE is the wrong way of doing it.”
Kinney on ICE and immigration:
“When they’re taking hundreds of people in, because they’re black or they’re brown and they’re being cruel and they’re not using due process, it has to be reformed.”
The post Who showed up for Wyoming’s US House debate and key takeaways appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Days before early vote begins, Arkansans rally for change at No Kings and Pride events
authors: Antoinette Grajeda, Tess Vrbin, Ainsley Platt
text:
Marchers at the No Kings rally in downtown Little Rock, Arkansas hold signs on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas voters who attended No Kings events and a Pride celebration Saturday cited healthcare and immigration as their biggest concerns, days before the first votes are set to be cast for the November election.
Hundreds marched to the state Capitol during a No Kings rally in central Arkansas where John Landosky of Little Rock said Republican policies have separated him and his family.
“I don’t like bullies. I don’t like people who use hate to further their agenda,” said Landosky, whose son is transgender and whose ex-wife is a pediatrician. “I mean, it doesn’t require me to have a trans child to vote against this, I’ll tell you that much. I would be voting either way.”
Landosky became emotional while saying he understood why his ex-wife and children moved to Oregon, pointing to a 2021 law which made gender-affirming medical care for minors illegal in Arkansas. The separation has been “devastating” for Landosky, who said this is just one reason he’s voting this year.
More than a dozen No Kings events were planned across the state as early voting is set to begin Monday for the Arkansas general election. Democrats, who haven’t won a statewide or congressional election in Arkansas since 2010, are hopeful that Trump’s unpopularity nationally may boost their chances in the predominantly Republican state.
Participants in the No Kings rally at the Arkansas Capitol in Little Rock hold signs protesting the Trump administration on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Patsy Stewart, a 77-year-old North Carolina resident who plans to move to Arkansas next year, participated in the march, and said climate change and how the Trump administration has treated immigrants motivates her to vote. 
“We need to be kind if we’re going to follow Jesus as a prophet,” Stewart said. “Most importantly for me is the climate, because that’s the end of the Earth that I grew up in.”
Pat Edmunds of Russellville and Joan Brooke of Clarksville said they both wanted to see Trump and his supporters “out of office.” Brooke said immigrants have been treated “terribly” while Edmunds said tariffs implemented by the Trump administration “are just crazy.” 
“One of the reasons we’re here is for our grandchildren — granddaughters in particular, their rights and their future,” Edmunds said. 
Pride and protest
Saturday’s No Kings rally coincided with Central Arkansas Pride’s festival and parade for a second year. While there were fewer attendees than last year, the message of solidarity against the Trump administration’s policies regarding immigrants and healthcare remained.
“I think everybody sees the potential for a lot of people’s rights regressing… and if that’s not scary, I don’t know what is,” said Tonya Nix from Bismarck.
Hallie Shoffner, the Democrat challenging Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, marched in the Pride parade alongside supporters, including one wearing an inflatable chicken suit and carrying a sign that said “Tom Cotton: Too Chicken to Debate.”
Cotton did not participate in Monday’s televised debate with Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin. The two major-party candidates will not debate each other in advance of the election after a conservative outlet announced it would not host a debate Shoffner and Cotton agreed to attend.
Cotton’s absence takes center stage at debate between Arkansas’ US Senate candidates

Newport resident William Mitchener said he’s seen firsthand that farmers have struggled financially and closed granaries in the past year.
An anti-Trump Republican, Mitchener also said the rising cost of gasoline frustrates people of all political affiliations.
“Other people are pro-choice, blah blah blah, but every one of us couldn’t fill up our tank today if we put $20 in,” he said.
Mitchener wore camouflage and carried both an American flag and a Pride flag up and down Capitol Avenue. He said he hoped his presence would dissuade anyone who might want to harass Pride attendees.
A small group of anti-LGBTQ+ counterprotesters held signs at the Pulaski Street intersection and shouted at passing paradegoers to “turn against sin and lust.” 
A larger group of pro-LGBTQ+ Christians marched in the parade, including retired Methodist pastor Don Moore, who said he believes “God loves all people and God creates people the way they are.”
Moore recently moved to Arkansas from central Texas, where he said he became fed up with anti-LGBTQ+ bigotry. Morre said he’s registered to vote in Arkansas, and one of the issues he considers most at stake in the midterms is the future of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he called “abhorrent.”
Voter education
In downtown Springdale, Indivisible Northwest Arkansas hosted a voter education event where local residents could sign up for rides to the polls, volunteer to provide voter protection and learn how to check their voter registration. 
The event also included protesters holding signs along a busy street and singing performances by the Raging Grannies of Northwest Arkansas. Raging Grannies is “an international disorganization of women over a certain age” who use satirical song and theater as a tool for political education. 
Kate Kowalski, a Fayetteville resident who started the local chapter in March 2025, said her biggest concern as a voter is healthcare. Kowalski said it “really distresses” her that in the world’s wealthiest country, many people don’t have access to care and worry about medical bankruptcy. 
Kowalski said she’s looking for candidates who, “at the very least,” won’t reduce access to healthcare by cutting back on Medicaid subsidies or who’s eligible for the program.
“Beyond that I would like to get us to a point where everyone in this country has healthcare, affordable healthcare and without having to jump through hoops; just as a right rather than as a privilege,” she said. 

The Raging Grannies of Northwest Arkansas sang during a voter education event in Springdale, Arkansas on Oct. 17,2026. Indivisible NWA hosted the event in conjunction with the No Kings nationwide day of action. #arpx
— Antoinette Grajeda (@grajeda.bsky.social) 2026-10-17T17:20:48.251Z

Mary Jennings, another Fayetteville resident who sings with the Raging Grannies, said she’s concerned about gun safety, especially in light of this week’s fatal school shooting in Oregon.
The economy and immigration are concerns for Tammra Fields, an Indivisible NWA volunteer from Elkins. During Saturday’s event, she signed up volunteers to help with the group’s voter protection efforts. Because of the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration crackdown, Fields said there are concerns about immigrants being hassled at the polls “just because of the color of their skin.”
“America’s always been racist, it has,” she said. “It’s always been divided in that sense and it’s long past time to break that habit.”
Stephanie Shufelt is a Springdale Democrat running for a seat on the Washington County Quorum Court in November. As a voter, Shufelt said she’s concerned about everyone in the community feeling safe — including immigrants — and infrastructure. 
“Our roads are crumbling, our roads have not been addressed,” she said. “Our kids ride buses over those bridges.”
Early voting starts Monday in Arkansas and continues until election day on Nov. 3. Arkansans can check their voter registration, view sample ballots and locate polling sites at www.voterview.ar-nova.org.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Analysts shift western Montana  congressional district to toss-up status
text:
Democratic U.S. House candidate Sam Forstag speaks at a rally in Missoula on May 28, 2026, ahead of Montana's primary election. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)Three political analyses this week moved Montana’s competitive western congressional race toward the Democratic candidate, with two shifting the race into “toss up” status. 
The race by Democratic smokejumper Sam Forstag and Republican veteran and radio host Aaron Flint has been Montana’s most competitive federal election since current Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke announced his retirement. Libertarian Nick Sheedy is also running. 
In rapid succession, Fox News, the Cook Political Report and Inside Elections all upgraded the race in favor of Forstag this week. 
Tuesday morning, before a congressional debate, Fox News released new “power rankings” shifting the race from “leans Republican” to “toss up.”
That was followed by a Thursday announcement by Inside Elections that the race had moved from “lean Republican” to “tilt Republican,” and on Friday the Cook Political Report changed the race to a “toss up.” 
“Montana families are fed up with corrupt politicians and political puppets like Aaron Flint telling us to ignore what we’re seeing and feeling every day while we fight to afford rent, gas, and groceries,” Forstag said in a statement. “We need leaders who will work to find actual solutions, not just talk about them on the radio. I’m so proud of the work we’ve done to rally our community around the struggles and solutions that can unite us.”
The Cook Political Report cited heavy investments from both the Democratic House Majority PAC and President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC as evidence that both sides view the race as close. 
According to Quiver Quantitative, a data aggregator, the race has seen more than $3.5 million in outside spending in the previous week alone. 
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally with U.S. House candidate Aaron Flint in Kalispell on Oct 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
Looking to boost turnout among his Republican base, Trump stopped in Kalispell on Wednesday night for a rally alongside Flint and the Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate, Kurt Alme. 
Before a few thousand attendees, Flint and Trump took the stage together, shared a handshake, a smile and remarked about the “dumbocrat” in the race. 
“We’re going to defeat far-left lobbyist, phony Sam Forstag, not respected at all,” Trump said. “And we’re going to elect a true American patriot, a fantastic man, a great guy, Aaron Flint, to Congress. He’s going to Congress to be a warrior.”
 Cross-partisanship appeal

Forstag’s campaign said the president’s visit was a sign Republicans are scared of the race.
While Trump was stumping in the Flathead, Forstag held a small rally outside Bozeman and on Thursday held a town-hall discussion in Libby with Marc Racicot, a former Montana governor and former Republican National Committee chairman. 
The event was the latest in a series of “civil discourse town halls” Forstag has held on the campaign trail aimed at finding common-ground solutions among individuals with differing political ideals. 
Racicot served as governor from 1993 to 2001, and ran President George W. Bush’s re-election campaign. 
Racicot has taken heat from the Montana GOP in recent years, including being disowned by the state GOP, after coming out against Trump during the 2020 and 2024 elections and endorsing Democrats. 
There is “an honest purpose, and a code of conduct in the ethics that Sam brings to this race,” Racicot told the more than 80 attendees. “He is a great student of what is going on in the country. He’s an extraordinarily kind and thoughtful human being. He’s principled and focused upon the best interest of the people that he lives with, that he wants to serve.”
The pair discussed a variety of topics including health care, limiting corporate spending in elections and best forest management practices. 
Racicot criticized the “Big Beautiful Bill” for transferring a trillion dollars from the Medicaid program and the SNAP program — formerly known as food stamps —  into tax reform. 
“That tax reform, as it ends up in the pockets of Americans, mostly goes into the pockets of those at the higher end of the wage spectrum or the wealth spectrum,” Racicot said. “As a consequence of that, we now are faced with a Medicaid emergency, and it’s only going to grow worse in January. 
Racicot also spoke about the administration taking a “hacksaw,” to the Forest Service budget, which was an impetus for Forstag getting into the race. 
“I was leader in my union’s Local when all the cuts started just over a year-and-a-half ago,” Forstag said. “I reached out to the person you should be able to call when our public lands are under attack, when working people’s livelihoods are under attack … our congressperson.”
When he got “crickets” in response, Forstag said he decided to get involved. 
Forest management is his primary background as a wildland firefighter, and Forstag said he wants to see forest management policies become proactive before wildfires become costly and dangerous, and help restore the state’s lumber industry. 
“We’re down to six sawmills across western Montana. We used to have 30 or 40,” Forstag said. “And the way that we rebuild that, I say this as a firefighter. It’s not just by fighting fire. It’s not by waiting until things are burning. It’s by fighting before they start.”
He added that responsible timber harvest will help with the housing crisis by boosting the state’s lumber industry. 
“I’d like to be part of making sure we’re reforming processes to make sure it doesn’t take five to six years to get a timber sale through in the front country on federal public lands,” he said. 
Forstag said that the town halls align with the premise of his campaign — just as important as fighting for specific policies, is fighting for a country where civil discourse is the norm. 
“We’re fighting … to get to a place where we can sit down with somebody we do not agree with on everything, and talk about all the values that we share in common and find common ground and solutions,” Forstag said. “Because that seems like an entirely lacking skill set in all the Congress today.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Trump parachutes to KY to stump for Republicans in safe seats, give GOP nod in ‘tight race’
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during his rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Kentucky. (Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern)HIGHLAND HEIGHTS — President Donald Trump returned to Northern Kentucky for the second time this year in hopes of swaying GOP voters in the commonwealth to back Republicans at the ballot box. 
Despite gaining attention from the Cincinnati area media market, the Saturday rally at Northern Kentucky University focused heavily on Republican seats in Kentucky. Signs for two Trump-endorsed candidates in Kentucky— U.S. Rep. Andy Barr in the Senate race and Ed Gallrein in the 4th Congressional District — lined the roads around the arena. Dates for Kentucky voting flashed on the arena’s jumbotron, such as the Oct. 20 deadline to request an absentee ballot and the start of early voting, Oct. 29. The only Ohio Republican candidate to address the crowd was Eric Conroy, in the Buckeye state’s 1st Congressional District. 
In addition to again promising $5,000 checks to adults if the GOP wins control of Congress this fall, Trump also had a Kentucky-specific promise.
Andy Barr, Kentucky Republican candidate for U.S Senate, speaks to attendees during President Trump’s rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Kentucky. (Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern)
“The Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Antheia to revitalize a gigantic drug manufacturing facility in Winchester, Kentucky,” Trump said. The Kentucky Lantern reached out to the U.S. Department of Defense for clarity but they did not respond as of publication.
Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s office said his office “has no information on this.”
“And if investments from the Department of Defense — or Trump’s ‘Department of War’ (DOW) — are conditioned on the outcome of an election, it’s time for the Department of Justice to investigate the DOW,” she added. 
Also in his remarks, which lasted for more than an hour and a half, the president encouraged voters “to pretend I’m on the ballot,” saying it helps Republicans pick up “a tremendous number of seats.” 
Trump used some of his time to talk about other political foes, like criticizing Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, who is running for an open U.S. Senate seat against former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley in North Carolina. He later called James Talarico, the Texas Democratic Senate candidate, a “freak” that should lose to Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton because he’s a “vegetarian,” despite Talarico eating meat this campaign cycle. 
“You don’t mind if I talk about other people,” Trump said to Barr. “Andy is doing so well, I think we can talk about other people.” 
A person, who was promptly booed by the crowd and removed by security, interrupted Trump’s remarks shortly after he took the stage. The president said to take the person “back home to mom” and claimed they were a paid protester. 
A protester is removed from President Trump’s rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Kentucky. Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern
“They get paid. We have them all over the place… but then they have to suffer because they go back home and the mother, especially if she’s a Kentucky mother, she slaps the hell out of him,” Trump said to cheers in the arena. “Slaps the hell and says, ‘I voted for that man. Don’t you ever do that again.’”
Kentucky’s most competitive race on the ballot this cycle — the Central Kentucky 6th District, currently held by Barr — was briefly mentioned by Trump, Barr and Gallrein and, as they encouraged voters to back Trump-endorsed candidate Ralph Alvarado. NKU is about a 90-minute drive from Lexington. 
Alvarado is “in a tight race with a lunatic,” Trump said, referring to Democrat Zach Dembo.   
“He is really a good guy, and I think he’s going to do very well,” Trump said of Alvarado. Winchester, where Trump said the Department of Defense investment would be pending the outcome of the midterms, is in the 6th Congressional District. 
Alvarado’s campaign manager Andy Westberry previously told the Lantern the candidate had conflicting events scheduled during the rally as part of the Court Day Festival in Mt. Sterling, “with long-standing commitments and speaking roles at GOP events with supporters from breakfast until evening.”
Throughout their speeches, Trump, Barr and Gallrein argued that Democrats have become engulfed by socialism, like GOP candidates around the country have done this election cycle. As he has done before, Barr likened his Democratic opponent, former state Rep. Charles Booker, to New York Mayor Zorhan Mamdami. Trump, too, attacked Booker, calling him “a communist lunatic.” Gallrein said he’d defended America from “socialists, communists, tyrants and terrorists” in other countries while serving as a Navy SEAL officer.
Ed Gallrein, Kentucky Republican candidate for the United States House of Representatives, speaks with members of the press before President Donald Trump’s rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Kentucky. Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern
“I’ve seen firsthand the devastation that communists and socialist agenda caused: food and gas shortages, high prices, long lines as families struggle to obtain life’s basic needs but live in utter misery,” Gallrein said. “If they like that so much why don’t those radical Democrats move there?” 
Barr blamed high gas prices in the U.S. on Iran and said Iran’s military capabilities have been diminished. The strait was closed earlier this year after U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. 
“The Ayatollah is dead, and its nuclear infrastructure is under rubble,” Barr said. “Thank you, President Trump, for making America and the world a safer place.” 
Republican Party of Kentucky Chairman Robert Benvenuti was first in the speaker lineup and encouraged GOP voters to cast ballots in upcoming elections and push back against the left, which he said “now tries to convince our friends and neighbors that not enough has been done to clean up their handspun destruction, and in some twisted way, they deserve your vote.”
“Folks, that’s bull—-,” he added. 
Trump previously came to Hebron in March to stump for Gallrein against U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie. Gallrein later defeated Massie in the Republican primary. 
What Dems say
While No Kings protests against the Trump administration had already been planned across Kentucky on Saturday, ahead of the November election, a few protesters did make it on campus to oppose Trump. Before arena doors opened to the public, a few protesters held signs near an entrance. One read, “I miss Obama.” 
Kentucky Democrats didn’t give Trump a warm welcome either. Ahead of the rally on Friday, U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, the state’s lone Democrat in Congress, argued the president should “explain why he has been lying to the American people and answer to the impact that it’s had on Kentucky.” McGarvey pointed to rising gas and grocery prices and GOP-backed cuts to Medicaid. 
Many Democrats, including candidates in Kentucky, have echoed McGarvey’s sentiments on the campaign trail this year. Asked if focusing on affordability issues would move voters, McGarvey said Kentuckians are “watching this happen.” 
“It doesn’t matter what politicians are saying. It’s what people are seeing. They are seeing the gas prices. They are seeing the grocery prices. They are seeing healthcare prices. They’re watching the corruption in this administration,” McGarvey said, recalling reports such as the U.S. accepting a plane as a gift from the Qatari government. 
As for the 6th Congressional District, McGarvey felt good about Dembo’s chances. Asked about Alvarado’s absence, the congressman said “just because somebody doesn’t go to a rally doesn’t mean they can run away from this president and his policies, which they have always supported.” 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. 
President Donald Trump speaks during his rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Highland Heights, Kentucky. Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s upcoming Nov. 3 general election top focus for Boise No Kings protest
text:
Crowds gathered Oct. 17, 2026, around the Idaho Capitol steps in Boise for the fourth No Kings protest. Early voting starts in many Idaho counties on Monday, Oct. 19. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Early voting, which begins Monday in many of Idaho’s 44 counties, was a focus of Boise’s fourth No Kings protest on Saturday. Idaho’s capital joined similar demonstrations nationwide. 
Speakers urged Idahoans to vote, volunteer with campaigns, and speak to friends and neighbors about candidates and ballot issues that matter to them ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Boise resident Lydia Aitchison, 31, who came to the Saturday event with her two sisters Nicki and Zarah, said she believes peaceful protest is part of her “civic duty to show what’s important to counters and to our country.” 
“And what’s important to us is non-tyrannical elements of government,” Aitchison said. 
For her, restoring legal abortion through Idaho’s ballot initiative, Proposition 1, was a top issue in the upcoming election. 
“I think people are so afraid of late-term abortions that they are taking away so many rights from a mother, and creating so much additional heartbreak,” Aitchison said. “And I think the question of making that choice for people is unconstitutional. I think that is someone’s specific right.” 
Zarah Aitchison, 20, said one of her top election priorities was keeping AI data centers out of Idaho. Nicki Aitchison, 27, said she wanted to see change in Idaho’s top elected positions, especially governor. 
In the 2026 election, voters will weigh in on all of Idaho’s statewide elected officials — such as governor, attorney general, secretary of state, and more — as well as two U.S. House seats, a U.S. Senate position, and all 105 seats in the Idaho state Legislature. 
Speakers at the No Kings rally emphasized early voting and participation in the 2026 general election at the protest held Oct. 17, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Protesters hold signs Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, at the No Kings rally in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) A crowd and information booths line the area in front of the Idaho Statehouse for the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings protest in Boise. The protest focused on voter registration, voting early and the importance of voter turnout before the Nov. 3 midterm election. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)A demonstrator holds up a sign during the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings protest held at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)
Boise resident Roy Heberger, an 81-year-old retired U.S. Fish and Wildlife biologist, said that amid this election, he’s very concerned about what’s happening in the federal government, primarily from President Donald Trump. 
“What he’s been doing is pulling the United States down,” Heberger said. “I’m very concerned about preserving our representative democracy.” 
He also underscored cuts to science in federal agencies. 
Randy French, 71, is another Boise resident and said he’s also concerned about Idaho officials who have supported the presidential administration. At the state level, he didn’t support recent legislative actions to cut income taxes, while he thought more money should go toward education. 
“When I went to college here, the state paid a much bigger part of college tuition,” French said. “And now it’s shifted to individuals.” 
Lisa Jones, 56, said she’s a retired healthcare worker and restoring legal abortion was a top issue for her this upcoming election, as well as addressing climate change. 
She also said she’s concerned about division nationwide. 
“What is happening and how people perceive and how people respond and react to one another is, I’ve never seen it before,” Jones said. “There’s so much hate.” 
Early voting runs until Oct. 30. Voters may find out if their county offers the option through their county clerk’s website. Absentee ballots may be requested from the Idaho Secretary of State until 5 p.m. Oct. 23. 
In-person Election Day voting will take place 8 a.m. to 8 p.m on Nov. 3. The Secretary of State’s Office has an online tool to find voters’ polling locations, which vary depending on home address.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: On No Kings day of action, Elizabeth Warren rallies for Jackson in Portland
text:
Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson rallied with U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts in Portland on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)With 17 days to go before the November elections, Democratic Party leaders, supporters, and candidates took to the streets across Maine on Saturday as part of a nationwide mobilization to get out the vote. 
Underscoring what she sees as the stakes of the midterms, particularly Maine’s Senate race, Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts told the more than 1000 people who rallied in Portland’s Deering Oaks Park that a vote for a Republican is essentially a vote for President Donald Trump’s agenda.
“Two years of Donald Trump and the Republican majority in the House and the Senate have never had the backbone to say no to anything,” she said. “Not an illegal war, not illegal tariffs, not tax cuts for billionaires, not taking away healthcare for millions of people, not to the biggest grifter in the history of the United States.”
Without naming U.S. Sen. Susan Collins but in an apparent reference to the longtime Republican senator’s approach to the Trump administration, Warren continued, “So here’s the deal, the time for polite requests for Donald Trump is over. No Kings means that we stand up, we show pride, we show backbone, we go to the polls, we go for a fighter, we vote for Troy Jackson.”
Jackson, Collins’ Democratic challenger, and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree also addressed the Portland crowd. 
Pingree, who previously served as speaker of the Maine House of Representatives, encouraged those assembled to spend the next two weeks volunteering, talking to friends, and encouraging others to vote on Nov. 3. 
“Democracy does not protect itself, it takes people,” she said, “don’t leave it to chance.”
Roughly 400 people rallied in Bath on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)The Oct. 17 No Kings national day of action was organized to encourage people to vote early for the Nov. 3 midterm elections. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree spoke to hundreds who rallied in Portland on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Hundreds rallied in Portland on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action, organized to encouraged early voting for the Nov. 3 midterm elections. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)
Though dubbed as a Defeat Collins rally, the Portland protest was among roughly 30 events held across the state Saturday, which was planned specifically to encourage people to vote early.
In several locations, turnout was lower than previous No Kings Day rallies in June and October 2025, and March 2026. 
In Bath, event spokesperson Jessica Mahnke said the events were deliberately less focused on Trump. ‘It’s a different event. It’s not a protest — it has a different temperament than the usual protests,” Mahnke said.
Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King, who made an appearance in Bath, said the purpose of the mobilization is “to demonstrate that we’re a democracy and we want to stay that way.”
Pam Giannatsis, who was among the estimated 400 people waving signs and flags along the Sagadahoc Bridge, said she came “to show solidarity and support what democracy needs to be, for everyone.”
In Freeport, organizer Kathleen Meade handed out “thanks but I voted early signs” to people who said they already cast a ballot. Roughly 75 people lined the main drag outside the L.L. Bean flagship store, much less than the roughly 3,000 that Meade said showed up for the previous No Kings rallies. 
Early, in-person voting started in Maine on Oct. 5. Voters can request a ballot through the Maine Secretary of State’s website or cast a vote at their municipal clerk’s office. Check out Maine Morning Star’s voter guide for more information.
According to the Secretary of State’s Office, more than 178,000 ballots have been requested, as of Friday, with more than 101,000 returned and accepted. That’s already more than the more than 84,000 who voted early in the June primary election. In 2022, the last gubernatorial election, a total of 252,135 absentee ballots were issued.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Thousands in NJ push for early voting at No Kings rallies against Trump
text:
Branchburg residents Dave Snyder, 64, his wife Sharon Snyder, 66, and Kate Fiore, 57 1(left to right), urged Americans to vote at the No Kings rally in Somerville on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]SOMERVILLE — Harvey Barry finds it tough to condense all the complaints he has about President Donald Trump, less than halfway through Trump’s second term in the White House.
So he picked one, immigration, put his sentiments on a sign, and bundled up for a brisk day outside the Somerset County Court House Saturday, where he joined hundreds of people protesting Trump at one of nearly 3,000 No Kings rallies unfolding nationwide.
“There’s too many things to mention for why I’m out here. I’ve never really been politically active, but with Trump and his administration, I just I couldn’t live with myself if I didn’t do something,” Barry said.
The theme of the day was early voting, with protesters aiming to energize voters in hopes of flipping control of Congress in the midterm elections next month. Early in-person voting in New Jersey begins Saturday, Oct. 24.
“Voting is so important,” said Douglas Anderson, 77, of Hillsborough. “That’s the one voice that we have, the one power that we have, and we can’t take that for granted. If we want change, we’ve got to use that power.”
Lisa Moor, 55, of Somerville, is a social studies teacher who tries to instill in her students the importance of their voting rights.
“I was really upset by the SAVE Act and limiting women’s right to vote by requiring women to have to go the extra step to prove that they are who they are and requiring them to show their birth certificate and the extra fee that’s involved — and even to get a passport if that’s how you’re going to show that you are indeed eligible and have the right to vote,” Moor said.
Harvey Barry, 77, of Tewksbury, protests President Donald Trump’s immigration policies at the No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Somerville. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
The No Kings rallies are billed as nonpartisan, but Somerville lies in a congressional district with the most competitive race statewide, with Democrat Rebecca Bennett seeking to unseat Rep. Tom Kean Jr., a two-term Republican.
So when Bennett showed up at Somerville’s No Kings rally Saturday, many rushed to say hello, pose for selfies with her, and otherwise root her on. She did not speak to the crowd, but an event speaker welcomed her from the stage, telling onlookers: “I don’t see Tom Kean here! That guy never shows up! When we need someone, Rebecca Bennett is here!”
Bennett told the New Jersey Monitor her goal during the 17 days until the Nov. 3 election is to meet as many voters where they are as possible. Bennett said voters are telling her to take on the cost-of-living crisis, tackle corruption in D.C., and put country over party.
“People are really fired up about flipping this seat,” Bennett said.
Corruption was a common complaint at the No Kings rallies, with Linda Mueller, 74, of Basking Ridge, calling Trump corrupt, narcissistic, and greedy.
“I’m horrified by the turn that so many people have taken to believe that someone like Trump could lead us anywhere but to disaster,” Mueller said. 
Other demonstrators said they were most concerned about the Trump administration’s violent and expansive immigration enforcement, its DEI rollbacks, its failure to release the Epstein files, religion creeping into the schools, and rising inflation and gas prices, among other things.

Foreign policy was another top worry among those who rallied Saturday, including the ongoing wars in Iran, Gaza, and Ukraine and the growing roles of Russia and Israel in shaping American foreign policy.
“I’m very concerned about the influence that Israel has on our politicians, our elections, and our military budgets in terms of the money that gets sent to Israel, which they then turn take and use against the population of Gaza,” said Claudia Bayait, 61, of Somerville.
Sara Gharavi of Bound Brook carried walking sticks that dangled plastic ears and skulls bearing the names of countries, to symbolize places where she said the U.S. has carried out war crimes without accountability. Her husband, Ali, who’s Iranian, carried a sign that said: “No war with Iran.”
“Not spending money on social needs and just spending money on defense and the military industrial conflict, all of that bothers us,” Sara Gharavi said. “We’re focused on stopping the forever wars. States are really concerned about being overrun by immigrants. Well, one of the ways to not be overrun by immigrants is to stop attacking countries, stop displacing their people, and stop interfering with their governments and the way they want to run their nations.”
Melissa Mariani, 50, of Stewartsville, regards Trump’s rhetoric on foreign policy, including his claim that he has ended eight wars, as part of the “lies and propaganda and gaslighting” that she said has characterized his time in office.
“It’s mind-blowing that he has any supporters at this point. I think that it really goes to show the propaganda machine has worked, and it’s really sad,” Mariani said. “We need a reality check. Our democracy is literally on the line. I fear that it’s too late at this point, honestly, because the damage that he’s done to us internationally, to our relationships with our allies, all that soft power that we had with U.S. aid, it’s all gone. And how long does it take to rebuild that kind of stuff? He’s hindered us for decades.”

title: Santa Fe, Las Cruces No Kings events focus on early voting
text:
Las Cruces' Oct. 17, 2026 featured a push for early voting amid anti-Trump sentiments. (Leah Romero for Source NM)In Santa Fe, organizers estimated close to 1,000 people attended the “No Kings: Vote Early” rally outside the Roundhouse on Saturday morning. As with previous No Kings events, participants such as Santa Fe Raging Grannies sang protest and folk songs reworked to criticize the Trump administration, and the crowds ballooned as more and more people lined the sidewalks, holding anti-Trump signs as passersby in cars honked and waved.
But Saturday’s No Kings event, iterations of which took place across the state and the country, differed in some ways by centering on the upcoming Nov. 3 general election.
Ellen Hill, chair of Indivisible’s Santa Fe chapter, told Source NM that the event aimed to spur early voter turnout. 
“Vote early, bank your vote, protect your vote,” Hill said. 
While early voting in New Mexican began Oct. 7, Saturday marked the start of expanded early voting locations. As of Friday, 4.3% of all registered voters across New Mexico cast either absentee or early ballots. 
Thousands rally in Albuquerque, Santa Fe for No Kings anti-Trump protest

Hannah Wetovsky attended the event and performed before a crowd a rendition of Chumbawamba’s tune “On the Day the Nazi Died.”
She told Source NM that she and her husband Nicholas planned on voting early after the event’s conclusion, and noted the importance of voting in a world that is “scary, where people are getting kidnapped and the rich keep getting richer.” 
Wetovsky, a millenial, added that she hopes to see more of her generation at the polls for the midterms. Many millennials, she said, feel disconnected from politics and that voting does not matter — a sentiment  with which she disagrees. The Trump administration “wouldn’t be trying to suppress the vote if voting didn’t matter,” Wetovsky said.
Speakers during the event expressed concern that the Trump administration might interfere with the midterm elections and presented early voting as a way to combat that fear.

(Photo by Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)At the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings event in Las Cruces, Terrye Doyle told Source NM, “I’m worried about the future for my children and grandchildren. It’s hard to see America just crumbling the way it is.” (Leah Romero for Source NM)
“Every vote gets banked the day that it’s voted,” Shari Hirst, an Indivisible organizer, said before a gathered crowd, adding that early votes “cannot be stolen by shenanigans.” 
Will Schmidt, a member of Santa Fe’s Indivisible chapter, handed out anti-fascist pins and buttons to attendees. He also expressed concern over the “monkey business” that the Trump administration “and his regime have tried with the post office. They’re trying to throw wrenches into the process wherever they can.” He urged people to vote early in order to “give the fascists as strong of a gut punch as we possibly can.”
Over the past several months, the Trump administration has launched failed efforts to obtain voter rolls from New Mexico and other states, and is currently pushing California to remove voters it says are non-citizens from its voter rolls. The administration has also raised concerns about mail-in ballots, raising ongoing concerns by states about federal interference during the midterm elections. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver on Oct. 13 issued a voter advisory reinforcing practical information and voter rights.
Hill told Source NM that based on online registration and participation, organizers expected just under 1,000 to attend the event. She added that she casted her ballot the first day early voting started because she is eager to see change. 
While speaking to the crowd outside the Roadhouse, Hill highlighted wealthy political donors, such as Elon Musk, who has been backing Republican midterm campaigns with $276 million in donations.
“But here’s the thing — he’s just one guy,” Hill said. “We’re a lot of people.”

In Las Cruces, several hundred protestors flocked to Albert Johnson Park for the No Kings: Vote Early Day of Action, with more than 50 people walking over to cast early ballots at Las Cruces city hall Saturday morning.
[Voter Guide: New Mexico Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Protestors lined the streets surrounding the park in downtown Las Cruces and drivers honked car horns in support of sign-holders, while protest songs sung by local group Volunteers of America could be heard in the background.
Many attendees told Source New Mexico that they were motivated to participate Saturday to call out authoritarianism in the White House.
“[President Trump] started an insurrection and still people voted for him. He was convicted of a number of felonies and it’s unbelievable what’s happening in this country,” Las Cruces resident Dean Williams told Source NM at the protest. 
He said if Democrats could take back control of Congress, it would be a “step in the right direction” as Republicans have shown that they will not “hold their people to account.” And having voted on both sides of the aisle in his time, Williams said he will be voting Democrat this election because the “Republican Party at the national level has just gone loco.”
Williams added that he is waiting to see if the negative impacts of rising prices across the country will be enough to motivate people to change how they vote. 
Las Cruces resident Laurel Brandi told Source NM Saturday’s No Kings protest had a different feel compared to previous ones, but said she believes it is important to keep showing up.
“Maybe I’m just projecting it, but it just feels a little less explosive and a little more dug in, like rooted in for the work,” she said. “Less reactive and more like grinding through.”
Brandi has a 5-year-old son and pointed to the recent fatal school shooting in Bend, Oregon as another motivator to get to the polls so she can send her child to school safely without worrying. “What can we do? What is there besides this, voting?” she said. Her son joined her at the polls when she cast her ballot on Oct. 6, the first day early voting opened.
At 11 a.m., organizers invited protestors to walk to city hall and cast their ballots early. Over 50 people lined up in the city hall lobby. Las Cruces resident Davena Norris told Source NM that her husband predicted there would be a line to vote, which she happily welcomed. 
“I was like, great, I’d love to stand in a long line because it means that there’s a lot of people that are getting out to vote,” Norris said. She said she “strongly” supports Daisy Maldonado for Doña Ana County Commissioner for District 1 because of her work in bringing the voices of the southern county to the table, particularly in regards to the controversial AI datacenter Project Jupiter under development in the area.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: In Florida, a first-time voter and fears of election interference at No Kings day of action
text:
Around 2,000 people crowded the lawn at Florida's Old Capitol on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 for a No Kings rally. Attendance was down from previous events. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix) Sam Kokales has a personal stake in the midterm elections. At 21, working toward a degree in business management from Florida State University, he finds himself in deep medical debt following two procedures for an abscess on his tonsils.
“We need better healthcare coverage — Medicare for all,” Kokales told the Phoenix during Tallahassee’s latest No Kings demonstration on the front lawn of Florida’s Old Capitol.
“I just looked at my bills again yesterday. I have over $94,000 as a student on a Pell grant. Insurance’s covering some of it, but it’s taken me five months to continue to talk to the insurance company and hospital and I still don’t have it solved,” he said.
Kokales, attending with Olivia Barber, also 21 and working on her master’s degree in public administration at FSU, was among the conspicuously few at the rally lacking gray hair.
He lamented that, “being in a college town, there’s not more people out. Hopefully, we’ll see more.”
Kokales said he canvasses for Democrat David Jolly’s campaign for Florida governor; Barber does the same for PJ Perez, a Tallahassee City Commission candidate.
“I just try to talk to people,” Kokales said.
Both planned to station themselves at the FSU student union for early voting beginning Monday.
Olivia Barber, left, and Sam Kokales attended the No Kings day of action rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Tallahassee. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)
 First ballot
Saturday’s rally unfolded under fleeting cloud cover with at times robust breezes, as attendance was down somewhat compared to a gathering nearly one year ago to the day. Similar rallies were unfolding the length and breadth of Florida.
The theme was “Vote Early.”
“We expected, across the nation, actually, that their own turnout would be a little bit less, just because it’s focused on getting out the early vote,” said Sabrina Harley of Indivisible Tallahassee, who emceed the event.
The No Kings movement’s earlier rallies “focused on kind of demonstrating and letting our voice be known about what we didn’t like,” she said. “Now the idea is just to coordinate across the nation and be ready to respond to any voter suppression.”
Halden Euridge, 18, majoring in history and economics at FSU, told the Phoenix he will vote for the first time this year. He attended Saturday’s rally with Donna Samara, his mother.
“I’ve always wanted to vote. I’ve always wanted to use my voice, so it was great when I got this opportunity,” Euridge said. “I think we should actually lower the voting age. Children also are affected by policy and they should have a say in elections.”
His friends are also politically engaged and some are canvassing for candidates, he said.
 Disruption feared
Fears that President Donald Trump could deploy Department of Homeland Security agents to interfere with voting was a major theme. Karen Woodall of Florida People’s Advocacy Center stationed herself at a table directing attention toward Floridians caught up in immigration enforcement.
“We’re all concerned that people will be afraid to come out and vote because of the ridiculous immigration activities — either by ICE or in Florida our own Florida Highway Patrol, our own state agencies — all of that’s designed to suppress the vote and scare people. People who are legally here, who are registered to vote but they’re immigrants,” she said.
“So, we need to be vigilant,” she continued.
“I’m hopeful we won’t have any problems here in Tallahassee, but no one should assume anything. We just have to have monitors, we need to have people present. People need to come out and vote. That’s how we’re going to take care of all this stuff,” Woodall said.
Alonzo Garcia, left, and Sarah Milan attend the No Kings rally on Oct. 17, 2026, in Tallahassee. They’re collecting petition signatures to undo Tallahassee’s agreement to cooperate in immigration enforcement. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)
‘Most egregious’
Alonzo Garcia staffed a booth for the Tallahassee Immigrant Rights Alliance, gathering petition signatures to rescind the city’s 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, allowing local police to work with ICE agents.
A former city manager signed the deal in 2025, and that October the City Commission voted, 3-2, to keep it.
“This is where right now the main, the most egregious abuses at the state, local, and federal level are happening, when it comes to immigration,” he told the Phoenix.
“While we recognize that elections are an important aspect of bringing change, they are not the only mechanism of change. We believe that through mass mobilization we can really bring changes, even outside of the electoral cycle, as we generally understand them in this country,” Garcia continued. “Because politicians don’t react only to just ballot results and percentages, but they also react to who’s the most organized, who’s the most agitated about an issue and how things move.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Latest No Kings protest urges Granite Staters to vote
text:
A crowd gathered at the New Hampshire State House in Concord, for one of over 2,500 official No Kings protests on Oct. 17, 2025. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)The theme of Saturday’s nationwide No Kings protest was “vote early.”
However, New Hampshire — which saw demonstrations in Portsmouth, Nashua, Littleton and other cities — doesn’t allow early in-person voting. All voting in New Hampshire, by state law, takes place on Election Day, which is Nov. 3 this year, or via mail.
No Kings is a left-leaning coalition that has organized protests across the country since President Donald Trump retook office early last year. Those protests have aggressively opposed Trump’s second-term agenda. On Saturday, they added a new goal: increasing voter turnout.
In Concord, a crowd amassed outside the State House, a common rallying spot for demonstrators, in the early afternoon. On the State House lawn, advocacy groups set up tents to hand out fliers and recruit members and protest organizers set up a stage where musicians sang and leaders rallied the crowd.
In the crowd of several hundred people was Jane Stapleton, of Concord. Her message: “Vote and know what and who you’re voting for.”
Jane Stapleton (front left), Bronnie Casey (back), Sarah Summerlin (center) and Frances Holland (right) hold signs outside the State House in Concord during the Oct. 17, 2026 No Kings protest. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“Because I wonder if the majority of people who voted for him in the last election are in support of and say that they’ve voted for what’s happening right now,” she continued. 
Trump’s approval rating among Republicans alone was 76%, according to a Fox News poll released Wednesday. That’s down 16% since March 2025. Amongst all respondents it was 36%.
“Wake up because democracy is falling under this administration,” Stapleton said. “That’s 100% what’s happening.”
She held up a sign that said “no kings and no liars, no pedophiles,” referring to Trump’s previously extensive ties to the notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
There were nearly 20 official protests in New Hampshire Saturday and more than 2,500 across the United States, according to the national No Kings organization. This is the fourth protest under the No Kings banner.
The first three were designed to “send a message that the American people were not simply going to sacrifice their constitutional rights, that they were willing to stand up,” Ezra Levin, co-founder and co-executive director of Indivisible which is part of the No Kings coalition, told States Newsroom. Saturday’s, he said “is therefore not just to protest and get attention to the fact that people aren’t afraid to stand up, but to use this tool that is available to us right now in October … your constitutional right to vote.”
Election Day is a little over two weeks away and Democrats hope to take advantage of Trump’s low approval ratings and the fact that parties in power typically do poorly in midterm elections.
The State House in Concord was the site of one of over 2,500 official No Kings protests across the United States Oct. 17, 2025. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Corydon protesters call on Hoosiers to vote early in latest anti-Trump ‘No Kings’ demonstration
text:
Around 100 "No Kings" attendees protest outside the Corydon Capitol State Historic Site in Corydon on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest for Indiana Capital Chronicle)
CORYDON, Ind. — A former electrical company employee, a couple wearing frog hats and a Franciscan friar were among about 100 protesters at a Saturday “No Kings” demonstration in Corydon — against the backdrop of the state’s first capitol. 
The latest in a string of nationwide protests since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, Saturday’s demonstrations were aimed at encouraging early voting and ballot education. 
Thousands of events were planned nationwide, including around 40 in Indiana, according to the No Kings event map. More than 130 miles away, participants rallied outside the Governor’s Residence. 
In Corydon, organizers with Progressive Voices H.C.F. — representing Harrison, Clark and Floyd counties — collected food and other donations for a community services group, and musicians played folk songs.
Susan Launder Becker and John Becker wear frog hats and hold papers calling on people to “Vote Out The King!” at a “No Kings” event in Corydon on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest for Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Tiffany Wolfe Garcia, president of Progressive Voices H.C.F., said grassroots progressive group Indivisible was organizing a carpool to the polls, and supporters of local political campaigns were also in attendance.
Though promoted as a “free, nonpartisan and family-friendly event,” most event attendees expressed discontent with the Trump administration. Others encouraged early voting.
Married retirees Susan Launder Becker and John Becker of Georgetown, who wore green frog hats and undershirts, held papers calling on people to “Vote Out The King!” The outfits were in reference to past colorful costumes in anti-Trump protests, including in Portland. After casting their ballots last Thursday, they also donned “I voted” stickers. 
Susan Launder Becker cited federal immigration policy and the cost of living as factors informing her vote. John Becker mentioned threats to voting rights and purported corruption in the Trump administration as other considerations. 
He said he hopes the demonstrations Saturday could “move the needle” in close races. Susan Launder Becker added that she felt concerns over federal officials “threatening polling places on” Election Day could boost early participation.
Father Vince Petersen of Mount Saint Francis Center for Spirituality said participation, no matter how people vote, is encouraged by the Catholic church, though he said the country faces the “existential” threat of tyranny today.
“There’s no kings,” he said. “My only king is Jesus, really.”
A protest sign evokes the the riot at the U.S. Capitol during a No Kings protest in Corydon on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest for Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Aim Me Smiley, a 56-year-old musician from Perry County, said she came out to protest a “rogue” president, data center expansion and the war in Iran, among other issues. She voted early the first day she could. 
Smiley wore a shirt backing Mary Allen, the Democratic candidate for Indiana’s 8th congressional district, and co-wrote a song for Allen’s campaign. Smiley also held a banner calling on people to “shape the future” by voting.
“People have the power to choose our leaders and our leadership, and they should reflect what we want in our lives to make our lives better,” Smiley said. “We don’t have that right now.”
Joe Dorgay, a 67-year-old from Lanesville, said he wanted to “open people’s eyes” via protesting. A constituent of Congresswoman Erin Houchin in the 9th District, he said the Republican has done some “impressive” things for the district but has acted as a “rubber stamp for Trump.” So he voted for her challenger, Democrat Brad Meyer.
“You got to stand up for the constitution, too,” he said.
