The America250 in Idaho Advisory Council in December voted to spend up to $28,500 to clean and refurbish the Liberty Bell. 
During the America250 in Idaho Advisory Council’s meeting on Thursday, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth floated the idea of installing a new liberty fountain in Idaho as a permanent landmark for this year’s America250 celebration. 
Ellsworth, who said she has already had Zoom meetings with state legislators on the subject, estimated the liberty fountain would cost $1 million, and encouraged the state to fundraise to generate the money for the fountain. 
“This is the gift that we want to give a lasting legacy to Idaho about America250,” Ellsworth said. 
Ellsworth did not say where the liberty fountain might be built. The advisory council did not take any action on the liberty fountain Thursday, but members encouraged Ellsworth to see if all the different officials and stakeholders who would need to support the project are on board and then report back during the council’s next meeting, which is tentatively scheduled for Dec. 10.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Scholten’s Grand Rapids office receives threatening letter containing unidentified white powder
text:
U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) speaks to reporters after visiting the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Mich. Feb. 17, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) says her office in Grand Rapids received a threatening letter containing unidentified white powder, prompting responses from local police and the FBI.
In a news release issued late Friday afternoon, Scholten said the letter, which purported to be from the Democratic Socialists of America, referenced an impending “civil war” following the election. The statement said the letter was similar to others sent to congressional offices across the country.
Scholten, a Democrat representing Michigan’s 3rd Congressional District centered around Grand Rapids, said her staff and first responders were her primary concern following the incident.
“My first thoughts today are with my staff who opened the mail and the first responders on the scene,” Scholten said. “Everyone is safe.”
Scholten said the Grand Rapids Police Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation responded to the incident, and that the substance found in the letter had not been identified.
Scholten called on the Democratic Socialists of America to condemn the threats made in its name or deny responsibility if the organization was not involved. She also criticized what she described as the group’s failure to adequately address extremism.
Unknown white powder in letter shuts down Secretary of State’s office

“Even as law enforcement works to verify the authenticity of these letters sent to congressional offices, it is the responsibility of the DSA to condemn these threats done in its name—and to refute responsibility if there is none. Unfortunately, this is another instance where the DSA has excused or ignored extremism,” Scholten said.
The congresswoman said threats and political violence should be rejected regardless of political affiliation.
“Regardless of party or origin, extremism must be rejected, condemned, and removed from our political discourse,” Scholten said.
She added that she and her staff would continue serving residents of West Michigan.
A request for comment was made by Michigan Advance to the Democratic Socialists of America. This story will be updated once a response is received.
The incident comes amid reports of similar incidents around the country. NPR reported Thursday on suspicious mailings sent to election officials in Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma ahead of the election, as well as the offices of U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California).

name: Nevada Current
title: Arizona joins Nevada lawsuit over Colorado River cuts
text:
The Central Arizona Project canal runs past homes in Peoria on June 8, 2023. The project carries diverted Colorado River water through a 336-mile long system to help serve 80 percent of the population of Arizona. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)Arizona has joined Nevada in a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s plan to drastically cut Lower Basin states’ share of Colorado River water.
The Arizona Department of Water Resources and Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs announced Friday they filed a motion to intervene in a lawsuit filed by the state of Nevada in August challenging the U.S. Interior Department’s plan to impose mandatory water cuts in Nevada, Arizona, and California.
In August, the federal government finalized a new operating plan for the river that requires Arizona, California and Nevada to reduce their water use by 1.25 million acre-feet in both 2027 and 2028, more than twice the largest reductions required under the current guidelines that expire at the end of the year.  
Upper Basin states – Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah – would not be subject to mandatory water reductions under the plan. 
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo welcomed Arizona’s decision to join the lawsuit, calling it “an important step in challenging a federal plan that unfairly burdens the Lower Basin and fails to require the Upper Basin to make meaningful reductions.”
“Nevada will not accept a framework that puts our water supply and the future of our communities at risk,” Lombardo said in a statement. 
Under the federal government’s plan, Nevada would have to give up 50,000 acre-feet of its Colorado River allocation over the next two years. An acre-foot is equal to 325,851 gallons — the amount of water needed to cover an acre of land a foot deep or enough water to supply two to three households for a year.
Additionally, Arizona would be required to reduce its water use by 760,000 acre-feet, while California will have to cut about 440,000 acre-feet under the plan.
But if conditions worsen, Nevada could have its 300,000 acre-foot Colorado River entitlement cut by more than 213,000 acre-feet or about 71% of its allocation. Nevada already has the smallest allocation of Colorado River water among the three Lower Basin states. 
In a statement, Hobbs called the proposed cuts “draconian” and said Arizona “will not accept a forced federal plan that solves this crisis on the backs of our families, farmers, and businesses.”
Nevada filed the lawsuit three days after the Trump administration released its 10-year plan for managing the Colorado River, and the nation’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, amid ongoing drought and record low water storage.
Tom Buschatzke, director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources, said in a statement that “Intervention in the Nevada lawsuit is necessary at this time for Arizona to protect its legal rights to Colorado River water while preserving a path forward to achieving a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada to protect the Colorado River system.”
John Entsminger, general manager of the Southern Nevada Water Authority, echoed that criticism saying that “Like Nevada, Arizona recognizes significant flaws in the federal government’s Environmental Impact Statement and the National Environmental Policy Act process used to develop the framework for post-2026 Colorado River operations.”
Lower Basin states have argued that the Upper Basin should be required to share mandatory water cuts in order to spare downstream states from taking steeper cuts. Upper Basin states argue they don’t have the infrastructure to store water during dry years like Lower Basin states, and are already restricted by available supply every year.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Musical chairs in the Maryland Senate president’s office and other political notes
authors: Danielle J. Brown, Christine Condon, William J. Ford
text:
David Schuhlein, director of communications for Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) will be leaving his post later this month after five years. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/ Maryland Matters)David Schuhlein will leave his role with the Office of the Senate President after five years of managing and coordinating the wide-ranging communication needs for Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City).
Ferguson said he was “deeply grateful” for Schuhlein’s work as director of communications in a statement announcing his departure, along with other staff changes.
“David has been an invaluable member of our team and a trusted advisor throughout some of the most consequential moments for the Senate of Maryland,” Ferguson said in the Friday statement. “His strategic judgment, communications expertise, and ability to navigate complex issues have helped strengthen how we communicate our priorities and connect with Marylanders.”
Since his appointment to the role in August 2021, Schuhlein has overseen communication strategy for the Senate president’s office, which includes updating Maryland residents on the Senate’s legislative efforts, coordinating with senators on legislative priorities, and serving as a point of access to the president for the Maryland press.
“I am humbled to have played a role in successfully navigating some of the most complex issues the state of Maryland has ever faced and incredibly proud of what we’ve accomplished together,” Schuhlein said in a text to Maryland Matters.
Schuhlein will be heading to Enterprise Community Partners, an affordable housing developer in Maryland, as the vice president of communications. He will continue working for the Senate President’s office until Oct. 27.
Another new gig, and a new hire
The announcement of Schuhlein’s departure came with notices for other staff changes in Ferguson’s office. That includes a promotion for Matt Jackson, who joined Ferguson’s team as senior adviser in January. Before joining the Senate, he worked “across the hall” as chief of staff to former House Speaker Adrienne Jones.
Friday, Ferguson announced that Jackson would take on a new role of senior counsel to provide legal and policy guidance to him and Senate leadership on upcoming legislative priorities.
Ferguson said Jackson’s “deep understanding of the legislative process” and “thoughtful approach to complex policy” will help him in his new role.
Jackson will take the position previously held by Ross Seidman, who left this summer.
Moving into Jackson’s seat as the senior adviser to Ferguson is Stephanie Hall, the chief government and legislative affairs officer for Coppin State University. She’s also previously served as the executive director for the Maryland Legislative Black Caucus and has a legislative background that will be “an incredible asset,” to the office, according to Ferguson.
“I am confident that our team will continue to provide the leadership, expertise, and dedication necessary to meet the challenges and opportunities ahead,” Ferguson said in his statement.
Maryland delegation supports Lapp
More Maryland politicians are piling on in support of David Lapp, the state’s top ratepayer advocate.
Maryland People’s Counsel David Lapp speaks at a news conference in February 2025 alongside Attorney General Anthony Brown. (Photo Courtesy of the Office of Baltimore City Council President Zeke Cohen)
This time, the vote of confidence is coming from Capitol Hill.
In a letter sent to Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown earlier this week, all nine Democrats representing Maryland in Congress urged Brown to keep Lapp as people’s counsel — even though his initial five-year term has expired.
The Democrats echoed a letter sent by more than 70 state lawmakers last week, noting that the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel has become “a more proactive and data- driven advocate for Maryland’s utility customers,” since 2021 under Lapp’s leadership.
“His continued leadership will help ensure that Maryland consumers have a strong voice as the State works to advance an affordable and reliable energy system while meeting its economic and clean energy goals,” the letter reads.
Brown’s office posted Lapp’s job earlier this month, with an application deadline of Oct. 13.
Brown told Maryland Matters it wasn’t a statement about Lapp’s job performance. Rather, he just wanted to hold a competitive process, especially since Lapp was nominated by his predecessor.
Still, Lapp has received a chorus of support, including from Maryland House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Anne Arundel & Prince George’s) and more than 70 House Democrats.
But Lapp has received pushback this year from Senate President Bill Ferguson (D- Baltimore City), and the post is subject to confirmation in the Senate.
Longtime Annapolis fixture retires
Susan Lawrence, who’s been in state government service for more than three decades, including almost three years as a lobbyist with the University System of Maryland, will retire at the end of the year.
Lawrence said Thursday she’s leaving her current position as vice chancellor for government relations with the university system.
Susan Lawrence
Chancellor Jay Perman wrote in a letter to system colleagues that announcing Lawrence’s departure “is hard to deliver and was hard to hear.”
“And given that we’re now gearing up for a challenging 2027 legislative session, it’s especially so,” Perman wrote. “Over Susan’s three years at the System Office, she’s been a highly respected and effective advocate for the USM, strengthening our relationships with policymakers, amplifying our voice in Annapolis and D.C., and securing meaningful outcomes for our universities and our people.”
Lawrence’s work includes 24 years in various positions in the General Assembly, where she was, among other positions, chief of staff to the chair of the Senate Finance Committee and legislative assistant for the Budget and Taxation Committee.
After she left the Senate, Lawrence began working in 2019 as director of government affairs at the University of Maryland, Baltimore. Perman announced Lawrence’s appointment to the lobbyist position in November 2023.
“I’ll miss Susan’s work and the obvious enthusiasm she has for it. I’ll miss her collaborative leadership and the strategy behind her every decision,” Perman wrote. I’ll miss her expansive connections that kept us tethered to those making the most consequential decisions affecting the System, our universities, our people, and our work.”
Perman expects to replace Lawrence before she leaves.

name: California
title: California presenta su demanda número 100 contra Trump, esta vez por el caso del ICE en los juzgados
text: This article is also available in English. Read it here.El fiscal general de California, Rob Bonta, ha presentado la demanda número 100 del estado contra el gobierno federal desde que el presidente Trump asumió el cargo por segunda vez en 2025. Bonta alcanzó ese hito en 21 meses. Durante la primera administración de Trump, los funcionarios de California demandaron al gobierno federal un total de 123 veces en cuatro años. La demanda presentada el jueves ante el Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Central de California alega que el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de los Estados Unidos (ICE) sobrepasó sus límites constitucionales al detener a personas en juzgados estatales, una práctica prohibida por un juez del Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos que, según la demanda, el ICE continúa empleando. Por ejemplo, el Departamento de Justicia de California descubrió que el ICE detuvo a 34 personas en juzgados estatales en junio de 2026. En julio de 2026, el mes siguiente a la orden judicial de dejar de realizar arrestos en juzgados , el ICE detuvo a 28 personas en juzgados. “La directiva del ICE sobre la aplicación de la ley en los juzgados y las actividades de control resultantes han tenido un profundo efecto disuasorio que ha obstaculizado la capacidad de California para hacer cumplir la ley y proteger la seguridad pública”, dijo el Departamento de Justicia del estado en un comunicado de prensa. Detener a personas en un juzgado puede tener un efecto disuasorio en testigos, víctimas e incluso sospechosos que temen presentarse ante el tribunal, declaró el año pasado Patricia Guerrero, presidenta del Tribunal Supremo de California. “Convertir los juzgados en un foco de control migratorio obstaculiza, en lugar de ayudar, a la administración de justicia, al disuadir a testigos y víctimas de denunciar y desalentar a las personas de hacer valer sus derechos”, dijo Guerrero. En septiembre, el gobernador Gavin Newsom promulgó una ley que exige a los agentes federales de inmigración presentar una orden judicial e identificarse antes de realizar arrestos a menos de 1000 pies de un tribunal estatal.

name: Nevada Current
title: Former coroner and deputy attorney general vie for public administrator job
text:
Patrick Michael Murphy, Stephanie Itkin-Goodman. (Candidate photos)The race for Clark County Public Administrator features Stephanie Itkin-Goodman (no relation to former Las Vegas mayors Oscar and Carolyn) who won the Democratic primary with 65% of the vote, and Patrick Michael Murphy, who garnered 66% on the Republican side. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]The public administrator secures the assets of deceased Southern Nevadans when there’s no will and no one has been designated to administer the estate. They search for relatives and for property, and may ultimately distribute it through court proceedings.
Itkin-Goodman, a newcomer to Nevada, previously served for just under two years in a New York City district attorney’s office and also worked in private practice.
She’s currently a deputy attorney general where she advises a variety of regulatory boards, including the Private Investigator’s Licensing Board, which also regulates armed security guards.
The board came under fire this summer at a legislative commission meeting when it proposed a regulation requiring eight hours of training for security guards who carry rifles and shotguns. 
Nevada law does not allow security guards to carry rifles or shotguns, lawmakers observed. 
“We need to find out who your DAG (deputy attorney general) is,” Sen. Rochelle Nguyen told the board’s executive director. 
Itkin-Goodman did not respond to the Current when asked whether she reviewed the proposed regulation before asking lawmakers to approve it. She later deferred to the executive director, noting she can only provide legal advice, but not require that the PILB accept it. 
“I think she’s new to the position,” said Murphy, her opponent, adding everyone should have a chance to “get up to speed. But it seems like publicly she’s kind of punted. The worst thing you can do is not make a decision. That’s what causes a lot of problems in organizations.”
Murphy served as Clark County coroner, an appointed position, from 2002 to 2015. His office was the inspiration for CSI, a popular network television program based in Las Vegas.   
He has become known as Clark County’s fix-it guy, stepping in to assume leadership of several agencies “that were either having trouble or where they needed a little extra assistance,” such as the Clark County Division of Juvenile Justice, which he ran while serving as coroner. 
He says he’s marketing his name and reputation in his bid for election. 
“I know the people in Henderson and North Las Vegas, and in Laughlin and Overton, so I don’t have to start from scratch,” he says. “I have a good reputation for getting the work done.”
From 2008 through 2015, budget cuts prompted the coroner’s office to perform duties of the public administrator on overnight cases.
“If I hadn’t been coroner, I wouldn’t know anything about running the public administrator’s office,” he said. He also served as Clark County’s legislative lobbyist in 2013 and 2015. 
Murphy moved to Southern Nevada in 1980 and went to work for the Boulder City Police Department. A decade later he was hired as Mesquite’s Chief of Police. He later went to work for City of Las Vegas Detention and Enforcement. 
After retiring in 2015, he worked for the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children in Washington, D.C. before being called back to take over when the coroner took early retirement during COVID in 2020.
In 2022, Clark County hired Murphy to restore order in the Public Administrator’s office, where then-Public Administrator Rob Telles was embroiled in scandal. Months later, Telles murdered reporter Jeff German, who was investigating allegations of wrongdoing by Telles. 
“I want the opportunity to go there and finish what I started,” Murphy said. He has never run for office, and says he’s surprised by the lack of prerequisites for candidates. “If you can plunk down $105, you’re in.” 
He’s been around long enough to know that voters, confronted with down-ballot races such as public administrator, often default to casting a vote in favor of party affiliation.
“The vast majority of people don’t even know what the office does. We absolutely want you to exercise your right to vote,” he says, adding the office should be nonpartisan, or better yet, appointed. “If you don’t know the candidates, don’t just vote for the party, because you might end up with some wild card.”  
Itkin-Goodman also says she doesn’t consider the public administrator to be a political role, and would support changing the law to allow county commissions in large counties, such as Clark and Washoe, to appoint the position.
Itkin-Goodman notes that she brings legal experience to the job and that she has spent her career “navigating complex legal matters, protecting vulnerable individuals, and ensuring accountability. The Public Administrator’s Office needs independent leadership, and my legal qualifications and commitment to transparency and accountability make me the best choice.”
Murphy notes that he ran the coroner’s office for 14 years without a medical degree. “You want your medical doctor doing medical work. You need the chief executive officer to be someone who has a background in business and ability to lead.” 
Both candidates say that if elected, they’ll increase outreach to the community in an effort to reduce the number of people who die without a will. 
Murphy says he’d like to have investigators fitted with bodycams and the ability to barcode, or “bag and tag” inventory in the field. 
A recent case turned up close to $200,000 in cash and hundreds of weapons – a scenario that frequently raises questions about integrity. “We need policies to protect beneficiaries and heirs, as well as employees.” 
Itkin-Goodman raised $41,000 as of Oct. 15 and has roughly $13,000 on hand.
She has a number of endorsements, including Culinary Local 226, SEIU Nevada, IATSE 720, Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, National Organization for Women (NOW), Make the Road, and PLAN Action.
Murphy has raised close to $87,000  and has roughly $26,000 in the bank as of Oct. 15. 
He is endorsed by more than a dozen law enforcement associations including the Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers, Clark County Firefighters, Juvenile Justice Probation Officers, several veterans organizations, and Ironworkers Local 433.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: No dark money in Alaska
text:
Voters line up at the polling site at Anchorage City Hall on Nov. 4, 2024. City Hall was one of the designated early voting sites in Alaska's largest city. It is not a designated site for Election Day voting. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Do you have enough extra cash to fund massive lobbying campaigns? Outrageously expensive political campaigns? Could you afford it year after year, decade after decade? The wealthiest in our country can. 
They use their funds to acquire special preferences in law and regulations. Tax rates, cuts, breaks, loopholes, credits, deductions, concessions, amortization schedules, accelerated depreciation and lower rates on types of income. The nearly endless list is now contained within 75,000 pages of IRS code, regulations and rulings.
Only the wealthiest few have the massive financial capacity it takes to twist the rules. They bend and distort society. The wealthiest include big corporations, big businesses and billionaires.
Their financial capacity and motivation to manipulate society for their own gain uses wealth to not only lobby for preferential changes but, importantly, to elect politicians willing to give to the few, without regard for the needs of all. When the wealthiest engage in class warfare against America’s middle class, society degrades. 
A risk to democracy arises when the richest and most powerful acquire such special treatment. 
When the richest and most powerful acquire and sustain their preferential advantage — their special treatment, the foundation of our democracy cracks. And what is that foundation? The middle class. In other words: The middle class recognizes they are left behind because they are.
The wealthiest create an unfair society where the rich grow much richer from preferential laws and government favors acquired over decades.  Those decades create an upward concentration of wealth and power. As Warren Buffett commented, about 20 years ago: “There’s class warfare, alright.” He continued: “But it’s my class, the rich class, that’s making war, and we’re winning.” Winning at the expense of the bottom 90%.
Buffett was upset because he saw actual injustice perpetrated by the rich class upon the vast majority of Americans. He saw and understood the effects of the preferential treatment given the rich class which resulted in his secretaries and clerks paying a higher share of their income than he did on his vastly higher income.
Starting from the early 1980s to 2020, more than $50 trillion transferred from the bottom 90% to the rich class. The per year transfer now from the bottom 90% is more than $2.5 trillion. Nearly all of the benefit of our nation’s growth is now captured by the very top. America’s bottom 90% is paid a fraction of their productivity as compared to the distribution of wealth from the end of WWII to the late 1970s. 
 Democracy can be lost when the nation’s financial system embeds ways to transfer wealth to the already wealthy. This dysfunction gives the already wealthy greater access to elected officials through lobbyists and capacity to donate to campaigns. Wealth concentration promotes dark money, anonymous and hidden money distorting and manipulating society. Dark money arises because the rich class doesn’t want specific names connected to the dastardly conduct they promote. Corruption increases as the mindset of the wealthiest people changes from simple greed to wanting it all. Corruption is used to transfer public money to the wealthiest and favored.
 Our nation seems to be a diminishing empire in which corruption and favoritism increases as rule of law decreases.
 As corruption increases, an ever-stronger belief arises that the political system is hopeless or meaningless. When you vote: are you for the bottom 90% or are you for the wealthiest?
 A result of unchecked corruption and favoritism is a government that cares more for corporations and billionaires than for average people. As a national sense of weariness increases, it displaces our nation’s optimism. The few “winners” rise much higher while the “others” sense the train has left without them.  
An unfair system provides for and protects the rich class. Those that are not within the rich class are promised a “trickle” which may come tomorrow. A pipeline flow for the rich and a trickle, maybe, for all others.  
When one man spends $290,000,000 to support a presidential candidate’s campaign and then is granted control of a new government agency, corruption and favoritism are surely nearby. How much will it cost dark money to purchase a U.S. Senate seat or state Governor’s office? Both wealth concentration and anonymous money shake the foundations of democracy.
Democracy can be protected. Massive lobbying and massive political campaign donations can be curtailed. Dark money can be banned. Our laws and regulations should be cleansed of preferential treatment which unfairly concentrates wealth.  
A starting point is a NO vote on Ballot Measure 2. No dark money should be allowed in campaigns or lobbying in Alaska.

name: California
title: Trump demanda a California por acusaciones de que personas no ciudadanas se registran para votar
authors: Jeanne Kuang and Ana B. Ibarra
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
La administración Trump demandó el jueves a California y al condado de Los Ángeles para prevenir que los funcionarios electorales cuenten las papeletas de potencialmente 20,000 votantes registrados, en una intervención extraordinaria a 19 días de unas elecciones nacionales trascendentales.
Esta semana, los fiscales federales del Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos escribieron a la secretaria de Estado de California, Shirley Weber, y al secretario del registro civildel  condado de Los Ángeles, Dean Logan, exigiéndoles que verifiquen la ciudadanía de una lista específica de votantes registrados o que aparten sus papeletas sin contarlas en noviembre.
Esto forma parte de una campaña nacional del gobierno de Trump para identificar casos de personas que no son ciudadanas estadounidenses y que votan ilegalmente en las elecciones. El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional afirmó recientemente que Nevada tenía casi 16,000 personas que no eran ciudadanas estadounidenses en su padrón electoral; sin embargo, solo enviaron al estado los nombres de 185 votantes, quienes, según confirmaron las autoridades de Nevada, eran todos ciudadanos estadounidenses.
California envía una papeleta de votación por correo a todos los votantes registrados; los secretarios de los condados de todo el estado ya lo han hecho antes de las elecciones del 3 de noviembre, en las que los californianos decidirán sobre un nuevo gobernador, 14 propuestas electorales estatales y varias contiendas reñidas que serán clave para determinar qué partido controlará el Congreso.
Las cartas del Departamento de Justicia , enviadas al condado de Los Ángeles y al condado de Weber por el fiscal general adjunto interino de los Estados Unidos, R. Trent McCotter, daban a los funcionarios 48 horas para cumplir con la solicitud de revisar una memoria USB que contenía una lista de votantes registrados que, según los fiscales federales, no son ciudadanos.
El miércoles, Logan declaró que no había revisado la unidad porque su formato no era seguro. Weber le escribió a McCotter diciéndole que había solicitado datos y metodología después de que funcionarios federales afirmaran sin pruebas en julio que 190,000 votantes de California “podrían ser” no ciudadanos, pero que dichos funcionarios nunca se los proporcionaron.
 El gobernador Gavin Newsom se burló el jueves de la demanda, calificándola de “un triste y desesperado intento de Trump de utilizar su politizado Departamento de Justicia para intentar suprimir el voto de los californianos a tan solo tres semanas del día de las elecciones”, y dijo que la petición de los fiscales de anular las papeletas “debería aterrorizar a todos los estadounidenses”.
 “Seguiremos celebrando elecciones libres y justas en California, y denunciaremos a este autoritario mientras intenta aplicar todas las tácticas propias de un dictador”, dijo Newsom en un comunicado.
 Señaló que la solicitud pide a los funcionarios electorales locales que violen la ley federal: la Ley Nacional de Registro de Votantes prohíbe la depuración de los padrones electorales dentro de los 90 días previos a una elección.
 Tanto la ley federal como la de California exigen que los residentes sean ciudadanos estadounidenses para registrarse para votar. El fraude electoral es extremadamente raro, según han demostrado numerosos estudios. 
Los demócratas de California instan a la gente a votar
 Las acciones de la administración Trump han alarmado a los líderes estatales, quienes afirman que equivalen a intimidación a los votantes.
 “Creo que esto es muy preocupante… porque muchos en California y en todo el país lo perciben como una forma de disuadir a la gente de votar”, dijo la presidenta pro tempore del Senado, Monique Limon, en un mitin en Los Ángeles el jueves por la mañana en apoyo del candidato demócrata a gobernador, Xavier Becerra.
 “Seguiremos defendiendo y protegiendo la integridad de nuestras elecciones. California cuenta con un sistema sólido para proteger nuestros comicios. Verificamos, comprobamos y damos seguimiento”, afirmó.
 En su discurso durante el mitin, Becerra no se refirió directamente a la acción federal, pero prometió luchar contra la administración Trump.
 “Ya sea votando, ya sea yendo a trabajar, ya sea teniendo buenas escuelas o ya sea protegiendo a nuestras familias contra los mercenarios de ICE, estamos aquí, estamos presentes , y lucharemos”, dijo Becerra desde el Monumento Histórico El Pueblo de Los Ángeles.
 Pero ahora mismo nuestra lucha es movilizar el voto, asegurarnos de que todo el mundo entienda que nuestro poder reside en nuestro voto”, dijo. 
Más citaciones judiciales para los condados de Orange y San Diego
 La demanda y las exigencias del Departamento de Justicia se producen semanas después de que los investigadores federales emitieran citaciones del gran jurado a los funcionarios electorales de Los Ángeles solicitando información sobre los votantes registrados.
 Según informó el medio de comunicación inewsource , los fiscales federales también solicitaron información sobre los votantes registrados en el condado de San Diego, así como en el condado de Orange, según consta en documentos no publicados anteriormente y obtenidos esta semana por CalMatters.
 El 10 de septiembre, el registrador de votantes del condado de Orange recibió tres citaciones judiciales para obtener información sobre votantes registrados. Las citaciones, dirigidas tanto al condado de Los Ángeles como al de Orange, fueron enviadas a petición del fiscal federal interino del sur de California, Bill Essayli, y del fiscal federal adjunto, Michael Wheat. Solicitaron a los funcionarios locales que entregaran la información a un investigador del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional.
 Una citación judicial solicitaba el archivo completo de votantes para obtener una lista censurada de lo que parecen ser 18 votantes registrados del Condado de Orange, incluyendo cualquier “declaración jurada sobre el estado de ciudadanía”; otras dos solicitaban registros más detallados de dos votantes diferentes, incluyendo información sobre si habían cambiado sus direcciones o afiliación política y “correspondencia relacionada con el registro de votantes”.
 Bob Page, registrador de votantes del condado de Orange, dijo que su oficina elaboró los registros y que no ha recibido ninguna otra solicitud o exigencia por parte de la administración Trump.
 “Desconocemos el motivo por el cual el gran jurado solicitó los registros de estas personas”, escribió Page en un comunicado enviado por correo electrónico. “La solicitud de esta información de registro no ha tenido ningún impacto en la administración de las elecciones generales de 2026”.

name: VTDigger
title: Pro-Phil Scott super PAC launches ad buy, another signal Vermont governor’s race could be close
text:
Democratic nominee for governor Amanda Janoo, left, and Republican Gov. Phil Scott. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
With Election Day around the corner, big bucks are rolling into Vermont from a pro-Phil Scott super PAC tied to the Republican Governors Association. His challenger, Amanda Janoo, hasn’t received the same support from the analogous Democratic organization — and says she doesn’t want it — though her campaign has raised more money than Scott’s, the latest campaign finance filings show.
The super PAC, called “A Stronger Vermont,” injected more than $460,000 into the governor’s race in recent weeks on Scott’s behalf, according to reports filed with the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office.
Under campaign finance law, the PAC can’t donate directly to Scott’s campaign but is able to spend an unlimited amount of money supporting him. The same organization has aided Scott before. In 2016, for example, it spent $3 million to help him get elected governor the first time. 
The spending reported so far this month, mostly on TV and online ads, is the PAC’s largest since 2018. It suggests the Republican Governors Association, which supports GOP candidates for that office nationwide, sees at least some need to campaign harder in Vermont this year.
Recent polls and campaign fundraising data indicate that this year’s reelection bid could be Scott’s toughest yet. Janoo raised more money for her campaign over the first half of October than Scott raised for his, according to new filings. Janoo also outraised the five-term governor in September.
Overall, campaign finance reports show Scott has raised just shy of $590,000 for his own campaign so far in this election cycle, while Janoo has raised about $890,000. Heading into the final weeks of the race, Janoo has more cash on hand — about $307,000 compared to Scott’s $202,000. 
Accounting for the super PAC’s cash, though, there has been far more pro-Scott money pouring into the race so far this month than pro-Janoo money, filings show.
Over the first half of October, the PAC spent just shy of $463,000, most of it on TV and online advertising, according to a Thursday filing with the Secretary of State’s Office. As of the end of September, it had reported spending just $300 so far this cycle with $70,000 in the bank. But on Oct. 8, its coffers were boosted by a $400,000 contribution from the Republican Governors Association, filings show. 
At least one recent ad funded by A Stronger Vermont describes Janoo as inexperienced and running a campaign with unrealistic policy proposals. A website displaying that same ad and urging voters to elect Scott also includes a picture that appears to show Janoo holding a glass of wine next to the words, “what kind of governor would Amanda Janoo be?”
Janoo’s campaign condemned the super PAC’s spending in a statement this week, calling the RGA “a D.C.-based political group aligned with Trump.” 

READ MORE

Last month, a super PAC called “Our Vermont” reported receiving $40,000 from the Democratic Governors Association, the national group that provides cash and campaign strategy to help elect Democratic governors. But Janoo’s campaign told VTDigger it did not want the organization to spend any money on its behalf.
Our Vermont reported spending $121,000 since the start of October on consulting and surveys but not on any advertising. Before this fall, the PAC last reported campaign spending in 2020 and hasn’t reported an ad purchase since 2016, filings show.
The RGA’s current chair, Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, is a close ally of Trump. Some of the organization’s big donors are also major supporters of the president. Among them is Elon Musk, the Tesla founder, and Miriam Adelson, the gambling magnate. 
At a press conference Thursday, Scott pushed back on the suggestion that the super PAC spending on his behalf tied him to Trump. “I think Vermonters know me,” he said. “I don’t know how I can separate myself any further from the president.”
Scott told reporters he would prefer to “just run our own campaign and do the best we can with giving our own message.” But he also said he did not have an issue with the ad that featured Janoo. 
“I don’t like the negative campaigning. But I thought it struck the right balance. It seems to be palatable,” he said.
In recent weeks, Janoo reported spending more than $200,000 on TV and online advertising, the first major media purchases she’s reported in the election cycle. Scott has been spending large sums of his campaign’s own money on digital, TV and radio advertising, too. The governor is also providing resources to Republican candidates for the state House and Senate, filings show.
Meanwhile, in the race for the state’s second-highest office, Republican Lt. Gov. John Rodgers has continued to outraise his Democratic challenger, Molly Gray. Rodgers brought in $75,240 over the first half of October, while Gray raised $41,290 in the same time period. Rodgers also outraised Gray last month. 
Gray enters the home stretch of the campaign with significantly more cash on hand, though — $122,700 to Rodgers’ $49,780.
The general election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pro-Phil Scott super PAC launches ad buy, another signal Vermont governor’s race could be close.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo joins Democratic colleagues for unannounced Massachusetts field office visit
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.), center, speaks with reporters after an unannounced visit to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s New England headquarters on Oct. 16, 2026. U.S. Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) is at left, and U.S. Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) is at right. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo's Office)U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo and two other New England Democrats made an unannounced visit Friday to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) regional headquarters in Burlington, Massachusetts to follow up on reports of detainees being housed there for multiple days and sleeping on concrete floors with limited food available.
Amo, who represents Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, spent 45 minutes touring the facility with U.S. Reps. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts and Becca Balint of Vermont to assess conditions for people held longer than the facility was designed to accommodate. Amo described the office as a temporary processing facility without a full kitchen.
“It’s ultimately important that we get an accurate view of what happens in there so that we can get the institution to do better,” Amo said in an interview after the 12:15 p.m. visit. “We don’t want to see a sanitized version of the facility.”
Over an hour drive from Providence, the Burlington office is primarily a place where ICE officers file paperwork and meet with people across New England for scheduled check-ins with immigration officials. It also serves as an intake center, where detainees are supposed to spend a few hours before they get transferred.
Several outlets have reported that detainees have been housed in the facility for multiple days.
Amo’s account of what he saw largely echoed those reports. He described a facility with no kitchen or dining area, just refrigerators and a sink.
“That’s insufficient,” he said. “If you’re going to have people in there for a period of time, you’re going to need food.”
Amo also described the sleeping arrangements for detainees held overnight, saying they are given thin mats rather than mattresses, along with pillows and lightweight, reflective thermal foil blankets.
A dozen detainees were in the facility during the tour, Amo said. The congressional delegates were not allowed to speak directly with them during the visit, he added.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, disputed claims of inadequate conditions at the Burlington facility, saying detainees have access to food, bedding and showers — along with medical treatment and opportunities to contact lawyers and family members.
“In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most US prisons that hold actual US citizens,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement to Rhode Island Current.
But the spokesperson, who did not sign their name, described Burlington as primarily a processing center, saying detainees are transferred to other facilities for longer-term stays.
“Illegal aliens are quickly processed and transferred to permanent housing at a detention facility,” the spokesperson said.
Amo said he would push for greater accountability for ICE, including scrutiny of its enforcement practices and the people it targets, while pursuing legislation to provide legal status to some immigrants who have lived in the United States for years.
But even if Democrats retake control of Congress in November, Amo acknowledged that advancing immigration reform will remain a challenge with Donald Trump in the White House for another two years.
“Does he want to be a president for the whole country, or does he want to continue to carry out chaos and cruelty on our streets?” Amo said.
Spokespeople for Auchincloss and Balint did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a video posted to social media at 2:19 p.m., Balint said she was alarmed that women were being held multiple days at a time.
“I am going to continue to keep the pressure on,” she said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Unusually high number of independent candidates seek South Dakota legislative seats
text:
The South Dakota Senate meets on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The Nov. 3 general election could be an independents’ day of sorts for South Dakota.
In addition to independent Brian Bengs challenging incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, the state’s legislative contests include 11 independent candidates — the highest number in recent memory.
At least one of those independents is guaranteed a seat in the state House of Representatives. That’s in District 27, a vast area including the Pine Ridge Reservation, where the ballot has four independents and one Republican vying for two House seats.
More than one victory for an independent would mark a historic moment for the South Dakota Legislature.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The last time an independent won a legislative seat in South Dakota was 2010, when Jenna Haggar — who’d later switch to Republican — was elected as a representative for a Sioux Falls-area district.
Prior to that, the last independent to serve was Alfred Burke, a Butte County senator from 1965 to 1972. The last time the Legislature had more than one independent serving at the same time was in the 1920s.
Independent victories this year would further adjust the shape of a Legislature already shaken up by a June primary election that produced the ouster of 16 incumbent Republicans.
The Republican Party will likely remain dominant in Pierre, however.
Fifty-two of the Legislature’s 105 seats are guaranteed to be held by Republicans in 2027, due to a lack of opposition: 21 seats in the Senate and 31 in the House. 
In South Dakota, there are more voters registered as independent or “no party affiliation” than as Democrats. Republicans have the highest numbers.
Advance voting is underway for the general election, and the voter registration deadline is Monday.
Partisan divide inspires some candidates
Neal Tapio is a former Republican state senator from Watertown who’s running as an independent to serve the same district as a state representative. Tapio said he still aligns with the Republican Party on most issues, but he’s come to see partisanship as a corrosive force.
“As you go through life, you realize that the country is just going more and more in the wrong direction, and it seems like partisan politics has gotten so bad that Republicans and Democrats don’t even talk to each other,” said Tapio. “The only thing they do is demonize each other.”
Tapio faces Republican incumbent Matt Roby and Republican former Rep. Byron Callies in a race for the district’s two House seats.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Joe Flood, a Massachusetts native who’s lived in Manderson on and off for two decades, is an independent running for a House seat in District 27. That race for two seats includes Flood, Republican incumbent Rep. Liz May of Kyle, and three other independents. 
Flood has always been registered as an independent, and said he’s approached politics with an independent mindset. He wants to work for his constituents, he said, not a party, even if party support might offer a hand up in an election.
The Harvard University graduate, author and educator said the major parties have done more to cheapen the discourse than earn his allegiance in recent years.
“I don’t think either party has covered itself in glory,” Flood said.
Path to independence differs
Tapio and Flood are among the independent candidates who told South Dakota Searchlight they’d always planned to run as independents. For others, running as an independent was the byproduct of missing the deadline for certification to appear on the primary ballot. For one, it was the result of a challenge to her nominating petitions. To get on the ballot, prospective legislative candidates need petition signatures from dozens of registered voters in their district, with the exact number depending on the party and the location. 
Rep. Peri Pourier, R-Rapid City, who is term-limited in the House, is on the ballot for Senate in District 27 as an independent. She’s running against Democrat Celestine Stadnick and Republican Anthony Kathol.
Democratic voter registration falls behind ‘other’ category in South Dakota

Pourier was serving as a Democrat when she announced her decision to switch to the Republican Party in 2025. 
She initially filed to run in the June Republican primary, but filed her petitions late. Pourier ultimately opted to re-collect signatures for the later deadline to run as an independent. 
She is still registered as a Republican, and said that if elected she would caucus with that party in the Senate. In a message to Searchlight, Pourier said she wants to be “up front about that,” but added that her status as an independent also reflects how she’d approach the job.
“What I offer is independent judgment, eight years of experience, and relationships that help me get work done,” she wrote.
Pourier’s Republican opponent, Anthony Kathol of Martin, challenged the validity of nominating petitions for Celestine Stadnick in the district’s Senate race and Elizabeth Lone Eagle in the House race.
In arguments that have reached the state Supreme Court, Kathol alleged inconsistencies between the candidates’ addresses as registered voters and those used on their petitions. He also argued some signers of Stadnick’s petition listed their county as “Oglala County” instead of “Oglala Lakota County,” which Kathol said ought to disqualify the signatures. 
The secretary of state threw out some signatures, but a circuit court ruled Stadnick, a Democrat, had enough valid signatures; the Supreme Court has yet to rule on Kathol’s appeal in that case.
His challenge to Lone Eagle’s petitions to run as a Democrat, grounded in similar issues, was successful. Lone Eagle was able to regather signatures and submit them to run as an independent. Lone Eagle told Searchlight that she aligns politically with Democrats, and would caucus with them if elected. 
Lone Eagle and Evangeline Poor Bear, who told Searchlight she’s a Republican and missed the March 31 filing deadline and therefore decided to run as an independent, are joined by Flood and Jay Yohner as independent candidates for the House seat in District 27. 
Rapid City race 
Samuel Hare Sr. of Rapid City considered running as a Democrat and said he received encouragement to do so, but decided to stay independent.
Nicole Uhre-Balk, who’s running for reelection as a Democratic representative for District 32, said Hare had suggested he run alongside her as a Democrat this spring, but she said “it becomes a little more challenging to know if we fully align on all the issues” with Hare running as an independent.
“It’s good for voters to have choices,” Uhre-Balk said, but “it’s a crowded race, for sure.”
In 2024 in her race for one of the district’s two House seats, Uhre-Balk asked people to “vote one, vote Nicole, because I was the only Democrat,” but “I’m not doing that this year.” 
“There are some people who think that really helped me, there’s some people who think it was all the doors that I knocked on,” Uhre-Balk said.
The other two candidates in the race are Republican Rep. Steve Duffy and Republican Zachary Martin.
Independent in Dell Rapids
Independent Bryan Breitling, like Tapio, has served in the Legislature before. 
When he was still living near Miller, Breitling successfully challenged then-Speaker of the House Spencer Gosch in the 2022 Republican Senate primary in District 23. 
Republican voters once again opt to oust incumbents from South Dakota Legislature

Breitling began what would become a permanent move to Dell Rapids in 2023, into District 25, before his term had ended. He did not run for reelection in 2024. 
District 25 Republican Sen. Tom Pischke took issue with Breitling’s residency prior to the 2024 session, but then-Senate President Pro Tempore Lee Schoenbeck dismissed those concerns, telling the Aberdeen Insider that Breitling “meets the minimum residency requirements.”
Breitling said he’d been encouraged to run against Pischke this spring, but that the window to register for the primary was too short by the time he decided to do so. 
“I’m a Republican running as an independent,” said Breitling. “That’s what I tell people when I’m knocking on doors.”
Breitling said his views diverge from Pischke’s on issues like education and economic development, and that he hopes to bring a more moderate, cooperative voice to Pierre. 
Pischke had no primary challenger. Shortly after the primary, though, he was charged with two felony counts of filing a forged or false instrument for allegedly signing and submitting candidate nominating petitions for county party precinct positions without those candidates’ knowledge.
The Minnehaha County Republican Party chairman, who’d clashed with Pischke, said he suspects Pischke was trying to add precinct officials to make it more difficult to conduct party business.
Pischke dropped out of the race over the summer.
The county party replaced him with Bart Sample, a former Flandreau City Council member who finished third in a four-way Republican primary race for District 25 House in June.

Neal Tapio, Watertown, District 5.
Garett Heinz, Ipswich, District 23.
Evangeline Poor Bear, Pine Ridge, District 27.
Elizabeth Lone Eagle, Kyle, District 27.
Joe Flood, Manderson, District 27.
Jay Yohner, Martin, District 27.

Clint Hoyer, Winfred, District 8.
Bryan J. Breitling, Dell Rapids, District 25.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: One step forward for West-East Rail
text:
WEST-EAST RAIL just got closer to becoming a reality.  
Gov. Maura Healey announced $130 million in federal funding for the Springfield Hub Modernization Project on Friday, the latest in the state’s push to upgrade rail infrastructure around Springfield Union Station and improve passenger rail service from Albany to Boston.  
The long-discussed West-East Rail is one part of the broader Compass Rail project — the Department of Transportation’s vision for intercity passenger rail within Massachusetts, with Springfield as the hub. It is a proposed 171-mile rail corridor linking Boston South Station with Albany–Rensselaer Station in New York, with stops in Worcester, Palmer, Springfield, and Pittsfield. Construction on the tracks between Springfield and Worcester is expected to begin in 2027, with the first trains to run by 2030.  
The modernization project is a key phase of the Springfield Area Track Reconfiguration Project, which will upgrade tracks, signals, and other infrastructure to ease a major rail bottleneck in the city by reducing conflicts between freight and passenger trains.  
The Healey administration said the funding will be used to improve on-time performance, reduce delays, and provide more schedule flexibility for Amtrak Vermonter and Valley Flyer passengers along the Connecticut River Line — also known as the Knowledge Corridor — while reducing unnecessary train idling, emissions, and operating costs. 
“The idea around Springfield is it’s a very busy area in terms of train traffic, both on the passenger side and the freight side, and the more we can separate the freight and passenger operations, the more flexibility we have for growing passenger service,” Meredith Slesinger, rail and transit administrator for MassDOT, told CommonWealth Beacon in March.
Healey made the announcement in Springfield’s Union Station alongside US Rep. Richard Neal.  
“With the federal resources we’ve delivered and the steadfast support of Governor Healey and her administration, we are full steam ahead on a project that will transform regional mobility and economic opportunity in every corner of the Commonwealth,” Neal said.  
The grant is an addition to the more than $150 million in federal funding that has already been allocated to the project over the last five years. Healey called it a “major win” for Western Massachusetts and a “big step forward” for West-East Rail.  
“This is about connecting Western Massachusetts to opportunities across Massachusetts and beyond throughout the Northeast,” Healey said. “When I was running, I campaigned and supported West-East Rail. I said we were going to get it done, and because of what we’re getting today, we’re going to get that going right in 2027.”  
The money was awarded through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements grant program. It is the last of the funding from the Biden-era Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that has provided around $8 billion in transportation investments to the state.  
In previous fiscal years, the Legislature has dropped line items from the final state budget that would have funded infrastructure improvements for West-East Rail. Instead, the Healey administration has relied mostly on federal funding opportunities.  
The state previously secured $108 million in federal funding for the Inland Route, which will connect Boston, Springfield, and New Haven, Connecticut with two daily Amtrak roundtrips in 2030.  
Last week, Healey also announced a new agreement between MassDOT and freight rail provider CSX to expand rail service in and around Pittsfield, calling it not only a big step toward permanent seasonal Berkshire Flyer service between the Berkshires and New York City, but also toward expanded passenger service from Boston to Western Massachusetts. MassDOT has proposed $31 million in its 2027-2031 Capital Investment Plan to support the work.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: What is news literacy and why do kids need it?
text:
ABC News correspondent Pierre Thomas speaks at the News Literacy Project conference in Salt Lake City on Oct. 9, 2026. The panel included Rep. John Arthur, D-Holladay, educator Patricia Hunt, Utah News Dispatch Editor McKenzie Romero, and Gretchen Zaitzeff, district library media specialist for Canyons School District. (Photo by Devin Captures Photography for the News Literacy Project) Growing up in a small town in Amherst County, Virginia, Pierre Thomas would gather around the table each night with his family to eat dinner and watch “World News Tonight with Peter Jennings” on ABC — in part because Jennings was their favorite evening news anchor, but also because it got the best reception on their TV.
That ritual instilled two strong beliefs in Thomas, now chief justice correspondent for ABC News based in Washington, D.C. 
In Salt Lake City last week during the first national conference of the News Literacy Project, Thomas said that night by night, as he learned about the world, he knew he always wanted to be an educated and informed person. He also decided he wanted to be a journalist.
Something similar happened to me.
When I was a kid growing up in Weber County, my parents subscribed to the Standard-Examiner, and I was often the one to grab it from the newspaper box and bring it inside. On the weekends, my dad and I would sit at the kitchen table eating cereal and flipping through the paper together, where I would check my favorite funnies and read the weekly musings of local columnist Mark Saal.
That’s how, from a young age, I knew if I wanted to learn more about what was happening in my community, local journalists would tell me.
Now I have a young daughter, and I wonder, what will be her equivalent of fetching the morning paper? How will she develop an interest in her community, and an awareness of where to find reliable information?
That’s a great question to ask the News Literacy Project, a cause championed by Thomas. The nonpartisan education nonprofit works with K-12 educators on teaching their students how to think critically about the onslaught of information they encounter, identify misinformation and bias, and understand the difference between news, advertisement, opinion and entertainment content.
Thomas moderated a panel for the Project’s Salt Lake event, which included John Arthur, a Democratic state legislator and Utah’s 2021 Teacher of the Year; Patricia M. Hunt, a social studies educator with 33 years experience who teaches at Wakefield High School in Arlington, Virginia; Gretchen Zaitzeff, district library media specialist for Canyons School District in Sandy; and me, representing local journalism.
In his remarks, Thomas emphasized that news literacy does not mean promoting any specific media outlet or political perspective. It is not partisan, it is teaching young people to discern for themselves where to find the best information to make their own decisions. And he believes developing that ability can make all the difference. 
“There’s so much negativity out there. People are so quick to retreat to their tribes and tribal positions. One of the few counters to what is happening is providing people with the tools they need to help themselves make some sense of it all,” Thomas said.
That’s where news literacy comes in.
Thomas continued, “Teaching students how to understand what the news is, how to pursue gathering information is more critical than it’s ever been. A public that is not informed cannot make good decisions about anything.” 
Utah schools were among some of the first to partner with the News Literacy Project. In Canyons School District, Zaitzeff has been working with 300 educators on how to teach information, news and media literacy to their K-12 students. 
Speaking on the panel, Zaitzeff said she sees news literacy as a vital skill that rounds out all of the subjects students are learning and prepares them for civic engagement.
“I would say that we can teach kids science and reading and social studies and health, but if we can’t help them find accurate information in those fields, what does it matter that they have this foundation, because they’re going to go out in the world and not be able to figure out what is out there and what they can trust,” Zaitzeff said. 
And of course, the final piece of promoting strong news literacy in young people is making sure they have quality news sources to turn to. Like Thomas, who said he strives with each story to be accurate and fair, or my reporters at Utah News Dispatch who clearly lay out the impacts of policy decisions in our state, or the journalists on the impressive list of strong Utah news outlets. 
Keeping that journalism in our communities requires looking to reputable news operations — which cite their sources, not their opinions — for information about what’s important to you rather than relying on social media screed. It can also mean supporting those news outlets by donating or subscribing, when you can. And it means sharing verified information from those quality news sources with the people in your lives, including kids, in order to spread the positive impacts of news literacy in our state.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Deer hunters welcome cooler, drier conditions as muzzleloader season starts
text:
Several deer at Jester Park in Polk County on Nov. 7, 2024. (Photo by Karsan Turner for Iowa Capital Dispatch)Cooler temperatures and harvested crop fields are welcome conditions for deer hunters in the state who have already started for the season or are gearing up to begin hunting, according to the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.
DNR tracks deer populations and hunter data throughout the year. Its 2026 spring spotlight survey, which scans for wildlife after sunset along gravel roads throughout the state, observed the lowest relative abundance of white-tailed deer in over a decade. 
Jace Elliott, state deer biologist for DNR, said the spotlight survey findings are commensurate with what the department is hearing from bow hunters, whose season started at the beginning of the month. The state’s early muzzleloader season begins Saturday.

“Bow hunters are our most avid hunting group, spending the most time in the field,” Elliott said in a news release from DNR. “And what we’ve been hearing from them in recent years is they are seeing fewer deer throughout much of the state.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The spotlight survey showed relative deer abundance declined 20% from 2025, and has the lowest estimated abundance since 2013. Deer populations declined across all regions of the state, though Elliott said “there is evidence” that deer populations in western Iowa are beginning to rebound. 
As a result of the observed population declines in the area, DNR implemented a new regional hunting zone this year in eight western Iowa counties that has limited quotas of county-specific licenses and a requirement to hunt antlered deer only.
All counties aside from Crawford, Ida, Lyon, O’Brien, Plymouth, Shelby, Sioux and Woodbury are considered part of Zone A and do not have the same restrictions, though there is an antlered-buck only restriction in certain Zone A counties during the first gun season. Hunters should consult DNR’s hunting guide for specific information before heading out to their tree stands. 
Iowa DNR implemented deer hunting zones in 2026 to encourage deer population growth in western Iowa. Counties shaded black are part of Zone B and have restrictions on doe hunting. All other counties are part of Zone A, and those shaded yellow have doe restrictions during the first gun season of the year. (Map courtesy of DNR)
According to DNR’s 2026 spotlight survey, the reasons for the decline in the relative abundance of deer in the state “remains unclear.” 
While deer in the state continue to be exposed to epizootic hemorrhagic disease — an often fatal disease spread by small insects – reported mortality from the diseases were relatively low in 2025. According to the spotlight survey report, mortality rates from hemorrhaging diseases were higher in the last several years though the relative abundance of deer remained stable.
The survey said it is possible that unaccounted for landscape or atmospheric conditions impacted the count. DNR said the survey also observed very low numbers in 2012, but that numbers shot back up the following year at rates that were “biologically improbable.” 
Chronic Wasting Disease continues to impact deer in Iowa and DNR tracks the disease with the help of hunters and additional population management in areas with high observations of the disease. However, CWD was not listed as a reason for the population declines across the state. 
According to DNR data, 192 deer in 29 counties tested positive for chronic wasting disease in 2025. The highest concentrations of the disease were detected in eastern and south-central Iowa. So far in the 2026-2027 hunting season, DNR’s database shows more than 240 samples have been taken, but none have been confirmed positive for the disease, which is always fatal to deer. 
Population, hunting, disease and car collision data gathered by the department helps inform deer management plans, county antlerless deer quotas and deer license types. The department’s management priorities for the current hunting season are primarily to maintain deer population in most of the state and to increase population in western Iowa. 
Hunters harvested 101,919 deer in the 2025-2026 season, which was a 1% increase from the previous year, according to DNR’s latest deer program report. While gun season harvest last season had around 5% lower harvests from the year prior, bow hunters harvested about 4% more deer last year than the year before. 
DNR said “Mother Nature hasn’t been cooperating” with bow hunters this fall as the state has seen warmer weather and near record-high rain totals in September. 
Elliot said bow hunters, whose first season stretches to Dec. 4, are “are getting excited” by cooler temperatures and a break from the rain.
“Due to all the rain, natural forage has been really prevalent this year and deer seem to be remaining in the timber where they have ample cover and food,” Elliot said.
Drier conditions the past couple of weeks have allowed farmers to make some progress on harvest, which Elliot said will also be beneficial for hunters. 
“Deer are still disbursed, but that can change as the crops come out and temperatures drop,” he said.
