title: JXN Water pushes for independent oversight of Jackson’s water system
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Jackson’s water and sewer systems would remain outside city officials’ control under a proposal by a federally appointed manager that would establish an independent, customer-governed authority to oversee the troubled utilities.
The 36-page transition plan JXN Water released Thursday blamed Jackson leaders for “decades of failure and the ultimate collapse of the water system.”
The manager, Ted Henifin, was especially blunt: “At bottom, there is no case to be made to return governance to the City in the foreseeable future.”
Henifin’s proposal would create a separate governing entity from the Metro Jackson Water Authority state lawmakers established earlier this year. A federal judge has partially blocked the state-created authority amid a legal challenge from Jackson officials over who should control the utilities once federal oversight ends.
During his State of the City address earlier this week, Jackson Mayor John Horhn acknowledged the ongoing strife.
“Our relationship with JXN Water has been tested. We are now having serious conversations about what comes next when the current arrangement ends,” he said.
“Let me be clear: Jackson owns these water assets. Jackson carries the debt. And the people of Jackson have a legitimate interest in the future of their water system.”
Henifin, who is expected to step down by July 2028, would be replaced by a court-appointed chief executive to lead the new authority – which could be in place as soon as next year.
The proposed authority, which would need court approval, would assume responsibility for the utilities while remaining under federal oversight. That oversight could end by December 2029.
In 2022, U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate placed Jackson’s struggling water system under Henifin’s control following a crisis that left much of the city without reliable running water. The following year, he placed Jackson’s sewer system under Henifin’s control, also.
Under Henifin’s plan, a federal judge would appoint the initial members of the authority’s governing board, with future members elected by ratepayers.
While Henifin considered privatizing the water and sewer systems, he concluded that doing so could prioritize profits over much-needed long-term investments.
Earlier this year, Henifin floated the idea of selling the city’s water and sewer system to an independent authority. The proceeds, he said, could help the city retire roughly $121 million in utility debt, potentially reducing the need for future rate increases.
The idea drew opposition from City Council members, some of whom argued that Jackson should not be forced to surrender ownership of its infrastructure.
Henifin’s transition plan outlines several possible scenarios for governing Jackson’s water and sewer systems.
His recommendation to establish an independent authority, he said in the report, would make it easier to get financing for infrastructure improvements and protect the system from political influence.
That influence is a key reason for his rejection of the legislative remedy adopted earlier this year. The Metro Jackson Water Authority would have board members appointed by  the governor, lieutenant governor and the mayors of Byram, Ridgeland and Jackson. Jackson’s mayor would also serve as a non-voting ex-officio member.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico early voting locations expand on Saturday
text:
The League of Women Voters of Southern New Mexico partnered with the Doña Ana County Clerk’s Office to register potential voters on Sept. 15, 2026, National Voter Registration Day, on the New Mexico State University main campus in Las Cruces. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Early voting locations for the Nov. 3 general election will significantly expand across New Mexico starting Saturday.
This year’s general election marks the first time New Mexicans will elect a new governor in eight years. The ballot will also feature contested races for the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, as well as several races for the state Legislature, along with constitutional amendments and ballot initiatives.[Voter Guide: New Mexico Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Early voting began on Oct. 6 at county clerks’ offices across the state, and will expand to additional early voting locations on Saturday that will remain operational through Oct. 31. The New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office’s website offers a comprehensive list of early voting locations, as well as sample ballots customizable to each user’s address.
As of Friday morning, just more than 63,000 registered voters across the state had cast either absentee or early ballots — about 4.3% of all registered voters in New Mexico.
Of those, nearly 37,000 were Democrats, about 17,000 were Republicans and nearly 9,000 registered as independent or “decline to state” voters, according to data from the Secretary of State.
Across the U.S. and New Mexico, a series of non-partisan No Kings rallies will also focus on early voting efforts. While past No Kings events have typically been protests, organizers say Saturday’s events are instead meant to educate attendees about registering and voting early.
The new focus comes amid ongoing concerns by states about federal interference during the midterm elections. On Tuesday, New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver and Attorney General Raúl Torrez issued a joint advisory to reinforce voter rights.
The next act for the No Kings movement: Early voting in the midterms

On Saturday, No Kings events are scheduled for more than two dozen New Mexico communities, including Albuquerque, Santa Fe and Las Cruces.
Rayellen Smith, the president of the progressive group Indivisible Albuquerque, told Source NM that from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday, volunteers will set up outside Bernalillo County’s busiest early voting locations waving large red arrows with messages such as, “vote early this way.”
A No Kings rally at Montgomery Park, off of San Mateo and Montgomery boulevards in Albuquerque, will also feature a giveaway. Smith said hundreds of attendees will receive a tote bag full of flyers, buttons and door hangers with early voting information. It’s designed to send people back into their communities, where they can educate their families, friends and neighbors about early voting resources.
“It is so critically important to get out there and get our votes counted,” Smith said, adding that national organizers hope Saturday’s effort will go down as the largest get-out-the-vote initiative in U.S. history.
On Oct. 30, 31 and Nov. 3 — the final two days of early voting in New Mexico and Election Day — Smith said residents can call 1-888-858-3421 to request a ride to the polls, as well.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota officials are jumpstarting next phase of effort to boost Bakken oil production
text:
Kyle Haustveit, under secretary of energy at the U.S. Department of Energy, talks about the potential of enhanced oil recovery during a press conference hosted by the North Dakota Petroleum Council on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)A coalition of oil industry leaders, state officials and a U.S. senator are rallying support for the next stage of an oil field research project that could have a significant impact on North Dakota’s economic future. 
The research centers on enhanced oil recovery, a collection of technologies that officials hope will double the amount of recoverable oil in North Dakota and extend the Bakken oil field’s longevity by decades.
“That’s an entire new oil boom without the infrastructure challenges,” said Gov. Kelly Armstrong. “This isn’t about the energy industry. This isn’t about western North Dakota. This is about the whole state.”
Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., is working with Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit, a Tioga native, to unlock $400 million in federal loan guarantees to help fund the expanded initiative. 
North Dakota’s stripper well tax break faces scrutiny

Ron Ness, president of the North Dakota Petroleum Council, said he expects there to be an ask for state funding during the upcoming legislative session. 
“This is the jumpstart for that discussion,” Ness said.
Enhanced oil recovery typically involves injecting a gas, like natural gas or carbon dioxide, into oil and gas formations underground in order to repressurize the reservoirs and increase the amount of oil that can be extracted. Oil companies have spent years testing the idea in small-scale pilot projects.
A coalition of government officials and industry leaders announced phase one of the current initiative in May. The $157 million effort involves six large scale pilot projects, planned to have 10 to 20 times the duration and volume of gas injections as earlier demonstrations, testing the technologies in the field. 
Those projects are ongoing. Three of the projects are underway, a fourth has received a permit and two more are awaiting approval from regulators. 
But the coalition is already working to launch the second phase of the effort. The goal is to secure funding for companies to move beyond single-well tests and implement the technology across a broader geographic area involving up to 200 oil wells. 
“We can’t continue to just wait another year to see what happens on phase one wells. We think this resource is so great that we can move now, and I think that’s the essence of today,” Ness said. “Phase two is jumping over the top of phase one.”
North Dakota’s governor said they are proceeding with multiple phases concurrently, rather than a linear progression of one phase after another, in order to accelerate the development timeline.
“It’s all gas, no brakes. We need an all-of-industry approach. We need an all-of-government approach,” Armstrong said. “I can promise you that your grandkids will benefit from the decisions that get made in these projects over the next six months.”
Hoeven said the technology needs to be in widespread use by the end of 2032 because that is when a federal tax credit for the use of carbon dioxide in enhanced oil recovery projects expires. 
Chord Energy CEO Danny Brown discusses enhanced oil recovery research during a press conference hosted by the North Dakota Petroleum Council on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Chord Energy, the largest operator in North Dakota and the only publicly-traded oil company that is exclusively focused on the Williston Basin, is part of the coalition of stakeholders. CEO Danny Brown said enhanced oil recovery is a fundamentally different approach to oil extraction than the techniques used in the Bakken today, such as drilling horizontally for miles and fracturing the rock formation. 
“It’s another potentially 10 billion barrels and decades of flatline production as we move forward. But it’s a fundamentally different way to approach how to extract oil,” Brown said. “We think there’s tremendous potential here.”
The stakes are high for North Dakota. 
“At one time, we were producing 1.5 million barrels of oil a day. Now we’re down to 1.1 million barrels of oil a day, and that’ll keep going down unless we do this enhanced oil recovery,” Hoeven said.
Armstrong said a new Bakken well can produce 1,000 barrels of oil per day when it comes online. But it declines quickly and can be producing 200 barrels of oil per day a year and a half later. 
Enhanced oil recovery could create a more stable revenue stream for governments and companies alike. The governor said the technology may be able to take an aging oil well producing 30 barrels of oil per day, increase production to 100 barrels per day and hold steady for decades. 
“The easiest way to explain it is like an annuity. It’s a long term investment in an oil well,” Armstrong said. 
He acknowledged there is risk in moving so quickly on the initiative. But he said the reward could be half a century of economic benefits like North Dakota has enjoyed over the last 20 years. 
“The opportunity cost of not doing anything is a significantly bigger risk, extraordinarily so,” Armstrong said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: New UI clinic pilots exercise treatments to improve health of cancer patients, survivors
text:
A new University of Iowa exercise oncology clinic is working with cancer patients and survivors to help with their symptoms and health. (Stock photo via Getty Images)When Casey Westlake had her first mammogram around a year ago, she was told everyone gets called back in. So when she was asked to stop by for another round of imaging, she knew not to panic. After that, however, Westlake got called in for a biopsy.
“I opened the biopsy results Sunday night, I think it was the Sunday before Thanksgiving, and I really thought there’s no way this is cancer, it’s not happening, and it was cancer,” Westlake said.
Westlake was diagnosed with stage 1B breast cancer, which she said was an early stage of the cancer. What followed was a winter with two surgeries, a spring filled with four rounds of chemotherapy and four weeks of radiation in the summer. She rang the bell to signal the end of her active cancer treatment on July 7 — just one day before her 41st birthday.
A new exercise oncology research clinic at the UI is helping Westlake and others dealing with cancer and its aftermath build back strength and trust in their bodies through exercise training.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The new clinic, housed in the UI’s new Health Sciences Academic Building near the Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center, is funded with $642,896 over three years through the university’s public-private partnership initiative. Jessica Gorzelitz, director and founder of the exercise oncology clinic, said she hopes the exercise treatment she’s researched and implemented here will eventually become part of cancer patients’ standard care.
Gorzelitz has been exploring the relationship between exercise and cancer since her own days as a college student, she said, and her lab and work at the UI focuses on how exercise can help improve cancer patient and survivor health and wellness.
“Across the United States, there are over 60 NCI-designated comprehensive cancer centers,” Gorzelitz said. “I can count on one hand the number of those cancer centers that even address physical activity, much less exercise oncology, so I think one component would be considering how we can set ourselves up as leading the field as a comprehensive cancer center.”
Iowa has become “infamous” for its number-two ranking in increasing cancer incidence rates, Gorzelitz said, but more and more people are also surviving cancer due to better treatments. It’s important to address the health outcomes of cancer survivors as well as those still going through treatments, she said.
Evidence from behavioral clinical trials she’s conducted shows that patients who exercise see differences in their symptoms, treatment outcomes and mortality risk, but Gorzelitz said the frustrating part is the difficulty in changing people’s behavior.
“There shouldn’t be this finger wagging of what people should be doing,” Gorzelitz said. “The question I have is how do we hit the easy button and build this into the clinical pathway so it’s part of cancer treatment, so that patients are seeing their oncologist, their radiologist, and then they have exercise oncology to support them on their journey as well.”
The clinic operates as a research trial, Gorzelitz said, with its main questions focusing on implementation — and measuring success — of exercise oncology treatments with cancer patients and survivors. The 30 women involved in the first pilot trial, including Westlake, had diagnoses of breast or gynecological cancers.
The University of Iowa Health Sciences Academic Building houses the new exercise oncology clinic. (Photo courtesy of the University of Iowa)
With the first pilot over the halfway mark and already seeing successes with participants, Gorzelitz said she and clinic staff are getting ready to open the doors to patients across Iowa with different types of cancer through remote consultations and training.
“Through this pilot, we’ve been able to identify inefficiencies and ways that we can do things better or clearer,” Gorzelitz said. “We’re also finding the importance of raising awareness both within our cancer center and educating the providers about this free, evidence-based service, then also thinking about strategies for outreach to rural areas and getting patients who might not live in Iowa City aware that this is available to them.”
As exercise is “inherently dangerous,” Gorzelitz said the clinic must go beyond the general aerobic and resistance exercise guidelines for exercise among cancer patients and figure out what would be safest for each patient in terms of exercise frequency, timing, progression and other areas.
What treatments patients are going through also must be considered, as they can cause fatigue or tingling in the hands and feet, and patients’ physicians sometimes need to be consulted for medical clearance and guidance.
Westlake said the different cancer treatments she went through left her feeling weak and fatigued, with medications she’ll need to be on for the foreseeable future also causing lower back and joint pain. Now, halfway through the exercise oncology pilot, she’s completing leg presses with the equivalent of her own body weight and can pick up her 7-year-old daughter, acts that she calls “empowering.”
“It’s been really amazing to do this because I know it’s a proactive way for me to prevent my cancer from recurring,” Westlake said. “It’s also been a really powerful experience in learning to trust my body again and rebuilding my strength after going through all this treatment.”
As the pilot reaches the latter half of its programming, Gorzelitz said participants have worried about what happens when the trial ends, and she has a goal of giving patients post-program resources or training that they can use in their own gym or home.
Both Westlake and Gorzelitz shared their dreams for where the clinic could lead, with the director wanting to find a way to keep the clinic sustainable and cost-free for its patients. She said she hopes Medicare, Medicaid and maybe even private insurers “see the value of these services” and cover them, and that the clinic is “institutionalized” to continue to receive UI support.
“In my dream world, every Iowan with cancer would eventually have access to this kind of care,” Westlake said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Medicaid changes impact, newest culinary trail: CT politics news
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Impact of federal Medicaid changes
U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, hosted a roundtable on Thursday morning in Norwich to discuss the impact of federal eligibility changes to Medicaid, known as HUSKY in Connecticut. Nonprofit leaders said people are confused and panicked that they will lose coverage. Representatives from groups representing patients with diabetes and multiple sclerosis said the new requirements will pose specific challenges for people with disabilities.
Department of Social Services Commissioner Andrea Barton Reeves walked through tools the state has created, including the website MedicaidMattersCT.org, which has a screener where residents can see if the eligibility changes apply to them.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CT recipients will see Social Security bump
Social Security recipients in Connecticut and around the country will see a bump in their checks due to a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment.
This will take effect in January for about 765,000 people in the state who get retiree, disability or survivor benefits.
Outgoing U.S. Rep. John Larson, who has pushed for legislation for years to bolster Social Security, said the increase is welcome news, but it’s a reminder Congress needs to act soon. “With insolvency looming, we are only a few years away from automatic benefit cuts for everyone on Social Security if Congress does not act,” Larson said. “It is time for a vote.”
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Blue Ribbon Commission eyes expanding regional centers
Members of Gov. Ned Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability heard proposals on Tuesday about how to expand the state’s six Regional Educational Service Centers, or RESCs.
RESCs serve multiple districts, making them a potentially powerful tool to regionalize certain services that may be too costly or cumbersome for individual districts to implement alone. Proposals included: creating state reimbursements for high-priority services; allowing RESCs to access state special education grants; staffing RESCs with fiscal advisors to help schools manage finances; creating formal state-RESC liaisons; and incentivizing districts to participate. The next full commission meeting is Oct. 29.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
CT’s latest culinary trail highlights “TV-to-table” successes
Connecticut has a new interactive tourism campaign, with officials announcing a trail highlighting popular chefs and food businesses that have appeared on national television.
The new “TV-to-Table” trail, announced last week in Stamford, highlights restaurants, bakeries and local chefs featured on shows like “Beat Bobby Flay,” “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives” and “Cupcake Wars.” During the launch event, Gov. Ned Lamont was joined by local chefs and television personality Scott Conant, a chef and Waterbury native.
State officials hope that its slew of experiential “trail” campaigns, including ones focused on pizza, supernatural lore, and Christmas movies, will encourage visitors to journey to businesses and popular sites across the state.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT awards $15 million in afterschool program grants
The Connecticut State Department of Education announced last week that $15 million in federal grant money will go to afterschool programs throughout the Nutmeg State.
The money comes through Title IV of the federal Elementary and Secondary Education Act. It will support a wide range of afterschool activities, including tutoring, arts, athletics, health and family literacy.
The education department said it received 55 applications, of which 25 won funding. Those include a mix of public school districts and local organizations like Boys & Girls Clubs.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Despite recent rain, drought has reached all areas of Maine
text:
The Wheeler Brook stream bed with low water levels on Sept. 9, 2026. The Maine Drought Task Force reports that the state never fully recovered from the 2025 drought, which is now worsening drought conditions across the state. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)The latest precipitation across the state still was not enough to alleviate Maine’s statewide drought, according to the Maine Drought Task Force. 
The task force convenes when abnormally dry conditions in the state compound with the aim of increasing communication and awareness. Members from state and federal agencies met Friday for the second time this year.
Since the task force last met in early September, drought conditions have expanded, now reaching all areas of the state. The latest report from the U.S. Drought Monitor, with data from Tuesday, had 4.64% of the state in extreme drought conditions, 43.10% in severe drought and the remaining 52.26% in moderate drought. 
The conditions are already affecting the fall harvest for farmers, and there has been a rise in the number of dry well reports. 
The midcoast region is experiencing extreme drought, with severe drought spreading wider across that area as well as much of Northern Maine. 
Sarah Jamison with the National Weather Service said the current drought might feel different from last year’s, which came on more suddenly, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t as severe.
“What’s very different from this drought compared to the same time last year is you could step outside and see it and feel it,” Jamison said. “Now if you drive around and you look at the lakes and the streams, you can see it. But generally, your lawns aren’t too bad.”
But, Jamison continued, “if you look under the hood, that’s where the problem lies.” 
Groundwater conditions
Nick Stasulis with the U.S. Geological Survey said that while the recent rain this week has boosted water levels in streams, it has not been enough to replenish the groundwater, and that’s a problem because it never fully recovered from last year’s drought.
Two monitoring wells in Oxford and Clayton Lake hit record low levels for October, Stasulis said. And both of those wells have more than 35 years of historical data. That means the current levels are falling below the levels from the 2000s drought, which is often considered the benchmark for severe groundwater conditions. 
And Stasulis said he expects other groundwater monitoring wells to follow suit.
“So without any recharge, my guess is by November there’ll be even more wells setting that period of record streak,” he said. “We’ve had a lot of droughts. We’ve met a lot over the last 10 years, and this is the first time we’re actually starting to see records be set for groundwater conditions.”
Jamison echoed his point that the recent rain just isn’t enough to improve groundwater. 
“We’ve been getting rain, all very, very beneficial,” Jamison said. “We’re seeing the effects of that at the surface level. We just need to get it down into the groundwater where we really, really need it. We’re fighting the seasonal declines in our groundwater too.”
Jamison looked at precipitation levels from Oct. 1, 2025 through Sept. 30, 2026, and found that different parts of the state got 5-18 inches less precipitation than normal. 
And further back, from June 2025 to the present, Jamison said only three months in that period saw above average precipitation: April, May and June of 2026. The other 13 months were below average.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Looking ahead, Jamison said the amount of rain needed to exit drought conditions varies in different parts of the state. Northern Maine would need to see 150% of normal precipitation in the next two months or before ground frost conditions, central Maine would need 180% and Southern and coastal Maine would need 200% of normal precipitation. 
And her colleague at the National Weather Service, James Sinko, said that relief doesn’t seem likely to come soon. Despite the rain Friday, he said the seven-day forecast doesn’t show a high chance of additional rain. 
Further out, he said, El Niño conditions could impact winter weather, which usually means warmer and wetter conditions in Maine. 
“So what that typically means is more rain, sleet, freezing rain events than we see for snowfall, and it also means we struggle typically to build a snowpack,” Sinko said. 
The concern in Maine is if the ground freezes, rain can’t soak into the soil to replenish groundwater, and the snow won’t be melting into the ground come spring as the ground thaws. 
“And that can be devastating when you don’t get a deep snowpack, so there are still some concerns in there that we’re worried about for any potential recharge that we need,” Sinko said.
On the ground impacts
Tom Gordon with the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry said the impact on farms has been significant. 
“We can really see a difference between the haves and the have-not as to whether the ones that have irrigation systems have done pretty well this year, the ones without, there’s definitely been impact on yield,” Gordon said. 
Gordon said he doesn’t have economic data on the impact yet, but he thinks potato and apple crops have done well despite the drought. 
Tommy Higgins with the U.S. Department of Agriculture said the agency’s farmer assistance programs are triggered by the length of a drought and its intensity, and many are already available to Maine farmers. 
The Emergency Livestock Assistance Program is available to farmers in all 16 Maine counties, the Livestock Forage Disaster Program is available in 13 counties and the Emergency Conservation Program is available in 10 counties. 
The agency is also anticipating a secretarial disaster declaration for seven counties in the near future, Higgins said, which triggers the availability of emergency farm loans. 
Paul Styslinger with the Maine Emergency Management Agency said the organization has gotten reports of 156 dry wells this year, the vast majority of those reports coming in the last month — although that may be because of increased attention to the report, rather than changing conditions. 
Paul Styslinger with the Maine Emergency Management Agency said the organization has gotten reports of 156 dry wells this year, the vast majority of those reports coming in the last month — although that may be because of increased attention to the reporting service, rather than changing conditions. 
“Well driller wait lists were a top item,” Styslinger said. 
Other members of the task force added that many well drillers are still working on the backlog of properties that ran dry last year, and there’s just not many people licensed to drill wells — and even among those who are, some are elderly and not actively working. 
The delays are a challenge for the Farmer Drought Resilience Fund, Gordon noted, which provides grants to farms to reach new sources of water. The state funding for the program typically must be spent within the two-year budget, Gordon said. So if a driller is not available, the contract could expire and the funding may not be available for that farm again.
The task force is encouraging residents to report dry wells to the Maine Emergency Management Agency and other drought conditions to the National Integrated Drought Information System. The Drought Task Force website also has a list of resources available for residents impacted by the drought.

name: WyoFile
title: Five takeaways from Wyoming’s superintendent of public instruction debate
text:
Wyoming political newcomer and Democrat Ana Cordova faced educator and long-serving Republican state lawmaker Steve Harshman in a well-mannered Thursday debate, where the superintendent of public instruction candidates discussed teacher pay, artificial intelligence in the classroom and school choice.
One of five statewide elected officials, the superintendent of public instruction leads the Wyoming Department of Education and serves on the powerful financial decision-making State Loan and Investment Board. Current Superintendent Megan Degenfelder ran for governor but lost to Eric Barlow in the August Republican primary. 
Degenfelder’s seat opens as lawsuits, policies, funding decisions and technological innovation pose major changes to Wyoming’s educational landscape. The Legislature passed a recalibration bill that represents a new funding model for school districts; Wyoming’s universal school choice program is rolling out even as it’s tied up in court and the state recently overhauled literacy standards and instruction. 
Here are five takeaways from the debate.
Despite an experience and party gap, the candidates agree on many issues.
Harshman’s 24-year tenure in the Wyoming House of Representatives makes him one of the longest-serving representatives in state history. He also has decades of experience teaching high school history and physical education and more than 40 years as a football, wrestling and track coach, which makes him well-known in the education world. 
As a standout 2004 graduate of Cheyenne High School who left Wyoming to pursue higher education and career opportunities before returning in early 2026, Cordova does not come with the same name recognition or classroom education. But Cordova, who earned a master’s degree in human genetics before obtaining her law degree, believes strongly in the value of education and the principles of evidence-backed decision-making, she said. 
“I really believe in the transformational power of public education,” she said. “I am a product of Wyoming public schools. I had a great experience. I had so many opportunities, and I’m really hoping to pass that on to future generations.”
Despite the party and experience gaps, the candidates found similar ground on issues like their stance on Proposition 1 (both adamantly oppose the property tax reduction measure); their belief that too much emphasis on standardized testing is detrimental and that the decision to go to a four-day school week should be up to a local school district. 
Harshman said teacher pay has improved; Cordova wants to pay them more.
Wyoming’s new K-12 school funding model, passed this year following a monthslong assessment process known as recalibration, raises average weighted teacher salaries to roughly $70,000, which is up from just under $60,000.
When given the prompt of “teacher pay” during the debate’s lightning round, Harshman said, “Teacher pay has improved dramatically, and that’s one of the good things [from recalibration]. We fully funded the teacher pay. It’s been underfunded for a few years.” 
Republican Steve Harshman shares his opinion on how cutting property tax would affect schools in Wyoming on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, during a superintendent of public instruction debate in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Staying on top of that, he added, will be critical. 
Cordova went even further. 
“I think that teachers should be paid more,” she said. “That is one of the failings of the recalibration in terms of teacher pay and being able to retain teachers, and also just trusting teachers as experts. They are the experts in their field and should be treated and compensated like that.”
Both believe cellphones bans and AI guidance are appropriate, but want to preserve local choice.
Education leaders across the U.S. are wrestling with how to manage artificial intelligence and cellphones in the classroom. 
Harshman called AI “a tremendous tool that’s changing lives,” but cautioned that it can seriously interfere with students’ learning. 
When asked if the state education superintendent should issue guidance on AI, Cordova said that yes, with the crucial word being “guidance.” That way, districts struggling to manage AI use can come to the state for best practices and up-to-date information. 
“That said, I don’t think the state superintendent should be putting out any mandates,” Cordova said. 
Both support banning cellphones during instructional time, but on that issue, Harshman was the one cautioning against state government overreach. 
“It’s not the job of the state superintendent or the authorization of this job to really tell school districts what you’re going to do,” said Harshman, who supported a bill that mandates districts create their own cellphone policy. 
They support different approaches to addressing behavioral issues.
Teachers are reporting a rise in behavioral and disciplinary issues in the classroom, particularly since the COVID-19 lockdown. 
It’s important to approach this issue through a multi-pronged strategy, Cordova said; behavioral issues can stem from problems like food insecurity, housing insecurity or other tumult in the household. 
Democrat Ana Cordova gives her opening remarks during the Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
“When it comes to behavioral problems in our schools, I think we can solve a lot of them through our schools, our school districts, our educators and our professionals working alongside other agencies we have here in Wyoming to help ensure that students come to school ready to learn,” she said. “So that means with a full belly after a full night’s rest in a place that feels safe with people who care about them.”
Harshman, meanwhile, focused on improved training and professional development for teachers. Administrative leadership, he said, is critical for ensuring teachers are equipped to deal with discipline problems.
Cordova criticized Wyoming’s school voucher program; Harshman didn’t.
Wyoming in 2025 passed a controversial law that created a universal school-choice voucher program, the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act. Through the program, Wyoming residents can apply to receive up to $7,000 in state funds per student to pay for costs associated with private K-12 education and preschool.
During the intense legislative debate that preceded its passage, Harshman opposed the program, warning his colleagues the universal voucher program would land in court. His warning came true; a judge will determine if the program is constitutional in an ongoing case. 
When given the prompt of “school choice,” in the lightning round, Harshman focused on the concept rather than Wyoming’s program. “Parents are the kids’ first and primary teacher,” he said. How to educate their children, he said “that’s their choice, 100%.”
Cordova addressed the funding mechanism, meanwhile. 
“I think that public money needs to stay in public schools,” she said. “So while parents definitely should have the choice on whether or not to send their kids to public school, I don’t think alternatives to public school should be funded by public money.”
The event concluded a series of debates hosted by Wyoming PBS. The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Make way for the corndog: Arkansas State Fair kicks off
text:
Roger Scott, an Arkansas radio personality, dons a costume to serve as the corndog at the Arkansas State Fair's inaugural corndog drop on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)It’s a bird, it’s a plane, it’s… a corndog?
To be more precise, it’s radio personality Roger Scott dressed in a corndog costume atop a scissor lift at the Arkansas State Fairgrounds on a somewhat-dreary Friday morning. 
To do what, you may ask? To inaugurate the newest tradition of the Arkansas State Fair — the corndog drop.
“Forget the ribbon cutting,” a news release from the fair read. “We’re dropping a corn dog.”

So in the minutes before the decades-old fair officially opened for its 2026 edition, rides such as the ferris wheel, Crazy Mouse and Polar Plunge were still and the fairgrounds located south of downtown Little Rock were occupied only by vendors and staff. 
A crowd was beginning to gather near the front gates as the clock approached 11 a.m. Cheerleaders with the Arkansas Diamonds, the minor league football team set to play its games at the fairgrounds’ Barton Coliseum, huddled close together, smiles never budging despite the windy chill.
They were joined by fair and rodeo queens young and younger, wearing sparkly tiaras and cowboy boots, while uniformed members of the Arkansas State Police and the Pulaski County Sheriff’s Office looked on. Some people looked nervously up at the sky. One person wondered aloud if it would rain.
As Scott hammed it up and Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders expressed relief that the bipedal corndog appeared to be wearing pants, Parkview Arts and Science Magnet High School’s marching band played stands tunes as its cheerleaders and color guard smiled and danced. Lt. Gov. Leslie Rutledge was also on hand.
“We are so proud to be out here to kick off the Arkansas State Fair tradition,” Sanders said. “(Her brother) and I have spent many hours and many days at a lot of fairs across the state of Arkansas, campaigning for my dad. I think we’ve been to at least about every county fair in the state of Arkansas.”
With a drum roll from the marching band, the scissor lift began to descend, the corndog dropped, and confetti and pyrotechnics followed, officially marking the start of the 10-day fair.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Richard E. Holmes, first Black student at Mississippi State University, dies at 82
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Richard E. Holmes, the first Black student to enroll at Mississippi State University, died Friday. He was 82. 
Holmes enrolled at the previously segregated university in Starkville on July 19, 1965, three years after James Meredith integrated the University of Mississippi amid violent opposition. 
MSU president Mark Keenum, remembered Holmes as a man of courage, vision and patience who left a lasting impact on the university. 
“Dr. Holmes cast a long, productive and impactful shadow over this institution, a shadow that also leaned forward,” Keenum said in a statement. “I will miss his company and his counsel.” 
Holmes, a Starkville native, earned a liberal arts degree from MSU in 1969 and a master’s degree in microbiology in 1973. He received his medical degree from Michigan State University in 1977 and later worked as an emergency room physician in Birmingham, Alabama. 
Holmes returned to Mississippi and joined MSU’s Longest Student Health Center in 2003, where he served as a staff physician. 
The university named its cultural diversity center in his honor in 1991 and recognized him in 2006 as its first Black National Alumnus of the Year. Holmes and his wife, Judie, also established an endowed scholarship supporting minority students. 
Mississippi State’s first African American student, Dr. Richard E. Holmes, died Oct. 16, 2026 at age 82. In August, MSU held a dedication and ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Dr. Richard E. Holmes Plaza. The monument marks Holmes’ significant contributions during his time as a student, staff member and alumnus. Credit: Grace Cockrell/Mississippi State University
Most recently, on Aug. 21, MSU dedicated the Dr. Richard E. Holmes Plaza in recognition of his contributions to the university. 
For generations of Black alumni, Holmes’ legacy extended beyond the university honors he received. 
Edward Sanders, co-founder of Mississippi State University Black Alumni Weekend, recalled bringing Holmes and James Meredith together during the event’s inaugural gala in 2016. Hearing the two men reflect on their experiences integrating Mississippi’s universities left a lasting impression, he said.  
“Both were full of wisdom and advice and it was one of the few times we got to see them interact together,” Sanders, a 2006 MSU graduate, said. “His passing will leave a huge void, but there are others from his time and era at Mississippi State that will continue to hold a torch.” 
Judy Meredith, James Meredith’s wife and a 2007 MSU graduate, said Holmes’ courage opened doors for generations of Black students. 
“He did it,” Meredith said. “And it allowed me to do it. For that, I’m grateful for him and his legacy.” 
Camille Scales Young, who became the MSU National Alumni Association’s first Black president in 2012, said Holmes’ legacy also inspired her own leadership. 
Alumni named a tailgating tent “Marvelously Maroon 1965” to commemorate Holmes’ historic enrollment. When she told Holmes about the tribute, Young recalled, he was honored and pleased. 
“All graduates have a responsibility of carrying on his legacy and dedication to the school he loved so much,” Scales Young said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In Concord visit, RFK Jr. renews attack on hep B vaccine that inspired state anti-vaccine bill
text:
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks to reporters about a new rural EMS program funded by the federal Rural Health Transformation Program at the New Hampshire Fire Academy in Concord on Oct. 16, 2026. To his left is GO-NORTH director Donalee Lozeau and to his right is Mark Wholey, director of New Hampshire fire standards and training & EMS. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)In a visit to Concord Friday, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cast doubt on the safety of the hepatitis B vaccine but wouldn’t comment on state legislation in New Hampshire that his agency inspired.
In June 2025, Kennedy fired every member of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, a panel of experts that creates national vaccine guidance, and subsequently replaced them with fellow vaccine skeptics. His new handpicked members ultimately rolled back the federal government’s guidance on the hepatitis B vaccine, among other immunizations. The panel voted that December to rescind the recommendation that infants receive the hepatitis B shot at birth unless the mother tested positive for the virus. However, the federal government’s vaccine schedule is just a recommendation. State governments enact requirements.
In New Hampshire earlier this year, state Rep. Kelley Potenza used the change as justification to similarly roll back New Hampshire’s hepatitis B vaccine requirement.
“New Hampshire has always followed, like I said before, the ACIP and CDC guidance on vaccines until now,” Potenza, who has long tried to eliminate state vaccine requirements, said in January. “This bill continues the tradition by aligning state law with the ACIP’s and the CDC’s updated hepatitis B recommendation.”
Asked if this was his intention or if he believed it was a positive development, Kennedy said it was ACIP’s decision and “the hepatitis B vaccine has been used for many years since 1991, but we don’t know what the risk profile is for that product because there was no randomized placebo-controlled trial prior to its licensure.”
However, according to the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, that’s not true. As early as 1980, a double-blind study published in the New England Journal of Medicine enrolled 1,083 subjects and randomized them to receive the vaccine or placebo and a subsequent study took place in 1984 in Hong Kong. CIDRAP argues that many who make this claim do so because no randomized placebo-controlled trials were cited in the Food and Drug Administration filing. However, that doesn’t mean that reputable scientists have never conducted trials. Specifically, it excludes those that were published in peer-reviewed journals but weren’t listed in a particular regulatory submission, per CIDRAP.
“Normally, we would not license a medical product without pre-licensing safety testing,” Kennedy continued.
Potenza’s bill — House Bill 1719 — was passed in the House but stifled by the Senate, which voted to continue studying the issue before taking any more action. Other anti-vaccine bills debated this year tried to eliminate nearly all vaccine requirements in New Hampshire outright (House Bill 1811), simplify the process for parents to request exemptions on religious grounds (House Bill 1022) and forbid state agencies from advertising vaccines (House Bill 1616).
On the federal level, Kennedy has elevated the growing anti-vaccine movement in the United States and been sharply condemned by the mainstream medical community throughout his tenure as health secretary. He and President Donald Trump have also cut hundreds of millions in funding for mRNA vaccine research for influenza, COVID-19 and other diseases, and they’ve fired roughly 10,000 federal health employees, though courts have halted some of his moves over questions on process and legal authority.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: State revenues projected to increase as Iowa’s billion-dollar budget deficit remains
text:
From left, Jeff Plagge, director of Northwest Bank in Spencer; Kraig Paulsen, the state budget director, and Jennifer Acton, director of the Fiscal Services division of the Legislative Services Agency, met for the October Revenue Estimating Conference at the Iowa Capitol Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa is expected to spend over $1 billion more than it raises in revenues in the current fiscal year, the Revenue Estimating Conference found Friday — but Iowa Department of Management Director Kraig Paulsen said this prediction remains in line with Republicans’ expectations about the initial impacts of income tax cuts.
The Revenue Estimating Conference, a three-member panel, met Friday to discuss the state’s expected economic outlook. When the conference last met in March, the members projected state revenues would decline by 9.3% in the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026, but that the state would see a 4.4% increase in revenue growth in fiscal year 2027.
With the books closed for FY 2026, Iowa saw a 7.1% decrease in revenue compared to the previous year — a drop of just under $635 million. Jennifer Acton, the director of the Fiscal Services division of the nonpartisan Legislative Services Agency, said this figure means revenues for the year were $205 million higher than the REC projected. But, she said, the year was still significant for being “the third year in a row with a net revenue decrease after 90 straight years of net revenue increases.”

These decreases are primarily driven by the changes to Iowa’s income tax structure in recent years. In 2025, Iowa’s law lowered individual income tax rates to a single 3.8% rate, making FY 2026 the first full fiscal year of implementation, Acton said.
Looking ahead to the rest of FY 2027, Acton said though “general fund revenues have been positive to start the year,” factors such as the Federal Reserve’s move to raise the interest rate, the effects of tariffs on agricultural exports and input prices, as well as tax changes made through the 2025 federal “One, Big, Beautiful Bill” Act, could have a negative impact on the state’s economy.
“While revenue growth and the overall economy are positive, concerns remain over persistent inflation, increased borrowing costs due to higher interest rates, and heightened geopolitical uncertainty with respect to gas and diesel prices,” Acton said. “These considerations are factored into LSA’s general fund revenue projections, which forecast modest growth for FY 27 and FY 2028.”
Jeff Plagge, director of Northwest Bank in Spencer, said the Community Bank Sentiment Index shows issues like higher interest rates, deficit questions and “stubborn inflation” all have an impact on economic outlooks.
“Uncertainty remains the common theme,” Plagge said. “Interestingly, though, bankers that I’ve talked to seem to be more concerned about the national economic issues and international unrest than conditions in Iowa or in their local communities.”
The panel predicts Iowa’s revenue will grow by 2.8% in FY 2027 in comparison to the previous fiscal year, taking in an estimated $8.54 billion. Though it represents roughly $60 million more in state revenue than previously projected, it remains below the $9.65 billion state budget approved by lawmakers earlier this year for the fiscal year that ends June 30, 2028.
This means the state will continue to draw from reserves and the Taxpayer Relief Fund to fill the more than $1 billion gap between state income and spending. Republican leaders have argued this disparity was expected when the Legislature approved income tax cuts, but Democrats and other critics have expressed concerns that the state will be left in a budget crisis.
Paulsen said he does not see the REC projections as a pessimistic outlook for the state, and said he believes “the Taxpayer Relief Fund will last long enough that the revenues will catch up.”
“I would say the state doesn’t have a revenue problem,” Paulsen said. “And we’re clearly in an extremely strong cash position, so assuming we continue to see the growth, which, that’s what we agreed to today in this meeting. Again, I think the state’s in a great spot.”
Gov. Kim Reynolds, who is not seeking reelection in 2026, said in a statement the latest projections “reflect a strong and stable financial outlook” for the state.
“For nearly ten years, my administration and the Republican-led legislature have prioritized the type of fiscal responsibility and conservative, pro-growth policies that generate measurable results,” Reynolds said. “Today, Iowa’s economy is well positioned to sustain growth, maintain stability, and continue to invest in the priorities Iowans value most.”
Common Good Iowa Executive Director Anne Discher said in a statement the REC estimate for FY 2027 — as well as the $8.83 billion revenue estimate for FY 2028 — show the need for Iowa to change course on its tax and budgeting practices.
“For the current fiscal year, FY 2027, revenue projections are more than $1.1 billion below the budget lawmakers approved in May,” Discher said. “For FY 2028, even if lawmakers were to approve what would be a deeply unpopular flat budget — further disadvantaging our schools and health care and all the other services Iowans depend on — we’d face a deficit of more than $800 million. This is not sustainable.”
Democrats said the latest REC projections show the need for a change in leadership ahead of the 2026 general election.
“With Iowa facing another billion-dollar budget deficit, today’s revenue estimate raises serious questions about the state’s fiscal priorities after 10 years of Republican lawmaker control,” Rep. Megan Srinivas, D-Des Moines, said in a statement. “While Iowa families are paying more for groceries, housing, and health care, wages aren’t keeping up with everyday costs. Today’s revenue estimates once again show that after a decade of the Iowa Republican trifecta, the economy is leaving middle-class Iowans behind while large corporations and the wealthy keep getting richer.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Berman, Cooke outraise their GOP incumbent opponents
text:
Campaign cash (Getty Images creative)Mitchell Berman and Rebecca Cooke, the two Democrats running to unseat incumbent Republican Reps. Bryan Steil and Derrick Van Orden in two of the most closely watched congressional races in the country, outraised their opponents in the most recent filing period. 
Both Democrats also received more individual and small dollar donations than Steil and Van Orden, who are more reliant on wealthy donors and the aid of GOP-aligned PACs. The latest campaign finance reports show that all four candidates will be funded enough for the final push to Election Day in both hotly contested races. 
In the 1st Congressional District, Berman is running closer than expected to Steil. He narrowly outraised Steil between July 23 and Sept. 30. 
Still, Steil spent four times as much money during the period and retains a massive cash-on-hand advantage.
Berman raised $897,321, with almost all of that coming from individual donations. He spent $710,725 during the reporting period and finished September with $338,069 in the bank. In the middle of the reporting period, Berman was added to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s list of target races — bringing national infrastructure and support to the campaign. 
Steil raised $783,582 during the period, including $215,637 from individuals, $268,500 from PACs and other committees, and $204,908 in transfers. He spent more than $2.9 million and had $4.2 million in the bank at the end of September. 
Steil’s fundraising has recently drawn scrutiny, with the Milwaukee Courier reporting on donations he’s received from industry groups shortly before taking votes related to their business interests. 
“Southeast Wisconsin is tired of politicians like Bryan Steil who get rich in office while working families pay more for everything,” Berman said in a statement about the finance reports. “Steil stood with Trump on tariffs, health care cuts, and a war that’s driving up prices, while handing billions in tax breaks to data center developers and his billionaire donors who are funding his campaign. No amount of dark money can cover up that record. I’m proud to have a campaign powered by the people of Southeast Wisconsin – not a dime of corporate PAC money – and in Congress, they’re the only ones I’ll answer to.”
In the 3rd Congressional District, Cooke has long been outraising Van Orden, but after a closer than expected Democratic primary election, her cash-on-hand advantage was depleted. For the cycle, she’s raised $12 million compared to Van Orden’s $9.3 million — a feat for a candidate who doesn’t have the fundraising advantage of incumbency. 
During the most recent reporting period, Cooke more than doubled Van Orden’s fundraising, bringing in $3.4 million, with $883,128 of that money coming from donations of less than $200. She spent about $4.3 million and ended September with $901,408 in the bank. 
Van Orden raised $1.2 million during the period, with $312,312 coming from donations of less than $200. He spent $3.8 million during the period and finished September with $2.1 million in cash and reported debts of $271,170.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: FBI investigates white-powder letters sent to election offices Louisiana, 3 other states
text:
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry. A mysterious white powder was found in an envelope opened by an elections division employee at the Secretary of State's office on Tuesday afternoon. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Federal officials are investigating letters containing an unidentified white powder that were mailed to elections offices and capitol buildings in multiple states this week, including Louisiana.
Officials in Arizona, Ohio and Oklahoma also reported receiving the letters, prompting building evacuations and an FBI investigation just three weeks ahead of the congressional midterm elections. 
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry reported Tuesday that one of the letters was received at the agency’s elections office. The state employee who opened the letter was taken to an emergency room as a precaution, and the building was evacuated for the remainder of the day. 
Testing later showed the powder was harmless, though state officials have not yet said what the substance was.
An Oklahoma state elections employee opened a letter Tuesday afternoon containing an unidentified white powder, prompting a building evacuation. 
A comparable mailing addressed to Ohio’s elections office was intercepted Wednesday by the U.S. Postal Service before it was delivered. 
Another white powder-filled letter was sent to the Arizona Secretary of State’s office on Thursday. Officials said the substance was not harmful based on preliminary tests. 
The FBI hasn’t yet announced if the letters sent to each of the states are connected. 
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors released a joint statement on Wednesday in response to the letters. The groups said they are “deeply concerned by these incidents.”
“Threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the organizations said in the joint statement.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Ag commissioner candidates tackle tariffs, farm crisis, data centers during debate
text:
Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring responds to his opponent, Democratic nominee Vern Thompson, during a debate on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring sparred with Democratic challenger Vern Thompson on tariffs, the farm crisis and more during a debate recorded this week. 
The debate also crystallized a key difference in how the two candidates view the role of government when it comes to overseeing the development of data centers and other industries.  
“The state of North Dakota has failed the people of North Dakota in this industry,” Thompson said. “People want government to work for them, not against them. And what’s happening right now is that government is working against them.”
Thompson has used the data center issue to gather momentum in his campaign to become the first Democrat elected to statewide office in North Dakota since Heidi Heitkamp’s U.S. Senate victory in 2012. He said during the debate, hosted by Rob Port and Chad Oban of the Plain Talk Podcast, there needs to be some basic regulation at the state level to help local governments navigate the permitting process for billion dollar projects like data centers. 
Goehring said data center developers need to do a better job explaining the purpose of their facilities, what the infrastructure demands will be and what benefits the projects can bring to communities. But he also emphasized that the government should not get in the way of a private property owner who wants to develop their land. 



“Respecting people’s private property rights also means we can’t stop you from doing certain things as long as it’s legal,” Goehring said. 
Thompson said the rights of others affected by the project, such as nearby landowners or other community members, need to be respected and they deserve to have a say. He said local control needs to take precedence.  
“A township should have the right to decide if they want industrial development in their township, irregardless of who sells the land,” Thompson said. “If we don’t have that, we’re losing part of the fabric that made North Dakota the state it is.”
Goehring said he is not a fan of NIMBY, or Not In My Backyard, attitudes that have led townships and other local governments to decide to exclude or place unreasonable restrictions on certain industrial development.
“It doesn’t respect private property rights. You can have reasonable and responsible zoning in place,” Goehring said. “We have to look at this, be balanced, reasonable, and we have to respect people’s ability and rights.”
Goehring is a third-generation farmer who has served as agriculture commissioner since being appointed in 2009. He has been elected four times. Thompson runs a trucking business in Fargo, spent years as a farmer and is a former state legislator.  
Vern Thompson, Democratic nominee for agriculture commissioner, during a debate against Republican incumbent Doug Goehring on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Commissioner’s role
The candidates also disagree on how vocal an agriculture commissioner should be in proactively developing policy solutions. Thompson said Goehring and other statewide officials have failed the people of North Dakota on data centers and other issues, like the ongoing farm crisis, by not being more active. 
“Nobody wants to do anything outside of their lane. Nobody wants to advocate. Nobody wants to work together,” Thompson said. “That’s how you solve problems. You work together. But right now, we have most everybody at the Capitol saying, ‘Well, I can’t do anything about it.’”
Goehring said the role of the executive branch is to “executive, implement and enforce,” and that the Legislature is responsible for setting policy in most circumstances. If state officials step outside of their lane, he said they can get called out in an audit report. 
“Your wings are going to get clipped. The Legislature is very clear about what authority you have and what you get to do,” Goehring said. 
Ag commissioner challenger highlights data centers; incumbent calls move ‘grandstanding’  

The agriculture commissioner said he’s involved in discussions with the Bank of North Dakota and the Department of Commerce to build a potential framework for fertilizer incentives to help farmers. He said his advocacy is behind the scenes, working with different stakeholders in government to develop solutions. 
“Those are things that everybody comes in with their different ideas. But you have to coalesce. You have to pull it together. You have to really figure out what works, what doesn’t work, and what you’re actually going to do,” Goehring said. 
Thompson, who has proposed using the natural gas expected to power data centers for fertilizer plants instead to lower input costs for farmers, disagreed with the incumbent. 
“I’m sorry, commissioner, you and the state of North Dakota have failed the people,” Thompson said. “I’m going to be out there advocating and talking to the people, and I’m going to use the bully pulpit that you haven’t used on this issue.”
Farm crisis and tariffs
Both candidates agreed the challenges facing ag producers in North Dakota constitute the worst farm crisis in 40 years, and that the tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump are part of the problem. 
“I don’t have the patience for people sitting silently on the sidelines. If it was a Democrat that did what they did with the tariffs or went to war, I’d stand up and say, ‘You’re wrong,’” Thompson said. “I haven’t heard the commissioner stand up and defend the people that are impacted by this.”
Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and Democratic challenger Vern Thompson shake hands after a debate on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Goehring, though he did not blame Trump, did condemn the tariffs and contradicted one of the president’s tariff talking points. 
“Countries don’t pay tariffs. The consumer pays tariffs. I’ve made that point over and over again. It’s just a tax. It’s a different form of tax. So I have a lot of problems with it, and we’re trying to work through those things,” Goehring said. “We’re not happy about it, but these are the cards we’re dealt. So we’re going to try and work through it.”
He said he has responded by providing feedback to federal ag agencies and attempting to promote North Dakota ag products to trade contacts elsewhere. Thompson questioned whether that’s enough. 
“Talking is good. That’s what we need. Communicating. That’s great. Where’s the plan? What kind of a plan have you got for the high cost of inputs in North Dakota?” Thompson said. “You, I believe, are a good person and could see this coming. Why didn’t you get ready for it?”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
The agriculture commissioner defended his record, noting he worked with the governor to make red-dyed diesel available for use on highways in the state and that he was involved in the Bank of North Dakota’s ag relief loan program for farmers last year. 
Goehring said farmers have to be “born of faith” to do their jobs in the face of all the market factors, from prices to weather, that they will never be able to control. Goehring, who was farming in the 1980s like Thompson, is optimistic about the future of agriculture and said investments into trade and research can help support farmers and ranchers in the state. 
“When it comes right down to it, we’re a blessed and fortunate nation. We are the land of abundance,” Goehring said. “How do we build on that? How do we support farmers and ranchers? One way is continuing to look at research to support their opportunities, technology, innovation practices, systems, and also trade.”

title: Cory Booker outraises GOP challenger Justin Murphy by factor of 50
text:
Sen. Cory Booker, the heavily favored Democratic incumbent, raised just under $1.8 million. GOP challenger Justin Murphy only brought in about $36,000. (Photo by Amanda Brown/New Jersey Monitor)U.S. Sen. Cory Booker (D) out-fundraised GOP challenger Justin Murphy by a factor of 50 in the most recent quarter, expanding an already chasmic fundraising gap between the two as Booker seeks reelection next month.
Booker reported raising about $1.8 million between July 1 and Sept. 30, dwarfing the $35,860 Murphy raised over the same period.
Booker spent a little less than $2.3 million during the quarter, with $1 million in the form of a transfer to the Democratic State Committee. He finished the reporting period with a little less than $22.6 million banked.
Murphy finished the reporting period with $9,578 banked after spending $26,404.
Murphy has joked about his minimal campaign cash on the campaign trail.
“I think my almighty creator, God, has made all currency on this planet allergic to me because it avoids me at everything I do in my life,” Murphy joked at a debate earlier this month.
“We’re not going to out-fundraise Cory Booker,” he added. “We can out-work him, but we’re not going to out-fundraise him.”
The gap grows wider when examining fundraising across the cycle. Since launching his reelection bid, Booker has reported raising nearly $35.4 million. For Murphy, that total’s about $75,205.
Even leaving fundraising to the side, Murphy faces a steep uphill climb to victory in November. Republicans have not won a U.S. Senate race in New Jersey since Sen. Clifford Case won reelection in 1972, and the GOP faces strong headwinds this year amid an unpopular president, an even less popular war in Iran, and a cost-of-living crisis.
The election is Nov. 3.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: In Senate debate, Tafoya and Flanagan can’t shake ties to unpopular men
text:
Republican Michele Tafoya (right) and Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan debate at MPR News in St. Paul on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota’s U.S. Senate candidates share a common burden: a connection to an unpopular man.
The shared baggage of Republican Michele Tafoya and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan was on display during a debate Friday on MPR News, the only one scheduled in the closely contested race.
Tafoya would not say if she would share a stage with President Donald Trump if he came to campaign in Minnesota, even after he endorsed her earlier this week.
Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan wouldn’t say whether she would campaign with Gov. Tim Walz, who dropped his bid for a third term earlier this year amid a widening crisis of fraud in social service programs that has dogged Flanagan’s campaign.
Flanagan and Tafoya sparred over the war in Iran, immigration and fraud, while each trying to tie the other to an unpopular politician.
Republicans see Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and conservative podcaster, as their best chance in years to end the party’s two-decade losing streak in statewide races. Tafoya is well known, good on television and a strong fundraiser. She has cut toward the middle on controversial issues like abortion — proudly calling herself a “pro-choice Republican” — and vowed to break from Trump when she disagrees with him.
Despite being far outspent, Flanagan handily won a bruising Democratic primary running as an uncompromising progressive: Medicare for All, universal childcare, $17-an-hour federal minimum wage and more. While Flanagan has said she isn’t responsible for waste and fraud, she has claimed credit for the successes of the Walz administration such as universal free school meals and a new paid family leave program.
Foreign policy
Flanagan said if elected she would not vote for any more funding for the war in Iran or for offensive weapons to Israel. She blasted Tafoya for her shifting stance on the war in Iran and accused her of standing by it only until it became a political liability.
Tafoya previously said that Americans complaining of higher prices caused by the war should “be patriots” about it and make fewer trips to Starbucks. She said during Friday’s debate that she thinks “there are some goals that have been achieved” but that she wants to see the war end quickly and “strategically.”
Tafoya criticized Flanagan for labeling the war in Gaza a “genocide.”
“I stand with Israel,” Tafoya said. “Calling it a genocide is an absolute misrepresentation.”
Flanagan and Tafoya also differ sharply on their assessment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who faces a pending impeachment resolution in the U.S. House after barely being confirmed by the Senate. He oversaw America’s launch of the war in Iran with Israel and has tried to reshape the ethos of the department, stating crudely, “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdoes. No wimps. No radicals — JUST WARRIORS.”
Tafoya wouldn’t give him a grade, saying it’s incomplete. She did say she was pleased Trump canceled plans to livestream an execution by firing squad, which is scheduled for later this year.
Flanagan gave Hegseth an “F.”
“He should be impeached,” Flanagan said. “I have seen enough.”
Operation Metro Surge
Tafoya called the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January at the hands of federal immigration agents “devastating.” She said former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem mishandled Trump’s incursion of some 3,000 federal agents to the state last winter, and that she was appropriately fired.
“America should be a nation of immigration and also a nation of law and order,” Tafoya said, noting she is the granddaughter of immigrants and adopted her daughter from Colombia.
Flanagan again bashed Tafoya for her shifting stance. She pointed out that Tafoya appeared to blame Good for her death by interfering with law enforcement and just last year suggested the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement be rebranded as National Immigration and Customs Enforcement — or NICE.
“Michele Tafoya again is trying to reinvent who she is just to get across the finish line,” Flanagan said. “The fact that she used roll-up footage in her campaign video from Operation Metro Surge, I think, tells you how she really feels.”
While Flanagan said she supports strong borders even as she calls to “tear ICE apart,” Tafoya accused her of selective compassion.
“I don’t hear Peggy ever crying about Sheridan Gorman or any of the other victims of these illegal aliens who have come in during Joe Biden’s reign,” Tafoya said, citing the case of an 18-year-old college student killed in Chicago.
Fraud and violent crime
Tafoya hammered home a point she’s been repeating throughout the campaign: Flanagan did nothing to prevent fraudsters from looting Minnesota’s social service programs and should be fired — not promoted to Senate.
She also criticized Flanagan for not being willing to say “Somali gang violence” after a string of suburban shootings (with the caveat that Tafoya said she doesn’t want to scapegoat an entire community either). Tafoya noted she has the endorsement of police groups, and rolled out a five-point public safety plan with the Minnesota Police and Peace Officers Association earlier this week.
Flanagan repeated that she opposes fraud and supported efforts to increase oversight and penalties. She pivoted to corruption in Washington under Trump — how he fired inspectors general responsible for cracking down on fraud, pardoned convicted fraudsters who support him, handed out government contracts to allies and enriched himself and his family.
“Michele Tafoya has nothing to say about that,” Flanagan said.
Tafoya said: “I am going to Washington to be an equal opportunity pain in the ass to any corrupt career politician … Donald Trump isn’t on the ballot. You and I are on the ballot.”
Social Security and Medicare
Flanagan said she would raise the income cap on Social Security contributions to shore up the program that is at risk of being depleted in six years.
“Social Security is one of the most successful programs our country has ever seen,” Flanagan said. “Our seniors who have paid into it, they’ve earned those benefits.”
Tafoya would not say if she would support raising taxes or increasing the retirement age in order to ensure solvency for Social Security.
“We’re not going to solve it in a 60-minute debate,” Tafoya said.
Flanagan said she would also fight to restore cuts to Medicare and Medicaid passed by Trump and Republicans in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Tafoya criticized the cost of health care, prescription drugs and insurance while calling Flanagan’s support for Medicare for All, “a pipedream.”
