name: Maryland Matters
title: Trump administration asks to reconsider Ocean City offshore wind permit
text:
A simulation of what the US Wind windfarm might look like from 84th Street in Ocean City. (Screengrab courtesy US Wind)Months after first threatening to do so, the Trump administration has officially filed a request to reconsider the construction permit it issued to an offshore wind project proposed off the coast of Ocean City, Maryland.
It’s just the latest episode in President Donald Trump’s battle against offshore turbines since returning to office last year. The Republican administration has halted coastal wind leasing, issued stop work orders to projects under construction and spent billions to buy back wind leases previously issued to developers.
When it comes to the Ocean City project, proposed by US Wind, the federal government is arguing that the project did not receive adequate consideration under a federal law known as the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
In their filing, Department of Justice officials cited possible adverse impacts of the project on: the North Atlantic right whale, “scenic and visual resources, some commercial fisheries, and scientific research.”
The administration is requesting to remand the permit “without vacatur,” meaning it would remain in place while the Department of the Interior reconsiders it.
The request sits before Baltimore U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher in a case originally filed nearly two years ago by the Town of Ocean City, opposing the construction permit for the project.
At first, the federal government defended its permit, issued by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, a subagency of the Department of the Interior. But after Trump took office, the feds did an about-face. In August, officials first signaled to Gallagher that they planned to request permission to reconsider it.
US Wind protested, asking Gallagher to issue an injunction preventing the federal government from revoking its permit. But Gallagher declined to do so, ruling that US Wind must “wait to see” whether the Interior Department “makes some decision that has some legal consequence.” Only then could US Wind challenge it, she ruled.
In a statement, the Town of Ocean City applauded this week’s filing from the Trump administration.
“The federal government has now told the court that its prior review and approval of the Maryland offshore wind project did not adequately address how the project’s significant impacts on ocean views, fisheries, marine life and other uses of the ocean are consistent with federal law,” the statement read. “Ocean City has raised these concerns from the start, and we welcome this acknowledgment.”
But US Wind said Friday it is “confident that a court will uphold” its permits’ validity, and “prevent any adverse action against them.”
“After over a decade of analysis, several federal agencies properly issued final permits to the project, which is one of the largest new energy projects in the region,” Nancy Sopko, US Wind’s vice president of external affairs, said in a statement.
In its filing, the federal government argued that the permit should be remanded because of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, meaning a few of Ocean City’s other concerns with the project are moot.
But the government did take issue with Ocean City’s claims against the National Marine Fisheries Service. It argued that the court should drop the town’s claims against the agency, commonly known as NOAA Fisheries, calling some “blatantly inaccurate.”
The town argued that the agency did not adequately consider possible harm to the North Atlantic right whale because of the construction. But the federal government argues it did consider the possible impacts to the marine mammals — and determined they would be minimal.
While experts at NOAA fisheries acknowledged that the whales could “experience temporary behavioral disturbance and associated physiological stress resulting from construction noise,” their documentation states that “all of these impacts . . . are expected to be temporary with normal behaviors resuming quickly after the noise ends” and are “not expected to affect the long term health of any whale or its ability to migrate, forage, breed, or calve.”
The agency also required construction crews for the project to follow certain rules to minimize disturbance to whales, including seasonal restrictions on pile driving and the requirement to use noise attenuation devices.
In sum, the agency “sufficiently analyzed all potential impacts to [Endangered Species Act]-listed whales from the Project and reasonably concluded that the Project is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of ESA-listed whales,” reads the filing.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Only 2 secretary of state candidates invited to televised debate next week
text:
Indiana secretary of state candidates, from left, Democrat Beau Bayh and Republican Max Engling. (Photos provided by campaigns)Republican Max Engling and Democrat Beau Bayh are the only candidates invited to a televised secretary of state debate set for next week.
The sponsoring TV stations FOX59/CBS4 in Indianapolis said Friday that Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings did not meet the qualification standards for participation. 
Those standards set by the stations’ parent company Nexstar include reaching at least 10% support level in nonpartisan polling.
A Free Press Indiana poll released Friday found Bayh with 43% support and Engling at 35%. Shillings had 6% support, with Ballard at 5% and 11% undecided.
The debate is scheduled for 7 p.m. Thursday and is set for broadcast on several Indiana stations.
All four candidates took part in an Oct. 7 televised debate sponsored by the nonprofit Indiana Debate Commission, as well as an August debate put on by the Indy Chamber.
The Ballard campaign objected to being left out of next week’s debate.
Nathan Gotsch, Ballard’s campaign manager, argued the poll cited was taken Oct. 8-11, just before the former Republican Indianapolis mayor’s TV commercials started airing around the state.
“One poorly timed poll shouldn’t determine which candidates Hoosier voters get to hear from,” Gotsch said. “A debate this close to Election Day is especially important because so many voters are still making up their minds.”

name: VTDigger
title: Addison County lands $3 million grant to fight addiction
text:
These officials represent organizations that will deploy the $3 million grant, recently won by United Way of Addison County, to boost services for people struggling with substance use disorder. Pictured from left are Chelsea Delisle of the Charter House Coalition, Jubilee McGill and Danielle Wallace of the Peer Revery Center; United Way’s Celia Heath, Heidi Melbostad of Mountain Community Health, Helena Van Voorst of United Way, and Taylor Morley of the Counseling Service of Addison County. Photo by John Flowers/Addison Independent

This story by John Flowers was first published in the Addison Independent on Oct. 15, 2026.MIDDLEBURY — Addison County experienced an opioid-involved death rate of 40 per 100,000 residents in 2023 — nearly double Vermont’s statewide rate — and yet the county has no inpatient detoxification facility, no residential treatment program and no hospital-based emergency psychiatric services. An estimated 75% of individuals who need substance use disorder treatment don’t receive it.
“Geographic isolation, provider shortages and pervasive stigma create compounding barriers that prevent individuals from entering and remaining in care,” reads a grant application submitted by the United Way of Addison County.
Now, through that application, the organization has landed a $3 million federal grant that will intensify local efforts to help folks battling substance use disorder.
The Rural Communities Opioid Response Program grant, awarded through the Health Resources & Services Administration, will unlock $750,000 during each of the next four years. It will fuel four Addison County nonprofits in their mission to improve access to treatment and recovery services for those fighting addiction, including opioid use disorder.
“There’s already so much good work happening in Addison County, and so many good partners doing this work really well,” United Way of Addison County Executive Director Helena Van Voorst said during an Oct. 8 meeting with the grant principals. “(The grant) is just going to strengthen the connection between those servicers, so that if somebody needs help, there’s no wrong door; wherever they land, they’re going to be able to get the help they need.”
United Way applied for the grant and will serve as its fiscal agent. The four local nonprofits that will draw from the funds to ramp up substance use disorder-related services are:

The Counseling Service of Addison County, providing outpatient behavioral health treatment and workforce development.
Mountain Community Health in Bristol, providing primary care and medication for opioid use disorder.
Peer Recovery Center of Addison County, providing peer recovery support, overdose prevention and street outreach.
Charter House Coalition, providing emergency shelter, coordinated entry and housing navigation.

Addison County’s rural character and a modest safety net for those struggling with drug addiction made this group a strong candidate for the grant award.
So how will the $3 million in funding be deployed?
United Way and its four nonprofit partners have a game plan that stresses identifying people needing help, engaging them, keeping them in treatment, measuring/maximizing positive outcomes, and getting them on a path to long-term recovery.
Early funding will provide for the purchase of a vehicle to ferry people to counseling and/or treatment; Narcan distribution; the hiring of two substance use disorder clinicians to be embedded at schools; making available opioid use disorder medication (buprenorphine) prescribed through an advanced practice registered nurse at the Peer Recovery Center’s drop-in center; more telehealth opportunities; expanded peer recovery support through newly hired specialists; more help for those seeking housing and related supports; and a countywide stigma-reduction campaign.
“What’s really exciting is that there are some tangible things that are going to happen in year one that will have a huge impact,” Van Voorst said.
Danielle Wallace is executive director of the Peer Recovery Center, which will see a staffing and programming boost from the new federal resources. The organization is already shopping for an electric vehicle.
“Transportation is always a barrier, whether it’s getting someone to treatment, or helping them get to appointments,” Wallace said, noting that public transportation can’t always reach folks in the most rural parts of the county in a timely fashion. A new hire at the center will, among other things, drive the new vehicle and help direct guests to sobriety-related services.
In addition, the grant funds will allow the center to expand its hours and bolster its street outreach efforts. As recently reported by the Independent, new guardrails on state funds recently cut off funding for Addison County’s street outreach program.
Heidi Melbostad, CEO of Mountain Health, said the new grant resources will give patients more access to peer recovery, as well as more telehealth options for medication-assisted treatment.
“We know when we treat substance use disorders, we’re most effective when we can meet people wherever they are,” she said of the importance of telehealth.
In addition to adding a nurse practitioner, the funding will allow Mountain Health to bring on a nursing care coordinator. Once they cross Mountain Health’s threshold, they’ll also have access to the health center’s primary and dental care services.
“Substance use disorders are chronic conditions, and they’re just one part of someone’s overall health and well-being,” Melbostad said.
Taylor Morley is executive director of the Counseling Service of Addison County. Morley said the grant money will help the service pivot to a Vermont-certified community-based integrated health center. This kind of center offers a wide range of services, including 24/7 crisis care, outpatient mental health and substance use disorder treatment, primary care screening and monitoring, and peer support services.
“As part of that change in our model, we are asked to do more with substance use disorder than we’ve done historically,” Morley said. “We view our role as being in collaboration with (Mountain Health) and Porter Hospital. We don’t see ourselves as becoming the primary provider in the county for those services, but we will be providing them to the folks we serve.”
Help in schools
The new infusion of grant money will allow the Counseling Service of Addison County to train and credential its current staff on best practices for substance use prevention and treatment techniques, rather than hiring new employees, according to Morley.
Officials at the service have for years been assisting local schools with mental health supports. Now the organization will be able to hire two substance use disorder clinicians to help youth and young adults.
Morley anticipates those new clinicians will begin their roles next fall.
Meanwhile, Middlebury’s Charter House Coalition will be able to use part of the grant money to help homeless folks struggling with addiction.
Many guests who find their way to the Charter House Emergency Shelter at 27 N. Pleasant St. in Middlebury are dealing with addiction.
Chelsea Delisle is a Charter House staff member and housing coordinator. She’s grateful the new grant will fund two full-time positions, one of whom will help integrate substance use into the shelter’s screening process to better serve those so afflicted and a housing specialist who will help guests transition to permanent residences.
What happens after the grant expires?
Local stakeholders plan to build a solid foundation with what they’ll be receiving.
“While it’s a four-year grant, the work that’s going to happen will have a much longer impact on our community and create a really strong system that will last beyond the four years of funding,” Van Voorst said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Affordability and accountability dominate Healey-Minogue finale
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY and Republican challenger Mike Minogue clashed over rising energy costs, abortion rights, and accountability for misconduct in state government Thursday night, as the candidates met for their second and final gubernatorial debate before Election Day.
Among the sharpest exchanges came when Minogue pressed Healey over her administration’s handling of former aide LaMar Cook, who faces new federal fraud charges after being arrested on state cocaine trafficking allegations, and when the candidates debated a State Police barracks scandal involving the alleged rape of a woman by a civilian who had stayed there.
A portion of Healey’s response to the barracks incident — “Do things happen? Sometimes things happen,” she said — gave Minogue an opening to question her leadership and prompted a sustained back-and-forth over whether the governor had adequately addressed misconduct in her administration.
The candidates also offered competing explanations for Massachusetts’s high energy bills, with Minogue blaming Healey’s opposition to earlier natural gas pipeline proposals and Healey arguing that the state needs more energy from multiple sources. On abortion, Healey accused Minogue of opposing protections for women, while Minogue defended his commitment to following the law without directly answering whether he supported an effort to repeal expanded abortion protections.
The debate, hosted by WCVB-TV at its studio in Needham, repeatedly returned to the central question of the campaign: whether Healey’s record in office outweighs voters’ concerns about affordability, or whether Minogue’s promises to cut costs and change the state’s direction offer a more compelling alternative.
Both candidates have proposed suspending the state gas tax, but they differ on the duration and approach. Asked what additional steps they would take to lower costs, Healey pointed to tax cuts enacted during her first year in office, along with investments in housing, health care, and energy.
Minogue called for suspending the gas tax immediately, cutting a third of utility fees and allowing families to benefit from a federal scholarship tax credit — one of his main policy priorities, which he repeatedly returned to during the debate. He called on Healey to opt into the tax credit several times, which she has said she is still reviewing.
He also brought up a specific remark Healey made during their first debate last week several times: “Again, ‘Massachusetts is a great place, if you can afford it,’ is what she said. She knows people can’t afford it,” Minogue said. He returned to the line three times, using it to challenge the governor’s economic record.
Healey argued that the state remained an attractive place to live and work, citing economic growth, housing initiatives, and job creation. She said governors should be “a cheerleader for our state” while acknowledging the challenges residents face.
The candidates’ housing debate highlighted a familiar disagreement over whether Healey’s administration has done enough to increase construction. Healey said she had cut permitting times from a year to 30 days, expanded opportunities for accessory dwelling units, and offered tax credits to developers.
“I did something that has never been done before as governor,” Healey said of her housing plan. “Mike, you got an idea to cut permitting times. I already did that.”
Minogue countered that Massachusetts continued to lag other states in permitting and argued that restrictive building requirements and local bureaucracy were preventing more housing from being built. He said the administration was celebrating projects set in motion under former Gov. Charlie Baker.
Healey cited 100,000 homes that had been built, permitted or brought under development during her time in office and said she wanted to double that figure in a second term. She also pointed to companies expanding in Massachusetts and the creation of 15,000 jobs in the past year.
“Sure, people leave and come and go all the time,” Healey said. “But I’m telling you, we are seeing companies expand here.”
The candidates then turned to education and racial disparities in homeownership, with Healey touting a first-time homebuyer program offering $25,000 toward a purchase and her administration’s investments in public schools and career training.
Minogue repeatedly pressed Healey to opt into the federal scholarship tax credit, arguing that it would give families more educational choices and help address achievement gaps.
“The federal tax voucher thing is a tax policy. It is not an education policy,” Healey said.
Minogue rejected that distinction, arguing that additional school spending had not produced better outcomes and that families in struggling communities needed more options.
“You did put more money in, but the outcomes are worse. Sixty percent are not proficient in grammar school and high school at reading and writing. That’s down from where it was in 2019. So we’re doing something wrong,” Minogue said.
One of the debate’s most contentious stretches began with a question about misconduct at the Massachusetts State Police. Healey was asked about a reported rape involving a civilian who was allegedly invited by a trooper to stay overnight at a State Police barracks on Martha’s Vineyard.
Minogue said the governor needed to establish a culture of accountability and criticized what he described as leniency toward people accused of wrongdoing in her administration.
Healey defended her selection of Col. Geoffrey Noble, whom she hired from outside the agency, and said she supported law enforcement while expecting misconduct to be addressed.
“Colonel Noble has come in and, with his management team, done a wonderful job, in my view. Do things happen? Sometimes things happen, but I can tell you, he and I make sure that swift action is taken,” she said.
Minogue seized on the remark.
“I think the governor just said, ‘Sometimes things happen.’ That is unacceptable. A woman was raped. Sometimes things happen is not acceptable,” he said.
He argued that leaders should remove people who violate the public trust and accused Healey of making excuses for misconduct.
The dispute widened to include Cook, Healey’s former aide, who was arrested on cocaine trafficking allegations and later faced federal charges involving SNAP and wire fraud. Minogue said Cook had not been adequately held accountable and criticized the administration’s handling of the case, including the payment of $22,000 in unused vacation time.
Healey said she fired Cook the day he was arrested and worked with law enforcement to pursue the case.
“I did fire LaMar Cook before he was even arraigned,” Healey said. “I fired him before he was even arraigned.”
Minogue countered that Cook was arrested rather than fired and questioned whether the administration had adequately investigated how alleged drug trafficking could have occurred.
Healey rejected Minogue’s account of the case, saying he had made inaccurate claims, and emphasized her record as attorney general prosecuting fraud and abuse.
In a post-debate scrum with reporters, Healey said, “I wish I never hired LaMar Cook.”
Asked whether she had known when he was hired about a 2001 arrest involving a firearm, she did not directly answer the question, instead reiterating that Cook had violated the public trust and that she fired him after his 2025 arrest.
The candidates’ disagreement over immigration enforcement was less personal and mainly retraced lines they went over during their last debate.
Healey defended her administration’s efforts to limit cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, describing the agency as a public safety threat and citing families afraid to go to school, work or seek medical care.
Minogue said he opposed violent criminals and drug dealers but argued that state and local authorities should coordinate with federal officials to target them. He said he would meet with affected residents and work to lower tensions.
On energy, Minogue blamed Healey for high utility bills, arguing that her earlier opposition to natural gas pipeline proposals had constrained supply and increased costs. He called for more natural gas, nuclear power and innovation, and proposed eliminating utility charges he said were unrelated to household consumption.
Healey defended an “all of the above” approach that includes natural gas, wind, solar, hydroelectric power, and geothermal energy. She said she was seeking federal approval to expand existing pipelines and argued that additional energy supplies were necessary to bring down prices.
She also called for an audit of utility companies to examine profits and rate increases.
WBUR’s Tiziana Dearing asked Healey whether Massachusetts should roll back its climate goals. Rather than immediately giving a yes-or-no answer, she said she was focused on bringing more energy online, including through natural gas, but the state “shouldn’t abandon” efforts to address climate change.
Pressed on giving a specific yes or no, Healey said, “We shouldn’t roll back climate goals, but goals are goals.” The state’s climate goals are legal mandates established through statute, and would need to be legally modified to weaken them.
Minogue criticized the response, arguing that the state’s energy strategy was too reliant on wind and solar power and that the administration had failed to prioritize reliable, affordable supplies.
The candidates also clashed over the productivity of the Legislature. Minogue gave lawmakers a “failing grade,” criticizing that they have not shown an interest in acting on a gas tax pause and calling for a legislative audit.
Healey gave the Legislature an “incomplete,” saying she wanted lawmakers to send her an energy cost-saving bill she originally filed. She said she had taken executive action where possible but could do only so much without legislative cooperation.
Later, when asked by reporters what she was doing to work with the Legislature to get that bill completed, she said, “I’ve continued to urge them.” Asked when her last face-to-face meeting with House Speaker Ron Mariano and Senate President Karen Spilka was, Healey said, “about a week ago.”
On abortion, Minogue faced repeated questions about an advancing 2028 ballot effort to repeal the law Healey signed lifting restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks. He said he would uphold the law but declined to say directly whether he supported repeal. He accused Healey of “politicizing” a “very sensitive, very difficult decision.”
“I will obey the law. I will follow the law. I believe in the separation of church and state, and when I become governor, I will swear an oath to do that. Now, I am still allowed to have my own beliefs, but my own beliefs will not get in the way of me doing what I’m supposed to do in upholding the law,” Minogue said.
Healey accused him of failing to protect women’s access to care and defended her administration’s purchase of a stockpile of mifepristone, an abortion medication, as well as a state’s expanded shield law protecting patients and providers.
“It’s not politicizing something when one in three women in America live without access to needed abortion care,” Healey said. “I trust women. I trust women and their doctors. Mike Minogue doesn’t.”
Healey said Minogue would “get rid of that stockpile” of mifepristone that she acquired in 2024 when President Donald Trump suggested he was open to restricting access to the pill.
“That’s not true,” Minogue said. “Mifepristone is FDA approved. You can buy it. It’s available. What you should be concerned about is buying a stockpile where the money is going to run out. You have to store drugs like that in air-conditioned or areas, they can expire. And the worst thing would happen is you buy a bunch of it, and it expires, and people get it, and it’s no longer valid.”
Healey replied: “Yeah, I know you’re a former biotech executive. I don’t need to be lectured about the storage of drugs.”
The stockpile cost $675,000 and was set to expire in September 2025, her spokesperson told the News Service in 2024 when the administration announced the rollout.
Minogue argued that the rhetoric had frightened residents unnecessarily.
“It’s legal. You can buy it. It was never going to be taken off the shelf,” he said.
Healey replied, “Well, it sure scared a lot of people.”
“You scared a lot of people,” Minogue retorted.
The governor said, “No, I protected people.”
The candidates closed with competing appeals on the state’s future. Minogue described the election as a “tipping point” and positioned himself as a political outsider who would focus on lowering energy costs, expanding manufacturing, and improving public safety.
Healey defended her record on taxes, housing, education, and transportation while acknowledging that affordability remained a challenge. She pledged to build more housing, expand primary care, and mental health services, and protect workers as artificial intelligence reshapes the economy.
Both asked voters for their support, leaving affordability and the question of accountability at the center of their final televised argument before the election.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lack of ‘moral outrage’ over Islamophobia is helping normalize religious hate, advocates say
text:
A Christian nationalist protest led by Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang prompted approximately 2,000 protestors and counterprotesters to gather in front of the Henry Ford Centennial Library in Dearborn on Aug. 18, 2026 (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance)As Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed held a campaign rally in rural Hart, Michigan on the weekend of Oct. 11, he was greeted by interested voters waiting to hear him speak in a part of the state that voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. 
Also waiting for him were more than two dozen self-styled Christian “crusaders” carrying crosses, dressed in military garb and calling for El-Sayed to be deported, citing his faith as a Muslim and Egyptian background.
The disruptive protest against El-Sayed was led by far-right agitator Jake Lang, who has organized similar protests, most recently in August with a march in the Muslim-majority city of Dearborn. While Lang’s antics could be characterized as performative activism, several advocates and experts told Michigan Advance that his rhetoric no longer exists in a vacuum of chronically online white nationalist streamers and influencers.
A Christian nationalist protest led by Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang prompted approximately 2,000 protesters and counterprotesters to gather in front of the Henry Ford Centennial Library in Dearborn on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance)
To the contrary, a new wave of Islamophobia has emerged throughout the 2026 campaign cycle from President Donald Trump to sitting lawmakers and candidates. That includes former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake), whose campaign has tried to tie him to terrorist movements like the Muslim Brotherhood. 
“An organization that supports the Muslim Brotherhood is one of his major funders,” Rogers claimed while speaking to Fox News. “He wrote an op-ed in Arabic a few years back, supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. This guy cannot tell the truth on this.”
Rogers’ campaign surrogates, including the National Republican Senatorial Committee, have repeatedly used El-Sayed’s full name  — Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed — in messaging while also circulating reports citing social media posts by El-Sayed’s half-sister in 2012 and 2013 that alleged family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. 
El-Sayed has repeatedly denied those claims, to the Washington Post and most recently to a crowd of supporters in Marquette to “judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” according to Semafor reporter Nicholas Wu.
“They don’t want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said in Marquette. “My mom and my sister are not running for office. I’m running for office.”
Rogers uses RNC midterm platform to attack El-Sayed as Dems push back against Islamophobic rhetoric

In response to El-Sayed’s comments, and as a reaction to this story, Rogers spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said that “Mike has been clear: This has nothing to do with how Abdul prays or what his name is–it has everything to do with how extreme his ideologies are.”
“Mike has repeatedly condemned hatred against all religious groups, including against the Muslim community,” Brouillet said. “The same can’t be said about Abdul El-Sayed, who continues to fan the flames of antisemitism, sympathizes with the terrorist attacker who tried to mass murder 140 kids in a Michigan synagogue, and refuses to disavow Hasan Piker, who calls Jews ‘inbred.’’
El-Sayed will be the first Muslim member of the U.S. Senate if he is elected in the November general election. That prospect brings the possibility of historical significance, but with it a deluge of attacks.
In the aftermath of El-Sayed’s win the August primary, the amount of Islamophobic content aimed his way has spiked.  The Washington, D.C.-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate found that posts focused on El-Sayed that included anti-Muslim bigotry averaged 155 per day from June 1 to Aug. 3, but then surged to 3,099 a day from Aug. 4 to 10, an increase of 1,900%.
Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, at the Michigan Democratic Party’s nominating convention on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Advocates say Islamophobia has become politically acceptable
For Dawud Walid, the executive director for the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the new turn to what he sees as unchecked Islamophobia is deeply troubling.
“Unfortunately, Islamophobia has become the only socially, politically accepted form of religious bigotry in the United States of America,” Walid told the Advance. “Politicians would be castigated if they made such sweeping generalizations against Christianity or Judaism, but it’s become socially acceptable in America, even to the extent that many Democrats won’t even push back and even speak out against it. It’s not just a Republican issue.”
Yasmin Moll, an associate professor at the University of Michigan specializing in religion, politics and the Middle East, agreed that Islamophobia is a centerpiece of current far-right rhetoric. The left also has a responsibility to push back, she said, if it truly cares about stamping it out.
“We have zero tolerance for anti-Black racism within the Democratic Party, for antisemitism, and that is absolutely as it should be,” Moll said. “And we should have zero-tolerance for Islamophobia. The lack of moral outrage from the opposition is contributing to the normalization of Islamophobia on the right.”
Moll told the Advance that although the current strain of political Islamophobia is alarming, it certainly isn’t new and is a direct evolution of negative media representations for Muslims and people of Middle Eastern and North African descent.
As of 2018, the Pew Research Center reports that there are around 3.5 million Muslim residents in the U.S., about 1.1% of the population. Over the past 50 years, media portrayals of their culture have been largely negative, Moll said, contributing to a predominantly negative image of the minority.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Oftentimes, the only depiction we see of Muslims in Hollywood films or in TV series is a Muslim who is a terrorist, or a Muslim who is being oppressed, or a Muslim woman who is being oppressed by a Muslim man or a Muslim terrorist,” Moll noted. “Very rarely do we see sort of normal, positive depictions of Muslims as people — complex people. Some are good, some are bad, some are whatever.”
Moll added that when those portrayals become the only information people have about a culture, that lends to a strong bias against them. The same could be said of conservative media transmitting similar messages about political figures or activists, much like El-Sayed, or New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota) before him. 
Walid said CAIR-MI has tracked polling that shows in 2026, 43% of the American public has negative views of Muslims and Islam. Walid noted that the sentiment saw an almost 20% increase over the past two decades.
What is most troubling for Moll is that the shift in the acceptance of religious bigotry is now coming from the top down.
Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Moll said former President George Bush made clear in public remarks that the attackers did not represent Islam or Muslims, and that any military action against the al-Qaida terrorist organization was not a war on Islam. 
While that was true, there were instances where others became victims of Islamophobia because they appeared to be Muslims, like Sikhs. Still, many political leaders had been wary to join in the anti-Muslim fervor, Moll said.
A key example of that came during the 2008 presidential election between former President Barack Obama and former U.S. Sen. John McCain (R-Arizona), at a McCain-hosted town hall.




Now, Moll said, it has become mainstream to deploy “a very kind of exclusionary, very dehumanizing rhetoric” and that it wasn’t just coming from “podcasters sitting in their basement.”
“These narratives burrow into and even become unconscious,” Moll said. “People may not even know they’re associating these things, which is why someone like Mike Rogers finds no problem at all releasing political attack ads that very much try to paint Abdul El-Sayed as some sort of dangerous Muslim male.”
On the national scale, U.S. Rep. Randy Fine (R-Florida), who has made Islamophobic remarks from the floor of the U.S. House of Representatives, has called for the deportation of American Muslims.
In the case of Mamdani, during his campaign for mayor in 2025, New York-based politicians on both sides of the aisle used Mamdani’s faith against him as a political cudgel, including Trump but also Mamdani’s independent rival, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo.
To Moll’s point, Trump initially framed Mamdani’s progressive policy proposals as coming from “Radical Left Jihadists” without naming him specifically. Trump stopped attacking Mamdani head-on after he met with him in the Oval Office, and the two found common ground on New York issues.
Anti-Muslim activism is finding political allies
With the gate open to accept that type of rhetoric, podcasters and influencers like Lang have found common cause with other political activists with real ties to lawmakers and candidates. 
When Lang came to Dearborn earlier this year, he did so in a march co-organized by conservative Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, who is a regular fixture within the Michigan Republican Party. Video taken during that “crusader” march showed Sewell also giving Lang a platform to speak at his church. Lang held a cross as he stood next to Sewell and delivered anti-Muslim invective.
Social media flyer used by Jake Lang to advertise his “Crusader March” on Dearborn in August 2026.
Not only has Sewell given benedictions at Michigan GOP functions, he has also done so at Trump rallies. Some of those rallies have acted as campaign events for candidates like Rogers and U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, the party’s gubernatorial candidate in 2026.
While Rogers’ campaign noted that the GOP nominee condemned Lang’s protest in Dearborn, it has not directly condemned Sewell, who remains a member of Rogers’ Faith Leadership Team. 
But it has insisted that El-Sayed’s connections to the Muslim Brotherhood were real based on reporting from the Washington Free Beacon, The Midwesterner, and the New York Post. The campaign has noted that the Free Beacon has reported that his campaign finance records include donations from individuals linked to the Muslim Brotherhood.
 Advocates call for a stronger response to religious bigotry

Pamela Shifman is the president of Democracy Alliance, a group of progressive donors focused on building organizing infrastructure for progressive platforms. While she has not formally endorsed El-Sayed in the general election, and neither has the group she leads, Shifman has been public in urging progressives to donate to his campaign. She has also written opinion articles in national publications praising El-Sayed. 
Shifman is Jewish, and one of her most recent op-eds was co-authored by Leena Barakat, the Palestinian-American president and CEO of Women Donors Action. Shifman and Barakat wrote that Jews and Muslims need to stand together against antisemitism and Islamophobia, and that El-Sayed’s race was a testing ground.
Pamela Shifman, president of Democracy Alliance. (Courtesy Photo)
In an interview with the Advance, she agreed with Moll’s assessment that Trump and others, who she deemed White Christian nationalists, have fueled new waves of Islamophobia, but also antisemitism, which she said go hand in hand. 
It was her belief that the Republican Party’s turn to Islamophobia was a sign that they have little else to run on other than fear and division.
“Their president is deeply unpopular,” Shifman said. “They have no solutions for the affordability crisis that is facing our country. They have no solutions for the healthcare crisis that is facing our country. They have nothing to offer, so they’re weaponizing Islamophobia because that’s all they have to talk about.”
To the converse, it was Shifman’s belief that El-Sayed, like Mamdani, was running on a much more popular platform, and that the attacks on him being a progressive — with the right trying to paint him as a socialist — and those about his faith were just low-hanging fruit to poke holes in his perceived momentum.
“Discrimination is the oldest trick in the book,” Shifman said. “None of us want this election to be about Abdul’s identity, but we have to forcefully reject hate always, and we have to constantly be calling it out every time it rears its head. Whether it’s anti-Black racism, whether it’s Islamophobia, whether it’s transphobia, whether it’s homophobia, we have to be vigilant about saying this is unacceptable. Full stop.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: LSU donor backs new capitalism research center, focused on its ‘greatest prosperity’
text:
LSU’s Memorial Tower rises above the trees on Monday, March 20, 2023, on Tower Drive in Baton Rouge, La. (Matthew Perschall / Louisiana Illuminator)The LSU Board of Supervisors Friday approved the creation of the Prosperity Institute, a research center in its business college that the founding donor hopes will definitively prove the superiority of capitalism. 
Roger Ogden, a New Orleans real estate developer and former LSU board chairman, has been a major donor to the university, He provided the endowment to create the institute, which he said has been in the works for a decade. LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom said the amount of the gift was not public. 
In his comments to the board, Ogden decried socialism and touted the virtues of capitalism.
“What powered me 10 years ago to begin exploring this was I realized in most media forms, profit was a dirty word. Capitalism was an even dirtier word,” Ogden said. 
Ogden said a lack of education about capitalism has led young people and the news media to support socialism and described the institute as a way to prove capitalism’s virtues. 
“Capitalism, when studied and compared — which is what will happen (at the institute) — to other major economic systems throughout history … by far creates the greatest prosperity for …  the most people than any other system that’s been employed in the world,” Ogden said. 
Russell Crook, LSU’s business school dean, said the institute will use research, teaching, study-abroad opportunities and a fellowship program to “accelerate knowledge” of various economic systems and their impact on various countries’ economies. 
Economics professor Areendum Chanda will direct the institute.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Career Pathways Commission releases draft, seeks public input
text:
Imagine being a high school student in Connecticut entering junior or senior year. You are unsure of what the future looks like and college doesn’t feel like the best fit. Between classes, extracurriculars and other obligations, you have your hands full. What happens after graduation, whether it is an apprenticeship, entry-level work or a deferred college degree, is an open question.  
This is the experience of some students in the state and it is being further complicated by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, rising college costs and limited exposure to jobs before graduation.
But a coalition of state leaders, educational representatives, advocates and business leaders hope that this experience changes in the coming years through the work of the Connecticut Career Pathways Commission. The body is tasked with developing a plan for work-based learning and career exposure in the state that will better prepare students of all ages for in-demand careers, creating pathway opportunities beginning in kindergarten through adulthood.
The commission was first discussed publicly in the spring, when Gov. Ned Lamont issued an executive order establishing the creation of group, charging it with crafting a plan to help prepare students not only for the jobs of today, but also for the  “jobs of the future.”
“We must have a system where students and job seekers can see the full arc of opportunity, a system where employers help shape the programs that prepare their future workforce, and a system where everyone — from classrooms to campuses to companies — is aligned around shared goals and shared outcomes,” Lamont said in a statement released earlier this year.
The commission, a 40-member body made up of representatives from workforce boards, higher education, labor, business, the legislature, student bodies and more, must create a five-year strategic plan that offers recommendations for a system that can help students across the state, creating clear and effective opportunities for students of all ages to access the information, skills and experience related to career pathways. 
The commission — led by former U.S. Education Secretary and previous state education official Miguel Cardona — must complete a draft report by the end of the year, with a final report due to the governor and the legislature by February 2027.
It must also make drafts of its proposals available to the public and collect feedback, incorporating public suggestions into future drafts of the report. It released its first draft of proposed recommendations for the creation and  structure of the pathways system earlier in October, with public comments being accepted online until Saturday, Oct. 17. On that day, the commission will also hold its final virtual comment sessions at 10 a.m. 
The current comment period is the first opportunity for the broader public to interact with the work of the commission, which has been meeting since May. Additional comment periods will be opened in future, as the body continues its work and prepares to submit its draft report later this year. 
In interviews with The Connecticut Mirror, commission members said the comment period is a key chance for them to show the progress they’ve made in recent months, and for the public to weigh in on the further direction of the work.
The goal
On paper, Connecticut has a vast network of resources and opportunities available to students looking to find a career path. By one count, there are more than 90 career pipeline-related programs, all of which are spread across more than a dozen state agencies — from the Department of Labor to the Department of Economic and Community Development.  
But these programs are disconnected and spread out across the state, creating a situation where students in one part of Connecticut may have access to opportunities that are walled off from students living elsewhere. 
“A lot of what’s going on across the state is pockets of opportunity based off of leadership interests, and that means it’s also ebbs and flows budget-wise based on the district’s priorities,” said Kate Dias, president of the Connecticut Education Association teacher union and a member of the commission. “It’s not necessarily the systemic commitment that we are really looking for.” 
Closing that gap and ensuring that students across the state not only have access and exposure to different career pathways, but can also develop clear skills that directly track with what local businesses and employers are looking for, is the central focus of the commission. 
“What the commission is really trying to do is ensure that opportunities are available to everyone and that they’re not based on where you live and what institutions you go to,” said commission member Kelli-Marie Vallieres, who serves as the state’s chief workforce officer and leader of the Office of Workforce Strategy. 
The Office of Workforce Strategy is also joining with the Governor’s Workforce Council to help coordinate with the Career Pathways Commission on the development and implementation of the career pathways plan.
The aim is for the commission’s work to build off already existing state programs, while also creating new opportunities for student engagement and learning. The pathways are also intended to closely connect with industry needs, giving students of all ages the ability to connect with career opportunities repeatedly over time. 
The focus on career pathways arrives at a key time for the state. There are more than 86,000 job openings in Connecticut, with employers reporting that they are having difficulty filling open roles. The Connecticut Business and Industry Association’s annual business survey, released in September, found that some 72% of respondents reported having difficulty finding and retaining workers, with skill gaps being a notable part of the problem. 
“We heard from businesses over and over, and we continue to hear, that they’re just not seeing the type of pipeline that they need in order to meet the 86,000 job offerings that we currently have in Connecticut,” said Chris DiPentima, president and CEO of CBIA and a member of the commission. “The students coming out of high school are not well enough prepared either from a technical point of view or just durable human skills.”
But rather than view that gap as an impediment, members of the commission say that it presents an opportunity: a chance for educators, industry and government to come together and create a better system, one that is more closely aligned with not only employer needs, but student interests.
That’s especially relevant amid a national resurgence in interest in skilled trades, an interest that has grown in recent years as college costs rise, and artificial intelligence threatens the type of work often done by entry-level administrative and white collar workers. According to a 2026 survey funded by a high school trades group and conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, 1 in 6 students reported trying to enroll in trades courses but being turned down due to a lack of space.
And that limited availability could further reduce the workers available for industries that are projected to be among the fastest growing in the state. Data from the Connecticut Department of Labor suggests that the state expects to experience a notable increase in employment between 2022 and 2032, with a significant portion of that growth expected to be in jobs that do not require a bachelor’s degree. That includes industries like hospitality, health care, transportation and manufacturing. 
These roles could account for more than 55% of job growth by 2034, with a CBIA Foundation report released earlier this year  arguing that the state must create a better pathways system that will help students connect and prepare not only for these fields, but for jobs that could exist in the future. 
“We have to have a transformational change, or we will continue to not see businesses stay in Connecticut and the economic growth and will miss the prosperity that this state can absolutely realize,” DiPentima said. 
Unpacking recommendations
There are many ways to create a career pathways system, however. 
The goal is to create a framework that “maintains the ability to stay current,” said Vallieres.  “We’re building the processes and the systems to make sure that we are updating these credentials and these pathways on a timely basis, so that we’re keeping pace with what industry demands are.” 
In its first set of draft recommendations, the commission is focusing on how it will structure that deeper work. The recommendations released this month focus on two broader objectives: creating a pathways system that is accessible to all learners in the state and building out the system that will support the work.
The recommendations offered in the report have been broken down into four “pillars.”
In the first pillar, the focus is on giving students a strong foundation, with the draft suggesting things like a statewide system for career readiness that includes clear skill building opportunities, career advising and job exploration opportunities. 
The second pillar calls for better preparing learners with industry-aligned skills and credentials, recommending that the state not only create clear dual credit and credential systems for students, but also improve the training pipeline for instructors, include community colleges in pathways work, and create clear sequences of studies that can be adapted to different groups of learners depending on age and skill level. 
The third and fourth pillars focus on work-based learning opportunities and the establishment of a clear unified system capable of managing the entire career pathways network, respectively. 
The draft document so far suggests that the task before the commission is a large one, requiring not only the creation of the career pathways system itself, but also of the evaluation, data collection, and broader management structures that will support what is ultimately created. 
A complicated process
With just a few months to go before the final report is due, commission members say that public input is incredibly important to the process, adding that the career pathways system that is created in the coming years will only be as effective as the engagement and participation that students and other stakeholders have with it.  
Dias of the CEA notes that teachers in particular will play a significant role, adding that with so many responsibilities already on their plates, the career pathways discussion will require a fundamental rethinking of the state’s education system to ensure that teachers can handle the new responsibilities expected of them. 
“At the end of the day, we’re talking about programmatic shifts that are going to involve transportation, bringing in different experts, creating regional resource networks for both industry and as well as school districts to create the network that is necessary to provide every student in Connecticut some sort of work-based experience,” she said. 
“You can’t keep adding to our system without subtracting,” she added. “There just aren’t enough hours in a day.”
But if the state can successfully pull the transformation off, it is a shift that Dias says will be worthwhile. “Our goals are ambitious, our ideas are not small, but I believe that if we do this well, the impact can be really important in terms of changing the outcomes for students,” she said. 
For Shannon Marimón, executive director of ReadyCT, a CBIA affiliate that focuses on providing career pathways support to students across the state, the commission has a tremendous opportunity before it. 
“We need to have the education system speaking to our employer community so that it can really align with where the workforce is currently and where it’s headed, because we want to make sure we’re setting young people up for the opportunities to be prepared and successful,” she said. 
But the actual implementation of the final recommendations will be out of the commission’s hands and will instead be up to the governor and the Legislature. The commission has not yet publicly released its specific policy recommendations or put a clear number on the amount of funding that will be needed to turn the career pathways plan to life. 
As the work continues, members of the commission are hopeful that their report will have an impact, saying that the state needs to make a change to give students a real shot at success. 
“We’re really working hard to set up something that we think is transformative,” Dias said. “I think that was always the goal: what can we do that supports the economic growth and development of the state of Connecticut that increases opportunities for our students?”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Freedom Caucus lawmakers vote to sponsor election bills, reject dark money resolution
text:
In some of the last votes they’ll make as state lawmakers, several Wyoming Freedom Caucus members and allies voted Thursday to sponsor a slate of legislation to revamp the state’s election system. 
At a legislative committee meeting in Casper, the group of Republican lawmakers also rejected a resolution intended to combat dark money — a political force the caucus has blamed for voters overwhelmingly rejecting their candidates in the 2026 primary election. 
Since the Freedom Caucus rose to power, a core part of its mission has included reshaping how elections are carried out in Wyoming. That focus has largely been aimed at restricting how and when people can vote. Some of those proposals succeeded at the statehouse, including 2025 legislation that added proof of residency and citizenship to the documents needed to register to vote. 
Other bills, however, including a ban on ballot drop boxes and measures to count votes by hand, have failed time and again. And after the caucus lost its House majority and backslid in the Senate in the primary election, those bills are unlikely to succeed in the 69th Wyoming Legislature.  
“One delicate issue is that there’s been an election in the intervening time between when these bills were proposed,” Joint Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions Committee Co-Chairman Cale Case said at Thursday’s meeting. The Lander Republican won his primary election against a caucus-aligned challenger.
“I believe that has real implications on how these bills will be received in the 2027 session,” Case said, adding that he did not think they would clear initial hurdles in the session’s process. 
Republican Sen. Cale Case of Lander during the 2025 legislative session. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
While Case is not associated with the caucus, most of the committee’s current membership is. His comments came in the late afternoon as lawmakers had reached the election portion of the agenda, which included consideration of 13 bills. When Case asked the committee how it would like to proceed, Casper Republican Rep. Tony Locke, a Freedom Caucus member who lost his reelection, asked for each bill to be heard and voted on. 
Lyman Republican Rep. Joe Webb, another Freedom Caucus member who lost in August, also asked that the committee forge ahead. 
“If another Legislature deems that these bills are not necessary, that is their responsibility and that falls upon their shoulders and not ours,” he said. “But I think we have the due diligence to proceed,” he said. 
Altogether, the committee voted to sponsor eight bills and move four more to its November meeting for consideration. The sponsored measures would ban drop boxes, restrict how ballots can be delivered and revise acceptable forms of voter ID, among other things. 
Ten Sleep Republican Sen. Ed Cooper, who is not on the committee, brought a resolution for the panel to consider sponsoring. 
“I do believe we have an election integrity problem in Wyoming and it comes down to money,” Cooper said. 
More specifically, he said, dark money, or political spending where the source of funds is not publicly disclosed, is affecting elections across the country, including in Wyoming. 
A large volume in dark money, in fact, was spent ahead of Wyoming’s 2026 primary election, including by groups both opposing and supporting the Freedom Caucus. 
Make Liberty Win, a Virginia-based political action committee, for example, spent $549,000 largely backing caucus candidates, as WyoFile previously reported. However, the PAC’s funding is obscured since it largely relies on funding from its nonprofit, Young Americans for Liberty, and is not required by federal law to publicly disclose its underlying individual donors. 
Meanwhile, opposition to the caucus was better organized and funded than it was during the last election cycle, as WyoFile reported in August. That included the PAC for a Better Wyoming, which spent about $191,000 opposing the caucus, according to campaign finance reports. Details about the PAC’s funding remain unknown to the public since it reported that Wyoming Donor Alliance, a nonprofit, was the single source of its funding. The caucus recently blamed this type of spending for its election defeat. 
At the meeting in Casper, Mills Mayor Leah Juarez told the committee dark money is no longer just a problem for statewide or national races. 
“I’m here today because the mayoral election in Mills, Wyoming, a community of 5,000 people, has become the target of organized political activity funded through a political action committee from Wisconsin,” Juarez said.
“The public has a legitimate right to know who is paying to influence its mayoral elections as well as everybody else’s elections in this room,” she said. 
Afton Republican Sen. Dan Dockstader brought a motion to move the legislation to the committee’s next meeting for a full discussion, public comment and notice. 
No one spoke against the motion, or the bill’s concept, but it failed on a voice vote when the committee’s caucus associates opposed it. 
Though Casper Republican Sen. Bill Landen did not run for reelection and is concluding his last term in January, he told the committee he’s hoping to see the state strengthen its campaign finance laws. 
“I think there’s a lot of work to do in the Secretary of State’s office on this front. I don’t think that our disclosure methods are adequate enough,” he said.
The committee’s next meeting is scheduled for November.

name: VTDigger
title: In his third congressional race, Republican Gerald Malloy is looking for middle ground
text:
Gerald Malloy, Republican candidate for Vermont’s U.S. House of Representatives seat. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger
It’s been six years and two big losses since “Deploy Malloy” first entered Vermonters’ vocabulary — but this time he’s taking a different tack.    
The slogan belongs to Gerald Malloy, a U.S. army veteran, former defense contractor at Lockheed Martin, Bowhead and Raytheon, and perennial congressional candidate in the Green Mountain State since 2022. He previously lost to two liberal U.S. senators in landslide races, and he’s now seeking a congressional office for a third time, challenging U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. 
His message? Lower bureaucratic barriers for business to develop in Vermont and bring balanced representation back to Vermont — representation that reflects red parts of Vermont as well as blue.
Malloy arrived on the Vermont political scene in 2022 with an endorsement from President Trump and conservative stances on issues like immigration and abortion, according to Middlebury College political science professor Matt Dickinson. He positioned himself to the right of Christina Nolan, the moderate Republican candidate whom Gov. Phil Scott endorsed, Dickinson added. Malloy also expressed his support for a border wall and disclosed that he had voted for Trump in past elections.
Now, political experts say Malloy may be changing his tune. He said he has broken with Trump on certain issues, such as the tariff war with Canada, the government’s military strategy in the Iran war and some current immigration enforcement tactics.
Despite some disagreements with Trump, Malloy said he still considers himself a conservative Republican. This time his platform centers around affordability and business. Vermont’s young people are leaving the state, he said, due to issues with affordability, and he wants to turn the tide.
Balint, the Democratic incumbent, is the third member of the Vermont congressional delegation that Malloy will face off against. First elected to national office in 2022, Balint champions issues like affordable housing, healthcare, climate action and reproductive rights. She is a vocal opponent of the Trump administration as well, encouraging Democrats to stand up against the White House. 
Polls indicate Balint is the clear favorite, with one recent survey from Vermont Public showing that if the election was held on the day of the survey, 43% of poll respondents would vote for Balint and 28% for Malloy.
It is notoriously hard to unseat incumbents in House races, Dickinson said, especially as a Republican in a blue state. Malloy’s previous opponents, U.S. Sens. Peter Welch and Bernie Sanders, won in landslides, with Welch taking 68% of the vote in 2022 and Sanders taking 63% of the vote in 2024. 
And Vermont is a special case, Dickinson added, noting that the last time an incumbent governor was ousted was in 1962.
“Vermonters generally stick with what they know,” he said.
Malloy disagreed. He’s been going door-to-door and talking to people all over the state, he said, and he’s heard a different message.
“Vermonters want change,” Malloy said. “They want balance. They want results, and they want accountability. We don’t have that right now.”
And Malloy has shown grit and connection with people on the ground throughout his campaigns, according to Paul Dame, chair of the Vermont Republican Party.
“I think Malloy is somebody who, even during his first run, was somebody who went everywhere to talk to everybody,” Dame said. “I mean that’s one of the reasons he was sort of the surprising win in the first primary, you know, against Christina Nolan, is he just puts in the work and he goes to people.” 
Malloy has always been a strong candidate in the primaries, according to Nicholas Charyk, the manager of government and public affairs at Downs Rachlin Martin — the largest law firm in Vermont — and a past campaign manager for multiple Vermont Democrats, adding that his win against Nolan came as a surprise to many in Vermont’s political community. He drew a comparison between Malloy’s 2022 campaign and Democrat Amanda Janoo’s recent gubernatorial primary win against Ali Richards, whom many political experts expected to win.

READ MORE

But after the primaries, the two candidates’ roads diverged, Charyk said.
“I think Amanda has continued to surprise people by gaining real traction and making it a real race,” Charyk said. “Malloy was unable to do that.”
Dickinson described Malloy’s 2022 platform as “hawkish,” with an emphasis on foreign policy and Malloy’s military experience, which inspired the slogan “Deploy Malloy.” He embraced Trump’s endorsement, Dickinson said. Malloy also expressed support for a nationwide abortion ban in June 2022, but he reversed course after Roe v. Wade was overturned.
“The problem is, as he found out when he was beaten easily by Peter Welch, is there’s a ceiling to being a MAGA type Republican in Vermont,” Dickinson said. “You’re not going to get more than 30% of the vote.”
Since 2022, Dame said there has been an effort from Vermont’s Republican party at large to bridge the gap between Gov. Phil Scott’s moderate stances and the more conservative national GOP. 
Supporting Gov. Scott has been a core facet of Malloy’s campaign platform in 2026, Dickinson said. Malloy argued that Scott has not been receiving the support he needs from Balint, Sanders and Welch, pointing out in an interview that all three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation endorsed Janoo, Scott’s opponent.
Balint countered that argument, highlighting collaborations between herself and Scott on housing, infrastructure, rural health care and the impacts of the tariff war with Canada.
“We certainly don’t agree on everything, but we do work together to get results for our state,” Balint wrote in a text to VTDigger.
It is difficult for her to “tease out” the exact reason why Malloy was running for a seat in the national congressional body, Balint said.
“He’s very focused on state issues, which I totally get,” Balint said. “We have a lot of them here, and a lot of the stuff he talks about is focused on state-level issues, which we in Congress don’t get to weigh in on.”
Malloy has drawn attention to expletives in statements made by Balint in previous cycles, which he argued are “disgraceful,” and called on Balint to resign.
“She’s committed misconduct and should not be in office,” Malloy said in the interview. 
Balint, for her part, said she’s seen a “different side” of Malloy, who she said has been quite “affable” over the years. She said she was surprised by the tactics in his campaign ads and his emphasis on her instances of “coarse language,” adding that she has a large body of work in healthcare, housing and other issues that shows her dedication to Vermonters. 
“You can make a case around policy for why you might not support what I believe,” Balint said in an interview, “but he is openly supporting a president who has said absolutely horrible things about women, about immigrants, about trans people — really horrific things.”
Some Vermonters remain skeptical about Malloy’s allegiances with Trump, and whether he will be willing to break with the president on key issues. Charyk said he sees clear evidence that Malloy’s stance has moderated lately, but he does not know if it will be enough for Vermonters.
“He was pretty full-throated in his support historically,” Charyk said, “but whether sort of a nuanced, slight differentiation is going to be meaningful to Vermont voters, I’m very, very skeptical.” 
Balint agreed, arguing that Vermonters have experienced real harm in the past few years through the decisions of the federal government.
“I think that Vermonters can see directly how this president’s initiatives have really hurt them, from, you know, the cuts to Medicaid, to letting the Affordable Care Act subsidies lapse, to the cuts to SNAP,” she said. “And so he doesn’t seem to have a clear case that he’s making to Vermonters that he will be a check on this president, because I think he’s still very much in support of this president.”
Charyk and Dickinson both emphasized one thing: Malloy has an uphill battle ahead of him. But Malloy said he likes his chances, and he will continue to fight for the Vermont he wants to see.
“I want Vermont to be a place to stay, live, and thrive,” Malloy said. “It’s not on that path right now.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota secretary of state office targeted amid probes into mailed election threats across US
text:
Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon received a threatening letter with an unidentified powder in the mail. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said Friday that a package containing a threatening letter and an unidentified white powder was intercepted before reaching his office, as federal investigations continue into similar packages mailed to election administrators and congressional offices across the U.S. amid midterm campaigning. 
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service is currently testing the material sent to Simon’s office, the secretary of state said in a statement.
“Threats against election workers are unacceptable and should not be tolerated,” Simon’s statement said. “Our office will not be deterred and will continue to support the thousands of election officials across the state as they administer elections to their communities.”
Similar packages have prompted responses in other states, including Arizona, Wisconsin and Nebraska. Election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma were evacuated after receiving suspicious mail containing powdery substances, while the U.S. Postal Service intercepted a similar package intended for Ohio’s secretary of state. 
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement expressing concern over the incidents, saying that threats against election officials “have no place in our democracy.”
The investigations come less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 general election. Early, in-person voting started Friday in Minnesota.
Simon said earlier this month that his office will be operating with “a war room mentality” on Election Day, coordinating with election administrators in all 87 counties and local law enforcement to prepare for potential threats and to combat misinformation.
In recent months, Minnesota has faced heightened federal scrutiny regarding its elections. In August, the U.S. Department of Justice sent election monitors to polling sites in two Minnesota counties. President Donald Trump has also made claims, without evidence, of election fraud in the state, and federal prosecutors recently charged 10 people with illegally voting or registering to vote in Minnesota elections.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: On the campaign trail for Republicans, Trump changes course and advocates for mail-in voting
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Menard Center in Wasilla. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting in this year’s midterm elections, the president is calling on voters to vote early and by mail as he campaigns in support of Republican candidates nationwide.
National polling has indicated that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting in this year’s elections than Republicans are, and control of the U.S. House and U.S. Senate is at stake in the election. If Democrats take control of one or both bodies, Trump and members of his administration likely will face investigations and could be impeached. 
“So vote early, vote by mail, or vote on Election Day, Nov. 3rd,” Trump said at a rally in Wasilla on Tuesday, urging voters to track their mailed ballot to ensure it is received.
Alaska has a limited ballot tracking service online; voters cannot tell until after the election whether their ballot was counted or rejected, and current state law does not allow voters to fix any technical problems that cause a ballot to be rejected.  
“Sort of follow your vote if you’re going to do mail-in,” Trump said.
Trump’s comments in Alaska followed a video he posted Oct. 3 that urged Republicans to vote early and by mail. 
“If your state has early voting, do not wait. Go out and vote. Vote early, vote by mail or vote in person on Election Day, Nov. 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left Dumb-ocrats in a midterm victory that is too big to rig,” Trump said in the video.
A week later, in New York on Oct. 9, Trump again urged voters to cast ballots by mail.
“We’re in the golden age of America. And if you’re voting by mail, make sure that you request your ballot by Oct. 24th, remember that, and have it postmarked by Election Day. I don’t know, I always like Election Day better, but what do I know about things like that?” he said.
While Trump has repeatedly tried to deter Americans from voting by mail, a voting method he attributes to his loss in 2020, he has also reversed course before. In 2024, he urged Republicans to vote by mail ahead of that year’s election despite denigrating mail-in voting for months beforehand.
Trump himself frequently votes by mail in Florida elections. 
Last week in Tennessee and in Ohio on Monday for a rally, Trump didn’t mention mail-in voting but noted that early voting is underway. “So get out and vote. And if you have to, you do it Nov. 3rd. I don’t care how you do it, but we have to do it,” he said in Ohio.
At rallies in Montana and Arizona on Wednesday, Trump did not mention mail-in voting but did note that early voting is already under way in both states. He did not say, as in Ohio, that supporters should vote early.
“For some reason, when you have a president, Republican or Democrat, it’s just brutal,” Trump said on Oct. 10 in Tennessee. “They don’t seem to win the midterms. But we’re gonna turn that tradition around.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana renews deals with 4 Medicaid providers; lawmakers want better health outcomes
text:
Louisiana has approved renewing the contracts of four managed care organizations that offer Medicaid healthcare plans to some 1.2 million state residents. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/The Missouri Independent)Louisiana lawmakers renewed state contracts Thursday with four private managed care organizations that provide Medicaid coverage, calling on state health officials to ensure the money results in better health outcomes. 
Louisiana will spend more than $16 billion on its managed Medicaid contracts in calendar year 2027, according to numbers shared at Thursday’s meeting of the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget. The deals range between $3.2 billion to $5.8 billion and cover some 1.2 million of the 1.3 million people in the state who use Medicaid. 
The four organizations are Atena, AmeriHealth Caritas, Humana Health and Louisiana Healthcare Connections. Two other providers — UnitedHealth and an Elevance Health-Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana joint venture — chose this year to pull out of the state.  
Most of the time spent on the contracts involved discussion about continued health struggles across the state.  
Sen. Regina Barrow, D-Baton Rouge, said her Google search before the meeting showed her Louisiana’s health ranking among states went from 49th in 2010 to 50th last year.
“We don’t need to continue to invest money in something that’s not working,” Barrow said.
Committee member Rep. Tony Bacala, R-Prairieville, shared his concerns about the state having spent more on Medicaid in recent years in direct payments to hospitals independent of the cost for its managed care contracts. Louisiana has raised its reimbursement rates for caregivers and facilities who accept Medicaid patients. But Bacala noted that more than half of Louisiana’s Medicaid enrollees are children, who tend to have fewer health issues   
“It just boggles my mind that we’re doing it,” Bacala said about needing to spend more on Medicaid.
Seth Gold, Medicaid director for the Louisiana Department of Health, told committee members the state’s higher Medicaid costs can also be attributed to healthcare inflation and the worsening health of enrollees.
“The average member is relatively sicker than they used to be, which means that we spend more per member than we used to,” Gold said.
Other lawmakers stressed to state health officials that Medicaid expenditures should be tied to better health outcomes. 
Barrow requested that the health department establish metrics for the four Medicaid providers so that lawmakers can track how they spend public dollars and whether the money improves the health of enrollees. 
Gold said the state Medicaid program will place more emphasis on accountability from providers and preventative health measures, such as well-baby visits. He also mentioned that providers would be directed to increase the availability of prescription medications to treat substance abuse. 
“We’re not going to pay anymore for bad outcomes,” Gold said.  
The federal government covers more than 75% of the cost of Medicaid in Louisiana, which is higher than the national average of just under two-thirds, according to Kaiser Family Foundation data. 
Some states could soon have to pay a larger share if they don’t fall in line with Trump administration policy changes, which include coverage limits for noncitizens legally in the U.S. that took effect this month and work requirements. Higher reimbursement rates for hospitals and doctors who accept Medicaid patients are also expected to increase state costs.
Just before the committee approved the Medicaid contract renewals, its members learned Louisiana Health Connections and Ochsner had reached terms to keep the health system’s affiliated caregivers and facilities in the Medicaid provider’s network. As recently as last week, Ochsner told the health department there was still no deal in place that included coverage for the 70,000 LHC enrollees who get their care through Ochsner.
Also at the meeting, lawmakers approved a three-year, $4.3 billion contract for health insurance through the state’s Office of Group Benefits, which covers state employees, retirees, K-12 public school teachers and their dependents. The plan also includes those who work at state colleges and universities as well as participating school districts and political subdivisions.
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana was the only bidder for the contract and will be paid 3% of the total value, which comes to $140 million. The other 97% of state dollars will cover plan participants’ claims over the contract period.

title: Colom out-raises Hyde-Smith, but incumbent has more cash on hand
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, raised almost twice as much money as his Republican opponent over the last three months, according to federal campaign finance reports.
But incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith still far outpaces him in cash on hand. Federal Election Commission reports show that Colom raised $1.3 million and has $991,802 in cash on hand. Hyde-Smith raised $642,988 last reporting cycle and has $2.4 million on hand.
READ MORE: Mississippi midterms: Colom trying to capitalize on economic discontent. Hyde-Smith trying to tie him to far left
“We are on track to win because Mississippians are paying attention, and they’re tired of a senator who works for the special interests instead of them,” Colom said in a news release. 
As national Democratic figures, including Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, visit Mississippi to campaign with Colom, the Democratic nominee hopes the national attention will energize  support in the Nov. 3 election and flip Mississippi’s Senate seat, long thought to be a safe Republican seat. 
Hyde-Smith has used the influx of out-of-state Democrats to tie Colom to the national Democratic Party to label him as out-of-touch with Mississippi’s conservative voters. 
Nathan Calvert, Hyde-Smith’s communications director, said in a statement that the Hyde-Smith campaign is not surprised “DC extremists are pouring money into Scott Colom’s campaign.”
“We planned for Colom to have plenty of resources,” Calvert said. “We are executing our own campaign plan with that in mind. We have a strong grassroots network statewide, and we believe we will once again win a majority of votes on November 3.”
Colom and Hyde-Smith are competing in the general election on Nov. 3. Independent candidate Ty Pinkins is also on the ballot. He reported raising $6,269 last cycle with $4,862 in cash on hand.
